title: The impact of dust and shading on pole-mounted PV - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
A year-long comparison of five PV configurations highlights how maintenance access, shading, and structural limits influence off-grid system selection. The researchers combined field measurements with analytical models to quantify these constraints and guide configuration choices.
Lior Kahana
02 Nov 2026
Research & Development
Commercial & industrial
Graphical abstract
A research team from Qatar’s
Hamad Bin Khalifa University
has investigated the techno-economic performance of different pole-mounted photovoltaic configurations with the aim of identifying the most suitable designs for off-grid applications in hot, arid environments with limited maintenance access.
These systems use solar modules attached to or integrated into poles to power off-grid equipment such as streetlights, cameras, sensors, and telecommunications devices.
“Pole-mounted solar systems have traditionally been selected based on a single metric: cost per watt. Our year-long field measurements show why engineers also need to consider maintenance access, shading, and wind loads,” corresponding author Khaled Aʼamar told
pv magazine
. “To our knowledge, this is the first framework for selecting off-grid, pole-mounted PV configurations grounded in a full year of experimental measurements.”
Aʼamar said the researchers developed indices to quantify the additional design requirements associated with different constraints, alongside a six-criterion framework to help engineers select the most suitable configuration for a given site.
“The next step is to take these findings from the test bench to the street,” he said, adding that Sunray Solutions, where he serves as chairman, is seeking partners for pilot deployments of pole-integrated systems.
The researchers monitored five PV configurations at the Qatar Environment and Energy Research Institute (QEERI) outdoor test facility in Doha between August 2025 and August 2026. The configurations included U-IBC and bifacial modules mounted at a 22-degree tilt or vertically, as well as an octagonal vertical PV tube. The team recorded electrical output and environmental conditions at one-minute intervals, retaining 311 days of data after screening.
Using low-irradiance data, the researchers sized PV arrays to meet a daily load of 1 kWh, assessed installation footprints, and estimated battery storage requirements based on three reference days. They used soiling measurements and geometric factors to estimate energy losses and cleaning requirements, while analytical models were used to assess shading and wind-related structural requirements.
The team calculated penalties associated with different constraints and ranked the configurations against six criteria: installed capacity, footprint, storage, maintenance, shading resilience, and structural compactness. Sensitivity analyses examined the effects of criterion weighting, temperature, and costs.
“Geometry makes a substantial difference to the impact of dust,” Aʼamar said. “When modules are never cleaned, tilted panels need 16.04% more PV capacity to compensate, compared with just 0.70% for the vertical photovoltaic tube – a 23-fold difference.”
He added that shading posed an even greater constraint under Doha’s conditions.
“Our model predicts that all the planar configurations stop producing above 67% shading, while the tube keeps operating,” he said.
“There is no single winner, though,” Aʼamar said. “Tilted bifacial modules need the least installed capacity when the site has no constraints. But when maintenance access, shading, space, or structural limits become an issue, the tube has the lowest combined penalty, even though its baseline capacity requirement is about 2.7 times higher.”
The findings are presented in the study “
Techno-Economic Analysis of Off-Grid Pole-Mounted Photovoltaic Configurations for Accessible and Inaccessible Sites in Arid Climates
,” published in
Solar Energy

title: Zwitterions could be much more than defect passivators in perovskite solar cells - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
Chinese researchers have reviewed the potential of zwitterions to improve the efficiency and stability of perovskite solar cells through defect passivation, crystallization control, and interface engineering. They found that these compounds could also enhance charge extraction, stabilize the perovskite structure, and suppress ion migration and electrode degradation.
Emiliano Bellini
02 Nov 2026
Research & Development
Cells & modules
Researchers at
Zhengzhou University
in China have reviewed the potential applications of zwitterions in perovskite solar cells, concluding that the compounds could improve device efficiency and stability through mechanisms extending beyond conventional defect passivation.
Zwitterions
are electrically neutral molecules containing both positively and negatively charged functional groups. “This dual-charge structure gives zwitterions a broader interaction scope than conventional Lewis acid/base passivators, single ionic additives, or some polymer-based modifiers,” the scientists explained. “Depending on their molecular structure and location in the device, zwitterions can participate in defect passivation, crystallization modulation, and interfacial energy-level tuning within one integrated molecular unit.”
Previous research has primarily focused on using zwitterions to passivate ionic defects in perovskite absorbers. More recent studies have explored their incorporation into precursor solutions and application at device interfaces to reduce non-radiative recombination, suppress ion migration, and improve charge transport.
According to the researchers, the effectiveness of these mechanisms depends on the molecular structure, incorporation method, and location within the device, making zwitterions promising multifunctional additives rather than single-purpose passivation agents.
Bulk engineering
The review identified three main functions of zwitterions within the perovskite absorber: defect passivation, crystallization regulation, and phase stabilization.
The researchers explained that the oppositely charged groups can interact with defects such as undercoordinated lead ions, halide vacancies, and defects associated with organic cations, reducing charge-carrier trapping and non-radiative recombination.
Betaine-type zwitterions have been the most extensively investigated, although amino-acid-based and other functionalized compounds have also shown promising results. In tin-based perovskites, for example, the addition of L-asparagine increased cell efficiency from 10.54% to 13.31%, while formamidine sulfinic acid enabled an efficiency of 22.06% in a wide-bandgap device.
Zwitterions can also influence precursor coordination, nucleation, and crystal growth, producing more uniform films with fewer pinholes and improved crystallinity. Depending on their chemical structure and processing conditions, they can accelerate or delay crystallization and modify grain size and orientation.
The review also highlighted their ability to stabilize the photoactive black phase, particularly in cesium- and formamidinium-based perovskites. Other reported benefits include reduced ion migration, improved lattice integrity, suppressed tin oxidation, and reduced residual mechanical stress.
Interface engineering
The researchers also examined the use of zwitterions at interfaces between the perovskite absorber and the electron transport layer (ETL) or hole transport layer (HTL), where they can simultaneously passivate defects and improve energy-level alignment.
At ETL/perovskite interfaces involving tin oxide (SnO2), titanium dioxide (TiO2), and zinc oxide (ZnO), zwitterions can interact with defects on both sides of the interface. Their molecular dipoles can also modify work functions and reduce electron extraction barriers, while influencing perovskite nucleation and crystal growth.
The review identified liquid-type zwitterions as a potential solution to the poor solubility and processing limitations of conventional solid-state compounds.
At HTL/perovskite interfaces, zwitterions can facilitate hole extraction, suppress surface recombination, and improve chemical stability. They can be applied as surface modifiers or incorporated directly into transport materials such as PEDOT and nickel oxide (NiOx).
In one study, a zwitterionic additive increased the average efficiency of PEDOT devices from 10.29% to 14.29%. Another approach using L-tryptophan at the NiOx/perovskite interface achieved efficiencies of 23.79% and 20.41% for devices with bandgaps of 1.56 eV and 1.68 eV, respectively. The latter devices also maintained stable performance for more than 1,600 hours.
Electrode engineering
The review also explored zwitterionic interlayers at electrode contacts, where molecular dipoles can adjust metal work functions, improve energy-level alignment, and facilitate charge extraction.
In one study, a zwitterionic polymer interlayer increased cell efficiency from 17.31% to 19.16%, while a carboxylate-based compound improved efficiency from 15.08% to 17.10%.
Beyond contact optimization, zwitterions can limit ion migration and electrode corrosion, particularly at silver contacts. The researchers highlighted a naphthalene diimide-based zwitterion capable of capturing both silver and iodide ions, thereby suppressing interfacial degradation.
Looking forward, the academics said future research on zwitterions should develop clearer design and evaluation frameworks. “By constructing a comprehensive database encompassing molecular descriptors, processing parameters, and device performance metrics, supervised learning models can be trained to predict optimal zwitterion candidates for specific functional layers. Furthermore, generative models could be explored to propose novel zwitterionic structures beyond the existing chemical space,” they stated.
“Zwitterions may evolve from important auxiliary modifiers in current high-efficiency perovskite solar cells into a key molecular platform for advancing perovskite photovoltaics toward long-term stability, scalability, and practical application,” the scientists concluded.
Their work was presented in the paper “
Research progress of zwitterions in perovskite solar cells
,” which was recently published in
Sustainable Chemistry for Energy Materials

title: Longi unveils 690 W back-contact solar module with 25.54% efficiency - pv magazine Global
content:
Chinese solar module manufacturer Longi has unveiled its Hi-MO X12 module series at All Energy Australia 2026, held in Melbourne on Oct. 28-29.
The new back-contact modules target residential and commercial and industrial (C&I) rooftop solar applications, with a focus on power density, interconnection design and long-term reliability.
The Hi-MO X12 series is based on Longi’s
hybrid passivated back contact
(HPBC) 2.0 cell technology and features an integrated conductive backsheet architecture that replaces conventional soldered ribbons with conductive metal foil circuits embedded in the rear encapsulation structure.
According to Longi, the design enables cells to connect directly to the conductive backsheet, eliminating more than 15,000 potential solder-joint failure points per module. The company said the architecture increases the current-carrying cross-sectional area by 85%, resulting in a power gain of 6 W to 8 W compared with conventional interconnection designs.
The modules also feature what Longi calls Full-Screen Technology, which combines shingled cell layouts with hidden busbars to reduce inactive areas and front-side shading losses. The manufacturer claims the design delivers an additional 8 W to 12 W, bringing the total power gain to between 14 W and 20 W.
The larger-format LR7-72WVD module for C&I applications is available in power ratings ranging from 660 W to 690 W, with a maximum module efficiency exceeding 25.54%, according to the manufacturer.
The smaller LR7-54WVD series is available in four power classes ranging from 495 W to 510 W, with module efficiencies of 24.25% to 24.99% under standard test conditions, according to the product datasheet.
The 108-cell, dual-glass LR7-54WVD module measures 1,800 mm × 1,134 mm × 30 mm and weighs 23.5 kg. It features a black anodized aluminum frame and front and rear semi-tempered glass layers measuring 2.0 mm and 1.6 mm thick, respectively.
The module has a temperature coefficient of -0.26%/C, an operating temperature range of -40 C to 85 C and a maximum system voltage of 1,500 V. The datasheet specifies front and rear static load ratings of 5,400 Pa and 2,400 Pa, respectively, as well as resistance to impacts from 25 mm hailstones traveling at 23 m/s.
Longi said the new interconnection design also improves mechanical durability. The company claims its ultra-thin stacking process reduces internal stress by 60%, while an integrated metal foil barrier reduces water vapor transmission by 90%.
The LR7-54WVD series comes with a 25-year product warranty and a 30-year performance warranty. Longi guarantees maximum first-year degradation of 1%, followed by annual degradation of 0.35%, corresponding to approximately 88.9% of the initial power output after 30 years.
The product datasheet lists IEC 61215 and IEC 61730 among the applicable certification standards and includes certification marks from TÜV Rheinland and TÜV SÜD.
Longi has not disclosed Australian pricing, initial shipment volumes or a commercial delivery schedule for the Hi-MO X12 series.
At the same event, the manufacturer also introduced its Hi-MO 9 Prime utility-scale module and showcased its LongiBank 3.0 and OneMatrix energy storage solutions, alongside the Longi Block modular PV system.

title: Mach launches Tier-1 autonomous solar mowing solution for utility-scale fleets - pv magazine Global
content:
Off-road autonomy developer Mach has introduced a commercial solar mowing solution tailored for independent power producers (IPPs) and large utility-scale solar asset owners.
Vegetation management consistently ranks among the most significant recurring operations and maintenance (O&M) expenses for ground-mounted solar arrays. Keeping grass managed beneath and between panel rows requires repetitive, labor-intensive scheduling across expansive, often remote geographic footprints. Mach’s newly announced system aims to alleviate this burden by bringing driverless capability directly to commercial mowing equipment via a factory-integrated approach.
“Utility-scale solar sites present one of the most demanding operational environments in off-road autonomy—narrow clearances, dense panel shadows, GPS-degraded zones, and zero tolerance for infrastructure strikes,” said Colin Hurd, CEO of Mach.
Mach’s platform incorporates several key technological layers designed specifically to handle the physical constraints of large-scale photovoltaic installations. Its factory-integrated architecture directly interfaces with commercial OEM drive-by-wire systems, enabling vehicle manufacturers to deploy autonomous mowers quickly without multi-year development overhead.
For precision navigation, the system combines Mach Perception, RTK-GNSS, and patented RadX phased-array radar to navigate reliably through dust, tall grass, and sun glare while actively detecting and avoiding tracker posts, guy wires, inverter pads, and hanging harnesses.
Furthermore, centralized fleet orchestration through Mach Ops enables a single remote operator to dispatch, monitor, and geofence multiple machines across nationwide portfolios. Maintenance is streamlined through dealer-supported serviceability, relying on established commercial platforms so that routine mechanical work, blades, and hydraulics are handled via existing nationwide dealer networks.
Mach will showcase its autonomous solar mowing platform at the upcoming RE+ 26 conference, running from November 16–19, 2026, at the Las Vegas Convention Center in the West Hall at Booth W16676.

title: Outer Space debuts solar pavilion with hidden battery storage decking - pv magazine Global
content:
While most solar and storage setups are designed around a home, the founding team behind outdoor living brand Outer is putting the tech to use in a new backyard pavilion in a new company called Outer Spaces.
Designed to fit anything from an outdoor kitchen or lounging space to an office or a gym, the team raised $8 million from venture capital with an aim to deliver what it calls an OS1 in 2027.
The approach by Outer Spaces is to make the solar and storage tech invisible in the OS1 in any configuration, but the specs are impressive. With a technical team that includes former Anker Solix members, the OS1 uses what it calls Horizon BladePack lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery modules, installed horizontally within the structure’s metal deck, with wooden decking over the top.
Each module has a nominal capacity of 7.83 kWh, with the system expandable to eight modules and 62.64 kWh. Each module measures 1,470 × 368.6 × 125 mm and weighs about 72 kg (158.7 lb).
The batteries use passive cooling, with integrated heating for temperatures below 0 C. The stated operating range is −20 C to 55 C, with output derated above 40 C. The modules are rated IP67 and carry a 10-year limited warranty.
The system uses a Fox ESS H1-11.4-US hybrid inverter and a 12 kW OS1 DC hub. Rated AC output is listed at 7.83 kVA with one battery module and 11.4 kVA with multiple modules. Motor-starting capability is listed at up to 80 A and 160 A, respectively.
OS1 supports AC coupling with an existing solar installation. Its energy management modes include self-consumption, time-of-use operation and backup standby. The system is also described as VPP-ready and supports PV black start, while generator support requires the Fox ESS Hub G2.
The pavilion comes in 12 × 12 ft and 12 × 24 ft configurations, with six or 12 solar panels, respectively. The supplied specifications put solar capacity at approximately 2.5 kW or 5 kW. Outer Spaces says the battery capacity can be expanded over time.
ESS News
had slightly conflicting information over if energy storage starts at 15 kWh, or two modules, or just one module at 7.83 kWh.
The company launched with an $8 million pre-seed round led by Upfront Ventures, with participation from Unlock Venture Partners, Mucker Capital, and Genius Ventures.
The company will be presenting at RE+ in Las Vegas in mid-November. No initial pricing was available.

title: A Breakthrough in Magnetism Could Make Computer Chips Use Dramatically Less Energy
content:
Researchers have overcome a longstanding obstacle that has prevented promising materials from being used in ultra-low-power computer chips.
A promising class of materials could help dramatically reduce the electricity needed for computing, but a persistent problem has kept them out of computer chips. When these materials are made thin enough for modern electronics, the electrical and magnetic properties that make them valuable can disappear.
Researchers at Brown University have now developed a way to overcome this limitation. Their technique produces ultrathin films of bismuth ferrite that retain their essential properties and develop an additional form of magnetism with potential advantages for future computing devices. The findings were published in
Nature Materials
Why Promising Materials Stop Working at Small Scales
Bismuth ferrite belongs to a class of materials called multiferroics, which have interconnected electrical and magnetic properties. Within their crystalline structures, positive and negative charges are displaced in opposite directions, creating electrical polarization. Applying a small voltage can reverse that polarization, allowing information to be stored as binary data (ones and zeros). Because the electrical and magnetic states are linked, the stored information could also be read magnetically, potentially enabling memory and logic devices that consume far less power.
The obstacle is a phenomenon known as the “dead layer” effect. When multiferroic films become extremely thin, their atomic structures and chemical environments can change enough to disrupt their functionality. At the same time, internal electric fields can destabilize their polarization. Together, these effects can eliminate the ferroelectric and magnetic behavior needed for electronic applications.
A New Method Eliminates the Dead Layer
The Brown team addressed both problems by carefully engineering the layers surrounding the bismuth ferrite. First, they grew the material on dysprosium scandate, a rare earth-based crystalline substrate with a smaller lattice spacing than bismuth ferrite. The mismatch places the film under compressive strain, helping preserve the atomic arrangement required for its electrical and magnetic properties.
The researchers also incorporated a metallic layer that screens unwanted electric fields, preventing them from destabilizing the film’s polarization. With both effects controlled, bismuth ferrite remained functional even at thicknesses of only a few angstroms. An angstrom measures approximately four billionths of an inch.
“We’ve established that we can get rid of the dead layer,” said Lucas Caretta, an assistant professor of engineering at Brown who led the work. “We show that you can make this material basically as thin as you want — down to a few angstroms — and it’s still ferroelectric, and it’s still magnetic.”
An Unexpected Magnetic Property Could Improve Future Chips
Beyond preserving the material’s original properties, the engineered structure enhanced its magnetic behavior. The researchers demonstrated that the thin film exhibits altermagnetism, a magnetic state with characteristics that could overcome some limitations of conventional magnetic materials.
“Ferromagnets are useful for memory and logic because they produce strong magnetic signals that are easy to read out,” Caretta said. “The challenge is that they are relatively slow, and their stray magnetic fields make it difficult to pack devices densely on a chip without interference. Antiferromagnets can operate much faster and avoid those stray fields, but their signals are much harder to detect. Altermagnets are kind of the best of both worlds — they can be fast, densely integrated, and still provide a strong electrical signal for readout.”
These characteristics could eventually support faster, more densely packed electronic components while reducing energy consumption. Although the researchers have demonstrated the material’s properties rather than a finished computing device, the technique addresses a major barrier to incorporating multiferroics into practical chips, particularly as artificial intelligence increases demand for computing power.
“We know the underlying properties are already there in the bulk materials,” Caretta said. “The trick is learning how to engineer them into a form that’s useful — and sometimes even better than what nature gives us.”

title: A Mysterious Explosion in Space Just Did Something Scientists Didn’t Expect
content:
Artist’s impression of GRB 260310A. A massive star collapses and launches a jet made by a narrow, ultra-fast core (white beam) wrapped in a broader and slower outflow. The jet points away from Earth. We first saw light from the jet’s outer wings and only later from its energetic core. The inset shows the image acquired by the Large Binocular Telescope, displaying the bright optical afterglow (marked) next to its host galaxy. Credit: Fortuna/Yang/ERC BHianca
An unexpected resurgence of X-rays weeks after a stellar explosion has challenged existing models.
An explosion that initially appeared unremarkable in gamma rays went on to produce one of the brightest afterglows astronomers have recorded in the past 20 years. Its visible light became brighter than its host galaxy, and its X-ray emission unexpectedly intensified again weeks later.
An international research team believes the extraordinary behavior can be explained by the direction of the explosion’s powerful jet. Rather than pointing directly toward Earth, the jet was viewed from an angle that initially concealed its most energetic region. The findings, published in
The Astrophysical Journal Letters
, suggest that some exceptionally powerful stellar explosions may be difficult to recognize from their initial gamma-ray flashes alone.
A Modest Gamma-Ray Burst With an Extraordinary Afterglow
NASA’s Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope detected the event, designated GRB 260310A, on March 10, 2026. Its initial burst of gamma rays lasted approximately 53 seconds and appeared to release relatively little energy. Over the following hours, however, its visible afterglow steadily grew brighter before eventually fading.
The contrast became even more pronounced at other wavelengths. Compared with samples of previously observed gamma-ray bursts, the event’s X-ray and optical afterglows ranked among the brightest 1%, while its radio emission placed it among the brightest 5%. Approximately three weeks after the explosion, the X-ray afterglow brightened again, remaining unusually luminous for more than a week and detectable for months.
“We see hundreds of GRBs every year, but the oddballs are the most informative ones,” says co-author Roberto Ricci, who led the radio observations. “We could explain individual features of this burst, but fitting them all into the same picture proved much harder.”
A Massive Star’s Death Viewed From an Unusual Angle
Gamma-ray bursts are among the most energetic explosions in the universe. Many occur when massive stars collapse and launch narrow jets of matter traveling at nearly the speed of light. As these jets collide with surrounding gas, they generate afterglows that can be detected in X-rays, visible light, and radio waves.
Astronomers typically observe the brightest gamma-ray flashes when a jet points almost directly at Earth. GRB 260310A appears to have been different. Its relatively weak initial emission, followed by an exceptionally bright afterglow, is consistent with a jet viewed from outside its most intensely beamed region.
“Much like a flashlight, the jet appears brightest when seen head-on. Most of our models are calibrated using events seen from that same perspective. This burst gave us a chance to look beyond that glare,” explains Yu-Han Yang, a postdoctoral scholar and lead author of the study.
How a Hidden Jet Can Become Brighter Over Time
The researchers propose that the explosion produced a jet with a narrow, highly energetic core surrounded by a wider, slower outflow. From Earth’s viewing angle, the broader outer regions would dominate the early afterglow, while much of the core’s radiation would initially be directed elsewhere.
As the jet slowed, its emission became visible across a wider range of angles. Radiation from the energetic core could then reach Earth, potentially explaining the delayed increase in X-ray brightness. This structured jet model offers a possible explanation for the unusual observations, although the precise configuration remains uncertain.
“We looked at it from a side angle. As the jet slowed down, its light became visible over a wider range of angles, allowing us to probe the jet’s shape, from its outer edges toward its inner core.”
The delayed X-ray brightening was particularly difficult to explain. “That was unexpected. At first, I thought another X-ray source was contaminating our observations. But the brightening really came from the afterglow,” recalls Yang, who coordinated the X-ray monitoring. “This prompted us to explore a more complex jet’s shape.”
An Explosion With Enormous Hidden Energy
To investigate the event, the international team, led by the ERC-funded BHianca group at the University of Rome Tor Vergata, combined observations from NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory, ESA’s XMM-Newton, the Einstein Probe mission, the Large Binocular Telescope, and the Karl G. Jansky Very Large Array. Additional observations from Calar Alto Observatory detected the signature of a supernova, confirming that the gamma-ray burst accompanied the death of a massive star.
The team’s models indicate that the jet’s central region may have carried vastly more energy than the initial gamma-ray measurements suggested. “What appeared to us as an unremarkable GRB might have looked like a monster explosion to an observer looking straight down the jet’s core,” notes Yang. “Our models suggest that the explosion packed roughly a billion years of the Sun’s energy output into a pencil-thin beam.”
The Search for Powerful Explosions Hidden From Earth
The findings also point toward a population of stellar explosions that conventional gamma-ray observations may overlook. As powerful new sky surveys, including those conducted by the Vera Rubin Observatory, expand their coverage, astronomers expect to identify more afterglows from jets that are not directed toward Earth. Such detections could help establish how frequently collapsing massive stars produce relativistic jets and how those jets escape through the stars’ outer layers.
“Gamma rays are not the most efficient route to spot these hidden jets: we find them once in a blue moon,” concludes Muskan Yadav, a graduate student who contributed to the study. “Upcoming surveys will pick up hundreds of them. Identifying them among millions of variable sources won’t be easy, but it’s a challenge I’m excited to take on.”

title: Depression Symptoms Improved in Just 48 Hours After a Single Psychedelic Dose
content:
Psilocybin is a naturally occurring psychedelic compound found in certain species of mushrooms, commonly known as magic mushrooms. In the body, it is converted into psilocin, which acts on serotonin receptors in the brain, altering perception, mood, and thought processes. Credit: Shutterstock
A single dose of psilocybin produced rapid antidepressant effects in a small Swedish clinical trial, with improvements lasting for weeks.
A single dose of psilocybin, the psychedelic compound found in magic mushrooms, produced rapid improvements in depression symptoms in a small Swedish clinical trial. After six weeks, 53% of participants who received psilocybin were in remission, compared with just 6% of those given a placebo.
Some participants reported improvements within two days, and the antidepressant effects persisted for more than three months in self-reported assessments. The findings come from Sweden’s first randomized, double-blind trial of psilocybin for depression, conducted by researchers at Karolinska Institutet and published in
JAMA Network Open
Hampus Yngwe Credit: Photo: Stefan Zimmerman
Testing Psilocybin for Common Depression
Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) are among the most widely prescribed treatments for depression, but they can take several weeks to work, cause unwanted side effects, and provide insufficient relief for some patients. Previous research has suggested that psilocybin may act more quickly, although much of that work has focused on treatment-resistant depression or depression associated with cancer.
The new phase 2 trial investigated whether psilocybin could also help people with more common forms of recurrent depression. Researchers enrolled 35 adults between the ages of 20 and 65 who had moderate to severe symptoms. Participants were randomly assigned to receive either 25 milligrams of psilocybin or niacin, a vitamin used as an active placebo because it produces noticeable physical sensations.
Both groups received psychotherapeutic support across five sessions before, during, and after treatment. During the dosing session, participants wore eye masks, listened to music through headphones, and were encouraged to direct their attention inward.
Depression Symptoms Improved Within Days
Researchers measured depression severity using the MADRS (Montgomery–Åsberg Depression Rating Scale), with assessments conducted by clinicians who did not know which treatment each participant had received.
Eight days after treatment, depression scores had fallen by an average of 9.7 points in the psilocybin group, compared with 2.4 points in the placebo group. The 7.3-point difference was statistically significant and considered clinically meaningful. The advantage remained evident at assessments conducted 15 and 42 days after treatment, while participants’ own ratings indicated improvement as early as the second day.
“Our results suggest that psilocybin can provide rapid, clinically meaningful improvement in depression and may serve as an alternative to standard treatment when fast symptom reduction is important,” says lead author Hampus Yngwe, consultant psychiatrist and PhD student at the Department of Clinical Neuroscience, Karolinska Institutet.
Long-Term Effectiveness Remains Uncertain
Although the initial results favored psilocybin, the difference between the groups was no longer statistically confirmed after one year. At that point, 53% of participants in the psilocybin group remained in remission, but many people who had received the placebo had also recovered.
Johan Lundberg Credit: Photo: Stefan Zimmerman
“However, the long-term effects are uncertain. Repeated treatments may be needed to prevent relapse. This needs to be investigated in larger studies.”
The findings suggest that a single supervised dose may provide relatively rapid symptom relief for some patients, but the small trial cannot establish how consistently those benefits will last or whether additional doses would improve long-term outcomes.
Side Effects and the Challenge of Blinding
Psilocybin was generally well tolerated, with most reported side effects being mild or moderate and temporary. However, two participants who received the psychedelic experienced severe, persistent anxiety that required medical attention.
“It is important to emphasize that the treatment is not risk-free and that some patients may need extra support,” says Johan Lundberg, professor at the Department of Clinical Neuroscience and the Centre for Psychiatry Research, Karolinska Institutet, who led the study.
Another limitation involved the difficulty of keeping participants unaware of their assigned treatment. Psychedelics produce distinctive psychological effects, and almost everyone in the trial correctly guessed whether they had received psilocybin or the placebo. Such awareness can influence expectations and make it harder to determine how much improvement comes from the drug itself.
“We want to understand how factors such as treatment expectations and lack of blinding affect the results, as previous studies may have exaggerated the treatment effects,” says Hampus Yngwe.
Investigating How Psilocybin Changes the Brain
Researchers are now turning to biological measurements collected during the trial to investigate how psilocybin might influence depression. Their next analyses will examine PET brain scans alongside blood and cerebrospinal fluid samples obtained before and after treatment.
One area of interest is synaptic density, which reflects the number of connections through which nerve cells communicate. Depression has been associated with disrupted communication between brain regions, while preclinical studies suggest that psychedelics may promote the growth of synaptic connections. Whether comparable changes occur in people receiving psilocybin remains an open question.
“Research suggests that the interaction between parts of the brain is impaired in depression and that this may be linked to changes in the connections between nerve cells, known as synapses. In preclinical studies, psychedelics have been shown to stimulate synaptic growth. We therefore want to investigate whether psilocybin alters synaptic density in the brain,” concludes Hampus Yngwe.

title: Einstein’s Equations Reveal an Unusual New Way Space-Time Can Transfer Energy
content:
A gravitational field is the region around an object where its gravity influences other objects. According to Einstein’s theory of general relativity, gravity arises from the curvature of space-time caused by mass and energy. Credit: Shutterstock
A new interpretation of Einstein’s equations reveals previously hidden rules governing how space-time evolves.
Einstein’s equations suggest that gravity may be capable of a process resembling the one behind powerful solar explosions. In a new theoretical study, physicists show how gravitational field structures can change their connections and transfer energy into matter. They call this process “gravitational reconnection.”
Luca Comisso of Columbia University and Felipe A. Asenjo of Universidad Adolfo Ibáñez in Chile describe the discovery in
Physical Review D
. Their work reveals a mathematical connection between gravity and the behavior of plasmas, electrically charged gases found in stars and throughout space.
The Physics Behind Explosive Solar Flares
In plasmas, magnetic field lines can become stretched and twisted until they rearrange through a process called “magnetic reconnection.” This releases stored magnetic energy and drives powerful events such as solar flares.
“Magnetic reconnection is when these field lines, in some specific configuration, break and reattach in a different configuration,” Comisso said. “When they break and reconnect, they release energy.” He added, “It takes energy from the magnetic field and gives it to the particles in the plasma, producing explosions, energetic events.”
How Gravitational Fields Can Reconnect
Gravity operates differently because Einstein’s theory describes space-time as a four-dimensional structure rather than three-dimensional space.
“Because space-time is four-dimensional rather than three-dimensional, gravity involves something like field ‘sheets’ rather than field lines,” explained Comisso. “Adding one dimension to a line gives you a plane. You can think of it as putting many lines together to form a ‘sheet.’”
These sheets are mathematical structures, not physical surfaces. The researchers found that when the conditions preserving their connections break down, the sheets can reconnect, allowing energy to transfer from the gravitational field into matter.
Hidden Rules in Einstein’s Equations
The researchers uncovered this behavior by expressing Einstein’s equations using different mathematical variables, revealing similarities with equations that describe plasmas. Their study builds on
earlier research
with Maricarmen A. Winkler that identified previously unrecognized constraints on how space-time can evolve.
“Einstein’s equations contain constraints on how space-time can evolve that are not immediately apparent,” said Asenjo. “By revealing these hidden new properties, we can begin to understand the fundamental rules governing how this gravitational reconnection process behaves.”
“Some implications are hidden in the equations, and they are not straightforward to capture just by looking at them,” Comisso said. “You need to rewrite them in a different way, and then you can exploit that behavior.”
What This Could Mean for Black Hole Collisions
One potential application involves merging black holes, where extreme gravity severely distorts space-time. Scientists rely on powerful computer simulations to predict the gravitational waves produced by these collisions, which detectors such as the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory (LIGO) are designed to measure.
The newly identified constraints could help researchers determine how gravitational fields must behave without calculating every detail of their evolution.
“It helps us predict some patterns of the space-time,” Comisso said. “Even without doing the full calculation, we know that space-time needs to behave in a certain way, that it needs to satisfy those constraints.”
Gravitational reconnection remains a theoretical discovery. Researchers must now investigate whether it occurs in astrophysical environments, how much energy it could transfer, and whether it might produce detectable signatures in gravitational waves.
Reference: “Reconnection of gravitational fields” by Luca Comisso and Felipe A. Asenjo, 28 October 2026,
Physical Review D
DOI: 10.1103/lmqy-pf9k

title: Human Bodies Are Producing Two Billion Tons of CO2 a Year
content:
Scientists have uncovered a largely overlooked component of the global carbon cycle, revealing how population changes are reshaping the amount of CO
humans produce. Credit: Shutterstock
A new study reveals that the amount of carbon dioxide produced by human metabolism has increased dramatically over three decades.
The carbon dioxide produced by human bodies as they convert food into energy increased by 74% over three decades, according to a University of Bath-led study. By 2015, the global total had reached an estimated 2.05 billion metric tons (2.26 billion U.S. tons) annually, highlighting a substantial component of the Earth’s carbon cycle that scientists had not previously quantified on this scale.
Unlike emissions from burning fossil fuels, the CO
humans exhale largely comes from carbon recently absorbed from the atmosphere by plants and transferred through food. Burning coal, oil, and natural gas releases carbon that has been stored underground for millions of years, adding it to the active carbon cycle.
Population Growth Drove Most of the Increase
To estimate global emissions from metabolism, the researchers analyzed thousands of real-world measurements of CO
production in people ranging from infants to older adults. They combined these findings with worldwide population and body weight data to calculate how human metabolic activity changed over time.
Professor Javier Gonzalez, who led the research at the University of Bath’s Centre for Exercise, Nutrition and Metabolism, explained:
“We all produce carbon dioxide simply by turning food into energy, but until now we haven’t had a good idea how much that adds up to worldwide.
Improving Our Understanding of the Carbon Cycle
“What we’ve found is that the increase is mainly because there are more of us. This gives scientists one more piece of the puzzle when working out where carbon comes from and where it goes. Ultimately, this information can help scientists more accurately predict how effective carbon reduction strategies may be.”
Human metabolism contributes to the continuous movement of carbon through the environment, particularly in densely populated cities. Accounting for that activity could help researchers develop more accurate carbon budgets and better assess the effects of strategies designed to reduce emissions.
Why Human Breathing Is Not Driving Climate Change
The researchers emphasize that their findings do not suggest people should exercise less, change their diets, or attempt to reduce the carbon dioxide they breathe out. The purpose is to improve scientific measurements of carbon movement, not identify respiration as a contributor to fossil fuel emissions.
Gonzalez stressed the distinction: “The important thing is that the carbon dioxide we breathe out is not the same as burning fossil fuels. We’re not saying that breathing is driving climate change.
“What this study does is give us a much clearer picture of how much CO
people produce around the world, and how that is changing as the population grows. This understanding can help improve the accuracy predictions of carbon reduction programs.”

title: Scientists Create a Tiny Electronic Device That Can Learn Like the Human Brain
content:
Innovative components based on an oxide interface, developed by researchers at the ctd.qmat Cluster of Excellence in Würzburg, electronically replicate key functions of neural networks and open up new prospects for energy-efficient hardware. Credit: Image: Jochen Thamm, think-design
A breakthrough in brain-inspired electronics could lead to devices that process information and learn without relying on conventional computing architectures.
A single nanoscale electronic component can perform three different jobs, switching electrical current, storing information through resistance, and remembering past electrical activity through changes in capacitance. Researchers in Germany have demonstrated this versatility using unusual oxide materials, opening a possible path toward computer hardware that processes information and adapts more like the human brain.
Today’s artificial intelligence systems can consume enormous amounts of electricity, particularly during the training of large models. One reason researchers are exploring alternative hardware is that conventional computers typically separate memory from computation, requiring information to move between them. The brain operates differently. Its neurons communicate through synapses, connections that can change in response to repeated or intense signals. This ability to adapt, known as neuroplasticity, helps the brain learn from experience.
An Unusual Material Interface That Can Learn
A research team at the University of Würzburg, working within the Würzburg and Dresden Cluster of Excellence ctd.qmat, has developed electronic components that reproduce several important behaviors of neurons and synapses. Their approach uses complex oxides, materials whose electrical properties can be adjusted to support different functions within the same system.
The devices rely on two materials: lanthanum aluminate (LaAlO₃, or LAO for short) and strontium titanate (SrTiO₃, or STO for short). Both are electrical insulators individually, but when brought together, they form an extremely thin conductive layer at their interface. This layer, called a quasi-two-dimensional electron gas, allows electrons to move through a region confined to the boundary between the materials.
Three Electronic Functions in One Tiny Device
Using this material platform, the Würzburg researchers created components that can act as a transistor, a memristor, or a memcapacitor. A transistor controls current flow, while a memristor stores information through changes in electrical resistance. A memcapacitor behaves differently: its ability to store electrical charge depends on its previous electrical state.
The researchers demonstrated that a single nanoscale component can provide any of these three functions depending on how it is connected electrically. This versatility could simplify the design of artificial neural networks built directly into electronic hardware.
“What makes our platform so exciting is that we can realize very different functions using the same material system. This brings us closer to hardware that not only computes but can also learn directly within the component and temporarily store information,” says Soumen Pradhan, a postdoctoral researcher at the Chair of Technical Physics in Würzburg.
Toward More Energy-Efficient Brain-Inspired Computing
“Brain-inspired computing” seeks to reproduce some of the brain’s information processing and learning mechanisms in electronic circuits. Rather than continually transferring data between separate processing and memory units, these systems aim to combine computation, information storage, and adaptation within individual components.
“Complex oxides are an especially exciting field for us because they combine many electronic properties in a single material platform. That is precisely what makes them so interesting for a new generation of energy-efficient and adaptable computer hardware,” says Ralph Claessen, spokesperson at JMU Würzburg for the Würzburg–Dresden Cluster of Excellence ctd.qmat and a co-author of the study.
Future Applications in Wearable Health Technology
One potential application is health monitoring. Wearable devices incorporating this type of adaptive electronics might eventually analyze physiological signals directly, without requiring separate computing hardware for every processing task.
Such “self-learning” sensors could potentially track heart rate, blood pressure, temperature, blood oxygen saturation, or blood glucose while adapting their responses to incoming data. Processing signals locally could also reduce the energy required to transfer information to external systems.
For now, these possibilities remain long-term goals. The research demonstrates the underlying electronic functions rather than a complete artificial intelligence system or medical sensor. Further development will be needed to establish whether the technology can deliver practical improvements in energy consumption, reliability, and performance.

Nature Communications

title: Scientists Discover That a Giant Bird Thought Extinct for Thousands of Years Never Actually Disappeared
content:
The common crane (pictured above) is the same species as a prehistoric giant crane once thought to be extinct, according to new ancient DNA research. Credit: Shutterstock
Ancient DNA analysis has challenged a 150-year-old belief about a giant bird thought to have disappeared after the last Ice Age.
For more than 150 years, scientists believed that enormous crane bones found in European caves belonged to a giant bird species that disappeared after the last Ice Age. Now, ancient DNA has overturned that identification, revealing that the supposedly extinct bird was actually a larger version of a species still living in Europe today.
Researchers at Bournemouth University (BU) found that the fossils attributed to
Grus primigenia
belonged to the common crane. Their findings also raise questions about whether other prehistoric birds classified as extinct species were simply larger forms of birds that survive today.
Ancient DNA Solves a 150-Year-Old Mystery
The mystery began in the 19th century when French biologist Alphonse Milne-Edwards examined unusually large crane bones discovered in caves in southern France. Believing they represented a distinct species, he named the bird
Grus primigenia
. The remains dated to the end of the last Ice Age and were long considered evidence of an extinct giant crane.
To investigate the bird’s identity, a team led by Dr. John Stewart, Professor of Evolutionary Paleoecology at BU, analyzed ancient DNA from 18 crane bones recovered across England, Wales, France, Germany, and the Balearic Islands. Working with the Centre for Palaeogenetics in Stockholm, Sweden, the researchers used genetic evidence to determine which species the bones belonged to.
“Previous studies had merely used the size and shape of the bones to attempt to understand these large birds. The use of DNA analysis has given us a more accurate picture of what they represent,” Stewart explained.
Why Scientists Mistook the Cranes for an Extinct Species
The genetic findings indicate that the oversized fossils belonged to common cranes rather than a separate extinct species. Stewart believes differences in body size between male and female cranes may have contributed to the original misidentification.
“We suspected that these large cranes were not extinct and instead represented larger, modern European common cranes. We believe that the reason for the mistaken identity was that cranes have large males and smaller females, and we think this contributed to previous speculation that there were two different species: the living, common crane we see today and the extinct, larger species,” Stewart said.
What Caused Ancient Cranes to Shrink?
Although the DNA evidence clarifies the birds’ identity, it leaves another question unanswered: Why were some prehistoric common cranes considerably larger than those living today?
“The challenge going forward is to investigate the reason for the cranes decrease in size. Wetland drainage and human land use changes are what we suspect, but more work is needed to resolve that,” Stewart said.
The researchers plan to investigate whether changes in wetland habitats and human land use contributed to the reduction in crane body size. These remain possible explanations rather than established causes.
Could Other Supposedly Extinct Birds Still Exist?
The findings suggest that some prehistoric bird species identified primarily through fossil measurements may need to be reconsidered. Differences in bone size do not necessarily indicate separate species, and ancient DNA could help determine whether other supposedly extinct birds were actually larger or smaller populations of surviving species.
“While it is true that many species of birds are vulnerable to human actions today, it may be that we have overestimated the number of extinctions in the past,” Stewart said.
“Some of these may instead represent size changes to living species,” he concluded.
Reference: “Ancient DNA study resolves the taxonomic status of the extinct large Palaearctic crane Grus primigenia Milne-Edwards, 1871 (Aves: Gruiformes: Gruidae)” by John R. title: Scientists Discover a Common Treatment for Chronic Tendon Pain May Not Actually Work
content:
Achilles tendinopathy is a common condition that causes pain, stiffness, and swelling in the Achilles tendon, which connects the calf muscles to the heel bone. Credit: Shutterstock
A major clinical trial is challenging the effectiveness of commonly used injections for chronic Achilles tendon pain.
A widely used injection treatment for chronic Achilles tendon pain may offer little lasting relief, according to a clinical trial published in
. Researchers found that high-volume injections, including those containing corticosteroids, did not significantly improve pain or physical function compared with a sham procedure after one year. The findings challenge the routine use of injections for a condition that can persist for years and interfere with everyday movement.
Achilles tendinopathy causes pain, stiffness, and swelling in the tendon that connects the calf muscles to the heel. Approximately 6% of people experience the condition during their lifetime, and although exercise-based rehabilitation is the recommended treatment, up to 44% of patients do not recover. Many consequently explore other options, including injections intended to reduce pain and improve tendon function.
Testing Popular Injections Against a Placebo
To investigate whether these treatments provide meaningful benefits, researchers conducted a randomized clinical trial involving 192 adults with midportion Achilles tendinopathy in Melbourne, Australia, between December 2019 and July 2022. Participants were 49 years old on average, and their symptoms had persisted for a median of two years.
The researchers divided participants into three groups receiving either a sham injection (64), a high-volume injection without corticosteroid (63), or a high-volume injection containing corticosteroid (65). The active injections delivered saline and local anesthetic around the affected tendon, with corticosteroid added in one group. Everyone also received the same exercise program, education, and guidance on modifying physical activity.
The primary measure was pain and disability after 52 weeks, assessed using the Victoria Institute of Sport Assessment-Achilles scale (0-100, where 100 is no pain or disability). Participants began the trial with an average score of 48.7, indicating substantial symptoms and functional limitations.
Steroid Injections Provided Only Temporary Relief
At the one-year follow-up, researchers obtained results from 181 participants (94%). Neither high-volume injection treatment produced a clear improvement in pain or disability compared with the sham procedure. The two active injection approaches also showed no meaningful difference in their overall outcomes.
Injections without corticosteroid failed to outperform the placebo at any assessment point. Adding corticosteroid produced small improvements after six weeks, but these benefits were short-lived. By 26 weeks, participants who received corticosteroid had worse outcomes than those given high volume injections without the drug.
An economic analysis found that corticosteroid-containing injections were less costly and generated more quality-adjusted life-years than sham treatment. However, the overall clinical results did not justify their routine use. No serious adverse events related to the trial treatments were reported.
What the Findings Mean for Achilles Tendon Treatment
The researchers acknowledged several limitations. Many participants were recruited through social media, which could affect how well the findings apply to other patient populations. Clinicians administering the injections also knew which treatment they were providing, and some observed differences may have resulted from chance.
Despite these uncertainties, the authors concluded that the evidence “should prompt clinicians to reconsider the rationale for using these injections in people with Achilles tendinopathy.”
In a linked editorial, John Orchard of the University of Sydney cautioned that corticosteroids are neither universally beneficial nor inherently inappropriate. Their use should depend on the patient’s circumstances, particularly when immediate symptom relief takes priority over longer-term outcomes (where short-term needs predominate over longer-term needs). He emphasized that patients should never be told corticosteroid injections will fix or cure tendinopathy.
“All clinicians recommending or performing corticosteroid injections for tendinopathy need to understand this trade-off and make every effort to explain the broader overview to the patient as part of the informed consent process,” he concluded.
Reference: “Efficacy and cost effectiveness of high volume injections with and without corticosteroid compared with sham for midportion Achilles tendinopathy (Inject trial): randomised controlled trial” by Peter Malliaras, David Connell, Anders Ploug Boesen, Rebecca S Kearney, Hylton B Menz, Dylan Morrissey, Shannon E Munteanu, Karin Gravare Silbernagel, Martin Underwood, Andrew Forbes and Terry P Haines, 28 October 2026,

title: Scientists Discover a New Type of Depression That Common Antidepressants May Miss
content:
Researchers have identified a possible subtype of depression linked to disruptions in the body’s internal clock. Credit: Shutterstock
For some people with hard-to-treat depression, the body’s internal clock may help explain why standard antidepressants fall short.
University of Sydney
researchers have identified a proposed subtype called “circadian depression,” marked by disrupted sleep and daily rhythms. It accounted for nearly a quarter of participants in a study of more than 10,000 Australians with severe, recurrent or persistent depression.
The findings, published in the
British Journal of Psychiatry
, suggest that recognizing this pattern could help clinicians identify people who may benefit from treatments targeting the body clock earlier in their care.
“Our research has identified circadian depression as a new subtype, affecting around a quarter of people in our study into those with severe, recurrent, or persistent depression,” said first author Dr. Emiliana Tonini, from the university’s
Brain and Mind Centre
A Depression Pattern Hidden in Sleep
Using clinical and genetic information from the nationwide
Australian Genetics of Depression Study
, the researchers classified nearly 25 percent (2,604 participants) as having circadian depression. Its features included seasonal episodes, sleeping longer when depressed, waking up exhausted, and a tendency to stay up late.
These symptoms point toward the circadian system, the body’s internal 24-hour timekeeping network that regulates sleep and wakefulness. The researchers identified genetic characteristics of the subtype that could help explain why treatments aimed at other brain pathways are less effective.
Participants with circadian depression were more likely to have developed depression earlier in life and experienced more severe symptoms (such as mania and higher levels of suicidal thoughts). They also had greater genetic susceptibility to inflammatory and cardiovascular conditions and major neurodevelopmental disorders, including ADHD.
“Depression is not a uniform illness, and understanding the characteristics of different subtypes means that we can give people earlier access to treatments that will be most effective for them,” Tonini said.
Why Standard Antidepressants May Fall Short
SSRIs (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors) and SNRIs (serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors) are commonly offered as initial treatments for depression. People with the circadian subtype reported less benefit and more side effects from these medications.
The researchers suggest that this group may respond better to behavioral and medical therapies targeting the brain circuits involved in circadian rhythms. Options include light therapy, melatonin, and antidepressants that act on melatonin pathways.
Co-senior author Dr. Jacob Crouse, from the Brain and Mind Centre, said, “Because circadian depression is linked to people’s internal body clock, treatments targeting the circadian rhythm, such as light therapy and melatonin, may be much more relevant, and clinicians should reach for these much earlier in people with this presentation.
“For those who find that antidepressants are not working for them, it is important to speak to your clinician for advice about your individual circumstances.”
Recognizing Circadian Depression Earlier
For young people, identifying this pattern early could help avoid unsuccessful initial treatments and additional side effects, according to Professor Ian Hickie, Co-Director of the Brain and Mind Centre and a clinical psychiatrist.
“We really want young people to receive the most appropriate treatment early in their course of illness.
“Most young people will be offered SSRIs first up, but for at least a quarter there are better circadian-focused medical and behavioral options to help treat and manage their condition.”

title: Scientists Finally Identify Mysterious Creature Nearly 90 Years After It Was First Found
content:
Colobothrix deckeri. Mesibov, 2026. Credit: Image by Ben Parslow, SAMA.
A mysterious millipede first collected nearly 90 years ago has resurfaced in South Australia.
A millipede first collected nearly 90 years ago in South Australia has finally been identified as a new species, challenging assumptions about where its moisture-loving relatives can survive. Named
Colobothrix deckeri
, the species belongs to the family Dalodesmidae, which typically inhabits damp environments. Yet its original collection site receives just 400 to 500 millimeters (15.7 to 19.7 inches) of annual rainfall, making it the first member of its family recorded from such a dry region of Australia.
The new species also possesses an unusual microscopic feature. Mature males in Dalodesmidae and certain other millipede families have tiny, ball-shaped structures on their legs called sphaerotrichomes, normally topped by a long, pointed bristle known as a seta. In
C. deckeri
, that bristle is reduced to a short, blunt rod. This distinctive anatomy inspired the new genus name
Colobothrix
, meaning “stunted hair.”
A Museum Specimen Overlooked for Decades
The discovery began with a specimen collected in 1936 on South Australia’s lower Yorke Peninsula. It remained unidentified in the South Australian Museum (SAMA) until 2015, when German researcher Peter Decker encountered it while examining borrowed museum specimens for his doctoral research on a different millipede family, Paradoxosomatidae.
Recognizing that the animal belonged to Dalodesmidae, Decker sent photographs of its microscopic features to Australian millipede specialist Robert Mesibov. The specimen provided the first evidence that this family occurred in dry South Australia. Mesibov searched the original collection area in 2016 and 2017, but neither expedition located another specimen. He later named the species in Decker’s honor, publishing the description in the peer-reviewed, open-access journal
A cluster of sphaerotrichomes on a leg of C. deckeri. Scanning electron micrograph image by Robert Mesibov. Credit: Robert Mesibov
An Unexpected Connection to Kangaroo Island
Unknown to the researchers at the time, additional specimens had already been collected about 50 kilometers (31 miles) south of the original location. In 2010, arachnologists Michael Rix and Danilo Harms were surveying spiders and leaf-litter invertebrates on Kangaroo Island when they discovered a remarkable
new assassin spider species
in the island’s relatively wet northwestern region. Their collections also included several unidentified millipedes, which were deposited in the Western Australian Museum (WAM).
The island’s devastating 2020 bushfires later destroyed the original collection site, raising fears that the rare assassin spider might be approaching extinction. During a follow-up survey in 2021, arachnologist Jessica Marsh found the spider at additional locations several kilometers (a few miles) away. Her collections of other invertebrates also contained specimens of the unidentified millipede.
A Rediscovery Nearly 90 Years in the Making
In early 2026, Mesibov discovered the Western Australian Museum’s millipede record online and contacted curator Mark Harvey. Close-up photographs supplied by Harvey confirmed that the Kangaroo Island specimens belonged to the same species collected on the Yorke Peninsula in 1936.
Mesibov subsequently visited Kangaroo Island and successfully located living specimens near the earlier collection sites. “Third time lucky!” said Mesibov. “I found the new millipede alive and well this year at relatively wet sites not far from its 2010 and 2021 localities.”
He collected several specimens for the formal species description and future genetic research. The specimens collected in 1936, 2021, and 2026 are now housed at the South Australian Museum.
Could the Millipede Be Hiding Beneath the Limestone?
Although
C. deckeri
has been confirmed on Kangaroo Island, researchers still do not know whether it survives at its original Yorke Peninsula location. That mainland site receives considerably less rainfall than the species’ known habitats in northwestern Kangaroo Island.
Mesibov suspects that the peninsula’s underlying limestone could provide a possible explanation for how the millipede survives in such a dry environment.
“The 1936 locality is underlain by limestone,” said Mesibov, “and the rock is broken where it is exposed at the ground surface. I wonder if the species survives in small voids in this bedrock, as a relict from wetter periods in South Australia’s past. That might explain why I couldn’t find it in 2016 and 2017, and how it could persist in such a dry climate.”
Reference: “Two new millipede genera and species from Kangaroo Island, South Australia (Polydesmida, Dalodesmidae, Spirostreptida, Cambalidae)” by Robert Mesibov, 23 October 2026,

title: Scientists Say This Medication Could Be the Next “Wonder Drug”
content:
Sotagliflozin, marketed under the brand name Inpefa, is an FDA-approved medication that blocks two proteins, SGLT1 and SGLT2, involved in glucose transport. Credit: Stock
A diabetes medication may protect against heart attacks and strokes through an unexpected biological mechanism.
Two medications used in people with type 2 diabetes produced dramatically different results when scientists tested their ability to prevent dangerous blood clots. In mice with injured blood vessels, sotagliflozin reduced clot formation by approximately 60%, compared with just 5% to 10% for the widely prescribed drug empagliflozin.
Researchers at Michigan Medicine also found that sotagliflozin suppresses excessive platelet activity, a process that can block blood flow to the heart or brain. Published in the
Journal of Clinical Investigation
, the findings suggest a possible explanation for the drug’s ability to reduce heart attack and stroke risk beyond its effects on blood sugar.
Why Sotagliflozin Works Differently
Sotagliflozin, marketed as Inpefa, belongs to a group of medications called sodium-glucose cotransporter (SGLT) inhibitors. These drugs interfere with proteins that transport glucose through the body. Common treatments such as empagliflozin (Jardiance) and dapagliflozin (Farxiga) primarily block SGLT2, a protein that helps the kidneys reabsorb glucose. Sotagliflozin acts on both SGLT2 and SGLT1, which is also present in other tissues.
Although SGLT2 inhibitors have established cardiovascular benefits, clinical trials have shown that sotagliflozin can also reduce ischemic events, including heart attacks and strokes. These occur when blood clots or other blockages restrict circulation. The researchers investigated whether the drug’s broader action on glucose transport proteins might help explain this protection.
“A drug that can both decrease the risk for diabetes along with the risk for having a heart attack or stroke could be a turning point in our ability safely treat this growing population in the US and abroad,” said Michael A. Holinstat, Ph.D., M.S., co-senior author and professor of pharmacology, internal medicine, and surgery at the University of Michigan Medical School.
A Powerful Effect on Blood Platelets
Scientists compared sotagliflozin and empagliflozin using blood samples from healthy volunteers and people with type 2 diabetes. Sotagliflozin significantly reduced platelet activation and made platelets less likely to clump together. Empagliflozin produced little or no comparable effect.
Platelets normally help stop bleeding by gathering at damaged blood vessels. However, excessive activation can produce clots inside arteries, potentially triggering a heart attack or stroke. Sotagliflozin’s ability to suppress this activity may contribute to its cardiovascular benefits.
“These experiments showed that sotagliflozin has a unique effect, and blocking SGLT2 alone is not enough to inhibit platelet aggregation,” said Eugene Chen, M.D., Ph.D., co-senior author and Frederick G. L. Huetwell Professor of Cardiovascular Medicine at the University of Michigan Medical School.
“Sotagliflozin may offer additional protection against blood clots, potentially lowering the risk of heart attack and stroke.”
Blocking SGLT1 Explains Only Part of the Effect
The researchers next investigated whether inhibiting SGLT1 alone could account for sotagliflozin’s effects. When they genetically removed SGLT1 from mouse platelets, blood clot formation decreased by approximately 40%. However, neither this genetic approach nor treatment with mizagliflozin, a drug that selectively blocks SGLT1, fully reproduced sotagliflozin’s results.
This suggests that other biological mechanisms contribute to the drug’s ability to prevent clot formation. One possibility involves SGLT1 in endothelial cells, which form the inner lining of blood vessels and interact with circulating platelets. Researchers have not yet established whether these cells contribute to sotagliflozin’s anti-clotting effects.
“Sotagliflozin appears to be in the sweet spot because compounds that have higher levels of SGLT1-selective inhibitors can cause gastrointestinal issues,” said Bertram Pitt, M.D., co-author and professor emeritus of internal medicine at the University of Michigan Medical School.
“We think this could be a wonder drug with potential to offer benefit for many conditions.”
Could the Benefits Extend Beyond Diabetes?
Sotagliflozin is FDA-approved to reduce certain cardiovascular risks in adults with heart failure and in adults with type 2 diabetes, chronic kidney disease, and additional cardiovascular risk factors. The researchers hope to investigate whether its effects on clotting could benefit patients with other conditions, including chronic kidney disease and atrial fibrillation, an irregular heart rhythm associated with increased stroke risk.
The laboratory and animal findings provide evidence that sotagliflozin affects clotting through mechanisms beyond conventional SGLT2 inhibition. However, further clinical research is needed to determine how much this platelet effect contributes to preventing cardiovascular events in humans and whether it can do so without increasing bleeding complications.
“The search for medications that reduce the risk of life-threatening blood clots without increasing the risk of bleeding has continued for decades,” Holinstat said.
“Sotagliflozin has now been demonstrated to serve both functions and may represent the next advancement in prevention of blood clots, heart failure and stroke in patients with and without diabetes.”

title: This Unusual Spider’s Genome Is Roughly 50% Larger Than a Human’s
content:
This trapdoor spider, named after comedian Stephen Colbert, has an outsized genome. Credit: Jason Bond / UC Davis
Scientists have sequenced the unusually large genome of a trapdoor spider named after comedian Stephen Colbert, uncovering surprising features of its DNA.
A spider no bigger than a quarter has a genome roughly 50% larger than the human genome. Known as
Aptostichus stephencolberti
, this elusive trapdoor spider lives beneath California’s coastal dunes and carries 4.6 billion DNA base pairs. Researchers at the
University of California, Davis
, have now sequenced its genome, uncovering features that could help explain how spider DNA has evolved.
“At 4.6 gigabases, or 4.6 billion DNA base pairs, it’s not the largest genome among the spiders, but it’s significant,” said Jason Bond, a professor in the UC Davis Department of Entomology and Nematology. The research, published in the
Journal of Heredity
, marks the first time scientists have sequenced the genome of a species in this spider family.
Why This Small Spider Has So Much DNA
The spider’s enormous genome is not packed with an unusually large number of genes. Instead, approximately 77% consists of repetitive DNA sequences, stretches of genetic material copied many times throughout the genome. Its DNA is organized into 52 chromosomes, compared with the 46 chromosomes typically found in human body cells.
Another feature involves telomeres, protective structures at the ends of chromosomes. Spiders lack the conventional telomere repeat sequences found in many other animals, a difference that may help explain why their chromosomes evolve more rapidly than those of vertebrates.
“It lends itself to broadening our understanding of spider genome composition and consequently how genomes have evolved across the animal Tree of Life,” Bond said.
A Secretive Predator Beneath California’s Beaches
A. stephencolberti
lives in coastal sand dunes between the San Francisco Bay Area and Monterey, often sharing beaches with people who never realize the spiders are there. Females spend their entire lives inside underground burrows lined with silk and concealed beneath hinged, camouflaged doors. They detect vibrations from approaching prey and rapidly emerge to capture unsuspecting insects and other small animals.
Although these spiders use venom to subdue their prey, they are not dangerous to humans. According to Bond, among the more than 50,000 known spider species, only about 30 to 50 have venom known to be toxic to people.
Rising Seas Threaten an Already Fragmented Habitat
The genome sequencing is part of the California Conservation Genomics project, a state-funded initiative developing genetic resources to support wildlife conservation. Because trapdoor spiders rarely travel far from their burrows, populations can become genetically isolated when their habitats are separated. Examining their DNA could help scientists identify distinct populations that may need protection.
“We Californians love our beaches and trapdoor spiders share them with us,” Bond said. “We’re hoping to understand how things like climate change, fire and urbanization might be impacting the genetic diversity of species.”
The spider’s limited coastal range makes it particularly vulnerable to environmental changes. Rising sea levels threaten the dunes where it lives, while invasive species place additional pressure on its habitat. “They’re going to be incredibly sensitive to sea-level rise, but they’re also very sensitive to invasive species,” Bond said.
How Stephen Colbert Got a Spider Named After Him
The species has an unusual connection to comedian Stephen Colbert. In 2008, after learning that Bond had named another trapdoor spider after musician Neil Young, Colbert demanded similar recognition. He made his case during the “Who’s Not Honoring Me Now?” segment of his former Comedy Central program, “The Colbert Report.”
Bond granted the request, naming the species
Aptostichus stephencolberti
(the “t” in Colbert is silent). The spider’s oversized genome now provides an unexpected scientific distinction for an animal named after a comedian known for playing an exaggerated, self-important television pundit.
Spider Venom Could Hold Untapped Compounds
Beyond conservation and evolutionary research, spider genomes may help scientists investigate venom compounds with potential medical or agricultural applications. Some molecules found in spider venoms are being studied for their possible use in pain relief, while others could offer new approaches to controlling agricultural pests.
The full range of these substances remains largely unexplored, and the newly sequenced genome could provide a foundation for further investigations.
“We don’t really know what’s out there in terms of untapped natural product diversity for venoms,” Bond said.
Reference: “Reference genome of the Californian trapdoor spider Aptostichus stephencolberti Bond 2008 (Araneae: Mygalomorphae: Euctenizidae)” by Stephen Richards, Emma Jochim, Lacie Newton, James Starrett, Ruta Sahasrabudhe, Oanh Nguyen, Eric Beraut, Colin Fairbairn, Samuel Sacco, William Seligmann, Merly Escalona, Robert D Cooper, H Bradley Shaffer, Erin Toffelmier and Jason E Bond, 8 September 2026,
Journal of Heredity
DOI: 10.1093/jhered/esag069
