title: India must tighten dealer rules to tackle informal lead recycling – Batteries International
content: India’s battery dealers must be made accountable for the collection and disposal of spent batteries if the country is to tackle its persistent informal lead recycling problem, according to L Pugazhenthy, executive director of the India Lead Zinc Development Association (ILZDA). Speaking at the 10th International Secondary Lead Conference in Colombo on October 26, Pugazhenthy (known informally as “Mr Pug”) called for tighter regulation of battery dealers, mandatory reporting of spent battery collections and regular audits of authorised recycling facilities. He warned that India’s Battery Waste Management Rules 2022, which introduced extended producer responsibility (EPR) requirements across battery chemistries, do not adequately address the role of dealers in directing spent batteries into legitimate recycling channels. Pugazhenthy identified battery dealers as a major route through which spent batteries are diverted into the informal recycling sector, arguing that their responsibilities are not sufficiently defined under the current regulations. He estimates that approximately 65% of India’s recycled lead production comes from authorised recyclers, while around 30% is attributable to the informal sector. India is one of the world’s largest secondary lead producers, with Pugazhenthy estimating annual secondary output at around 1.6 million tonnes. He also cited authorised recycling capacity of approximately 3.5 million tonnes, based on figures from the Central Pollution Control Board. Despite the country’s substantial investment in formal recycling infrastructure, he said the continued presence of informal operators remained one of the industry’s most pressing concerns. “The most important concern as far as lead battery, as far as lead is concerned, [is] to eliminate or to minimise the role of informal sector,” he said. “We cannot go on talking about that disorganised sector for a long time because of safety concerns and human exposure.” His proposed solution places battery dealers at the centre of a more accountable collection system. “All the battery dealers have to be made accountable. Let them get registered. Let them submit periodical returns,” he said. Under such a system, dealers would be required to disclose the quantities of spent batteries collected, the volumes transferred for recycling and the identities of the recyclers receiving them. Pugazhenthy argued that this information should be submitted regularly to regulators, allowing authorities to track the movement of used batteries and identify where material is being diverted away from authorised facilities. He also called for stronger oversight of licensed recycling operations, warning that obtaining regulatory approval should not be treated as a one-off exercise. Registered recyclers, he said, must be subject to periodic audits to establish whether environmental and occupational safety standards are being maintained. “They all need to be audited periodically as they are really following all the best practices, or only one-time exercise, and after that they get the approval. Everything goes away. That cannot go on.” Pugazhenthy also questioned whether India’s recycling industry should continue to accommodate facilities operating at widely differing scales. He suggested that an individual firm’s minimum annual recycling capacity of 10,000 to 12,000 tonnes could provide a more appropriate operating benchmark, although he presented this as a proposal rather than an existing regulatory requirement. The recommendations come as India’s lead consumption continues to expand, supported by automotive batteries, backup power systems, telecommunications and renewable energy installations. Pugazhenthy forecasts that total Indian lead consumption could reach approximately two million tonnes annually by 2030. But he insisted that growth must be accompanied by stronger environmental safeguards and greater accountability throughout the battery supply chain. For India’s formal recycling industry, the challenge is not simply to increase processing capacity, but to ensure that spent batteries reach the facilities equipped and authorised to handle them safely. title: Iranian manufacturer begins commercial production of graphene-enhanced lead battery – Batteries International
content: Iranian battery manufacturer, Platin Iran,  has begun commercial production of a graphene-enhanced lead battery, claiming the technology can increase capacity by more than 60% and significantly extend service life. The development follows four years of research involving Platin Iran, the Graphene and Advanced Materials Laboratory at Amirkabir University of Technology in Tehran and the Institute for Color Science and Technology. The company says its technology uses three-dimensional graphene incorporated into both the positive and negative active materials of conventional lead batteries, improving performance without changing the underlying chemistry. Mehdi Orouji, research and development manager at Platin Iran, said the project began in 2021 and had progressed through laboratory testing and pilot production to industrial manufacturing and commercialisation. “After four years of research and development, the project reached the stages of industrial production and commercialization,” he told Iranian news agency Tasnim. According to Orouji, testing has demonstrated capacity improvements exceeding 60% and service-life gains of at least 10% compared with conventional batteries. The company also claims its batteries could last twice as long as some commercial alternatives, potentially reducing operating costs by as much as 50% over their lifetime. However, the performance figures have been reported under different testing conditions and have not been independently verified at commercial scale. The technology is intended to address some of the longstanding weaknesses of lead batteries, including positive grid corrosion, hydrogen evolution and sulphation, which can accelerate degradation and shorten operational life. Orouji said hydrogen gas release had been reduced by at least 10%, while graphene’s conductive and capacitive properties contributed to improved battery performance. The company is targeting industrial and stationary applications, including telecommunications, power generation, electricity networks, data centres and solar energy storage. Although Platin Iran describes the technology as having reached commercial production, sales remain at an early stage. Two batteries were sold during the previous Iranian year, with one supplied to Iran’s Nanotechnology Development Headquarters and the other to the Tabriz Gas Transmission Company. The company has also pursued international patent protection for its graphene-based technology. A US patent application covering porous carbon-based materials for lead batteries was published on October 29. Earlier this year, Platin Iran said its graphene-enhanced batteries could offer approximately twice the cycle life of conventional products at a purchase price around 30% higher. The development comes as manufacturers continue to investigate advanced carbon additives as a means of improving the performance and competitiveness of established lead battery technology. For Platin Iran, the next challenge will be demonstrating whether the reported laboratory improvements can be reproduced consistently in commercial production and sustained under real operating conditions. title: Japan's lead recyclers face scrap shortage as competition drives prices higher – Batteries International
content: Competition for used batteries is intensifying across Japan, pushing up scrap prices and putting pressure on recyclers. Meanwhile, the country’s lead battery manufacturers are facing higher costs and an uncertain long-term market. Japan’s secondary lead industry is facing growing competition for used automotive batteries, with shortages of recyclable material pushing scrap prices higher despite uncertainty over the longer-term outlook for lead battery demand. According to the Japanese metals newspaper Japan Metal Daily , prices for spent automotive lead batteries reached ¥115–¥120 ($0.75–0.80) per kilogram in early September, compared with ¥100–110 during the first half of 2026. On October 2, Nikkan Sangyo Shimbun , a daily Japanese newspaper,  reported that spent automotive lead-acid battery prices had reached approximately ¥115/kg, close to their highest level of the year. The paper attributed this to reduced battery replacement and vehicle-scrapping volumes, together with stronger competition among collectors. On October 10 a Kyoto scrap buyer was reported by ScraPrice, an international online platform that tracks and compares scrap metal prices, as paying ¥123/kg for automotive lead-acid batteries. Japan Metal Daily attributed the overall increase to competition among collectors and recyclers for limited supplies of scrap. Even the winter replacement season, traditionally an important source of spent automotive batteries, failed to generate the volumes dealers had expected. The shortage reflects changes taking place across Japan’s lead industry. Domestic recyclers are competing with new entrants, including Chinese secondary lead companies, while primary smelters are increasingly turning to recycled material as supplies of lead concentrates become more difficult to secure. Industry presentations suggest that two or three Chinese-backed secondary lead operations are already active in Japan. Although the number of established Japanese recyclers has remained relatively stable, the additional competition is increasing pressure on scrap collection networks. Japan’s dependence on imported raw materials complicates this further. In 2024, the country imported almost 120,000 tonnes of lead ores and concentrates, worth approximately $314 million, principally from Australia, Mexico, Bolivia, the US and Peru. Meanwhile, battery manufacturers are confronting their own cost pressures. In June, GS Yuasa announced price increases of at least 20% across its replacement automotive, motorcycle and cycle-service lead battery ranges, effective from August. The company cited higher raw material, energy, logistics and labour costs, together with continuing uncertainty over international procurement The broader market remains substantial. GS Yuasa, Energywith and Furukawa Battery are Japan’s three principal domestic lead battery manufacturers, although industry observers expect production to consolidate over time. Electrification and Japan’s ageing population present longer-term challenges, but the replacement battery market remains resilient. GS Yuasa forecasts Japanese lead battery sales of ¥117 billion for fiscal 2026, up from ¥108 billion the previous year, although the increase reflects revenue rather than necessarily higher battery volumes. The company is also developing auxiliary lead batteries for hybrid and electric vehicles, where dependable low-voltage power remains essential. For recyclers, the immediate concern is less about disappearing demand than obtaining sufficient scrap to meet it. Japan’s experience illustrates how a mature battery market can face tightening raw material supplies even as its long-term growth prospects diminish. Japanese automotive trade reporting identifies increases of at least 10% from Furukawa Battery and Energywith (which took over the battery operations of Showa Denko Materials in December 2021), and approximately 10% from Panasonic Automotive Systems in 2026. title: Secondary lead industry launches training academy at 10ISLC – Batteries International
content: An initiative to preserve technical knowledge, develop new talent and improve understanding of lead recycling across the industry was launched in Colombo, Sri Lanka last week alongside the 10th International Secondary Lead Conference. Opening the 10th International Secondary Lead Conference, organiser Mark Stevenson said the new training academy had evolved from discussions dating back four or five years about how the industry could address gaps in technical knowledge and professional development. The academy, Stevenson said, was intended to provide a broader foundation of knowledge for everyone involved in lead production, recycling and associated activities, including regulators, non-governmental organisations and newcomers to the sector. Four factors had driven its creation: the need to preserve expertise accumulated by experienced industry professionals, growing demand for information from governments and NGOs, support from industry associations and the need to attract younger people. Stevenson recalled discussions with Dr Mike McDonagh about the failure of experienced professionals to pass on their knowledge to succeeding generations. “We both said, ‘Let’s do something different,'” he told delegates. He also highlighted the importance of providing a common foundation of understanding for people approaching the industry from different backgrounds. “Let’s bring people together and start teaching them, so their foundation is just as strong as ours, and it includes everybody.” The initiative has received support from Battery Council International, the International Lead Association and the Indian Lead Zinc Development Association. The Colombo meeting also marks a departure from the conference’s traditional format. The International Secondary Lead Conference has normally been held alongside the Asian Battery Conference, but was separated this year to accommodate the academy and mark its tenth edition. The first conference was held in Macau 17 years ago. Stevenson said the event would return to its association with the Asian Battery Conference next year. ILA managing director Andy Bush, speaking at the opening, said understanding developments in secondary lead markets, regulation, worker health and production technologies was essential to the industry’s future. Stevenson also envisaged the conference becoming a training ground for younger professionals, giving them opportunities to chair sessions and present papers before moving on to larger international battery conferences. He stressed that the academy’s remit extended beyond established manufacturers and recyclers to include those working to improve lead recycling practices in countries such as Nigeria, Ghana and India. The objective, he said, was to encourage knowledge sharing across the entire lead industry rather than treating its different sectors as separate communities. title: AI’s Expansion Hits the Limits of Local Power
content:
Grid connection delays and local resistance are extending development timelines as operators race to add AI-related capacity, though analysts differ on whether those constraints are already limiting AI development.
Data center projects are taking longer to reach construction as developers struggle to secure electricity connections and
local approval
, complicating expansion plans intended to meet growing AI demand.
Projects that broke ground between the third quarter of 2025 and the third quarter of 2026 waited an average of just over two years after being announced, according to
GlobalData
. That compares with about 18 months for projects that started construction between early 2020 and mid-2025.
Martina Raveni, senior analyst on GlobalData’s Strategic Intelligence team, told
Data Center Knowledge
that grid access and public opposition are the two biggest constraints.
“The grid is the hardest to fix because it is structural: new grid infrastructure takes five to 15 years to build, while a data center takes one to three,” she said.
Related:
The Power Challenge Behind Hyperscale AI Expansion
GlobalData forecasts annual data center electricity consumption will rise from 590 terawatt-hours in 2025 to 1,520 TWh in 2030. Meeting that demand will require developers to address power, permitting, and construction bottlenecks that investment alone cannot quickly overcome.
Grid Access Determines What Can Move Forward
A project’s other development challenges can become secondary when there is no available electricity connection. Luis Fernandes, IDC senior research manager for cloud and data centers within enterprise infrastructure, told
Data Center Knowledge
that discussions with developers, designers, and large operators consistently point to
grid access
as the dominant obstacle.
“It is by a long shot the biggest cause for delay in projects, to the point that we haven't seen delays in projects for any other reason, given that the lack of grid connection halts the entire exercise,” Fernandes said.
Raveni said developers in
Europe’s main data center hubs
can wait up to a decade for a connection. Skilled labor shortages add another constraint, with insufficient electricians and other trades pushing some delivery schedules back by around a year.
Delays are expected to be more common than cancellations, with Fernandes suggesting some stalled projects could change hands as other operators seek opportunities to acquire and complete them.
“Speed in construction [comes at] a premium, and a paused construction site is still bleeding cash,” he said.
Related:
Data Centers Can Delay, Not Dodge, the Power Crunch
Raveni cautioned that it remains too early to quantify eventual cancellations, although projects in grid-constrained locations or facing strong local opposition are particularly exposed.
Community Pushback Makes Timelines Harder to Predict
Community resistance can disrupt projects even when developers have customers and funding. Concerns about electricity bills, water consumption, noise, and land use can affect permitting and construction schedules.
Ya-Han Brownlee-Chen, DP World’s vice president of data center strategy in the Americas, told
Data Center Knowledge
that local acceptance is becoming one of the sector’s most significant barriers to development.
“There's a growing tension between the demand for AI infrastructure and communities' willingness to accommodate the physical facilities required to support it,” she said.
That tension complicates site selection and makes construction timelines harder to predict. Brownlee-Chen also pointed to
rising costs
for land, equipment, and other resources, with owners seeking premiums for sites that could accommodate data centers.
Those pressures can affect whether a delayed project remains financially viable. She said outcomes will depend on developers’ ability to resolve local objections, obtain infrastructure, and execute within a workable schedule, rather than on demand alone.
Related:
New PCE Metric Could Recover Stranded Data Center Power
On-Site Power Can Reduce Delays but Add New Risks
Developers seeking alternatives to delayed grid connections can face additional environmental and permitting challenges. Raveni said on-site gas generation can bridge a power gap, but redundancy requirements may necessitate generating capacity substantially greater than the data center’s normal needs.
Air pollution and water concerns can then intensify the same local resistance developers are trying to resolve.
“The real risk is that a temporary fix becomes permanent and pushes emissions up just as grids are decarbonizing,” she explained.
Power and cooling decisions also need to account for their combined demands on local resources. Joe Johnston, executive vice president and president of applied water at Xylem, said the infrastructure challenges need to be addressed together.
“Some of the biggest barriers to data center growth are tied to physical infrastructure, particularly power availability, water resources, and cooling capacity,” Johnston told
Data Center Knowledge
Johnston called for more efficient and resilient water and cooling infrastructure to support expansion while reducing pressure on community resources. GlobalData, for example, identified closed-loop cooling, water stewardship, and diversified power supplies among operators’ responses, although it describes progress as uneven.
The Effect on AI Remains Unclear
Longer development schedules raise questions about when infrastructure constraints will limit AI deployment, beyond increasing the cost of new capacity.
Raveni said access restrictions are already emerging, citing cloud providers rationing capacity, customers needing to reserve further ahead, and usage caps affecting large AI companies. Fernandes, however, offered a more measured conclusion.
“In terms of compute capacity, there is no hard evidence that we can point to [showing] that being a limitation to AI development,” he said.
He attributes the rise in computing costs more to material shortages, including
pressure on memory supplies
associated with high-end GPU manufacturing. His assessment distinguishes delays in building facilities from demonstrated limits on AI development.
For developers, the immediate task is to establish credible power and construction schedules while addressing the concerns that can prevent projects from securing approval. Neither demand forecasts nor proposed community benefits establish that a site can be delivered on time.
Raveni said developers should engage before opposition becomes entrenched and focus on the impacts residents expect to experience.
“Companies should focus on addressing people’s main concerns – electricity bills, water, and land use – early and transparently, rather than offering generic benefits once opposition has already formed,” she said.

title: Cloud Revenue Hits $168B as AI Capacity Expands
content:
Cloud providers are bringing data center capacity online for higher-priced AI services as enterprise cloud infrastructure spending accelerates, reinforcing demand for construction even as power constraints complicate delivery.
Worldwide spending on cloud infrastructure services reached $168 billion in the third quarter of 2026, up 55% from a year earlier, according to a Synergy Research Group
. The market has doubled in eight quarters, and AI-specific services now account for roughly one-third of total revenue.
John Dinsdale, chief analyst at Synergy, told
Data Center Knowledge
that three factors are driving the surge: additional capacity coming online, higher pricing, and a continued shift toward more expensive AI services.
“A lot of the additional capacity that is coming online is specifically targeting more valuable, higher-priced AI services,” he said.
That shift in pricing and service mix helps explain how cloud revenue can grow faster than the data center capacity supporting it. JLL’s August midyear
illustrated the construction demand behind that expansion.
Related:
Zombie Workloads Haunt Data Center Efficiency Efforts
Hyperscalers accounted for 59% of North American data center tenant demand, while 28 GW of owner-occupied capacity was under construction, according to JLL.
Neoclouds
– specialized cloud providers offering GPU-as-a-Service to enterprise customers – represented another 11% of demand, while AI companies accounted for 7%, broadening the customer base competing for facilities.
The buildout is expected to continue. Global data center capital spending is projected to exceed $3 trillion by 2030 as hyperscalers, sovereign AI programs, and specialized cloud providers expand their infrastructure to support growing AI workloads, according to an August
AI Changes the Cloud Customer Mix
The cloud market’s expansion is also reshaping which companies need infrastructure and how they compete. Amazon retained the largest share of worldwide cloud infrastructure revenue at 26%, followed by Microsoft at 19%, and Google at 16%, Synergy reported.
“AI has totally transformed the cloud market in terms of service capabilities, customer demand, and growth opportunities,” Dinsdale said.
Microsoft and Google grew faster than Amazon, while Oracle and neocloud providers, including CoreWeave, Crusoe, and Nebius, were among the fastest-growing companies outside the top three. Synergy said neocloud expansion is eroding the market shares of some established providers.
For data center operators, that changing mix raises questions about tenant durability and contract stability, particularly if some fast-growing providers consolidate. Dinsdale said he expects the underlying infrastructure to retain value even if an individual neocloud’s prospects change.
Related:
The Vanishing Value of VMware: A Wake-Up Call
Construction Demand Persists Despite Power and Tenant Risks
CBRE’s August
on North American data center trends found 7,481 MW under construction across eight primary markets in the first half of 2026, up 24.8% from a year earlier. More than 80% was preleased, up from 74.3% a year earlier. Power constraints continued to extend completion schedules, leaving customers competing for capacity that has yet to be delivered.
Those commitments mean operators evaluating expansion must weigh
construction schedules
and tenant stability alongside cloud revenue growth.
Dinsdale said he expects data centers, installed equipment, and existing customer contracts to find new owners if neocloud providers consolidate or fail. That suggests consolidation would redistribute infrastructure rather than leave large amounts of it unused, though the financial outcome would vary significantly by asset.
“Whatever happens to a neocloud company and its prospects for carrying on as an independent entity, there will be valuable assets that will not go to waste,” he said. “Valuations will vary greatly, but I don’t imagine too many stranded assets being trashed.”

title: Liquid Cooling Retrofits: Hard, but Sometimes Worth It
content:
There is little question that
liquid cooling
is becoming an increasingly attractive way to manage rising heat loads inside data centers, especially as operators deploy denser racks and more AI infrastructure. In many scenarios, liquid cooling can improve thermal efficiency and reduce dependence on large volumes of airflow. It can also help operators curb water use in designs that would otherwise rely heavily on evaporative cooling.
The challenge, however, is that most existing data centers were not designed with liquid cooling in mind. Retrofitting an older facility to support liquid cooling can be technically feasible, but it is rarely simple.
Here’s a look at why retrofits are difficult – and when the investment may still make sense.
Why Liquid Cooling Retrofits Are Difficult
Related:
Liquid Cooling Is Changing What Data Centers Need to Measure
It is much harder when an operator wants to retrofit an existing facility, whether to replace or supplement a traditional air-based cooling design. In that case, several challenges tend to stand in the way.
Space Constraints Complicate Piping
Liquid cooling systems require supply and return lines to run close to servers and other heat-generating IT equipment. In many existing server rooms, however, available space is already constrained, and much of it is occupied by networking and power cabling.
Addressing that problem may require repositioning racks, reworking cable pathways, or creating new routes for coolant distribution. In some cases, operators may even need to expand white space or make other physical changes to the facility. All of that is possible, but it can be expensive and disruptive.
Heavier Racks Can Strain Raised Floors
The structural components of liquid cooling systems, combined with coolant itself and higher-density compute hardware, can significantly increase rack weight. In AI-heavy environments, fully loaded racks can exceed
3,000 pounds
The added weight is especially challenging in facilities with
raised floors
. Raised-floor designs are common in older data centers because they support airflow management for conventional air cooling. But they may not be able to support heavier liquid-cooled racks without reinforcement or redesign. That can mean extensive structural work before a retrofit can move forward.
Downtime Is Hard to Avoid
Even for operators willing to make the investments needed to support a retrofit, downtime is often a major concern. Structural modifications, mechanical upgrades, and rack-level changes can take months, especially if servers must be moved or workloads shifted elsewhere during the transition.
Related:
Where Solid-State Micro-Cooling Fits in Data Centers
Even when no major building work is required, some disruption is likely as systems move from an existing cooling model to a liquid-assisted design. That might be manageable for organizations with spare capacity in other facilities or the ability to burst into the cloud, but it is a much harder proposition for sites supporting mission-critical workloads.
Mechanical Systems May Need Major Upgrades
Adding liquid cooling requires supporting infrastructure to remove heat from the building, which may entail changes to pumps, heat exchangers, water loops, or dry-cooling equipment.
Older facilities may not have enough capacity in their mechanical plant to support those changes. Even when they do, integrating new liquid cooling equipment with legacy systems can be complex. Operators must also consider factors such as leak detection, water quality, redundancy, and maintenance procedures.
Liquid Cooling Adds Operational Complexity
A retrofit can also create ongoing operational challenges. Liquid cooling introduces new equipment, maintenance needs, and failure scenarios that require staff training and updated procedures.
Related:
Rethinking the Blind-Mate Connection
When a Liquid Cooling Retrofit Is Worth It
Given the cost, complexity, and disruption involved, many operators will conclude that a full liquid cooling retrofit is not the right move for their facilities.
Still, there are cases where the economics and the operational logic are compelling.
One is a partial deployment. Instead of replacing an entire cooling architecture, an operator may add liquid cooling only for the highest-density racks while leaving the broader air-cooling system in place. That reduces structural changes and the risks of downtime. It is also the approach many
colocation providers
have taken as they add support for liquid-cooled deployments without converting entire facilities.
Another scenario is the single-tenant data center, where one organization directly captures the long-term efficiency and capacity benefits. In those cases, it is often easier to justify the capital expense because the operator and the beneficiary are the same.
Retrofits can also make more sense in regions facing
water constraints
or regulatory pressure around resource consumption. Where water availability is limited or sustainability targets are becoming harder to meet, the case for moving at least some workloads to liquid cooling can grow stronger.
Finally, a retrofit may be attractive when the alternative is building new capacity from scratch. If an operator needs to support denser server hardware but does not want to add another facility, liquid cooling may provide a way to
increase compute capacity
within an existing footprint. In that scenario, retrofitting may be less expensive than expanding the data center portfolio.
Retrofitting an existing data center for liquid cooling is difficult, and in many cases the costs will outweigh the benefits. But not always. For operators facing higher rack densities, tighter sustainability requirements, or limited room to expand, a carefully targeted retrofit can be a practical way to prepare an existing facility for the next generation of workloads.

title: Acciona Energía to add 42 MWh of battery storage across Dominican solar farms - Energy Storage
content: Acciona Energía has announced plans to build three co-located battery energy storage systems totaling 21.2 MW / 41.7 MWh across its operational solar portfolio in the Dominican Republic, targeting commercial operation in late 2027. Spanish renewables developer Acciona Energía will install 21.2 MW / 41.7 MWh of battery energy storage systems (BESS) across three of its operational solar photovoltaic assets in the Dominican Republic. The installations will be co-located at the Pedro Corto (82.7 MWp), Calabaza I (58 MWp), and Cotoperí Solar (162.6 MWp) plants, which together represent 303.3 MWp of installed solar capacity. The developer plans to commission all three sites in the final quarter of 2027. By co-locating the systems, the developer aims to cut capital expenditure through shared balance-of-plant infrastructure, avoiding additional land acquisition and utilizing established substation and grid connection points. The investment follows recent regulatory shifts within the Dominican Republic’s National Interconnected Electrical System (SENI), as grid operators contend with reduced system inertia and rising curtailment, with battery storage mandates and ancillary service market structures. Acciona generally operates its assets alongside local investment partners, holding 51% stakes, with pension and regional impact capital showing that institutional investors in the region view storage as an investable, bankable asset class. Acciona has not yet disclosed EPCs, BESS OEMs, or system integration partners. title: China’s Mengxi grid tops 20 GW of storage as renewables approach 60% of capacity - Energy Storage
content: China’s western Inner Mongolia power grid has surpassed 20 GW of operational new-type energy storage capacity, as rapid growth in wind and solar generation increases the need for flexible electricity resources. According to data released by Inner Mongolia Power Group on October 28, the grid had 20.23 GW/70.47 GWh of operational storage capacity as of October 27, accounting for 11.5% of its total installed power capacity. The figures imply an average nominal storage duration of approximately 3.5 hours. New installations reached 6.555 GW during the first ten months of 2026, up 47.9% year on year, supported by the commissioning of several large independent storage projects, including facilities in Wuchuan and Baotou. The western Inner Mongolia grid, also known as the Mengxi grid, is operated by Inner Mongolia Power Group and serves eight prefecture-level areas in central and western Inner Mongolia. It operates separately from the eastern Inner Mongolia grid, which is managed by State Grid. Wind and solar power account for nearly 60% of the Mengxi grid’s installed generation capacity, making the region an important test case for operating power systems with high renewable penetration. On October 22, renewable generation on the grid reached a record 720 GWh, representing 60.2% of total electricity generation that day. Wind power contributed 560 GWh, also setting a daily record. The increasing role of energy storage is reflected in operational data. According to the grid operator, cumulative charging and discharging volumes reached 15.78 TWh and 14.04 TWh, respectively, by October 27, with both increasing by more than 400% year on year. Storage has also become an important resource for emergency power supply. During the first ten months, the grid conducted 95 emergency storage dispatch operations. The maximum reported power contribution reached 12.25 GW, equivalent to 33% of the grid’s electricity load at the time. To coordinate these operations, Inner Mongolia Power Group has connected 126 storage stations to a centralized intelligent monitoring platform, enabling operators to monitor and control facilities across the grid. The operator said it has adopted a dispatch approach combining market-based optimization with centralized emergency interventions. Under normal conditions, electricity market mechanisms guide charging and discharging decisions, while grid operators can call on storage resources when supply shortages arise. This approach reflects an obvious shift in China’s storage sector, as independent and market-participating facilities increasingly complement batteries installed alongside individual renewable energy projects. Inner Mongolia Power Group is planning to advance six self-invested storage projects, including developments at Chunkunshan, Hanhai and Erzihao, while supporting grid connections for nearly 10 GW of new storage capacity during 2026. The rapid expansion highlights the growing importance of large-scale storage in China’s renewable-rich regions. title: Italy authorizes nearly 7 GW of battery storage - Energy Storage
content: Italy’s Ministry of Environment and Energy Security (MASE) issued five new single authorizations (AU) on Oct. 30 for battery energy storage system (BESS) projects with a combined power capacity of 722.5 MW. Including previous approvals, 24 storage projects totaling 3.7 GW received authorization in October, exceeding the 3.2 GW approved in September . The largest of the five projects approved on Oct. 30 is Castra Energiae Umbriae, for which Rinascita Botticelli Srl, a subsidiary of Rinascita Holding, obtained authorization under Decree 322/2026 . The 434.5 MW project will be located in Castel Giorgio, in the province of Terni, and will comprise 340 battery containers, each with a capacity of 4.472 MWh, for around 1.5 GWh in total, and 2,040 inverters rated at 213 kW. Construction is expected to take around 17 months. The other four projects are all in Puglia. Nuveen, through CS Bess 2 Srl, received authorization for the 103 MW Valle del Forno 2 project in Castelluccio dei Sauri, while Reden subsidiary Electricity Time Shifting 4 Srl was authorized to build a 50 MW battery in San Severo. GR Value subsidiary GRV BESS Srl received approval for a 35 MW project in Stornara, and RNE IT SPV 41 Srl for the 100 MW Bari Loseto project. Construction is expected to take 24 months for the Nuveen and Reden projects and nine months for the GR Value project. Leading developers Engie received authorization for the 140 MW Leini project in the province of Turin, through Engie Produzione Spa, alongside its combined-cycle power plant in Leinì. It also secured approval for a 122.4 MW BESS developed by Engie Puglianello Srl in the municipalities of Amorosi and Puglianello, in the province of Benevento. The two projects total 262.4 MW, adding to the 104 MW Andria project authorized in September. Milan-based ACL Energy secured authorization for the 116 MW Bari Ovest BESS, through ACL SPV 3, and the 250 MW Lucera 1 BESS, through ACL SPV 16, for a combined 366 MW. Including the Carpi and Castelverde projects authorized in September, the group now has four authorizations totaling 728 MW over two months. Naples-based Energy Total Capital obtained two authorizations through special-purpose vehicles registered at the same address: 198 MW in Manfredonia, Foggia, and 51 MW in Santa Maria Capua Vetere, Caserta, for a combined 249 MW. The group had already secured authorization for the 222 MW Sant’Agata di Puglia project in September. Two more authorizations went to companies established following the split of GRA BESS Srl. Santa Maria Srl received approval for 104.4 MW across Santa Maria La Longa and Pavia di Udine, while Casei Srl secured authorization for 100.8 MW in Casei Gerola, Pavia. Both projects have the same plant configuration. The other four projects are all in Puglia: a 103 MW project by Nuveen in Castelluccio dei Sauri, a 50 MW project by Reden in San Severo, a 35 MW project by GR Value in Stornara, and a 100 MW project by RNE IT SPV 41 in Bari. Construction is expected to take 24 months for the Nuveen and Reden projects and nine months for the GR Value project. Other recipients include Urus Storage, with a 250 MW project in the Macchiareddu industrial area near Cagliari; Portugal-based Greenvolt in Copertino, Lecce; NPD Italia II in Civitavecchia; Viola Rinnovabili in Borore, Nuoro; Myt Renewables in Castelnuovo Scrivia, Alessandria; Agave; HorizonBess; Grottaglie Solar BESS; Galatina BESS 2; and Casetta Storage. Puglia received 12 of the 24 authorizations, totaling around 2,237 MW, or 60.6% of the month’s authorized capacity. Even excluding the large Brindisi project, Puglia would remain in first place, with more than 1.2 GW. The province of Foggia had the largest concentration, with six projects totaling around 752 MW. Outside Puglia, notable projects include the 435 MW development in Castel Giorgio, Umbria, and 305 MW across Macchiareddu, Cagliari, and Borore, Nuoro, in Sardinia. Northern Italy accounted for around 11% of the total, or 420 MW, across five projects in Piedmont, Lombardy, Friuli Venezia Giulia and Emilia-Romagna. Two of these projects, in Casei Gerola and Castelnuovo Scrivia, will connect to the same Terna substation, Castelnuovo Scrivia, on the border between the provinces of Pavia and Alessandria. October ended with two fewer authorizations than September, at 24 compared with 26, but around 440 MW more capacity. The average project size therefore rose to around 154 MW, from 125 MW in the previous month. The figure is inflated by the Brindisi project, however, with the median remaining effectively unchanged at 100 MW. Most projects are smaller than 200 MW, and 12 have a capacity of no more than 100 MW. The smallest is Myt Renewables’ 25 MW project in Castelnuovo Scrivia, with 104.16 MWh of storage capacity. Few decrees specify energy storage capacity. Where figures are available, durations range from around 3.5 hours for Castel Giorgio to more than 4.5 hours for Brindisi and Santa Maria La Longa, with Civitavecchia (70 MW/282.15 MWh) and Castelnuovo Scrivia at around four hours. title: Former CAKE team is back in the kitchen with a new electric motorcycle
content:
Electric Motorcycles
Micah Toll
| Nov 3 2026 - 5:53 am PT
If the new ReBake Abler electric motorcycle looks like it might share a bit of DNA with Sweden’s dearly departed CAKE, there’s a good reason for that.
ReBake Motors
has officially unveiled its first electric two-wheeler at EICMA 2026 in Milan, introducing the Abler as a highly modular, utility-focused electric moped and light motorcycle.
Behind the new Swedish company is founder and CEO Karl Ytterborn, who spent eight years at CAKE from its founding in 2016 through 2024. CAKE famously built
some of the most interesting minimalist electric motorcycles and utility bikes on the market
before ultimately collapsing after failing to secure additional funding. Ytterborn says ReBake is intended to apply many of the lessons learned during that experience, while eliminating unnecessary cost and complexity.
And the Abler certainly looks the part.
Its chunky 42mm aluminum tube frame isn’t just a styling exercise. ReBake designed it as a mounting system, allowing cargo accessories to attach directly to the frame at multiple locations. That means riders can configure the bike for everything from carrying groceries and passengers to more serious utility duties.
There are two versions. The Abler45 is an EU L1e-B moped with a 45 km/h (28 mph) top speed, 4 kW nominal motor and 5.12 kW peak output. It starts at €3,990 including VAT.
The €4,990 Abler80 steps up to the A1 light motorcycle category, increasing nominal power to 6.14 kW and peak power to 7.68 kW while pushing the top speed beyond 80 km/h (50 mph). Both versions use a direct-drive rear hub motor.
Energy comes from removable 2 kWh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries weighing 17 kg (37.5 lb) apiece. The Abler45 comes standard with one battery but can carry two, while the Abler80 includes two for 4 kWh of total capacity. With both batteries, ReBake claims up to 160 km (99 miles) of low-speed urban range on the Abler45 or 114 km (71 miles) on the Abler80. Each battery can be charged either on or off the bike from a normal 230V outlet, reaching a full charge in four hours.
The rest of the hardware includes 14-inch cast wheels, 140mm of front suspension travel, dual rear shocks, front and rear disc brakes with combined braking, regenerative braking, and full LED lighting.
Perhaps more interesting than any individual specification, though, is simply seeing another Swedish electric motorcycle startup emerge from CAKE’s ashes.
CAKE demonstrated that there was plenty of appetite for unconventional, lightweight electric motorcycles. Unfortunately, it also demonstrated just how difficult it is to turn that enthusiasm into a sustainable business.
ReBake appears to be getting another crack at that equation – this time with eight years’ worth of lessons already baked in.

content:

Kia is eyeing its fourth consecutive annual US sales record after another record-breaking October. With the new 2027 EV3 arriving,
is “confident” the momentum will carry into Q4 and well into 2027.
Kia extends record-breaking US sales streak in October
“With six consecutive months of record-breaking sales, Kia is accelerating toward a fourth straight annual sales record,” Kia America vice president of sales Eric Watson said on Tuesday.
Kia sold 80,008 vehicles in the US last month, up 16% year over year and marking its best
October sales
month ever.
Kia said electrified and hybrid vehicles drove the growth, with sales up 112% and 114% YOY, both setting new sales records.
Several Kia models posted strong YOY sales growth, including the three-row electric EV9 (+111%), Telluride (+63%), EV6 (+58%), Seltos (+43%), Sorento (+31%), Carnival (+17%), K4 (+14%), and Sportage (+12%).
Regarding its fully electric vehicles. Sales of the EV9, Kia’s three-row electric SUV, are now up 5% year-to-date, with 13,835 units sold through October.
Although EV6 sales rebounded slightly last month, they are still down 39% YTD, with 7,067 units sold through October.
2027 Kia EV9 (Source: Kia)
Kia’s new entry-level electric SUV, the EV3 (
check out our review
), is now in showrooms nationwide. After it went on sale in mid-August, Kia sold 1,496 EV3s in its first two months.
The 2027 EV3 is Kia’s most affordable fully electric vehicle, starting at $29,890. That’s for the base EV3 Light model, which uses a 58.3 kWh battery that provides up to 221 miles of range.
Higher-priced trims, including the Wind, Land, GT-Line, and GT, use an 81.4 kWh battery for up to 321 miles of range.
2027 Kia EV3 (Source: Kia)
Front-wheel-drive (FWD) models have a single 201-horsepower electric motor. Upgrading to all-wheel-drive (AWD) costs $3,200 and adds a rear electric motor for a combined 261 horsepower.
All variants have a native NACS port so that drivers can use Tesla Superchargers without a separate adapter. Charging the 58.3 kWh battery from 10% to 80% takes around 29 minutes, while the larger 81.4 kWh battery takes about 31 minutes.
2027 Kia EV3 interior (Source: Kia)
Inside, all EV3 models feature Kia’s latest ccNC (connected car Navigation Cockpit) with standard wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto.
The setup provides nearly 30″ of combined digital screens, including a dual 12.3″ instrument cluster and touchscreen infotainment, plus a 5″ climate control display.
Kia describes the EV3 as an “entry-level EV SUV that offers many of the advanced amenities of the EV9,” but in a smaller, more affordable package.

title: Maximo milestone: friendly robot robot has completed 300,000 tasks
content:
Solar power
Jo Borrás
| Nov 3 2026 - 4:32 am PT
After completing the first half of the Bellefield complex last summer
, Maximo engineers have put their helpful robot friend into high gear, with the latest version 3.0 robot-equipped construction crews installing as many as 24 solar panel modules per hour, per person. And now, the company is reporting that Maximo has completed its 300,000th construction task. (!)
If that 24 modules per hour, per person rate sounds fast,
that’s because it is
. At full tilt, the latest Maximo robot-equipped crews have nearly doubled the output of traditional installation methods at similar solar locations throughout Southern California. Now,
with 300,000 tasks under its belt
, the robot is proving to be both fast
durable.
“The future of solar construction depends on bringing together the experience of our people and new technology,” explains Matt Tetrault, President of Primoris’ Renewables business.
Max’ed out
Image by Maximo Robotics.
Like just about everyone these days, Maximo is playing up its machines’ NVDIVIA hardware, re-branding its robots’ repetitive automation as “physical AI.” That’s not to say the robots don’t work, however – as their deployment at Amazon’s Bellefield solar field is proving.
(By) leveraging NVIDIA AI infrastructure together with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries and NVIDIA Isaac Sim open robotics simulation framework, the Maximo team was able to develop, test and refine robotic capabilities through physics-based simulation and AI driven modeling before deploying updates in the field. The combination of AI, vision, robotics and simulation driven engineering reduced development and validation timelines and increased confidence in field performance as the robotic fleet scaled.
Amazon Web Services (AWS) powered the development, deployment, and operation of Maximo’s AI-driven field systems. AWS provides scalable computing, automated software delivery, and advanced data analytics, including real-time construction intelligence, enabling Maximo to collect operational robotics data and continuously improve performance.
The rapid deployment of solar panels at utility scale projects like this one,
which is set to eventually reach over a GW of solar generating capacity
, will help companies like Amazon reduce their carbon footprint, of course –
but also save them big money as the price of fossil fuels continues to climb
The Maximo team says it has plans to extend its robots potential use cases beyond solar and into construction tasks that require similar pick and place and feeding and attaching movements, site logistics, and site cleanup. And like just about every other business that demands a high degree of physical labor, the construction industry is facing huge labor shortages,
making machines like Maximo that provide real efficiency gains welcome additions to the job site

title: Tesla wins trade zone status for Texas Megapacks, but China tariffs stay
content:
Tesla Energy
Tesla Megapack
Fred Lambert
| Nov 3 2026 - 6:15 am PT
Tesla’s Megapack factory in Brookshire, Texas, is now officially a foreign-trade zone, a US customs program that lets manufacturers defer duties on imported parts. The FTZ Board’s approval,
on Monday, runs for 14 months.
It’s easy to read this as Tesla getting a pass on tariffs for the Chinese LFP cells inside its Megapacks. Tesla’s own application says otherwise: parts hit by Section 301, 232, or 122 tariffs still pay them.
What Tesla asked for
Tesla filed the request on May 20 for Subzone 84AM, part of FTZ 84 in the Houston area. That’s the factory where
Tesla started Megapack 3 production in August
, with a planned capacity of 50 GWh per year.
application
lists roughly 80 imported components Tesla wants to bring in under zone procedures, from coolant pumps and transformers to busbars, wiring harnesses, circuit boards and battery cells. Duty rates on those parts go up to 6.5%, while finished Megapacks and Bento inverters range from duty-free to 3.4%.
That gap is the usual reason companies set up an FTZ. A manufacturer in a zone can normally elect to pay the finished product’s lower rate instead of the rate on each imported part.
The tariff catch
But the application spells out the limit. Components subject to duties under Section 122 of the Trade Act, Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act, or Section 301 “require subject merchandise to be admitted to FTZs in privileged foreign status,” according to the notice.
Privileged foreign status locks in a part’s own classification and tariff treatment when it enters the zone. So a Chinese LFP cell that ends up in a Megapack sold in the US still pays the Section 301 tariff on Chinese non-EV lithium-ion batteries, which jumped from 7.5% to 25% on January 1, 2026. Tesla just pays it later, when the finished Megapack leaves the zone.
Here’s what Tesla actually gets out of it:
Duties are deferred until a Megapack ships out of the zone, which helps cash flow while the factory ramps up
No US duty on Megapacks exported directly from the zone
The lower finished-product rate on parts that aren’t caught by China, steel, or other special tariffs
No duty on scrap, and fewer customs filings
Useful. Not an exemption.
Same deal everyone else got
The approval came with the same wording the FTZ Board has used all year. Production was “authorized on a limited basis,” and “further subject to a fourteen-month time period.”
Tesla got an
identical decision
for Megapack and inverter production at Fremont, Livermore and Lathrop in California this summer, with a one-year limit instead. Eastman Chemical, battery pack maker Rose Batteries, and chipmaker Qorvo all received similar time-limited, “limited basis” approvals in 2026.
The 14-month clock puts the expiry around the end of 2027. That’s roughly when
LG Energy Solution is due to start supplying Tesla with LFP cells from Michigan
under a $4.3 billion contract for Megapack 3, with mass production expected in the second half of 2027.
Tesla’s China cell problem
Tesla hasn’t hidden the issue. When tariffs escalated in April 2025, CFO Vaibhav Taneja said the impact on energy storage would be “outsized since we source lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery cells from China.” We wrote at the time that
Tesla’s only growing business was kneecapped by Trump’s tariffs
Tesla has since brought up its own
LFP cell factory in Nevada

title: This electric microcar just got a 50 mph upgrade, plus a secret Turbo mode
content:
microcar
Micah Toll
| Nov 3 2026 - 7:00 am PT
The adorable little Eli ZERO electric microcar is growing up. At this year’s EICMA motorcycle show in Milan, Eli Electric Vehicles is unveiling a faster, more powerful version of its pint-sized electric car, along with a sporty new limited-edition model that even includes a hidden Turbo mode.
teased last week
, the new Eli ZERO MX is the company’s first L7e-class electric vehicle, allowing it to reach speeds of up to 80 km/h (50 mph). That’s a significant jump from the 45 km/h (28 mph) top speed of the original L6e version
that we originally reviewed
, opening the door to a much wider range of driving scenarios.
And perhaps most importantly, the company managed to squeeze that extra performance into the same tiny package.
Eli ZERO MX: Same tiny car, more power
Eli ZERO MX
retains the original’s ultra-compact 2.25-meter (7.4-foot) length, making it considerably smaller than even the smallest conventional passenger cars.
But under that tiny exterior, the MX now packs up to 20 kW (27 hp) of peak power, compared to the 12 kW (16 hp) of the original Eli ZERO.
The upgraded model also features a 14.4 kWh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery, providing a claimed range of up to 200 km (124 miles) per charge.
That’s a pretty respectable figure for a vehicle designed primarily for short urban and suburban trips.
The rear-wheel-drive microcar features selectable ECO and SPORT driving modes, a 30% climbing capability, and a tight 7.2-meter turning circle. Charging is handled by a 3.3 kW onboard charger, allowing owners to plug in at home or use public AC charging stations.
Despite its diminutive size, the Eli ZERO MX also includes a surprisingly long list of features normally associated with much larger cars.
Those include air conditioning and heating, a panoramic moonroof, soft-close doors, keyless entry and start, electric power steering, ABS, front and rear disc brakes, and an electronic parking brake.
There’s also an 8.8-inch digital instrument cluster, a reversing camera with rear radar, and an optional 10.1-inch infotainment display with Apple CarPlay.
The MX is available in four colors: Pearl White, Arctic Silver, Graphite, and Champagne.
The biggest difference, though, is the vehicle’s classification. While the original Eli ZERO falls under Europe’s L6e light quadricycle category, the new MX qualifies as an L7e heavy quadricycle. That means it generally requires a higher-level driving license, but also allows for considerably more performance.
For drivers who love the idea of a tiny electric runabout but need something capable of keeping up with faster suburban traffic, the MX could be a much more compelling option.
A sporty Race Edition with a hidden surprise
Eli isn’t stopping at a faster version of its microcar.
The company is also introducing the Eli ZERO Race Edition, a limited-production model available in both the original L6e and the new L7e configurations.
Finished in an exclusive Turbo Red paint job, the Race Edition features racing stripes across the hood, roof, and body panels, along with a rear spoiler and special wheel badging.
Inside, the sporty treatment continues with a two-tone Race Red microsuede and light gray interior, including special upholstery, dashboard accents, and embroidered seats.
But the most interesting feature isn’t immediately visible.
Eli has included a secret Turbo mode activated by pressing and holding the hazard light button. After four quick chimes, the digital instrument cluster switches to Turbo mode and the car’s acceleration response becomes sharper.
Importantly, the feature doesn’t increase the vehicle’s top speed or exceed its regulatory performance limits. Instead, it changes the way the car responds to accelerator inputs, giving it a sportier driving feel.
It’s a fun little Easter egg in a vehicle that already has plenty of personality.
Eli is also offering a new Carbon Aero Kit, consisting of a carbon fiber front splitter, side skirts, and rear wing. The kit is compatible with both the Race Edition and other Eli ZERO models.
Small electric cars finding their place
Eli has spent years developing its vision of a smaller, lighter, and more efficient alternative to conventional cars, particularly for the short trips that make up much of our daily driving.
The company has already launched its second-generation Eli ZERO, which shares the same 96V electrical architecture and aluminum chassis as the new MX.
A 28 mph (45 km/h) microcar makes plenty of sense in dense urban centers, but its usefulness quickly drops off when drivers need to venture onto faster roads. A 50 mph (80 km/h) version, on the other hand, could make the same tiny vehicle practical for considerably more people.
The Eli ZERO family is currently available through authorized dealers in several European markets, including Italy, Norway, and the Netherlands, with prices starting at €10,500 (approximately US $12,000) for the base model. Pricing for the new MX and Race Edition hasn’t yet been announced.
Eli also has a pilot program underway in the United States, though the new models are being introduced primarily for the European market.
Both the Eli ZERO MX and Race Edition will be on display at EICMA 2026 in Milan from November 3–8.
For a vehicle that takes up less than half the space of a conventional car, the Eli ZERO is certainly finding ways to make a bigger impression!

title: Yamaha unveils new NMAX E, bringing electric power to its popular motorbike lineup
content:
Electric Motorcycles
Micah Toll
| Nov 3 2026 - 3:28 am PT
Yamaha is expanding its electric two-wheeler lineup with a much more capable machine, unveiling the new NMAX E as an electric version of its popular NMAX sport scooter.
2027 Yamaha NMAX E
is being positioned as a 125cc-equivalent electric scooter, putting it firmly above the
low-speed urban electric scooters
that have made up much of Yamaha’s electric lineup thus far.
At its heart is Yamaha’s new compact eAxle drive unit, which sends power to the rear wheel through a belt drive. The electric motor produces 6.7 kW (9 hp) of nominal power and peaks at 7.5 kW (10 hp), along with 33.3 Nm (24.6 lb-ft) of torque.
Yamaha hasn’t published a top speed in the specifications, but the NMAX E’s A1 classification puts it in the same general category as 125cc combustion scooters rather than urban mopeds.
Power comes from a centrally mounted 3.5 kWh lithium-ion battery, which Yamaha says provides up to 104 km (65 miles) of range on the WMTC Class 1 testing cycle. The L-shaped battery is mounted low and centrally in the chassis to help maintain a low center of gravity.
Unlike many electric scooters that rely on removable batteries, the NMAX E uses a fixed pack. Yamaha has compensated for that with an onboard 800W charger, allowing riders to plug the scooter directly into a household outlet or an AC Type 2 public charging station. A full 0-100% charge takes around 5.5 hours.
Riders can choose between three riding modes. Sport (S) mode offers the quickest acceleration, Touring (T) provides smoother power delivery for everyday riding and carrying a passenger, and Eco (E) reduces acceleration and top speed while maximizing range. Regenerative braking is also included.
The rest of the scooter is fairly well equipped, including traction control, ABS, 245mm front and rear disc brakes, 13-inch wheels, a 33mm fork, dual rear shocks, and even a reverse mode to make low-speed maneuvering easier.
A five-inch TFT display includes smartphone connectivity through Yamaha’s Motor On app, providing turn-by-turn navigation as well as battery status, ride information, maintenance reminders, and other connected features. There’s also keyless ignition, USB-C charging, LED lighting, and illuminated underseat storage large enough for a full-face helmet, depending on its size.
Perhaps most importantly, the NMAX E looks like a proper Yamaha scooter rather than an electric experiment. Its dual headlights and distinctive side panels closely follow the styling language of Yamaha’s existing MAX family.
That could prove important as established motorcycle manufacturers increasingly attempt to bring electric models into their existing lineups rather than treating them as separate curiosities.
Pricing and exact market availability haven’t yet been announced, but Yamaha is positioning the NMAX E as a 2027 model for the European market.

title: Zero Motorcycles unveils $8K electric motorcycle, street-legal dirt bike, and much more
content:
Electric Motorcycles
Zero Motorcycles
Micah Toll
| Nov 3 2026 - 7:30 am PT
Zero Motorcycles is celebrating its 20th anniversary with a major wave of announcements at EICMA 2026, unveiling several new electric two-wheelers alongside some important technology upgrades that could make its existing motorcycles even more appealing.
The biggest news is an entirely new lightweight electric street motorcycle known as Project Ventura, designed to bridge the gap between the increasingly popular world of electric bikes plus lightweight e-motos and the full-size electric motorcycle market. But that’s far from the only news coming out of Zero’s booth in Milan.
The electric motorcycle maker is also announcing a new street-legal version of its XE electric dirt bike that was previously only street-legal in Europe, introducing its LS3 electric scooter to Europe, introducing a redesigned smartphone app, and sharing more details about its upcoming DC fast-charging system.
There’s quite a bit to unpack here, so let’s get into it.
Zero Project Ventura: A new electric motorcycle for under $8,000
Perhaps the most exciting announcement is Project Ventura, a new lightweight electric motorcycle that
hopes will attract an entirely new generation of riders.
With supermoto-inspired styling, 17-inch wheels, and a more approachable design than the company’s larger street motorcycles, Ventura appears aimed squarely at riders who want something more substantial than a typical lightweight e-moto but aren’t necessarily looking for a full-size, high-performance motorcycle.
And with a targeted price of less than US $8,000, it could be one of Zero’s most accessible street motorcycles yet.
The bike features a new electric powertrain producing over 20 kW (27 hp) of peak power, delivering a sustained top speed of 65 mph (105 km/h) and a momentary maximum speed of 81 mph (130 km/h).
That’s a particularly interesting distinction, as it positions the bike as being able to briefly reach highway-capable speeds with the occasional burst of extra performance, but perhaps not for longer sustained highway stretches.
Importantly, we don’t yet know the battery capacity, though Zero is giving us a hint by publishing a range estimate. The company is quoting an estimated real-world range of 93 miles (150 km), but without a real battery capacity figure to parse, it’s hard to take that range estimate at face value.
We do know that the bike will feature onboard Level 2 charging, allowing riders to plug into public AC charging stations without carrying around a separate external charger – something more common on the
smallest of electric motorcycles
that attempt to cut down on weight and cost by using an off-board charger.
Other features include standard ABS, Bluetooth connectivity, integration with Zero’s upcoming smartphone app, and a chassis designed to accommodate a passenger.
The riding position is upright, and the bike’s supermoto-inspired geometry is intended to deliver agile handling and a playful riding experience.
Perhaps most interestingly, Zero isn’t hiding the fact that it sees the explosion of e-bikes and smaller electric motos as
a potential gateway
to motorcycle ownership.
“When we set out to build Project Ventura, we had three guiding principles: first, build a bike so good-looking you’d want its poster above your bed. Second, make it a proper electric motorcycle that feels like a natural next step for the millions of riders who’ve spent the last four or five years on e-bikes and e-motos. And third, make it ridiculously fun to ride,” explained Jim Callahan, Zero’s Chief Product and Partnerships Officer.
That’s a notable strategy for a company that has historically focused heavily on higher-performance electric motorcycles. However, the
launch of Zero’s smaller Sur Ron-style electric dirt bikes last summer
showed that the motorcycle maker did see the writing on the wall in terms of the success of the e-moto market compared to larger flagship bikes.
Instead of trying to convince existing gasoline motorcycle riders to make the electric switch, Zero is increasingly looking toward younger riders who may have already fallen in love with electric two-wheelers and are ready for something faster and more capable.
But for those interested in the new Ventura, they’ll have to wait just a bit longer. The motorcycle is expected to become available in summer 2027.
Zero XE electric dirt bike is finally going street-legal
Another major announcement is a new street-legal version of Zero’s XE electric dirt bike.
The original XE was introduced as part of Zero’s
more affordable X Line of lightweight electric off-road motorcycles
, offering a more accessible entry point to the brand than its traditional street and dual-sport models. While the model was available in street-legal format in Europe, the US versions were purely off-road affairs.
Now Zero is taking that same general concept and making it legal for public roads, opening up significantly more riding possibilities.
The new XE is fully homologated and features the necessary street equipment, including a headlight, taillight, and centrally mounted dashboard. A small integrated flyscreen and black bodywork give the motorcycle a more refined appearance, while wide dual-sport tires help it transition between pavement and dirt.
Zero has also revised the gearing, using a rear sprocket designed to balance off-road performance with the higher speeds required for street riding.
The result is a claimed top speed of 60 mph (97 km/h), making the XE capable of considerably more than simply putting around the neighborhood, though with a slight torque sacrifice.
For riders who live near off-road riding areas, the appeal is obvious. Instead of loading a dirt bike into a truck or trailer to reach the trails, owners could potentially ride directly from home to the trailhead, provided local regulations allow it.
That’s a particularly useful capability for a lightweight electric dirt bike, where much of the appeal comes from its simplicity, low maintenance, and ability to explore places that larger motorcycles might struggle to reach.
The new street-legal XE is expected to launch in spring 2027, with pricing starting at US $6,295.
Zero LS3 electric scooter makes its European debut
Zero is also expanding its electric scooter offerings with the European debut of the LS3, a faster and more capable scooter designed for urban transportation and longer commutes.
While Zero has traditionally been associated with electric motorcycles, its growing interest in scooters represents another effort to reach riders who prioritize everyday transportation over outright performance.
The LS3 offers a top speed of 75 mph (121 km/h), which puts it well beyond the typical low-speed urban electric scooter category.
Zero also quotes a range of up to 93 miles (150 km), powered by a battery system consisting of three onboard batteries with a combined capacity of 5.6 kWh.
Interestingly, one of those batteries is removable and located beneath the seat. Riders can remove it to free up additional storage space, offering some flexibility between maximum battery capacity and cargo-carrying convenience.
That could prove useful for commuters who don’t always need the scooter’s full range but would appreciate extra room for everyday items.
The LS3 also comes equipped with heated grips and a heated seat, features that should be particularly welcome to European riders commuting through colder months.
Connected technology rounds out the package, including compatibility with Zero’s upcoming smartphone app.
The LS3 is expected to become available in Europe in spring 2027.
Zero is developing a completely new smartphone app
Beyond the new vehicles, Zero is also working on a redesigned smartphone application that promises to give riders considerably more control over their motorcycles.
The new app is being developed for the LS3, 2027 Street and Dual Sport motorcycles, and Project Ventura.
One of the more interesting features is the ability to customize riding modes. In addition to preset modes that adjust power delivery and regenerative braking, riders will be able to create a custom mode and individually tune parameters including speed, power, torque, and regeneration.
The app will also include a charging-station finder, allowing riders to search for nearby chargers and filter them by charging speed, network, and availability. Apple Maps integration will provide route guidance to selected charging locations.
An optional ride-history feature can automatically record trips, including their distance, duration, and route previews.
Riders will also be able to customize their motorcycle’s dashboard layout, choosing which information appears in each quadrant of the display.
Battery management is getting some attention, too. The app will provide controls for scheduled charging, target charge levels, charging limits, and long-term battery storage settings.
Zero is also adding integrated feedback and support tools that allow owners to report problems or suggest improvements directly through the app, including photos and diagnostic logs.
The redesigned app is expected to arrive in 2027.
DC fast charging is finally coming to more Zero motorcycles
Perhaps the most consequential technology announcement, at least for riders who want to take their electric motorcycles beyond short commutes and weekend rides, is
Zero’s continued development of DC fast charging
Zero says it is targeting a 2027 launch for its new fast-charging system, which will support compatible Street and Dual Sport motorcycles.
The system is being designed to charge compatible batteries from 20% to 80% in less than 30 minutes.
That’s a major improvement in convenience compared to the longer AC charging stops that have traditionally been associated with Zero motorcycles.
Importantly, the company is developing the system for both North America and Europe, with different charging connectors for each market.
European motorcycles will use the CCS standard, while North American models will feature NACS connectors.
The latter is particularly interesting given the
growing adoption of NACS charging infrastructure across North America
, potentially making it easier for electric motorcycle riders to access a wider range of charging locations.
Zero is also developing a retrofit option for eligible existing motorcycles, meaning some current owners may eventually be able to upgrade their bikes rather than purchasing entirely new models to take advantage of the technology.
The company hasn’t yet announced pricing or a complete list of compatible motorcycles, and the retrofit option remains under development.
Still, the prospect of adding significantly faster charging to existing electric motorcycles could be an important development for the brand.
Electrek’s Take
There are several exciting announcements here, but I think the biggest takeaway is that Zero seems to be increasingly focused on making electric motorcycling more accessible through smaller and more affordable options.
For much of its 20-year history, Zero has been a pioneer in the electric motorcycle industry, often offering impressive performance and technology, but at prices that made its motorcycles difficult for many riders to justify. The bikes have long won acclaim, but $20k was a big ask.
Now we’re seeing a different approach.
The company’s more affordable X Line bikes have already demonstrated that Zero is interested in attracting riders who might never have considered one of its larger electric motorcycles. The street-legal XE takes that concept a step further, and Project Ventura could be an even more important addition.
I’m particularly intrigued by Zero’s explicit acknowledgment that millions of people have spent the last several years riding e-bikes and smaller electric motos, and that many of those riders may be ready to graduate to something bigger.
That’s an audience
I’ve been watching grow
for years. These are riders who are already comfortable with electric drivetrains, who appreciate the simplicity of twist-and-go riding, and who don’t necessarily have any attachment to gasoline engines or traditional motorcycle culture.
For those riders, a lightweight, fun electric motorcycle capable of 81 mph and priced below $8,000 could be an awfully compelling next step.
The new street-legal XE is similarly exciting, especially for riders who want to combine urban transportation with off-road adventures without needing a truck to haul their bike around.
And while the new motorcycles are likely to get most of the attention, I wouldn’t overlook the DC fast-charging announcement. Charging speed has long been one of the biggest limitations facing electric motorcycles, particularly for riders interested in longer trips. A sub-30-minute charging stop isn’t quite gasoline-level convenience, but it’s getting much closer to something that can work for real motorcycle touring.
Of course, several important details remain unknown, and we’ll have to wait until 2027 to see how these products and technologies perform in the real world.
But taken together, these announcements suggest Zero is making a serious effort to expand beyond its traditional audience and build electric motorcycles for a much broader range of riders.
And after two decades of helping pioneer the electric motorcycle industry, that’s exactly the kind of evolution I’d like to see.

title: 亿纬锂能成立大洋洲新子公司
content:
集邦光储观察获悉，10月27日，亿纬锂能大洋洲子公司在澳大利亚墨尔本正式成立。
在现场，亿纬锂能还发布Mr.Big Family系列6.9MWh储能大电池系统、LF702S高能量电芯、“磐盾系列”6C/10C高倍率园区备电柜四款储能新品。
活动现场，亿纬锂能大洋洲子公司与Akaysha Energy、EPEC Group、EWE Group、Hitachi Energy四家企业进行战略合作签约。各方将围绕电网侧长时储能、分布式备电、电网调频、项目开发、技术协同及本地化交付等方向开展深度合作。
在10月23日举行的电话会议中，亿纬锂能表示，随着国际客户交付增加，2027年储能电池业务海外占比将大幅增加。
亿纬锂能还披露，2026年前三季度公司实现营业总收入733.90亿元，同比增长约63.08%；归母净利润52.40亿元，同比增长86.11%。
出货量方面，2026年前三季度动力电池出货66.17GWh，同比增长91.30%；储能电池出货67.52GWh，同比增长39.46%。
亿纬锂能还表示，目前，公司储能电池产品需求旺盛，大方型电池备受青睐，公司将尽力满足交付。从亿纬锂能出货目标来看，其2027年动力和储能业务预计均将实现较大增长。

title: 天合储能滁州100GWh储能系统项目发布新进展
content:
集邦光储观察获悉，10月26日，滁州市生态环境局对《天合储能（滁州）有限公司年产100GWh集成舱（储能系统）及研发中心项目生态环境影响报告表》发布批前公示。
公示信息显示，该储能项目建设主体为天合储能（滁州）有限公司，选址落于安徽省滁州市滁州经济技术开发区。本项目租赁厂房面积约10万平方米，规划购置PACK产线、集成舱产线及电芯研发配套设备。
此前，在9月17日发布的环评公示中显示，天合储能（滁州）拟投资35亿元，建设本次公示项目。项目建成后，将形成年产100GWh的储能系统集成舱的生产能力。
图：批前公示信息
图源：滁州市生态环境局
此外项目还将设置研发中心，开展高储能密度、长寿命、高安全性等锂离子电池技术及产业化研发。
项目预计工期为12个月。按照环评审批流程，批前公示期间，公众可向滁州市生态环境局提交书面反馈意见。公示若无重大异议，项目后续将取得正式环评批复文件。

title: 拟募资最高6.39亿港元，远信储能启动港股招股
content:
集邦光储观察获悉，10月30日，深圳市远信储能技术股份有限公司正式启动全球招股，计划于11月9日在香港联合交易所主板挂牌上市。
根据招股书，本次全球发售H股共计5754.05万股，其中香港公开发售575.45万股，国际发售5178.60万股。发售价区间为每股8.54港元至11.10港元，按最高发售价计算，预计募集资金总额约6.39亿港元（未扣除相关发行费用）。
本次招股于10月30日上午9时开始，至11月4日中午12时结束，预计于11月5日确定最终发售价，并于11月6日公布配发结果，11月9日正式开始买卖。
根据招股书，本次募集资金将主要以下方面：
其中，约45%将用于硬件及软件产品研发，包括采购相关产品、招聘研发及运营人员；
约25%将用于拓展海外业务，包括建立海外本地化团队、拓展业务合作及探索海外生产机会；
约20%将用于浙江乌镇新工厂建设、设备采购及实验室相关费用；
剩余约10%将用于营运资金及其他一般企业用途。

title: 晶科、楚能等5企披露最新储能订单动态
content:
集邦光储观察获悉，近期，晶科储能、楚能新能源、因湃电池、远东股份及巡鹰储能相继披露储能业务新进展。
楚能新能源签澳洲储能订单
10月28日，楚能新能源携全场景储能系统解决方案亮相澳大利亚能源展，现场与Leistung Energie Group签署战略合作协议。根据协议，双方将围绕M5 APEX及M6电池预制舱展开深度合作。
目前，588Ah大容量电池及M6电池预制舱已具备200GWh产能规模，全面开启规模化量产交付，为澳洲客户的大规模集采提供坚实保障。
晶科储能德国新签20MWh储能订单
近日，晶科储能在德国新签20MWh独立储能项目群，由三个市场化储能项目组成，容量分别为5MWh、5MWh和10MWh，将参与德国电力市场运营，为当地电力系统提供灵活调节能力。
据悉，三个项目均采用晶科储能蓝鲸5.01MWh液冷储能系统，面向电力市场化交易场景。
因湃电池中标800MWh储能项目
11月2日，因湃电池宣布成功中标博州博乐市200MW/800MWh储能项目储能系统设备采购。
本项目位于博尔塔拉蒙古自治州博乐市，总规模200MW/800MWh，采用100MW/400MWh构网型+100MW/400MWh跟网型组合方案。项目由中能启源（江苏）能源投资、新疆雄匠储能联合开发，总投资约8.56亿元，计划工期180天。
根据此前公布的中标候选人信息，因湃电池总投标报价为66545.44万元，折合0.832元/Wh。
巡鹰储能50MWh移动式储能系统交付
近日，巡鹰储能首批移动式集装箱储能系统正式发运交付，总容量达50MWh，标志着公司进一步拓展移动储能应用市场。
据悉，本次交付的产品采用标准化20尺集装箱设计，针对极寒、极热、高风沙、高湿度等复杂环境进行适应性设计，并配备多层级安全防护体系，以满足长途运输及不同场景下的部署需求。
应用场景方面，移动式储能可根据用能需求灵活转移，主要覆盖电网调峰、应急保电、离网供电，以及船舶港口、矿山油田等场景，与固定式储能形成互补。
远东股份10月新签1000万储能订单
11月2日，远东股份发布公告称，2026年10月，公司收到子公司中标/签约千万元以上合同订单合计为人民币14.98亿元，同比增长41.04%，环比增长6.06%。2026年1月至10月，公司收到子公司中标/签约千万元以上合同订单合计为194.46亿元。
其中，智能电池储能业务方面，公司10月中标/签约千万元以上合同订单为1000万元，1—10月公司中标/签约千万元以上合同订单为29.2亿元。

title: 通威股份拟收购丽豪清能，发行价调整至9.12元/股
content:
集邦光储观察获悉，11月2日，通威股份披露发行股份及支付现金购买资产并募集配套资金预案（修订稿），拟收购青海丽豪清能股份有限公司100%股权。
与此前预案相比，本次修订主要调整了发行股份购买资产的定价基准日及发行价格，发行价格由原来的15.20元/股调整为9.12元/股。根据修订稿，标的公司100%股权预估交易总对价不超过48亿元。
发行价格调整至9.12元/股
根据修订稿，本次交易拟通过发行股份及支付现金的方式，购买段雍、海南卓悦、海南豪悦等57名股东持有的丽豪清能100%股权，同时向不超过35名符合条件的特定投资者发行股份募集配套资金。
本次发行股份购买资产的定价基准日调整为通威股份第九届董事会第十四次会议决议公告日。定价基准日前20个、60个及120个交易日，公司股票交易均价分别为11.39元/股、12.06元/股和12.82元/股，对应80%分别为9.11元/股、9.65元/股和10.26元/股。经交易各方协商，本次发行价格确定为9.12元/股，较此前降幅约40%。
对于此次调整，通威股份表示，自原预案披露以来，光伏行业市场环境等影响本次交易的因素发生明显变化，且交易各方仍在协商交易具体方案，因此重新召开董事会确定本次交易的定价基准日及发行价格。
预估交易总对价不超过48亿元
交易标的方面，丽豪清能主营业务为高纯晶硅的研发、生产和销售。本次交易完成后，通威股份将持有丽豪清能100%股权。
修订稿披露，经交易各方初步协商，丽豪清能100%股权预估交易总对价不超过48亿元。不过，截至预案签署日，标的公司的审计、评估工作尚未完成，最终交易价格仍将以符合规定的资产评估机构出具的评估报告为基础，由交易各方协商确定。
财务数据方面，截至2026年9月30日，丽豪清能总资产为100.31亿元，总负债为55.44亿元，所有者权益为44.87亿元。
2026年前三季度，公司实现营业收入16.22亿元，营业利润亏损8.14亿元，净利润亏损6.76亿元。2025年，公司实现营业收入26.51亿元，净利润亏损3.79亿元；2024年实现营业收入39.59亿元，净利润亏损7.38亿元。上述财务数据均未经审计。
通威股份表示，本次交易旨在进一步完善公司产业布局，具体交易方案仍在协商中。后续交易尚需完成标的资产审计、评估工作，并经公司董事会、股东会审议，上交所审核及中国证监会注册等程序，能否最终实施及实施时间仍存在不确定性。
