title: How “reverse game theory” could keep AI agents in check
content:
How “reverse game theory” could keep AI agents in check
Borrowing from disciplines like economics could help AI safety researchers control AI models, even if they don’t understand them.
A new approach known as “reverse game theory” aims to control powerful AI models by designing systems that incentivize them to stick to the rules.
As AI models become more capable, safety researchers are scrambling to ensure they are “aligned” with human desires—to make sure, in other words, that rogue agents don’t break the law, hack into unauthorized servers, or release poison gas into major cities and kill us all.
Until now, this work has mostly focused on trying to peer into an AI’s “brain” to understand what it is “thinking,” or training models to hew to values that we hold dear. Claude, for instance, has its constitution—a sort of moral code.
The trouble is, these techniques don’t seem to work particularly well: Models have been shown to deliberately underperform on tests, hide their intentions, and mislead their evaluators.
Now some alignment researchers believe that reverse game theory, also known as mechanism design, might get better results. Where game theory tries to predict how rational actors will behave when given a particular set of rules, reverse game theory attempts to design rules that will elicit the kinds of behavior we want to encourage.
An example of mechanism design in the real world might be the classic strategy for splitting a piece of cake in two: One person cuts the cake and the other gets the first choice of pieces. This incentivizes the cutter to make the pieces as even as possible. Other examples include surge pricing in ride-hailing apps, which encourages drivers to be available at busy times, and second-price auctions, where the winning bidder pays the price of the second-highest bid instead of the highest. Platforms use these auctions to sell online advertising because they encourage buyers to bid close to the maximum they are willing to pay.
In AI, mechanism design starts from the premise that we may never be able to understand enough about the internal workings of frontier models to make sure they are aligned. This means we should design mechanisms that incentivize agents to behave in ways that we want, regardless of what’s actually going on under the hood.
A recent preprint paper by Stephen Morris, an economist at MIT, along with colleagues from Yale and Columbia suggested some potential mechanisms that could stop agents from “sandbagging” tests (pretending to be worse than they actually are—for example, to avoid triggering safety mechanisms).
Instead of being rewarded only for how well it does on a test, a model could be rewarded for how well its answers predict what a second model will say. Deliberately playing dumb becomes a losing bet. “AI agents have a very good understanding of what other AI agents can achieve,” Morris says. “So it does seem like a context where this cross-checking could work more practically.
The paper also suggests pitting agents against each other, creating a competitive dynamic that incentivizes them to perform their best, or pairing agents that are known to be biased in opposite directions and rewarding them depending on how closely their outputs match, thus incentivizing them to reach an optimal answer.
A second approach, as envisioned by Elad Hazan, a professor of computer science at Princeton, is to design mechanisms that take inspiration from the ways human society keeps people “aligned”: social norms, the justice system, the monetary incentives of free-market capitalism. “We want to align superintelligent AI,” he says. “Why don’t we first talk about humans? How do we align humans?”
Hazan’s suggested mechanism involves having AI models take turns as either “solvers” that tackle problems or “auditors” that check the others’ work. “One agent acts like law enforcement; the other agent acts like the citizen,” he says.
During training, the models are rewarded depending on outcomes: Solvers that get caught cheating are punished, but so are auditors that fail to catch the cheaters. In situations where there’s a disagreement between auditors and solvers, the case can be sent to “trial”—perhaps a human expert will decide who is right.
There is, Hazan admits, a risk that agents will collude with each other—as auditors have colluded with the businesses they’re meant to be auditing, or corrupt police officers have colluded with criminals. But that problem can be solved by rewarding the auditors well enough, so that being caught isn’t worth the risk (a lot easier in the world of AI training than the real one, where money for police salaries is tight), and by auditing the auditors using techniques akin to employing mystery shoppers.
Hazan points to Nobel Prize–winning work by the economist Gary Becker, who introduced the idea of the “rational offender” in the 1960s. Criminals don’t break the law because they’re inherently bad people, he said. Instead, they do it when it’s the most rational choice given the incentives on offer. Crime makes sense only when the proceeds outweigh the potential punishment.
Alignment shouldn’t be thought of as a property of a model, he argues, but as a descriptor of its behavior at a particular moment. “You are, like, a nice person,” he says. “Are you aligned? I don’t know. Probably you are aligned most of the time, but there could be a situation where you’re not.”
One potential issue with applying mechanism design to AI: It relies on the assumption that AI agents behave rationally. Mechanism design has a mixed record with humans, who often fail to behave the way economic models say they should.
It’s ironic: Economists have spent decades trying to reduce human behavior to mathematics, and now, in large language models, we’ve built mathematical systems that run on human language and could be just as inscrutable. AI models exhibit behaviors that seem more human than machine, and they can be swayed by subtle factors that are difficult to understand and explain. “Is it even reasonable to assume that they will respond to incentives?” asks Helen Qu, a research fellow at the Flatiron Institute, a nonprofit dedicated to advancing scientific discovery through computational methods, who has written about mechanism design and AI safety.
“Obviously, AIs are not rational,” Morris says. “They’re just algorithms at work.” However, as economists have found with humans, treating them as if they’re rational could still be useful if it helps to predict and control their behavior.
Qu sees mechanism design as just one layer in a “defense in depth” strategy for keeping AI models aligned—alongside interpretability, regulation, and training, not instead of them. But there are a lot of questions to be answered before the approach can be implemented in actual frontier models. It’s unclear, for instance, how these theories will apply to real models, or whether mechanisms designed for one task will carry over to another in practice. Models could find loopholes that no one anticipated. (Anthropic and OpenAI did not respond to requests for comment on whether they are working on this.)
Whatever these mechanisms look like, they will ultimately have to slot into the biggest mechanism of all: the free market. “We play by the rules of economics,” says Hazan. A more aligned model may be good for the world, but if it’s slower or more expensive than a less aligned one, does our current system of rules and regulations actually incentivize any of the frontier labs to release it?
“It’s a mechanism that’s responsible for a lot of prosperity for humankind,” he says of the market, “but it could be ultimately responsible for something very terrible.” Perhaps the entities really in need of a better mechanism design are the labs themselves.

Here’s how reverse game theory could help make AI agents behave.

title: Exploring DP World’s Circular Seabed Sunglasses
content:
Exploring DP World’s Circular Seabed Sunglasses
Prioritise Us
on Google
DP World is helping fishing nets gain a new life through its circular sunglasses project. Credit: DP World
DP World is unlocking business opportunities with a new circular initiative, explains Jimena Rodriguez, Oceans and Biodiversity Senior Manager at DP World
Around the world, thousands of fishing nets have been abandoned, lost or discarded in the ocean.
Made of synthetic materials, the fishing gear of recent operations take hundreds of years to degrade, polluting the oceans and putting marine life at risk.
To help clear up the ocean and drive circularity,
DP World is undertaking a collaborative project
to turn ghost nets into sunglasses.
A call for sustainable solutions
Ghost nets are pieces of fishing equipment that have been left or lost in the sea, with much of it coming from large commercial fishing operations. These nets, once adrift, continue to catch marine life, impacting fish, dolphins, whales, turtles and sharks.
As they trap a range of creatures, they have a major impact on biodiversity and marine food chain stability – and coral structures can become damaged by the nets. When the materials degrade, the ghost nets fragment into microplastics, which are ingested by animals, leading to malnutrition and death. When ingested by fish, these microplastics enter the human food chain.
pollution in the seas
and the disruption to the oceanic ecosystem is having a major impact on the environment, adding to the instability of supply chains. Global warming, made worse by pollution, is impacting global supply chains – resulting in adverse weather patterns and poor crop yields. This knock-on effect has a major impact – though ocean acidification and other forms of pollution,
food supply chains are weakened
through the disrupted quality, quantity and safety of seafood.
“Sustainability is not something a business “finishes”. We move forward one practical solution at a time,” says Jimena Rodriguez, Oceans and Biodiversity Senior Manager at DP World on LinkedIn.
Oceans and Biodiversity Senior Manager at DP World
“Working alongside colleagues across DP World, I see this journey as one of constantly connecting knowledge, local context and business thinking to find better ways forward.
“That is why I love the simplicity of this initiative. It brings science, business and circularity together to create value while reducing pressure on nature.”
Key facts
Ghost nets can take up to 200 years to degrade
More than 1,000 m² of nets will be removed from the seabed
The project will collect approximately 800kg of materials
Some of the material has been collected from 50 metres deep
Each pair of sunglasses will have coordinates from where the material was found
Collaboration for recovery
Moreover, the lost nets act as a lost economic benefit for fisheries – once lost, fisheries need to purchase new fishing equipment, rather than being able to re-use the gear and gain full ROI on it.
DP World is working in collaboration with Deniz Yaşamını Koruma Derneği (Türkiye’s Marine Life Conservation Society) in order to clean up the Sea of Marmara. Together, these organisations are removing the nets from the ocean in order to give the material a second life.
The aim is to remove more than 1,000m² of nets from the area around the Princes’ Islands. This totals approximately 800 kg of material.
“Protecting our seas requires collaboration, and the private sector has an important role to play,” Volkan Narcı, Chairman of Deniz Yaşamını Koruma Derneği says.
Volkan Narcı, Chairman of Deniz Yaşamını Koruma Derneği
“The partnership with DP World allows us to create a greater and more lasting impact on the health of the Sea of Marmara.”
Through reports, technology, sea charts and local knowledge, the Deniz Yaşamını Koruma Derneği team finds the abandoned nets. They then carefully remove them from the seabed – attempting to limit the further damage – before recording the weight, size and location of each net.
In making these records, the companies can gain further information of where lost equipment has been accumulated, helping them track movements and potential damage to the ecosystem.
Much of the work takes place around the Princes’ Islands and the deeper waters around Istanbul – many have been recovered from more than 50 metres below the surface.
“A great example of how environmental responsibility, collaboration and innovation can come together to create meaningful impact,” states Alişan Koyuncu, Corporate Communications Specialist at DP World on LinkedIn.
Alişan Koyuncu, Corporate Communications Specialist at DP World
“It’s inspiring to see materials that once threatened marine life transformed into something valuable.”
Circularity and the economy
Once the material is recovered, the process of giving them a second life begins. The nets are processed into recycled plastic granules and turned into custom-designed sunglasses. This means the material gains a new life with a longer lifespan.
The coordinates and the depth of where the original net was found are stamped inside the frames. By creating a direct link to the waters, it offers these glasses an exclusivity and a reminder of the ecological benefits of the sunglasses.
“Ghost nets are a threat to marine life long after they have been lost. This project gets them out of the water and puts the material to a completely different use,” explains Nicholas Mazzei, Vice President of Sustainability, Europe at DP World.
Nicholas Mazzei, Vice President Sustainability at DP World
“Turning a net recovered from the seabed into a pair of sunglasses makes the idea of reuse very real. And stamping the location inside each pair creates a connection to where it came from.”
DP World is also working with SUSAKO, the Sustainable Art Women’s Cooperative (Sürdürülebilir Sanat Kadın Kooperatifi). This partnership works to support the economy on a more local level, running workshops where members of the public can turn the plastic into jewelry. This acts as an example of how material can be repurposed – educating the communities on
circularity and waste reduction
– and aims to support women’s participation in the economy.
Through the project, there will also be work with local fishing communities in order to raise awareness of ghost nets, helping to prevent the gear from being lost or abandoned in the first place.
DP World is focusing on its Source to Sea approach, aiming to restore water ecosystems, enhance natural carbon sinks and support biodiversity. In conducting these projects, it is driving circularity and supporting local economies while working to reduce the environmental impact of marine operations.
This is helping to restore balance to ocean quality, which helps stabilise food supply chains. Moreover, the demonstration of how these ghost nets can be used for circular purposes helps local communities think about the
circular economy and the opportunity
to create more projects with other waste products.
I see this journey as one of constantly connecting knowledge, local context and business thinking to find better ways forward.
Jimena Rodriguez, Oceans and Biodiversity Senior Manager at DP World
Approximately 800kg of ghost net will be recycled. Credit: DP World
Key partners
DP World
DP World is a leading global supply chain and logistics company headquartered in Dubai, United Arab Emirates. Operating across six continents with locations in over 78 countries, it specializes in cargo logistics, port operations, and maritime services. Founded in 2005, DP World handles approximately 10% of global container traffic, employing over 103,000 people and facilitating international trade through innovative infrastructure.
Sürdürülebilir Sanat Kadın Kooperatifi (Sustainable Art Women's Cooperative) is a Turkish women-led initiative promoting economic empowerment through sustainable artistic practices. The cooperative supports female artisans by preserving traditional crafts while incorporating eco-friendly methods and materials. Members create handmade products, generating income and fostering entrepreneurship. The organization emphasizes women's independence, cultural heritage preservation, and environmental responsibility through collaborative creative work and fair trade principles.
Deniz Yaşamını Koruma Derneği
Deniz Yaşamını Koruma Derneği (Marine Life Conservation Association) is a Turkish environmental NGO dedicated to protecting marine ecosystems and biodiversity. The organization conducts research, rehabilitation, and conservation projects focusing on threatened species, particularly sea turtles, Mediterranean monk seals, and cetaceans. Through beach monitoring, rescue operations, and education campaigns, the association works to mitigate threats from pollution, overfishing, and habitat destruction.

title: FarEye: Reducing the Cost of Carrier Fragmentation With AI
content:
FarEye: Reducing the Cost of Carrier Fragmentation With AI
Prioritise Us
on Google
Last-mile delivery costs are rising, but FarEye is looking at ways to optimise planning. Credit: Getty
As last-mile delivery continues to face ongoing challenges, Kushal Nahata, CEO and Co-founder of FarEye explains that visibility is key to success
FarEye has published findings from its Eye on the Last Mile EMEA 2026 research, exploring the challenges within the logistics sector.
In the past year, supply chains have faced significant volatility, but the rising costs of last-mile delivery have been a major focus of the report.
As a critical and complicated aspect of the journey, the last mile needs to be as accurate as possible – and FarEye is aiming to simplify spend.
Modern supply chain challenges
Logistics companies have been put under much pressure in recent years, faced with geopolitical instability, rising costs and heightened demand. Businesses are working out where to cut spend, while also meeting rising expectations for sustainable operations – such as alternative fuels and electrification.
Last-mile is already a complex challenge,
being what the customer sees. As a result, it is critical to ensure the last-mile operates without issue. Recent years, however, have increased consumer scrutiny, alongside more congestion to tackle, more instability from weather and rising costs of fuel.
According to FarEye’s report, last-mile delivery costs across EMEA rose by 9% over the last 12 months, and 96% of firms paid more money per delivery. Much of this has been attributed to the ‘fragmentation tax’, which consists of hidden costs from disconnected carriers, data and systems.
The report found that 51% of fully outsourced firms cited unreliable carrier information as their biggest challenge, whereas 22% cited cost.
"Businesses may outsource execution, but they cannot outsource accountability for cost and customer experience," explains Kushal Nahata, CEO and Co-founder of FarEye.
Kushal Nahata CEO & Co-Founder of FarEye
"The last mile is still waiting for its container moment."
To ensure businesses operate cost-effectively, Kushal states leaders must know the location of each delivery, carrier allocation and cost at all times, with full visibility into operations. Exceptions and failed attempts need to be tracked, and there needs to be options for delivery – some customers prioritise reliability, whereas others prioritise speed.
Kushal also recommends leaders integrate AI on trusted data, with standardised milestones, exception definitions and more, all while maintaining human oversight.
At a glance
Last-mile delivery costs across EMEA rose by 9% in the last year
51% of fully outsourced firms state unreliable carrier information is the largest challenge they face
41% of total supply chain cost is in the last mile
Own-fleet operators are 2.3x as likely to see costs outrun revenue
69% of leaders are building with AI
Cost concerns
In a year which has been incredibly volatile, balancing cost and customer experience is a difficult task but a crucial skill to have. Shipping through the Strait of Hormuz was disrupted due to the conflict in Iran, meaning that insurance premiums have been heightened, fuel prices have increased and time taken to deliver products has gotten longer.
According to the study, 41% of total supply chain cost sits within the last mile, making it even more exposed to disruption. Balancing the cost and customer experience requires technology, people, carrier relationships, agile operations and capital.
Leaders need to have full visibility into the costs and demands of each necessity, but this is another challenge on its own. The report found that fuel and insurance both rose in the last year, meaning that nearly everyone is paying more to deliver their products, though there is a disparity within this.
Out of respondents, 76% report costs growing at least as fast as revenue. Though the typical rise was 9%, one in four respondents saw rises of 15% or more. Own-fleet operators are likely to see costs outpace revenue, meaning it becomes more cost-effective to outsource – but reliability and trust is lacking.
Businesses who outsource more find issues in failed deliveries, unreliable information, lack of customisation and poor customer experience. If the final mile is being poorly managed, the company risks its reputation.
FarEye is using AI agents to simplify logistics (Credit: FarEye)
AI integration
To help manage changing demand better, more teams are turning to AI. Within the study, 69% of teams are already building with AI, though as few as 18% are running it at scale. This is limited by expertise and trust, poor data quality and unclear ROI.
However, integrating AI successfully can help leaders grow capabilities in demand forecasting, customer support,
delivery time prediction and route optimisation
FarEye, therefore, aims to simplify last-mile logistics, using real-time insights to create meaningful action points and create improved value for customers and companies.
Its AI-driven orchestration platform unified planning, routing and real-time execution in order to make delivery faster, smarter and more sustainable. FarEye helps businesses forecast capacity up to 12 months in advance, predicting cost per delivery with accuracy and running what-if simulations at scale. This helps organisations plan their yearly budget and be able to roll out contingency plans if something goes wrong.
The platform completely reimagines the last-mile with AI, tailoring workflows to suit each need and scaling solutions with agility. As logistics becomes more unpredictable, FarEye offers some clarity to leaders, making use of AI tools in an
end-to-end network
in order to keep operations moving and customers satisfied.
The last mile is still waiting for its container moment.
Kushal Nahata, CEO and Co-founder of FarEye

title: Loadsmart Adds AI Agents for Enterprise Shippers
content:
Loadsmart Adds AI Agents for Enterprise Shippers
Prioritise Us
on Google
Marine services provider SSA Marine implemented Opendock at its Port Arthur, Texas and Gulfport, Mississippi locations in 2021, before expanding its use to three further locations. Credit: SSA Marine
Loadsmart CEO Felipe Capella launches new logistics AI agents to automate dock and yard management for global enterprise shippers.
Enterprise shippers are under constant pressure to streamline complex freight lifecycles and reduce manual data entry across their supply chain networks. Addressing this operational bottleneck, logistics platform Loadsmart has expanded its digital ecosystem by adding five new AI agents to its enterprise suite. The new agents cover: detention handling, purchase order follow-up, warehouse customer service, dock door management and yard task orchestration.
The newly added AI agents expand the number of AI agents supported by Loadsmart to eleven. The platform launched AI agents in September to handle scheduling, tracking and status updates, document collection, tender failures, load audits and claims. The expanded platform now automates repetitive tasks spanning from initial purchase orders all the way through to final dock door scheduling.
The evolution of freight technology is rapidly mirroring the expanding use of AI in the autonomous vehicle sector. While most enterprise shippers currently operate at automation levels one or two - in other words, relying on software to simply flag issues for human intervention - the integration of agentic AI is pushing the envelope of industry applications. By 2030, industry leaders expect supply chains to reach levels three and four, where AI agents execute autonomous decisions within strictly defined shipper rules.
The most valuable commodity in global logistics is time, not data or fuel. Our autonomous technology is designed to buy back that operational time, empowering entire freight teams to step away from manual systems and focus on strategic execution
Felipe Capella, Chief Executive Officer of Loadsmart
Felipe Capella, CEO of Loadsmart
Automating the Freight Lifecycle
To manage this digital transition, Loadsmart’s newly expanded AI agents work directly on top of the Transportation Management Systems (TMS), Warehouse Management Systems (WMS), and Yard Management Systems (YMS) that shippers already utilise. Functioning through everyday communication channels like email, phone, and chat, these autonomous agents successfully complete 70 to 90 percent of logistics tasks on their own.
For the remaining exceptions, human freight experts intervene to guarantee 100% task resolution, ensuring supply chain continuity without disruptions. During a recent live demonstration at the Sightline 2027 event in Chicago, the platform successfully processed a single load from order to settlement, with an AI agent autonomously making a phone call to reschedule a delayed dock appointment.
Ralph Moyle uses Loadsmart's Opendock tool to coordinate up to 500 appointments per week. Credit: Ralph Moyle
Extending AI into the Dock, Yard, and Warehouse
The five newest AI agents are specifically designed to eliminate the manual emails and phone calls that historically plague warehouse and yard operations. The targeted logistics workflows include:
Detention Handling:
Autonomously warns the warehouse dock before a truck exceeds its free time, accurately reports detention fees owed, and automatically approves carrier requests that match gate records.
Purchase Order Follow-up:
Scans the system for purchase orders lacking a dock appointment and proactively contacts the supplier or carrier to book, ship, or reschedule the freight.
Warehouse Customer Service:
Directly manages incoming warehouse emails and phone calls regarding truck arrivals, receipt confirmations, and updated Estimated Times of Arrival (ETAs).
Dock Door Management:
Optimises the physical flow of inbound and outbound trucks, autonomously handling late arrivals, carrier no-shows, and unexpected dock door closures.
Yard Task Orchestration:
Intelligently generates and assigns yard moves, temperature checks, and safety inspections in the correct order triggered by specific supply chain events.
Aaron Thomas, Director of Engineering, Dock and Yard at Loadsmart, and Nate Allan, VP of Enterprise and Partnerships at Loadsmart discuss applications of AI in Dock, Gate and Yard management. Credit: Loadsmart
Key Logistics and Technology Tools
Loadsmart
: Operating as a premier connected logistics platform, Loadsmart spans the entire global freight lifecycle. By combining advanced artificial intelligence with experienced human operators, the company provides enterprise shippers with customised automation tools. Their agent-led execution model transforms how logistics professionals interact with core systems, ensuring 100% resolution across highly complex supply chain networks.
Opendock
: Functioning as a critical component of the broader logistics software ecosystem, Opendock provides specialised dock, yard, and gate scheduling solutions. By integrating directly with enterprise AI agents, the platform allows warehouses to seamlessly automate inbound and outbound freight appointments, drastically reducing truck detention times and optimising physical facility throughput for enterprise shippers.
ShipperGuide
: Serving as a robust transportation management system (TMS), ShipperGuide centralises freight procurement, routing, and carrier tracking. When paired with autonomous AI agents, the platform eliminates repetitive manual data entry. It enables supply chain operators to transition from merely clicking through software workflows to actively managing intelligent agents that execute strategic logistics rules.

title: EDENenergy builds storage systems from used e-scooter batteries - electrive.com
content:
Freiburg-based startup EDENenergy is developing stationary commercial energy storage systems from used e-scooter and e-bike batteries. The first storage system with 70 kWh capacity has already been delivered. In the future, different battery types could also be integrated.
The first tested used batteries still showed more than 90 percent of their original capacity.
Image: EDENenergy
EDENenergy, a start-up spun off from the Fraunhofer Institute for Solar Energy Systems ISE, aims to give used batteries from micromobility a second life. To achieve this, the Freiburg-based company is developing modular energy storage systems for commercial and industrial customers. In mid-October, the first storage system, with a capacity of 70 kWh, was delivered to a customer.
The system integrates 112 used e-scooter batteries connected in series. Before deployment, the batteries are tested for their technical condition. According to the company, the initial results exceeded expectations: among around 350 batteries examined, the remaining capacity was partially well above 90 per cent. Originally, EDENenergy had calculated with a State of Health of 80 per cent.
The technical foundation is power electronics developed at Fraunhofer ISE. This technology enables the combination of batteries with different form factors and varying battery management systems into a single stationary storage system, without the need to disassemble individual batteries. However, EDENenergy currently relies primarily on larger suppliers, such as e-scooter and e-bike fleet operators, to obtain sufficient batteries of the same type.
EDENenergy plans storage systems with up to 300 kWh
One advantage of the modular concept is the replaceability of the batteries. EDENenergy monitors the individual modules remotely and can replace them during operation if necessary. This approach is intended to maintain the storage capacity at a constant level over the long term. The company expects to still provide the original 70 kWh even after ten years. Batteries that are no longer usable are subsequently sent for recycling.
Initially, the offering targets small and medium-sized enterprises with their own photovoltaic systems that wish to increase self-consumption or reduce peak loads. EDENenergy also sees potential applications for municipal utilities and electricity trading. In the long term, the start-up aims to expand its storage systems to capacities of up to 300 kWh.
A challenge remains the diversity of available batteries. For each new battery type, connectors, battery management, and communication protocols must be adapted. In the long run, EDENenergy therefore considers uniform communication standards and clear legal frameworks essential for the stationary reuse of mobile batteries.
Other companies are also working on repurposing used batteries from micromobility. For example, in 2025, e-scooter rental provider Lime and US battery recycler Redwood Materials
agreed to cooperate on battery recycling in Germany, the Netherlands, and the USA
. While this initiative aims to recover valuable raw materials for new batteries, EDENenergy initially focuses on reusing functional batteries in stationary storage systems before they are sent for recycling.
For further development, the company is seeking additional pilot customers from the regional commercial sector. Through the Baden-Württemberg funding programme “Mittelstand trifft Start-ups”, corresponding projects can reportedly receive 50 per cent funding. EDENenergy also receives support from the Sustainability Performance Centre and the BW Pre-Seed programme. The first investor is JobRad founder Ulrich Prediger.

title: Rio Tinto expands lithium production in Argentina - electrive.com
content:
Mining giant Rio Tinto has commissioned two additional lithium projects in Argentina. The 'Fénix-1B' expansion and the 'Sal-de-Vida' plant in Catamarca province are now ramping up. At full capacity, they are expected to achieve a combined annual production capacity of 25,000 tons of lithium carbonate equivalent.
Image: Rio Tinto
Rio Tinto has announced the official opening of expansion project ‘Fénix 1B’ and the ‘Sal de Vida’ lithium operation in the province of Catamarca. According to the British-Australian mining giant, it has invested a total of around US$1.4 billion (approx. €1.25 billion euros) in the two projects. Production at both sites reportedly began ahead of schedule in the second quarter of 2026, as stated in an accompanying release. The projects are intended to strengthen “Rio Tinto’s standing and Argentina’s position as a leading supplier of lithium for global markets.”
Background: ‘Fénix’ is considered Argentina’s first commercial lithium operation and began production in 1997. The ‘Fénix 1B’ expansion is said to have increased the annual capacity of the existing facility by 10,000 tonnes of lithium carbonate equivalent (LCE), bringing the total on-site capacity to around 40,000 tonnes. ‘Sal de Vida’, on the other hand, is a completely new lithium carbonate operation located approx. 20 km northeast of ‘Fénix’, with a targeted annual capacity of 15,000 tonnes. Both sites are located in Catamarca, a province in northwest Argentina. Rio Tinto also operates or plans additional lithium projects in the Argentine provinces of Jujuy and Salta, including the flagship lithium project ‘Rincón’, which is expected to have a long-term capacity of 60,000 tonnes per year. Commercial operations there are set to begin in 2028.
Commenting on the launch of the two operations in Catamarca, Simon Trott, CEO of Rio Tinto, said: “Today is a proud moment for Rio Tinto and an important milestone for Argentina’s lithium industry, as we grow our position as a leading global supplier. […] These two projects build on nearly three decades of lithium production in Catamarca and the expertise of our Argentine workforce. They demonstrate our industry-leading project delivery capability, as we execute with discipline towards our global target of 200,000 tonnes lithium carbonate equivalent annual production capacity by 2028.”
Rio Tinto has also long had an interest in developing a lithium project in Europe – namely, in Serbia.
However, the company pulled away from the so-called Jadar project at the end of last year
and stated that it would prioritise other ‘short-term opportunities’. The pause on the project in Serbia, which was still in the permitting phase, was one of several measures taken by Simon Trott, who was appointed CEO of Rio Tinto in August 2025, to rationalise operations and reduce costs. One of his first decisions was also to reorganise Rio Tinto into three business units: iron ore, aluminium combined with lithium, and copper.
In general, Rio Tinto has made significant investments recently, including earlier this year
in the Canadian company Nemaska Lithium
. Rio Tinto also incurred substantial costs in 2024 for the
acquisition of lithium producer Arcadium
in a US$6.7 billion deal. This was also because the mining company announced plans to massively invest in its first proprietary lithium mining site in Argentina to expand its battery materials offering.
In recent years, Rio Tinto has pursued the goal of establishing lithium not only as a fourth pillar alongside iron ore, aluminium, and copper mining but also of becoming one of the world’s largest lithium producers. The geographical focus is on Argentina. However, it remains unclear to what extent Rio Tinto will continue to invest so heavily in its lithium business during times of increasing rationalisation.

title: AGIBOT puts six humanoid robots in 24-hour convenience store challenge
content: Chinese robotics company AGIBOT launched a 24-hour convenience-store challenge featuring six G2 humanoid robots working alongside human customers. The livestream, titled “Robots Never Clock Out,” ran from November 2 to November 3, giving viewers an extended look at the robots performing everyday retail tasks. Their assigned duties included stocking shelves, preparing coffee and hot food, greeting customers, and clearing rubbish. According to the firm, the challenge was designed to test the robots across different store conditions, including rush-hour crowds, overnight operations, and the morning breakfast rush.Humanoids tackle retailAGIBOT deployed six G2 humanoid robots in a convenience store for a 24-hour challenge designed to demonstrate their ability to perform everyday retail tasks. The event gave viewers an extended look at the robots operating in a real-world retail environment alongside human customers and store staff.The robots are expected to handle several tasks, including stocking and organizing shelves, preparing coffee and hot food, greeting customers, and clearing rubbish. AGIBOT has divided the challenge into four operating periods: the lunch rush, evening rush, late-night duty, and breakfast preparation.Robots Never Clock Out | AGIBOT G2’s 24-Hour Convenience Store Challenge Six AGIBOT G2 take on a 24-hour shift as convenience store trainees. From rush-hour crowds to late-night solo duty and the morning breakfast sprint, can they keep up with nonstop customers and…— AGIBOT (@AGIBOTofficial) November 2, 2026The schedule was intended to expose the machines to different working conditions, from periods of heavy customer activity to overnight operations and the morning breakfast rush.The convenience-store setting brought together several technical requirements. The G2 robots navigated spaces shared with people, interacted with merchandise, reach and manipulated objects, and responded to customer requests while other activities continued around them.These tasks require more than basic movement. Stocking shelves involves locating merchandise, reaching for individual items, and placing them in the appropriate positions. Preparing coffee and hot food requires the robots to interact with equipment and objects in a controlled manner, while customer-facing duties involve responding to requests and operating around people.The different operating periods also introduce variations in the environment. During rush hours, robots must work around increased customer activity and potentially obstructed routes. Overnight operations provide a different set of conditions, while breakfast preparation introduces another sequence of tasks.AGIBOT tests autonomyThe 24-hour livestream offered a longer observation window than a short demonstration, allowing viewers to see not only successful task completion but also potential pauses, repeated attempts, and recovery from difficulties.For example, an item may be hard to grasp, a customer may block a robot’s route, or an unexpected request may interrupt an ongoing task. How the machines respond to these situations could better indicate their practical capabilities than isolated demonstrations of individual movements.The challenge followed AGIBOT’s AI Day announcements, which included new AI models, the G2 Max robot, and a proposed Worken measure of productive robot work. The company presents the convenience-store event as a practical demonstration of its technologies working together in an everyday environment. However, the announced 24-hour duration refers to the livestream and does not establish that each robot operates continuously without charging, maintenance, or human assistance.The promotional material reviewed also does not specify a complete intervention policy or a scoring system for measuring task success. Experts highlighted that these details will be important when evaluating the robots’ performance. The number of tasks completed, time required for individual activities, frequency of human intervention, and ability to recover from unsuccessful attempts would provide useful measures of their effectiveness.For now, the livestream offers an extended opportunity to observe six G2 robots performing a range of retail activities in a shared environment. It could provide a more detailed picture of how humanoid robots handle routine work beyond controlled demonstrations, although the event’s duration alone is not evidence of fully autonomous, uninterrupted operation.

title: China debuts world's first 800V DC power system for smart data centers
content: A Chinese green tech company has recently made history with the launch of the world’s first commercially deployed, fully integrated 800-volt direct current (DC) power system at a massive artificial intelligence (AI) data center.Shanghai’s Envision Energy announced the technology on Monday, November 2. It is currently powering live computer workloads at the company’s Galaxy AI data center campus in Ulanqab, Inner Mongolia, China.The platform combines solid-state transformers, battery energy storage, as well as smart controls to deliver electricity from the grid to computing equipment. As per company representatives, it could cut energy loses, lower infrastructure costs, and support more powerful AI servers within the same space. Kevin Huang, Envision Energy’s senior VP, pointed to the technology’s potential. “AI data centers need power systems that coordinate renewable energy, energy storage, and the grid to meet computing demand,” Huang explained. Powering AI serversAs AI data centers expand, they require more electricity to run. Reports show that global data center power demand could surge by 160 percent by 2030. Moreover, research suggests data centers alone could require as much as 68 gigawatts (GW) of capacity worldwide by 2027, roughly equivalent to California’s power grid. But delivering that power efficiently remains a massive challenge. Traditional data center power systems utilize multiple conversion stages to deliver electricity from the grid to servers. These stages require additional equipment, cables, and space.To address these challenge, Envision came up with a new system that can convert electricity directly from a 10-kilovolt (kV) medium-voltage input to an 800-volt DC power system. It reduces the need for extra equipment and copper cables, leaving more room for computer hardware.To maintain a stable electricity supply, the firm integrated solid-state transformers with battery energy storage. The batteries can also respond to sudden changes in power demand within seconds and provide backup power for several minutes. At the same time, Envision’s Dubhe Controller, coordinates both the transformers and the batteries through its Dubhe Energy Foundation Model. As a result, the system can respond to rapid changes in electricity demand within milliseconds.Targeting more powerEnvision’s Galaxy AI data center campus began operations in August 2026. It has a planned capacity of three gigawatts (GW). Once fully developed, the facility is expected to support up to one million AI accelerators operating simultaneously.Huang said the system uses renewable energy to power AI workloads. “This is a critical step in turning power-compute coordination from a strategic vision into an operational reality,” he concluded in a press release.In the future, the company aims to source more than 80 percent of the campus’s electricity through direct renewable energy connections. The power architecture could serve as a reference for other data centers as the industry moves toward 800-volt DC infrastructure. “Already operating commercially ahead of wider industry adoption, the system provides a reference for the industry’s transition to 800V DC,” the firm stated. It also aims to expand the technology via its Mission Gobi initiative. It targets five GW of green AI data center capacity across desert regions worldwide by 2030.

title: Hackers turn freezers into 122-degree ovens in six-country attack
content: Cyberattacks against supermarket refrigeration systems have disrupted grocery operations across Europe, with hackers remotely manipulating temperature controls and destroying perishable food. The incidents affected dozens of stores across several countries, exposing the risks associated with connecting industrial equipment to remotely accessible digital systems.Refrigerators and freezers reportedly reached temperatures exceeding 120 degrees Fahrenheit during Monday’s attacks. Affected retailers operate across Sweden, Belgium, Ireland, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and Estonia. The incidents also follow a similar wave of attacks against French supermarkets in October.Investigators have yet to identify those responsible. No hacking group has claimed responsibility for either wave of incidents.Major grocery chains affectedSeveral major European grocery retailers experienced disruptions across their store networks. Belgian and Luxembourg grocery groups Ahold Delhaize and Colruyt reported incidents involving their refrigeration infrastructure.Colruyt recorded five affected locations. Belgium also saw disruptions at 15 Carrefour stores, according to Reuters. In Ireland, hackers targeted 13 SuperValu supermarkets.Sweden’s grocery sector experienced similar problems. Seven Coop supermarkets reported refrigeration disruptions. Swedish retailer ICA also suffered an overnight incident affecting a limited number of locations.The attacks extended beyond conventional grocery retailers. Hackers affected at least one IKEA location in Belgium. The Swedish furniture retailer operates food departments across its stores, including restaurants and grocery sections. Refrigeration failures therefore threatened food inventory beyond traditional supermarket operations.An ICA supermarket in Stockholm experienced particularly severe damage. Its freezers reportedly reached 122 degrees Fahrenheit, destroying stored food products. Such temperatures can rapidly compromise frozen inventory and make affected products unsuitable for consumption.Connected refrigeration systemsSome refrigeration units affected during Monday’s incidents used temperature management technology developed by Danish manufacturer Danfoss. The same technology appeared in French supermarkets targeted during October’s cyberattacks.Modern commercial refrigeration systems increasingly depend on electronic controllers. These devices regulate cooling cycles and maintain temperatures across storage areas. Remote management capabilities also allow operators to monitor equipment and adjust settings without physically accessing individual units.However, network connectivity introduces additional cybersecurity risks. Attackers who compromise refrigeration controllers could potentially manipulate operating parameters remotely. Changing temperature settings can compromise entire storage facilities without requiring physical access to supermarket premises.Researchers at cybersecurity firm Claroty previously identified security weaknesses in Danfoss refrigeration controllers. Their August report documented vulnerabilities that could expose connected equipment to cyberattacks. Danfoss subsequently addressed the reported issues through a software update.The connection between the French and European incidents raises questions about whether attackers exploited similar weaknesses. However, investigators have not established whether both campaigns involved the same vulnerabilities or perpetrators.France faced earlier attacksOctober’s incidents affected hundreds of French grocery stores, including Carrefour, Monoprix, Intermarché and Cooperative U. Attackers similarly manipulated refrigeration equipment, causing widespread food spoilage across affected locations.The financial damage extended across multiple retail groups. Intermarché’s parent company, Les Mousquetaires, estimated losses worth several million euros following the incidents.The repeated attacks demonstrate how compromising industrial control equipment can disrupt essential commercial operations. Refrigeration systems play a critical role in preserving perishable inventory throughout supermarket supply chains.Their increasing dependence on connected controllers creates another potential entry point for cybercriminals. The incidents also illustrate how relatively small changes to industrial equipment settings can produce substantial physical and financial consequences.

title: Longi launches 690 W solar panels with 25.54% efficiency for rooftops
content: Chinese solar manufacturer Longi has introduced rooftop solar modules rated up to 690 W, using a conductive backsheet that replaces conventional soldered ribbons to boost output and reduce potential connection failures.Unveiled at All Energy Australia 2026 in Melbourne on October 28–29, the Hi-MO X12 series targets residential, commercial and industrial rooftops. The modules combine the company’s hybrid passivated back contact (HPBC) 2.0 cells with a redesigned electrical interconnection structure.Longi said the design removes more than 15,000 potential solder-joint failure points per module. Australian pricing, initial shipment volumes and a commercial delivery schedule have not been disclosed.Metal foil replaces soldered ribbonsThe new architecture embeds conductive metal foil circuits within the module’s rear encapsulation structure. Solar cells connect directly to this conductive backsheet, replacing the conventional soldered ribbons used to link cells.According to Longi, the design increases the current-carrying cross-sectional area by 85 percent, delivering an additional 6 W to 8 W compared with conventional interconnection designs.The modules also incorporate what the manufacturer calls Full-Screen Technology. This combines shingled cell layouts with hidden busbars to reduce inactive areas and shading on the front of the module.Longi attributes a further 8 W to 12 W gain to that arrangement, bringing the combined power increase to between 14 W and 20 W.The company also claimed its ultra-thin stacking process reduces internal stress by 60 percent, while an integrated metal foil barrier cuts water vapor transmission by 90 percent.Two formats for rooftop installationsThe larger LR7-72WVD module, intended for commercial and industrial applications, offers power ratings from 660 W to 690 W. Longi reported a maximum module efficiency exceeding 25.54 percent.The smaller LR7-54WVD series comes in four power classes between 495 W and 510 W. Its datasheet lists efficiencies ranging from 24.25 percent to 24.99 percent under standard test conditions.This 108-cell, dual-glass module measures 1,800 mm by 1,134 mm by 30 mm and weighs 51.8 pounds (23.5 kg). It uses a black anodized aluminum frame, with 2.0 mm front glass and 1.6 mm rear glass.The datasheet specified a temperature coefficient of -0.26 percent per degree Celsius, an operating range of -40°F to 185°F (-40°C to 85°C), and a maximum system voltage of 1,500 V.Warranty covers 30 years of performanceThe LR7-54WVD series carries a 25-year product warranty and a 30-year performance warranty.Longi guaranteed no more than 1 percent degradation in the first year, followed by annual degradation of 0.35 percent. That corresponds to approximately 88.9 percent of the module’s initial power output after 30 years.The datasheet lists front and rear static load ratings of 5,400 Pa and 2,400 Pa, respectively. It also specifies resistance to impacts from 25 mm hailstones traveling at 23 m/s.IEC 61215 and IEC 61730 are listed among the applicable certification standards, alongside certification marks from TÜV Rheinland and TÜV SÜD.At the Melbourne event, Longi also introduced its Hi-MO 9 Prime utility-scale module and displayed LongiBank 3.0 and OneMatrix energy storage solutions, together with its Longi Block modular photovoltaic system.

title: New process targets rare earths in discarded computer hard drives
content: Discarded computer hard drives could become a source of critical raw materials for electric vehicles, wind turbines and other technologies. Researchers in Germany are testing two processes to recover valuable metals from old magnets, including a method that uses ammonium chloride instead of conventional hydrochloric acid.The work is part of the European Union-funded NEO-CYCLE project, in which researchers at the Fraunhofer Institute for Ceramic Technologies and Systems (IKTS) are working with TU Bergakademie Freiberg to recover neodymium, iron and boron from discarded hard disk drives (HDDs).Neodymium-iron-boron magnets are among the strongest permanent magnets available. They are used in electric vehicle motors, wind turbines and electronic products such as speakers, smartphones and hard drives. However, recovering their constituent materials at the required purity for reuse is technically challenging.Neodymium is particularly important because around 90 percent of the material is imported from China, according to Fraunhofer. Much of Europe’s collected magnet waste is also sent to China for processing before the recovered materials are imported again.Recovering metals from old magnetsThe NEO-CYCLE researchers are evaluating two approaches to separate valuable materials from magnets found in discarded computers and laptops.The first is solid-state chlorination, which is being developed by project partner TU Bergakademie Freiberg. Instead of conventional hydrochloric acid, the process uses ammonium chloride added to a mixture containing neodymium, iron and boron recovered from magnet waste.When heated, the mixture is converted into metal chlorides and a high-purity ammonia solution. The approach builds on a patented process already used to recycle fluorescent lamps, which researchers are now testing for magnet recovery.Initial results indicate that the method can separate metal chlorides from magnet material more efficiently, allowing nearly all the metals to be extracted while using comparatively small amounts of chemicals.The second approach uses electrochemical processing. Researchers place powdered magnet waste in an electrochemical cell, where an electrolyte such as diluted sulfuric acid provides the medium for chemical reactions.This process initially extracts boron into a solution, which can then be concentrated for use in the chemical and pharmaceutical industries.Separating valuable materials for reuseAfter the initial processing, researchers at Fraunhofer IKTS use hydrometallurgical techniques to separate the resulting materials. The team applies selective processing to recover neodymium and iron, allowing the metals to be obtained in pure salt forms.The recovered materials can then undergo further processing by project partners for applications across several industries. These include chemicals, pharmaceuticals, hydrogen production, and fertilizers.The researchers are also exploring ways to turn the recovered materials into higher-value products rather than simply extracting them from waste. This could help establish a circular supply chain in which discarded electronic components become feedstock for new industrial applications.The four-year NEO-CYCLE project is funded through the European Union’s Horizon Europe program. Researchers have completed laboratory-scale testing of the recovery approaches, while plans for a pilot plant are underway.The aim is to develop an economically and environmentally viable process that can recover high-quality materials from end-of-life magnets while reducing chemical and water consumption. If successful, the approach could help Europe make better use of its electronic waste and reduce its dependence on imported critical raw materials.

title: New satellite handoff tech cuts network switching to milliseconds
content: Your phone could soon stay connected even when it moves beyond cellular tower coverage, switching seamlessly to satellites instead.AT&T and AST SpaceMobile have demonstrated what they believe is the industry’s first successful handoff between a ground-based cellular network and a direct-to-device satellite network.The milestone could help smartphones switch between conventional cell towers and satellites without dropping calls or losing data connections, bringing seamless satellite connectivity closer to commercial use.The demonstration took place on October 21 at 8:15 a.m. PT near Granite Falls, Washington. It builds on earlier tests in which AST SpaceMobile’s BlueBird satellites supported voice calls, text messages, and video calls using everyday smartphones. The latest test addressed a different challenge: transferring a connection between two networks operating through very different infrastructure.Bridging two network worldsUnder the arrangement, AT&T provides the terrestrial wireless network, while AST SpaceMobile operates the satellite network designed to connect directly with standard smartphones. Ericsson and Nokia supplied the technologies needed to coordinate the transition between them.Ericsson provided AT&T with combined radio and core network technology, alongside intelligent network automation. According to the company, this technology is designed to reduce handoff transition times between ground-based and satellite networks from seconds to milliseconds, helping minimize interruptions as phones move between the two types of coverage.Nokia supplied radio access technology and mobility software for AST SpaceMobile’s satellite network. These technologies support the transfer of connections between terrestrial networks and satellite coverage, helping maintain service continuity as users move between them.The companies are working to make satellite connectivity function as an extension of existing mobile networks rather than a separate service that users must manually activate. This could allow smartphones to move between available ground-based and space-based coverage without requiring users to change devices or network settings.The approach is particularly relevant to areas where conventional cellular infrastructure is difficult to establish or maintain. Remote communities, highways and disaster-hit locations could benefit from satellite coverage that complements existing wireless networks.Moving toward commercial serviceFor AT&T, the satellite network is intended to extend its existing wireless coverage rather than replace terrestrial infrastructure. The company said the integration could help keep customers, first responders, and essential workers connected in locations where traditional mobile coverage is limited.The latest demonstration is an important step, but the technology is not yet ready for widespread commercial use. AT&T said the next phase is expected to include beta services under real-world conditions, allowing the companies to further refine network performance before moving toward commercial deployment.Robert Walters, AT&T’s senior vice president of network, described the successful handoff as a significant milestone, while noting that further testing remains necessary.AST SpaceMobile is developing its BlueBird satellite constellation to deliver 4G and 5G cellular broadband directly to standard, unmodified mobile devices. Its satellites use large communication arrays designed to connect with smartphones without requiring specialized satellite handsets.The companies have not announced a firm commercial launch date for the seamless handoff service. The upcoming beta phase will help determine how reliably the technology performs outside controlled demonstrations and across different coverage conditions.If successful, the development could make satellite connectivity a more seamless part of everyday mobile networks, allowing users to remain connected even when they move beyond the reach of conventional cell towers.

title: OpenAI builds custom Git backend in 10 weeks after 2,442% commit surge
content: OpenAI has developed a new Git backend called Pando to handle the growing volume of code changes generated by its engineers and Codex agents. The system now powers development across OpenAI’s monorepo, processing nearly one petabyte of Git data daily.The infrastructure addresses a problem that emerged as Codex accelerated software development. More engineers and autonomous agents now work on separate code changes simultaneously. Their activity creates a growing stream of branch updates, code reviews, merges, and repository downloads.OpenAI says Pando has reduced median Git push latency by nearly 80 percent. It has also improved merge reliability to 99.99 percent, compared with earlier periods when reliability sometimes dropped below 90 percent.Codex pushes Git to its limitsOpenAI’s monorepo experienced a sharp increase in development activity over the past year. Its quarterly commit growth reached 2,442 percent in Q4 2026 compared with Q1 2024.Traditional Git infrastructure struggled to accommodate the resulting workload. Engineers encountered slower pushes and downloads, alongside failed merges. Multiple automated jobs also fetched identical commits after individual code submissions.We built Pando, a new Git backend for our monorepo, to handle more pushes and fetches without changing how our engineers and agents use Git.Pando cut push latency by ~80% and now serves nearly a petabyte of Git data a day. We can grow Git capacity alongside agent usage. pic.twitter.com/4c0YXOfKqK— OpenAI Developers (@OpenAIDevs) November 3, 2026OpenAI wanted to address these bottlenecks without replacing Git or forcing developers to adopt unfamiliar tools. Its engineers therefore designed Pando around the existing Git protocol and command-line client.The approach preserves familiar development workflows while changing how servers coordinate updates and distribute repository data. It also allows improvements to the underlying Git client to benefit the wider developer community.Conventional Git infrastructure can struggle when thousands of developers update different branches simultaneously. Some distributed systems coordinate changes across multiple repository replicas. Others rely on a shared write-ahead log to establish update order.Both approaches introduce potential bottlenecks. Coordinating updates across replicas increases communication overhead. A shared log can also force unrelated branch updates to compete for the same resource.Pando takes a different approach through causal consistency. It coordinates updates independently for individual branches instead of imposing one global sequence. When a developer pushes code, Pando stores the incoming Git packfile in cloud object storage. Its metadata service then records the updated branch version and its dependencies.This arrangement allows unrelated branches to accept updates concurrently. However, readers examining multiple branches might see different update versions. Individual branch updates remain consistent. Pando also reuses previously generated packfiles during downloads. This reduces the computing work required to serve identical repository data repeatedly.Caches accelerate repository downloadsThe architecture uses regional caching to distribute Git data closer to developers and automated systems. Its Express delivery service stores packfiles in regional caches.OpenAI reports cache hit rates exceeding 99 percent. The company has also demonstrated clone and fetch operations saturating 10-gigabit-per-second network connections.Background compaction further improves performance. Workers combine smaller packfiles into larger groups, reducing download overhead and speeding up repository history searches.Built with Codex in 10 weeksOpenAI says it developed Pando with Codex in just 10 weeks. A single engineer designed its core architecture, while teams of agents handled implementation.The system entered production in April 2026. OpenAI implemented it in Rust and developed extensive testing tools to identify concurrency bugs.Pando has since handled more than 57 terabytes of Git packfiles in a single hour. The company says it achieved this using more than 99 percent locally cached data.OpenAI also plans to explore broader applications for Pando. Its architecture could support other environments where large numbers of software agents collaborate on shared repositories.

title: OpenAI expands security testing with help from external experts
content: OpenAI is bringing outside security researchers into its next internal security sprint, giving them access to its models to help find weaknesses in its defenses.The company is partnering with Cathedral Systems, whose researchers will work alongside OpenAI’s teams to test its systems and help strengthen protections across its platforms.The planned exercise builds on an earlier sprint that involved 25 percent of OpenAI’s product engineers. Alongside the partnership, the company is increasing its Security Bug Bounty rewards, with exceptional findings eligible for up to $172,000, including bonuses.OpenAI has not specified when the next sprint will begin. It framed the effort as part of a broader push to use AI continuously to identify and fix vulnerabilities before attackers can exploit them.Outside researchers join defense testingCathedral’s researchers will use OpenAI’s models alongside the company’s own security teams to challenge its defenses. OpenAI said the partnership would bring different expertise and approaches to identifying weaknesses.The collaboration will also involve testing fixes, according to Gavin Kliger, Cathedral’s CEO and co-founder.“OpenAI is setting an important example by partnering with outside security firms and using its own models to continuously test and strengthen its defenses. Every company should be thinking about how to put these capabilities to work,” Kliger said.“We’re excited to collaborate with OpenAI’s teams, combining their models and security expertise with our research to find weaknesses, test fixes, and strengthen this approach to continuous defense,” he added. The announcement describes a planned collaboration rather than completed findings. It does not identify specific vulnerabilities discovered through the new partnership or detail the systems researchers will examine.Higher rewards for critical findingsOpenAI is also more than quadrupling rewards for critical findings under its Security Bug Bounty program. The maximum payment of $172,000, including bonuses, applies to exceptional findings.The company said it wants researchers to challenge its assumptions and strengthen both its systems and the methods used to defend them.During the previous internal sprint, engineers used Codex to investigate findings, reproduce vulnerabilities in isolated environments, and prepare patches for review. OpenAI dedicated a quarter of its product engineers to that effort.The next sprint is intended to build on this work by bringing new researchers and security partners together with internal teams.Expanding access to AI defense toolsOpenAI said traditional cyber defenses alone are no longer sufficient, pointing to recent industry incidents as evidence of how quickly threats can emerge. Its stated goal is to build continuous defensive loops that find and fix weaknesses before attackers do.Beyond its internal systems, the company is making its most capable models available to Daybreak customers. It has committed $1 billion in subsidized access over six months for frontline defenders protecting essential services and digital infrastructure.OpenAI is also sharing its architecture and lessons from its previous sprint, along with a blueprint for empowering cyber defenders across industry and government.The company said it would keep advancing its models, applying them to its own defenses and expanding access for trusted defenders as AI becomes better at finding vulnerabilities.

title: Scientists build virtual Earth to help search for alien life
content: Scientists have built a computer model of Earth without life to help determine whether distant planets could host living organisms or merely have conditions that resemble those of an inhabited world.Researchers at the University of Washington developed a simulation that models how chemicals move between a planet’s core, mantle, crust, surface and atmosphere over billions of years. The model could help astronomers identify atmospheric signals on rocky exoplanets that cannot be explained by geological and other non-biological processes.The distinction matters as scientists search for signs of life beyond our solar system. Astronomers have cataloged more than 6,000 exoplanets and are examining the atmospheres of promising worlds for gases that could indicate biological activity. However, finding a potentially habitable planet does not establish that life exists there.To address this challenge, the researchers simulated Earth’s geochemical evolution over five billion years, covering its formation around 4.5 billion years ago and extending roughly 500 million years into the future. The model excludes the influence of living organisms, allowing scientists to examine how a planet’s systems could evolve without biology.Simulating a lifeless EarthThe simulation builds on an earlier model developed in the laboratory of Rory Barnes, an associate professor of astronomy at the University of Washington. Previous versions included the planet’s core, mantle, crust and stellar radiation but did not account for the surface and atmosphere.Lead author Samantha Gilbert-Janizek expanded the model to include those missing systems, creating a more complete picture of how chemicals move throughout a rocky planet. The simulation reproduced 19 planetary properties, including heat flow through Earth’s mantle.The model provides a baseline for understanding what a planet’s atmosphere might look like without life. Researchers can adjust its inputs to represent other rocky exoplanets and test whether their observed atmospheric conditions can be reproduced through non-biological processes.This could help scientists avoid mistaking geological activity for evidence of extraterrestrial organisms. A planet might have an atmosphere containing chemicals associated with life, but those gases could also arise from interactions between its interior, surface and atmosphere.Distinguishing life from geologyEarth offers an example of why this distinction is important. Living organisms continually release gases such as oxygen and methane into the atmosphere. These gases react with one another, so their simultaneous presence can suggest that biological processes are replenishing them.An astronomer observing Earth from another star system might therefore consider the combination a possible sign of life. But scientists first need to understand whether non-biological processes could produce similar atmospheric conditions on other worlds.The new model allows researchers to test that possibility. If a planet’s observed atmosphere can be reproduced without including life, the findings may offer a non-biological explanation. If the simulation cannot reproduce the observations, the planet could become a more interesting target for further investigation.The researchers say the work could also inform the design of future space telescopes, including NASA’s proposed Habitable Worlds Observatory, which is intended to study potentially habitable planets around other stars.The study does not identify an inhabited exoplanet or detect extraterrestrial life. Instead, it provides a tool for improving how scientists interpret atmospheric observations and distinguish potentially biological signals from the natural evolution of a planet.The study appears in The Planetary Science Journal.

title: Solid-state battery survives 400°F heat test, targets 600-mile range
content: Next-generation all-solid-state batteries are gaining attention in the electric vehicle battery market, with several battery makers expanding research in the sector. Sunwoda, a Chinese battery manufacturer, has recently announced advances to its polymer-composite approach used for building solid-state batteries.The company claimed that its latest 20 Ah all-solid-state battery, Xin Bixiao, withstood extreme thermal heat without catching fire or exploding.Built with a nanoscale high-entropy silicon anode, a single cell of these polymer batteries showed strong thermal performance, passing the hot-box test with temperatures raised to 400 degrees Fahrenheit (200 degrees Celsius).High-density, long-rangeThe model has previously achieved an energy density exceeding 400 Wh/kg and a cycle life of more than 1200 cycles at a low external pressure of 1 megapascals (MPa). This it stated is a breakthrough for long-range electric vehicles (EVs), offering a range of over 600 miles (1000 km).With over 1,200 cycles and capacity retention above 80 percent, the company claimed the battery could support vehicle use for over a decade, assuming annual driving of more than 12,000 miles (20,000 km).However, the company noted that the thermal and lifespan performance results were not obtained after integrating the entire battery pack in a vehicle. The testing process started earlier this year in May and is still ongoing.Going forward, the company also plans to build a second-generation sulfide battery by next year at its pre-commercial solid-state battery production line. This manufacturing unit is designed to handle an annual capacity of 0.2 gigawatt-hours (GWh), which is considered small in the battery world, making batteries enough for nearly 2600-2700 electric vehicles per year.Next stop: Aviation batteriesBeyond the planned automotive batteries of 400Wh/kg capacity, the Chinese battery maker is also eyeing developing aviation battery cells of at least 450Wh/kg. For this project, the company is working with the Guangdong Engineering Research Center. Another segment that the company is aiming to make its mark in is the electric vertical take-off and landing (eVTOL) aircraft batteries. The company is targeting a continuous discharge power density of at least 1,000 W/kg for these aircraft.However, the company has not yet committed to an official deadline for any of these high-energy-density batteries, nor has it defined the scale of production volumes or commercial orders.Meanwhile, Contemporary Amperex Technology Co., Limited (CATL), another leading Chinese battery manufacturer, is developing its next-generation solid-state batteries using bisulphide chemistry, a different electrolyte technology. The company announced its 20 Ah solid-state prototype two years ago and has reaffirmed its 2027 target for a small-scale batch production trial.Earlier this year, Sunwoda unveiled its latest fast-charging EV battery technology that can add about 62 miles (100 km) of range per minute and charge from 10 percent to 97 percent state of charge (SOC) in 9 minutes at room temperature. The claims were made for its new 15C lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery.The company said the battery can go from 10 percent to 70 percent in about 5 minutes, then reach 97 percent in another four minutes.

title: US Navy's 1,200-mph Super Hornets to carry four hypersonic missiles
content: The U.S. Navy is preparing to add a new class of high-speed strike weapons to its carrier-based fighter fleet. Chief of Naval Operations Adm. Daryl Caudle recently examined Blackbeard, a hypersonic missile developed by defense startup Castelion, during a visit to Naval Air Station Patuxent River in Maryland.The October 28 visit provided a closer look at the weapon’s progress toward integration with the F/A-18E/F Super Hornet. The Navy has already conducted an initial flight evaluation, with further testing planned before the missile enters operational service.Caudle inspected the weapon at Air Test and Evaluation Squadron 23 (VX-23), which handles weapons testing at the installation. The visit also included discussions about the Navy’s broader approach to developing autonomous aircraft and extending the reach of carrier-based operations.Hypersonic weapon nears testingBlackbeard falls into the hypersonic category, which covers weapons capable of exceeding Mach 5. Its flight profile also allows it to change direction during atmospheric flight. This combination could complicate interception attempts by adversary air defense networks.Integrating the weapon onto the Super Hornet has already produced several testing milestones. A Navy presentation in August showed two Blackbeard test articles mounted beneath the fighter’s wings.Engineers took the next step on September 18. A Super Hornet departed Patuxent River carrying two missiles during a developmental flight. The aircraft completed the sortie without releasing either weapon, allowing the Navy to evaluate how the fighter handles their additional weight and external configuration.Coming soon to a theater near you…BLACKBEARD!@USPACOM @CENTCOM @PAEAviation pic.twitter.com/KgBtIqdf8I— NAVAIR (@NAVAIRNews) September 25, 2026Footage released by the Navy on September 25 documented the flight. The service ultimately wants each Super Hornet to accommodate four Blackbeard missiles, potentially giving individual aircraft a substantial strike payload.Navy increases missile ordersCastelion has positioned Blackbeard as a more affordable alternative to existing American hypersonic weapons. The California-based startup was founded by former SpaceX engineers and aims to simplify production to increase manufacturing capacity.The Navy awarded the company a $105 million agreement in April to advance integration with the Super Hornet. The program also includes preparations for live-fire evaluations in the Indo-Pacific.Procurement activity has gathered pace since then. In June, the Navy purchased 50 pre-production missiles for $23.4 million. A September agreement added a production order worth up to $200 million. USNI News reported that the deal covers 444 missiles.@USNavyCNO, meet Blackbeard. pic.twitter.com/xgu5pBVEJJ— Castelion (@Castelion) November 2, 2026The Pentagon has also outlined much larger ambitions for the weapon. A framework agreement calls for at least 500 missiles annually once testing concludes. The Department of War has also indicated plans to seek funding for more than 12,000 units over five years.Multiple launch platforms plannedThe Super Hornet represents just one potential application for Blackbeard. Castelion is pursuing compatibility with several other military platforms.The U.S. Army’s HIMARS rocket artillery system is among the planned launch platforms. The company has also begun adapting the weapon for the Air Force’s F-16 under a research agreement.Naval operations could eventually involve unmanned vessels, too. Castelion intends to demonstrate a launch from Saronic’s Marauder unmanned surface vessel in 2027.The Navy is working toward early operational capability, which would allow a limited missile inventory to reach frontline units. Additional developmental flights at Patuxent River will help prepare the weapon for subsequent live-fire evaluations.An important milestone remains outstanding. The Navy has yet to announce a date for Blackbeard’s first live launch from a Super Hornet. That test will provide a clearer indication of the weapon’s readiness for deployment.
