title: US rival tests cruise missile cluster warhead with 6-hectare reach
content: North Korea has tested a dispersal warhead designed for a strategic cruise missile, claiming it can devastate a target area of up to 6 hectares. The test also assessed the missile’s ability to strike targets vertically, as Pyongyang continues to expand its range of weapons systems.The tests were conducted on Monday, November 2, and overseen by Full Gen. Kim Jong-sik, a member of the ruling Workers’ Party of Korea’s Central Military Commission, according to the Korean Central News Agency (KCNA).North Korea’s Warhead Institute, which operates under its Missile Administration, said the medium-sized dispersal warhead could turn an area of 5 to 6 hectares into ashes at what it described as the highest-density power.The country’s Cruise Missile System Institute also reported improvements to the missile’s terminal maneuverability, saying the changes had established its ability to conduct vertical strikes while accounting for the natural and geographical characteristics of the target area.Cruise missile gains vertical strike capabilityThe reported test involved two assessments: the destructive power of the dispersal warhead and the missile’s flight characteristics during a vertical strike. North Korea did not provide details about the missile’s range, flight profile or the technical changes behind the claimed improvement.A dispersal warhead is designed to release multiple smaller explosive devices, known as submunitions, over a wider area. Such weapons can threaten several targets within the affected zone rather than concentrating their effects on a single point.The Missile Administration’s director described the tests as a demonstration of “practical combat power.” The official also said developing different weapon systems was increasingly urgent, arguing that the country’s armed forces needed to defend national security and deter external threats.Cluster warheads expand weapons optionsThe cruise missile test followed another weapons trial on Saturday, October 31, when North Korea tested a cluster warhead designed for tactical ballistic missiles.KCNA reported that the standard Type 2 cluster warhead could devastate an area of 12 to 13 hectares at its highest density. That figure is separate from the 5-to-6-hectare area claimed for the dispersal warhead tested on Monday.North Korea’s Missile Administration said its cluster warheads fall into four categories, depending on their intended purpose. An official said the country planned to make the different types available to military units by the end of 2026, allowing them to select weapons based on operational requirements and target characteristics.The two tests indicate that Pyongyang is working on dispersal warheads for both tactical ballistic missiles and strategic cruise missiles. However, the claims about their destructive power and improved flight capabilities come from North Korean state media and have not been independently verified.North Korea has also tested other weapons systems in recent weeks, including attack drones, a precision-guided torpedo system and an intermediate-range hypersonic missile. The latest trials add to its efforts to broaden the capabilities of its armed forces.

title: US strikes target Iran's Qeshm Island and underground missile base
content: The U.S. military has quietly expanded its campaign against Iran, conducting limited strikes on Qeshm Island as Washington weighs diplomatic options and prepares for a possible return to wider combat.U.S. officials confirmed Monday’s operation, describing it as a defensive response to Iranian surface-to-air missile threats against American assets. The strikes also aimed to limit Tehran’s ability to threaten commercial shipping near the Strait of Hormuz.The operation signals that American forces remain engaged despite President Donald Trump’s public suggestions that the conflict has largely ended. It also raises questions about whether Washington can maintain its military pressure without triggering another major confrontation.Strikes target strategic islandQeshm Island occupies a critical position near the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world’s most important energy shipping routes. Iran operates strategic military infrastructure there, including an underground missile facility and a naval base.The island also hosts a major desalination plant, making it an important part of the region’s infrastructure. Its location gives Iranian forces a strategic position near shipping lanes used by commercial vessels.Explosions reportedly occurred across parts of Qeshm on Monday, according to social media reports. The U.S. has previously targeted the island during earlier phases of the conflict.Washington has also considered seizing the territory, according to reports. However, Monday’s strikes appeared limited and did not indicate preparations for an immediate ground operation.American officials told the Wall Street Journal that Washington had conducted similar attacks secretly in recent weeks. The administration has avoided publicly announcing these operations to prevent signaling a return to large-scale warfare.Pentagon prepares wider optionsThe latest strikes follow weeks of military planning inside the Trump administration. Senior officials have discussed additional airstrikes and presented the president with several options.Those options reportedly include tighter economic sanctions and expanding restrictions on Iranian trade. U.S. Central Command has also prepared for broader military operations.Adm. Brad Cooper, head of U.S. Central Command, visited the White House last week. He briefed Trump on the conflict and potential military responses.The Pentagon has strengthened its regional posture in recent weeks. American forces have moved additional missile defenses and munitions into the region.Washington has also warned Gulf countries about a possible short, intense military operation after Tuesday’s midterm elections. Such preparations suggest the administration wants to retain the ability to escalate quickly.Trump keeps diplomacy openTrump has recently softened his public position on renewed military action. On Monday, he dismissed suggestions that another round of major strikes would immediately follow the elections.Speaking to reporters, Trump said the United States had already won its confrontation with Iran. He questioned whether the current situation even qualified as a war.The president also suggested that negotiations could produce an agreement. Vice President JD Vance echoed that assessment, saying Washington and Tehran had made progress toward ending hostilities.Iranian officials have maintained that any agreement depends on American concessions. Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei said Tehran had clearly communicated its demands.Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei has also warned that Iran would retaliate if Washington reignited the conflict. His threats extend beyond the Middle East.The competing signals leave the region facing an uncertain military outlook. Washington continues to strike Iranian targets while keeping diplomatic channels open.Whether those negotiations can prevent another major confrontation remains unclear. The limited operations on Qeshm demonstrate that the United States has not abandoned military pressure.

title: US student's jet drone claims world record with 491 mph flight
content: A jet-powered drone built in the dormitory of a U.S. university broke the world record for the fastest jet-powered aircraft, according to a social media post by the Georgia Tech aerospace engineering student Tomas Salvo.​The aircraft, which he named Reaper, hit a speed of 491 miles per hour (790km/hr) and carried a payload of 2.6 pounds (1.2 Kg).​The radio-controlled (RC) drone climbed a maximum height of 6500 feet, covering a total range of 31 miles at the full speed and maintained the flight at that speed for four minutes.Smallest jet-powered drones​He built three such models, and each of them achieved the record speed, Salvo said, claiming them to be “the world’s fastest small jet-powered drones.”​The engineer added the aircraft he built can be launched either from a truck or railway track, reaching peak heights in less than 20 seconds.​”Reaper can be rail- or truck-launched, climb to 2,000 m (6,600 ft) in under 20 seconds, then fly for 50 km (31 mi) at full speed,” he posted on his social media account.​In a video posted online, Salvo, along with two others, was seen demonstrating the launch from an open field, with screeching sounds heard in the background as the aircraft engine ignited before giving it a final thrust for the launch.3D-printed titanium nozzle​Built using 3D-printing, his aircraft has a titanium nozzle on its engine that replaces the stock nozzle. This allows the engine to sit comfortably much further forward and improves the center of gravity without adding extra weight in the frontal region. The exterior is made of custom-molded carbon fiber with a laser-cut internal structure, keeping it lightweight at a total of 11 pounds.​Young engineers claimed record speeds, yet he is still far from reaching Mach 1, which stands at 767.3 mph (1,234.8 km/h).​Earlier in October, a team of graduates from Bath University made a similar attempt to reach 0.8 Mach speeds with their 3D-printed, jet-powered remote-controlled aircraft, Kingchaser. The aircraft, which measured just under a meter, was made out of thermoplastics, Polyethylene Terephthalate Glycol-modified (PETG), carbon fiber-reinforced polyphenylene sulfide (PPS-CF), carbon-fiber rods, and aluminum.​It reached a top speed of 205 mph (330 km/hr) when propelled by a miniature jet turbine capable of generating 63 newtons (N) of thrust.​The initial plan involved housing a 150 N jet engine to hit the speed of 614 mph (988km/h). However, the team opted to build a 20 percent larger craft that weighed nearly 20 pounds (9 Kg), heavier than Salvo’s reaper.​The team also used Titanium in their design but limited it to the exhaust sheets to protect the aircraft from the engine’s heat. The main skeleton was composed of an aluminum frame and reinforced with steel to mount the engine.​In the latest demonstration by the U.S. student on October 30, Reaper exceeded the peak speeds reached by Kingchaser by nearly 2.5 times, showcasing a robust engineering design and performance.After his latest tests, Salvos was confident that he has built a reliable and repeatable system. He hopes to push the top speeds past 500 mph (800 km/hr) with small optimization tweaks during his future tests.

title: Behind-the-meter generation could deliver five times more grid relief than data center load shifting - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
An Ember analysis finds that data center load shifting could reduce peak electricity demand by up to 1.5% in Ireland by 2030, offering limited grid flexibility. Behind-the-meter generation and storage could provide nearly five times more relief, with potential reductions of up to 2.7 GW in Texas.
Pilar Sánchez Molina
03 Nov 2026
Markets & Policy
Energy Storage
Highlights
Utility-scale
The rapid deployment of data centers is placing substantial new loads on electricity systems that, in many cases, are not expanding at the same pace. An analysis published by Ember in October 2026 examines the extent to which data centers can provide grid flexibility through two mechanisms: shifting computing workloads and using behind-the-meter generation or storage. The study covers nine markets across the United States, Europe, and Southeast Asia, with particular relevance to Ireland, the United Kingdom, and Germany.
Ireland faces one of the largest impacts on electricity demand
Data centers could account for a significant share of peak electricity demand as their capacity expands. In Ireland, one of Europe’s leading data center hubs, they already account for approximately 19% of peak demand. In January 2025, when system demand peaked at 6 GW, data centers accounted for an estimated 1.1 GW. Ember projects that this share could rise to 24% by 2030, with data center demand reaching 1.6 GW against a system peak of 6.5 GW.
The challenge is particularly acute because of the mismatch between data center construction timelines and electricity infrastructure development. A large data center can require between 200 MW and 500 MW of power capacity and be built within 18 to 24 months, while conventional grid expansions can take four to 10 years.
Load shifting offers limited flexibility potential
Load shifting involves moving certain computing workloads to different times or locations to reduce demand during periods of grid stress. However, the composition of data center workloads significantly limits this option.
Cloud services, enterprise workloads, and artificial intelligence (AI) inference require low latency and currently account for most data center capacity. Ember estimates that these workloads will represent approximately 87% of global data center capacity by 2030. By contrast, AI model training offers greater flexibility, as workloads can be interrupted or relocated with fewer operational consequences.
Under Ember’s assumptions – 35% flexibility for AI training workloads, 5% for inference, and none for traditional data centers – approximately 6.5% of global data center capacity could theoretically be shifted. Factoring in an average utilization rate of approximately 48%, the capacity effectively available to respond to periods of grid stress falls to around 3%.
The impact on peak demand would therefore be limited. In Ireland, load shifting could reduce peak demand by approximately 100 MW by 2030, equivalent to 1.5% of the projected peak. Across the other markets analyzed, estimated reductions range from 0.1% to 0.6%.
Behind-the-meter generation and storage
An alternative offering greater flexibility involves maintaining computing workloads while temporarily replacing grid electricity with on-site generation or storage. This approach, known as bring-your-own-capacity (BYOC), can combine renewable generation, batteries, and other backup technologies.
The study finds that this approach could provide nearly five times as much grid relief as load shifting. For two large data centers analyzed in Texas, with a combined projected load of 5.6 GW, load shifting could reduce grid demand by approximately 0.55 GW during periods of stress, while on-site generation could reduce it by up to 2.7 GW.
Although the Texas example is outside Europe, it is relevant to the European regulatory debate because it illustrates the scale of flexibility that behind-the-meter resources could provide when grid connections become a bottleneck.
Ireland offers a European regulatory precedent. Initial proposals by the country’s energy regulator to impose flexibility requirements on data centers were replaced, following public consultation, with requirements for facilities of 10 MW or more to provide generation or storage capacity.
Energy sources determine system benefits
On-site generation does not automatically deliver decarbonization benefits. If it relies on fossil fuel-based technologies, it could lock in infrastructure and emissions for decades. There is also a risk of duplicating investments: a data center could install its own firm capacity while the system operator procures additional capacity to meet the same potential demand.
The report recommends integrating behind-the-meter resources into grid planning and connection requirements. Renewable generation and storage could enable data centers to reduce grid demand during critical hours without passing the costs of additional infrastructure on to other electricity consumers.
Storage is particularly relevant to this approach, as it can partially decouple data center electricity consumption from real-time grid availability and supply power during periods of congestion or peak demand.
Ember’s analysis indicates that no single flexibility solution is suitable for all data centers. Traditional computing and AI inference workloads, which could account for 87% of global data center capacity by 2030, offer limited scope for load shifting. For these facilities, renewable generation and behind-the-meter storage could be the primary means of reducing grid dependence during peak periods. Data centers dedicated to AI training, by contrast, offer greater potential to shift workloads across time or locations.

title: Hanwha Q-Cells shifts focus to research and development in Europe - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Hanwha Q Cells has denied rumors of a market exit but confirmed plans to focus its European operations on research and development. The restructuring will lead to job cuts in sales and business development, while the company expands its R&D workforce in Germany.
Sandra Enkhardt
03 Nov 2026
Markets & Policy
Cell production at the Hanwha Q Cells facility in South Korea.
Rumors are circulating in the solar industry that Hanwha Q-Cells is preparing to withdraw from the market and shut down operations by early 2027. The speculation has been fueled by reports of the company’s products being sold at unusually low prices.
In response to an inquiry from
pv magazine
, a company spokesperson firmly denied the rumors. “Q-Cells is not ceasing its operations in Europe,” he said. However, the spokesperson confirmed that, following “ongoing reviews and close monitoring of its subsidiaries,” parent company Hanwha Q-Cells has decided to refocus its German subsidiary exclusively on its core business.
Hanwha Q-Cells GmbH’s core business in Europe is research and development (R&D). “This decision involves a restructuring,” the spokesperson said. Although he initially declined to provide further details, he confirmed that “the restructuring will, however, result in some job losses within the sales and business development departments.”
Hanwha Q Cells also recently announced its involvement in a new German research project focused on space photovoltaics. The spokesperson said the company is expanding its R&D workforce.
The market speculation extends beyond the company’s German and European operations, with rumors suggesting that Hanwha Q-Cells could withdraw from PV manufacturing altogether. The spokesperson also rejected these claims.
“In its core business areas—research and development, as well as the production of solar cells and modules—Q-Cells is guided by global market interests and economic factors,” he said. “All other regions, including the U.S. operations you asked about, remain unchanged.”
Just over a year ago, Hanwha Q-Cells announced that it would discontinue direct sales of residential PV systems in Germany and instead rely exclusively on its network of approximately 1,000 authorized partners. At the time, the company cited weak demand in Germany’s residential solar market as the reason for the decision.
The move also resulted in job cuts, although Q-Cells declined to disclose how many positions were affected.
The sales division now facing closure is based in Berlin, while Hanwha Q-Cells’ German R&D center is located in Bitterfeld-Wolfen.

title: Hybrid wind-solar-battery plants can power Kazakhstan’s demand growth - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
Ember analysis finds that hybrid wind, solar and battery plants could supply electricity at an average cost of $56/MWh in Kazakhstan, compared with $70–170/MWh for new coal, while meeting up to 90% of typical demand.
Patrick Jowett
03 Nov 2026
Markets & Policy
Research & Development
Asia-Pacific
Batteries
Energy Storage
Highlights
Utility-scale
Hybrid power plants pairing wind and solar power with a battery can supply up to 90% of Kazakhstan’s typical demand profile for a delivered cost below $60/MWh, according to the
latest report
Ember’s report says Kazakhstan needs “new power capacity quickly”, with its electricity demand rising 16% in the last five years. Coal still dominates Kazakhstan’s electricity mix, supplying 62% of electricity generation in 2025, but its coal units are on average over 50 years old, leading to frequent equipment failures. Ember says there were 891 incidents of various severity between January and July this year.
“To replace its ageing infrastructure and keep pace with fast-growing demand, Kazakhstan needs to build more capacity quickly and ensure its availability during peak periods, including winter demand spikes,” Ember’s report says. “The capacity also needs to be built close to where demand is to relieve pressure on the transmission network.”
Ember’s research analysed 15 sites, chosen for their proximity to a major demand centre and an existing power line, across all three of Kazakhstan’s power zones. It tested 125 combinations of wind, solar and battery capacity at each site, producing 1,875 simulations. Each configuration was simulated hour by hour over a 30-year project life using site a typical hourly demand profile that represented national demand patterns and was scaled to a peak of 100 MW.
Results found the best-performing configurations at each site could supply between 70% and 90% of the electricity in a typical demand profile, hour by hour, over 30 years, at a delivered cost below $60/MWh.
“This cost represents the plant’s lifetime cost per MWh actually delivered, including the cost of curtailed output,” Ember’s report says. Across all 15 sites, the average delivered electricity cost is $56/MWh. Ember says this is significantly cheaper compared to new coal, which costs $70-170/MWh, depending on the region and technology.
Kostantsa Rangelova, Senior Battery Analyst at Ember, told
pv magazine
that while there is real potential for solar-plus-battery projects in Kazakhstan, the potential is even greater when wind is added.
“Solar is really cheap and very fast to build here,” Rangelova said. “Shifting some of it to the evening with a battery unlocks its full value, making its potential contribution to electricity supply larger than with standalone solar.”
Rangelova added that the challenge for solar lies in the Kazakh winter, which often brings cloudy days that mean solar-plus-storage produces less when demand is highest.
“Solar-battery projects do not need wind to be viable, but on their own they are a summer-heavy source of power,” she continued.
“Kazakhstan’s advantage is its vast untapped wind, which is strongest in exactly those winter months. Combining wind and solar behind one grid connection, overbuilding generation capacity and accepting some curtailment by design means only a small battery is needed to reach a high capacity factor at low cost.”
Ember’s hybrid simulations feature curtailment by design in order to minimise the battery need and make it possible to meet over 70% of winter demand at most sites. The report explains that deliberately oversizing the generation means there is enough generation even on less windy and sunny days when paired with a small battery.
This offers a capacity factor comparable to that of a baseload power station, it continues, but at a lower cost than new coal.
Rangelova also told
pv magazine
the report findings can be very relevant for renewable energy procurement schemes, explaining that while hybrid plants provide flexibility for the power service, their service needs to be rewarded and priced into procurement costs.
“An auction that asks for a specific supply profile and lets bidders find the lowest-cost mix of wind, solar and battery to meet that profile would price that flexibility in and lower system costs,” she suggested.
Rangelova also recommended batteries have access to balancing, reserve and capacity revenues in order to provide the best value for the investment made in them.
“Batteries co-located with renewables under a mandate that only shift their own plant’s output remain underused and never deliver their full value to the system,” she said. “It is like owning a Swiss Army knife and only ever using the blade.”
Figures released by Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Energy in April put the country’s cumulative renewables capacity at 3.7 GW, including
1.37 GW of solar
. At the time, the ministry said it planned to commission 245 MW of renewables this year, including five solar projects with a combined capacity of 92.6 MW.
Additional figures from Ember’s report says wind and solar could supply 23% of Kazakhstan’s electricity generation by 2035, up from 6% in 2025, bringing total renewables generation to 35%.

title: Key takeaways from All Energy Australia 2026 - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
The outlook for Australia’s renewable energy transition appears positive with supportive government policies and renewable energy targets, a surge in battery installations, and a strong pipeline of grid-scale solar and storage projects helping to fuel confidence.
David Carroll
03 Nov 2026
Markets & Policy
Batteries
Commercial & industrial
Residential
Utility-scale
The sense of optimism within Australia’s renewable energy sector was on display at All Energy Australia 2026 conference and trade show in Melbourne on Oct. 28 and 29, where energy security, growing demand, and investment and market certainty featured prominently in discussions.
Batteries were also a major topic of conversation with the strong presence of both grid and small-scale battery suppliers on the expanded exhibition floor showcasing a growing confidence in the market.
RX Global, which organises All Energy alongside the Clean Energy Council (CEC), said more than 22,000 people attended the event this year – up about 5,000 on 2025 figures – and more than 490 national and international companies and organisations exhibited on the trade show floor.
Batteries big and small were prominent among the displays with exhibitors keen to be part of the surging small and grid-scale markets.
More than 550,000 residential battery systems have been installed by Australian homeowners in the 15 months since the launch of the federal government’s Cheaper Home Batteries program – that subsidises approximately 30% of the cost of an eligible home energy-storage system. The growth pattern has steadied since the initial boom in installations, but the industry is confident there is still plenty of upside in the small-scale sector.
“Residential has stabilised over the past few months but there is still a lot of potential in that segment,” EP Cube Sales Manager Sudeesh V said. “Metropolitan areas like Melbourne and Sydney might be slowing but areas such as South Australia, Western Australia, Queensland, even the Northern Territory, there’s a lot of growth potential.”
The large-scale battery sector is also experiencing record growth with nine projects representing 2.3 GW / 7.1 GWh of storage capacity switched on in the first six months of the year, surpassing the 2 GW / 5.1 GWh added during 2025. In addition, 13 projects totalling 1.6 GW / 6.5 GWh reached financial close in H1 2026.
“We see a very, very significant penetration of battery storage and looking ahead, we’ll see this scaling up even more,” Rystad Energy Renewables and Power Vice President Sally Bogle said, adding that battery energy storage systems are serving as “a silver bullet for the power market.”
“They have quite a multi-faceted role,” she said, highlighting their ability to mitigate the curtailment of daytime solar in our markets.
“Asset performance wise, that is really, really valuable,” she said. “It allows a solar or wind facility to really maximise their asset and optimise the grid connection.”
The outlook for Australia’s solar market is also buoyant with the federal government’s recent raising of the Small-scale Renewable Energy Scheme (SRES) eligibility cap from 100 kW to 1 MW tipped to drive growth in the commercial and industrial (C&I) segment.
The expansion extends financial incentives through the Small-scale Technology Certificate (STC) mechanism, reducing the upfront cost of qualifying mid-scale systems by approximately 20%.
“This will definitely unlock a lot of small to medium commercial projects,” said Charles Guo, Australian manager with module manufacturer Gorkin Solar.
Government policy appears to be accelerating large-scale solar development also. Australia is targeting 82% renewables share in the National Electricity Market (NEM) by 2030 while Western Australia recently committed to a renewable energy target of 75% by 2031 for its main electricity grid.
Australian Energy Market Operator data shows a record 80.9 GW of new generation and storage projects now in the pipeline but as ageing coal-fired power plants retire and electricity consumption forecast to grow by more than 40% over the next decade, getting new capacity built will be critical.
Victorian Energy Minister Jaclyn Symes said Australia said capital is available but providing investors with certainty is key.
“Investors need clear policy, predictable approvals, and confidence that the infrastructure connecting projects will be delivered,” she said.

title: Shenzhen Nanshan Power seeks majority stake in Trina Solar’s tracker business - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Shenzhen Nanshan Power plans to acquire a 51% to 70% stake in Trina Solar’s tracker business through a cash transaction. The proposed deal could provide Trina Solar with additional capital as it navigates financial pressure and intensifying competition in China’s solar sector.
Vincent Shaw
03 Nov 2026
Markets & Policy
Utility-scale
Trina’s Agile tracker is designed for one in portrait or two in landscape module installation.
Shenzhen Nanshan Power, a Chinese power producer backed by state-owned capital, plans to acquire a controlling stake in Trina Solar’s tracker business.
According to an Oct. 30 announcement, Shenzhen Nanshan Power signed a preliminary equity acquisition agreement with Trina Solar and its wholly owned subsidiary, Trina Solar (Changzhou) Science & Technology.
Under the proposed transaction, Shenzhen Nanshan Power would acquire a 51% to 70% stake in the Changzhou-based company operating TrinaTracker, Trina Solar’s solar tracking unit.
The target company, established in February 2019, is currently wholly owned by Trina Solar through its Changzhou subsidiary. If completed, the acquisition would give Shenzhen Nanshan Power control of the business and allow it to consolidate the subsidiary’s financial results.
The acquisition would be financed entirely in cash and is expected to qualify as a major asset restructuring under Chinese securities regulations. It would not involve the issuance of new shares or a change in Shenzhen Nanshan Power’s controlling shareholder.
The companies have yet to agree on the final equity stake, valuation or payment schedule. The purchase price will be determined following an independent asset valuation, while performance commitments and compensation arrangements are expected to be negotiated as part of a definitive agreement.
TrinaTracker supplies solar tracking systems, including its Vanguard-1P and Vanguard-2P products, alongside intelligent control technologies. According to Trina Solar, the business had delivered more than 43 GW of tracking systems across more than 70 countries by the end of 2025, with annual global production capacity exceeding 15 GW.
Wood Mackenzie ranked TrinaTracker second in its 2026 global tracker manufacturer assessment, which evaluates companies based on service capabilities, research and development, supply chain resilience and financial strength, rather than shipment volumes alone.
In comments to Chinese media on Nov. 2, Trina Solar said it intended to introduce a strategic partner to strengthen operational synergies. The company said it would continue to focus on its solar and energy storage businesses while developing integrated energy solutions and technologies for AI data centers.
The proposed sale comes amid continued financial pressure on China’s solar manufacturing sector. Trina Solar reported a net loss attributable to shareholders of CNY 1.94 billion ($285 million) for the first nine months of 2026, on revenue of CNY 47.98 billion.
Selling a majority stake in the tracker subsidiary could provide Trina Solar with additional capital while allowing it to retain a minority interest. The arrangement could also preserve opportunities for cooperation between its module and tracking systems businesses, although the companies have not disclosed any post-transaction supply or cooperation agreements.
The proposed deal reflects a broader push among Chinese renewable energy companies to explore ownership restructuring and strategic partnerships as they seek to balance investment requirements with business specialization amid intense competition.
Both companies stressed that negotiations remain at a preliminary stage. Due diligence, financial audits, asset valuation and corporate approvals must be completed before a binding agreement can be signed.

content:
Applications & Installations
A tender is open in Slovenia for the development of a solar-plus-storage project at a former waste landfill site. The deadline for applications is November 19.
Patrick Jowett
03 Nov 2026
Applications & Installations
Batteries
Energy Storage
Utility-scale
Slovenian state-owned energy company Holding Slovenske Elektrarne (HSE) has administered a tender for a solar-plus-storage project.
Available tender details
state the tender covers a 1.38 MW solar power plant to be tied to a 1.25 MW/5 MWh battery energy storage system.
The project will be built within the area of Kamnolom Zagorje, a closed municipal waste landfill located in the municipality of Zagorje ob Savi, central Slovenia. It forms part of HSE’s wider work in developing renewable energy projects in brownfield areas in Slovenia’s Zasavje region.
The chosen contractor will be responsible for the design, supply, assembly, testing and connection of the hybrid plant.
HSE announced securing a building permit for the project in late September. At the time, it said part of the funds for the project will be provided by the EU’s Just Transition Fund.
“As part of the project, measures to drain stormwater more efficiently and reduce its seepage into the body of the landfill will also be implemented to further contribute to the appropriate and sustainable management of the area,” HSE said. “The building permit is an important milestone on the path towards implementing the investment, which is planned for 2027.”
Prospective bidders can submit questions requesting additional information until November 10. The deadline for applications, which must be submitted electronically, is November 19.

title: Solar PV cuts Spain’s electricity costs by €17.02 billion over 18 months - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
A study by Spanish solar association UNEF estimates that solar PV generation reduced Spain’s wholesale electricity costs by €17.02 billion ($19.03 billion) between January 2025 and June 2026. Without solar generation, average daily market prices would have been 86% higher, according to the analysis.
Pilar Sánchez Molina
03 Nov 2026
Markets & Policy
Highlights
Utility-scale
Solar PV reduced Spain’s wholesale electricity costs by an estimated €17.02 billion between January 2025 and June 2026, according to Spanish PV association UNEF.
The association estimates that average day-ahead electricity prices would have been 86% higher without solar generation.
The study compares actual day-ahead market prices with a modeled scenario excluding generation from utility-scale PV plants and self-consumption systems. Without solar, the average price would have reached €112/MWh, compared with the recorded €60.2/MWh, representing a 46% reduction.
Utility-scale PV accounted for €14.23 billion of the estimated savings, while residential and commercial self-consumption contributed €2.79 billion. The total comprised €10.86 billion in 2025 and €6.16 billion in the first half of 2026.
UNEF attributes the effect to the marginal pricing mechanism of the day-ahead market. Solar generation, with its low variable costs, displaces more expensive electricity sources, lowering the market-clearing price. Self-consumption contributes by reducing demand from the grid, benefiting consumers beyond those with rooftop installations.
The association also estimates that every euro invested in solar PV generates €8 in wholesale electricity price savings.
Greater impact during periods of high solar generation
The price effect was particularly pronounced in June 2026, when the average day-ahead market price stood at €69.6/MWh. UNEF estimates that it would have reached €162.7/MWh without solar generation, a difference of €93.1/MWh.
The analysis uses data from Iberian electricity market operator OMIE, Spanish grid operator Red Eléctrica and UNEF to model market clearing without utility-scale PV and self-consumption. It also considers how other generation technologies would respond to changes in electricity prices.
However, the findings do not translate directly into equivalent savings on consumers’ electricity bills. The analysis covers the day-ahead wholesale market but excludes other cost components, including technical constraints, balancing services and forward contracts.
UNEF also acknowledges that the response of other technologies, particularly combined-cycle gas plants and hydropower facilities, could differ under substantially altered market conditions.

title: Waaree doubles Texas solar module manufacturing capacity to 3.2 GW - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
Waaree Solar Americas has started commercial production on two new 800 MW solar module manufacturing lines at its Brookshire facility in Texas, doubling the plant’s annual production capacity.
Uma Gupta
03 Nov 2026
Technology & Products
Highlights
Waaree solar manufacturing facility in Texas
Waaree Solar Americas Inc. (WSA), a wholly owned subsidiary of India’s Waaree Energies Ltd., has started commercial production on two new solar module manufacturing lines at its facility in Brookshire, Texas.
Each line has an annual production capacity of 800 MW, bringing the facility’s total installed module manufacturing capacity to 3.2 GW.
The expansion forms part of Waaree’s broader manufacturing plans in the United States. WSA is also expanding its Arizona module manufacturing facility from 1 GW to 1.6 GW, which is expected to bring the company’s total US module manufacturing capacity to 4.8 GW in fiscal 2027, which in India runs from April 1, 2026, to March 31, 2027.. Waaree’s global module order book exceeds 25 GW.
Commercial production on the new lines began on Oct. 29, 2026, following an expansion approved by Waaree Energies’ board of directors in April 2025. The additional capacity doubles the Brookshire facility’s manufacturing capacity and strengthens WSA’s ability to supply US solar developers, utilities and engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) contractors with domestically manufactured modules, according to the company.
Waaree said the expansion comes amid changes in US trade policy, including measures under Section 232, that are affecting the economics of imported solar modules. The company said its investments in domestic manufacturing are intended to strengthen its position in the US market.
Revenue from Waaree’s US manufacturing operations increased to INR 13 billion ($146 million) in the second quarter of fiscal 2027, from INR 7.32 billion a year earlier. The US domestic business accounted for 43.8% of the company’s INR 592 billion order book, up from approximately 36% at the end of the preceding quarter.
“Shifting trade policy has strengthened the case for local manufacturing, and that is exactly where we have invested,” said Sunil Rathi, director of Waaree Group. “With Brookshire now at 3.2 GW and Arizona expanding, we are serving American customers from American factories, and our US order book continues to grow every quarter.”
The expansion is part of Waaree’s strategy to manufacture solar products in both India and the United States to serve domestic and international markets.
Waaree’s consolidated revenue from operations rose 23.9% to INR 75.18 billion in the second quarter of fiscal 2027.
The company is also expanding its upstream manufacturing operations in India. It plans to increase its solar cell manufacturing capacity from 5.4 GW to 15.4 GW in fiscal 2027 and commission a 10 GW ingot and wafer manufacturing facility in fiscal 2028.

title: Yingfa Ruineng establishes 7.5 GW PV manufacturing plant in Indonesia - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
The facility is the Chinese manufacturer’s first overseas base. It will produce n-type TOPCon solar cells for Indonesia’s domestic market while also acting as a regional supply hub for Southeast Asia and the Middle East.
Patrick Jowett
03 Nov 2026
Markets & Policy
Asia-Pacific
Highlights
Manufacturing
Chinese solar cell manufacturer Yingfa Ruineng has unveiled a 7.5 GW solar cell manufacturing plant in Indonesia. The facility, presented at technology launch event hosted by Yingfa Ruineng’s subsidiary BCI, will produce n-type tunnel oxide passivated contact (TOPCon) solar cells.
A statement released by Yingfa Ruineng explains the facility is intended to serve as a regional supply hub for Southeast Asia, the Middle East and other international markets.
The company adds it will also support Indonesia’s
100 GW solar power program
alongside the country’s efforts to strengthen domestic manufacturing and local content.
“For project developers, contractors and module manufacturers, local cell production can offer shorter supply routes, closer technical coordination and greater flexibility in supply planning,” the statement explains. “BCI’s local capabilities are also intended to help Indonesian module manufacturers address [Indonesia’s official local content requirement] TKDN, subject to relevant product certification and regulatory requirements.”
The facility is Yingfa Ruineng’s first overseas manufacturing base, adding to its three in China. Together, the four bases have a combined effective capacity of 51.5 GW, according to figures released by the company, including 45.5 GW of n-type TOPCon capacity.
The launch event also highlighted Yingfa Ruineng’s half-cell passivation, multi-cut cell designs and back-contact (BC) solar cells. The company says it is advancing both its TOPCon and BC platforms and claims to have also completed an initial end-to-end fabrication process for perovskite/BC tandem solar modules.
Yingfa Ruineng
ranked second
for global solar cell shipments in the first half of 2026, according to PV industry research firm InfoLink, behind only Tongwei.

title: Batteries to dominate Belgium’s capacity remuneration mechanism - pv magazine Global
content:
Belgian transmission system operator
Elia Transmission Belgium
has published the
results of three capacity remuneration mechanism (CRM) auctions
, covering the 2027-28, 2028-29 and 2030-31 delivery periods. In line with the volumes set by the energy minister, it contracted the capacity required to help ensure Belgium’s security of supply. Supply exceeded demand in all three auctions, while batteries accounted for a significant share of contracted capacity for 2028-29 and 2030-31.
Introduced in the context of Belgium’s partial nuclear phaseout, the CRM provides financial support to market participants that make electricity capacity available. Open to the entire market and technology-neutral, it contributes to the country’s security of supply.
A total of 6.5 GW was contracted for 2027-28 through the various CRM auctions, at a total cost of around €200 million ($223.7 million) and a weighted average price of €30.944/MW/year. No additional capacity was contracted in the Y-1 auction. The scenario adopted by the energy minister had changed compared with previous auctions for this delivery period. After accounting for cross-border contributions and capacity available on the electricity market but not seeking to participate in the auction, the required volume fell to zero.
The Y-2 auction contracted 1.6 GW for 2028-29, bringing the total volume already secured for the delivery period to 5.8 GW. New batteries accounted for around 0.5 GW of the selected capacity. Some of these battery projects will enter operation earlier than stipulated in their multiyear contracts and will therefore be able to contribute capacity sooner.
Two-hour batteries accounted for just 5.98% of selected volumes, while four-hour batteries were favored, representing 31.74% of volumes, behind combined-cycle gas turbines. The auction cost around €34 million, at a weighted average price of €21.643/MW/year.
The Y-4 auction contracted 0.8 GW for 2030-2031. Including previously awarded long-term contracts, the total volume secured for this delivery period now stands at 4.9 GW. New batteries accounted for around 0.5 GW of the selected capacity, split between one-year and multiyear contracts. Following the same trend as in the 2028-29 auction, no two-hour batteries were selected, while four-hour batteries represented 61.75% of volumes, well ahead of other technologies.
Supply exceeded demand by 3.1 GW. The auction cost around €14 million, at a weighted average price of €18.143/MW/year.

title: Canadian province opens tech-neutral capacity call to replace coal - pv magazine Global
content:
Nova Scotia’s independent grid operator has opened a technology-neutral call for on-demand capacity, inviting battery storage, pumped hydro, long-duration storage and other projects to bid as the Canadian province prepares to shut its coal plants by 2030.
The Nova Scotia Independent Energy System Operator (IESO Nova Scotia) launched the request for qualifications on Oct. 30. It is open to projects of at least 10 MW in the province, with submissions due by Jan. 30, 2027.
Eligible technologies include battery storage, pumped hydro, long-duration storage, geothermal, biomass, thermal generation, hydrogen combustion, hydrogen fuel cells, small modular reactors and hybrid facilities. The call also includes requirements supporting Mi’kmaw participation and economic development.
“There is no single technology that can meet all of Nova Scotia’s future electricity needs. Different resources contribute in different ways to the grid’s reliability, and they come at different costs,” said Chris Milligan, vice president of planning and procurement at IESO Nova Scotia.
The operator said it has received feedback from more than 20 organizations. The final version of the call clarifies that hybrid projects, such as storage co-located with wind or solar, can take part. It also adjusts scoring to recognize a range of storage durations and broadens the development experience that counts toward qualification. IESO Nova Scotia has not said how much capacity it intends to procure.
Bids will be assessed alongside the operator’s separate gas procurement through energy system modeling to determine the most cost-effective mix. That tender, launched in July as IESO Nova Scotia’s first competitive procurement, seeks up to 600 MW from one or two 300 MW gas-fired plants in Pictou County that must be designed to switch to non-fossil fuels. Its deadline has been extended to Jan. 21, 2027. It targets commercial operation by July 2030 but will consider dates up to July 2032.
In September, IESO Nova Scotia said feedback that competing technologies should be considered more fully had contributed to its decision to accelerate and expand its storage procurement into the technology-neutral call. The operator expects qualified bidders to move to the next stage in spring 2027.
The operator said Nova Scotia needs new on-demand capacity to avoid rotating outages during low-wind periods, “which can last for days at a time.” Coal supplies about 40% of the province’s electricity, and provincial law requires coal to be phased out and 80% of generation to come from renewables by 2030.
The province’s Clean Power Plan calls for about 1,000 MW of new onshore wind, at least 300 MW of larger-scale solar and 300 MW to 400 MW of battery storage by 2030. Nova Scotia Power inaugurated
three 50 MW/200 MWh batteries
in September, and IESO Nova Scotia’s resource plan includes 250 MW of further battery procurement.
IESO Nova Scotia was created under the province’s More Access to Energy Act in 2024 and took over system planning, procurement and grid operations from Nova Scotia Power, the province’s main utility.
The province is also adding renewable generation. In September, it
launched a second round of its Green Choice renewable procurement program
, which allows large electricity customers to buy power from new renewable projects.

title: Fraunhofer ISE spin-off repurposes used e-scooter batteries for C&I storage - pv magazine Global
content:
German startup Eden Energy is developing commercial battery storage systems using retired e-scooter batteries that still retain much of their original capacity. The Freiburg-based spin-off from the Fraunhofer Institute for Solar Energy Systems (Fraunhofer ISE) has delivered its first 70 kWh storage system, built from 112 used batteries.
“With this storage capacity, we are initially targeting small and medium-sized enterprises in the region that already have a photovoltaic system but lack a storage solution,” said Florian Bierwirth, who previously worked in Fraunhofer ISE’s power electronics department alongside co-founders Daniel Seeger and Hannes Kurzmann.
The storage systems could also appeal to municipal utilities, as they can be used to optimize self-consumption, reduce peak demand, and facilitate electricity trading.
According to Eden Energy, around 1 million high-performance batteries from e-bikes and e-scooters are discarded in Germany each year, although many retain much of their original capacity. Unlike second-life batteries from electric vehicles, these smaller batteries have not been widely used for stationary energy storage, largely because of differences in battery designs, cell types, and battery management systems.
Eden Energy aims to address this challenge using power electronics developed at Fraunhofer ISE. “It allows for the interconnection of different storage units and enables communication across various modules, all without the need to dismantle the battery packs,” said Bierwirth.
Few other systems currently offer comparable flexibility when integrating batteries with different designs or levels of degradation. Exceptions include multilevel battery storage systems developed by companies such as Stabl and Sax Power.
Batteries retain more than 90% of original capacity
The 112 e-scooter batteries used in the company’s first storage system underwent initial screening before being connected. Eden Energy currently sources batteries primarily from large e-bike and e-scooter fleet operators, ensuring access to sufficient quantities of identical battery types.
In the future, however, the power electronics developed at Fraunhofer ISE are expected to enable the integration of different battery types. This requires adaptations to connectors, battery management systems, and communication protocols – a significant challenge given the wide variety of batteries on the market.
In the longer term, standardized communication protocols for battery storage systems and regulations governing the second-life use of mobile batteries in stationary applications will be needed.
Initial tests of 350 batteries conducted by Eden Energy highlight the potential for reuse. While the company had expected the batteries to retain around 80% of their original capacity, some retained well over 90%.
The results suggest that the batteries could remain useful in stationary storage applications, where they would be exposed to less mechanical stress, such as vibrations, and fewer temperature fluctuations.
Seeking additional pilot customers
Eden Energy’s technology also enables individual battery modules to be replaced while the storage system remains operational. The modules are monitored through a tracking system and sent to partner companies for recycling once they reach the end of their service lives.
According to Eden Energy, this modular approach turns a potential disadvantage into a technical advantage over conventional battery storage systems. By replacing individual modules, the company says it can maintain the system’s overall storage capacity at a constant level, even after 10 years of operation.
Eden Energy, which now employs three part-time staff in addition to its three founders, plans to scale its storage systems to capacities of up to 300 kWh.
The company is also seeking additional commercial pilot customers in the region. Under the state-funded “Mittelstand trifft Start-ups” (SMEs Meet Start-ups) program, participating businesses can receive a subsidy covering 50% of the cost of an EdenEnergy battery storage system.

title: Gokin unveils latest additions to back-contact PV module portfolio - pv magazine Global
content:
Chinese wafer and module manufacturer
Gokin Solar
has introduced a new single-glass solar module series for the Australian residential and commercial markets. The framed glass-backsheet panel features 108 N-type back-contact (BC) half-cells sourced from fellow Chinese manufacturer Aiko.
“We have a lot of partners like Jinko, Trina, Astronergy, and Aiko that we sell our wafers to, and in turn we buy cells from them,” Gokin Australia Manager Charles Guo said.
“Because we control our own wafers, we can buy these cells with no limitations. Our BC cells are from
and we source TOPcon cells from other partners.”
Guo said the arrangement allows Gokin to provide premium products for its customers with the company claiming its BC platform produces 6–10% more output than TOPCon products for the same installed area.
“Where the roof plane is the binding constraint, this differential directly reduces the number of modules required and the associated mounting and cabling labour,” Gokin said.
The BC GK-3-54HGF module series includes four variants ranging from 495 W to 510 W. All modules are Clean Energy Council (CEC) certified. Maximum module efficiencies range from 24.3% up to 25%, with a maximum system voltage rating of 1,500 V and a 25 A maximum series fuse rating.
The single-glass panel measures 1,800 mm × 1,134 mm × 30 mm and weighs 21.4 kg. For mechanical durability, the module is rated for a 5,400 Pa front load and 2,400 Pa back load, while the 3.2 mm tempered glass offers hail resistance capable of withstanding impacts up to 25 mm at 23 m/s.
The modules feature a black anodised aluminum frame, an IP-68 rated junction box, and are rated for operating temperatures of −40℃to +85℃.
Gokin backs the BC GK-3-54HGF module series with a 25-year product warranty and a 30-year linear performance guarantee covering a maximum first-year power degradation of 1.0% followed by an annual degradation rate of 0.35%, guaranteeing at least 88.85% of original nameplate output at year 30.
Guo said he expects the BC GK-3-54HGF module series to be available in Australia from early 2027.
The unveiling of the modules series coincided with Gokin announcing it had signed agreements with OSW, GBP, and Peak Energy.
The company said these partnerships mark a significant step in expanding Gokin’s footprint across the Australian market.

title: Grid-forming vs. grid-following in residential solar-plus-storage - pv magazine Global
content:
Scientists at the Bucharest University of Economic Studies in Romania have compared the performance of grid-following (GFL) and grid-forming (GFM) inverters in residential solar-plus-storage systems under low-inertia grid conditions and have found that GFM technology offers significant advantages in terms of grid stability, frequency and voltage recovery, islanding capability, and economic returns, with a relatively short payback period for the additional investment.
The researchers explained that most existing studies focus on control design, dynamic stability, and large-scale integration, with limited attention paid to country-specific economic assessments, particularly for prosumers in emerging electricity markets such as Romania. Their study addressed this gap by combining an analysis of GFM dynamic performance, including frequency stability, voltage regulation, rate of change of frequency (RoCoF), and islanding capability, with a techno-economic assessment based on net present value (NPV), internal rate of return (IRR), adjusted levelized cost of energy (LCOE), and payback period. It also identified an indicative transition point toward inverter-dominated operation based on installed-capacity trends and long-term Romanian grid scenarios.
For the technical comparison, the researchers used MATLAB/Simulink to model a 5 kW residential PV system coupled with a 10 kWh lithium iron phosphate battery. Both inverter configurations were evaluated under identical operating conditions using detailed electromagnetic transient simulations. Two disturbances were considered: a 1.2 kW load increase and a 20% voltage sag lasting 200 milliseconds. The performance indicators included frequency deviation, voltage deviation, stabilization time, and RoCoF.
The economic assessment compared capital expenditure, operating costs, self-consumption savings, grid export revenues, and energy arbitrage. It assumed a 15-year project lifetime, a 6% discount rate, and initial investments of €7,000 ($7,851) for GFL and €8,500 for GFM. The analysis also accounted for ancillary service revenues, avoided outage costs, battery degradation, and reduced renewable energy curtailment.
The researchers found that, under GFL operation, the system relies on external grid references and primarily optimizes self-consumption and energy storage. By contrast, GFM independently establishes voltage and frequency references, enabling active grid support and islanded operation. GFM also improves power-flow management, voltage regulation, frequency stability, and continuity of supply during outages.
The simulations showed that GFM reduced maximum RoCoF from 18.99 Hz/s to 6.34 Hz/s, a decrease of approximately 66% compared with GFL. Maximum frequency deviation fell from 0.62 Hz to 0.18 Hz, while frequency settling time decreased from 7.5 seconds to 3 seconds. Maximum voltage deviation also declined from 0.20 per unit (p.u.) to 0.08 p.u., with recovery time falling from 5 seconds to 2 seconds.
The economic analysis showed that GFM achieved an annual net cash flow of €1,142, compared with €615 for GFL, reflecting additional flexibility and resilience benefits. These included ancillary service revenues, avoided outage costs, reduced curtailment, and improved energy management. GFM also achieved a positive NPV of €2,591 and an IRR of approximately 10.4%, compared with an NPV of −€1,027 and an IRR of around 3.7% for GFL.
Although GFM had a higher conventional LCOE of €0.206/kWh, compared with €0.174/kWh for GFL, its adjusted LCOE fell to €0.118/kWh when flexibility and resilience benefits were included. Under the assumed economic conditions, the additional €1,500 investment required for GFM was recovered in approximately 2.85 years.
Sensitivity analyses showed that GFM remained economically attractive across the electricity-price, ancillary-service revenue, and battery-cost scenarios examined. However, the researchers noted that its profitability depends on access to flexibility markets, the economic value assigned to grid services, and assumptions that require further validation using seasonal operating data.
“Even under unfavorable conditions such as lower electricity prices, reduced ancillary service revenues or higher battery investment costs, GFM maintains positive profitability indicators and economic viability,” the scientists said. “In contrast, GFL remains significantly more sensitive to market variations and often fails to achieve attractive financial performance.”
The researchers said future work should investigate the coordinated operation of GFM-equipped prosumers, aggregators, and energy communities, as well as artificial intelligence-based adaptive control. They also identified integration with vehicle-to-grid systems, hydrogen storage, and peer-to-peer energy trading as potential research directions to improve grid flexibility and resilience.
Their findings are presented in the study “
Can grid-forming inverters pay off? A techno-economic analysis of photovoltaic and battery systems in low-inertia power systems
,” published in the

title: Huawei plans 5% to 15% price increases for solar, storage equipment - pv magazine Global
content:
Huawei Digital Power, the energy technology business unit of Chinese technology group Huawei, has notified customers of planned price increases of 5% to 15% across several solar and energy storage product lines.
In a customer notice dated Oct. 20 and reported by Chinese industry media on Oct. 29, the company outlined proposed increases of 5% to 15% for residential solar-plus-storage products, commercial and industrial (C&I) systems, and utility-scale PV inverters and related equipment. Grid-forming utility-scale energy storage solutions, including power conversion systems (PCS), face smaller increases of 5% to 10%.
Huawei Digital Power said it had absorbed some of the additional manufacturing costs through internal efficiency measures but could no longer maintain existing prices without compromising product quality, delivery reliability or service commitments.
The company did not specify an implementation date, saying price adjustments would be negotiated individually with customers.
Huawei attributed the planned increases to rising prices for commodities, printed circuit boards (PCBs) and memory components since 2025. Copper is widely used in power electronics equipment, including busbars, cables, magnetic components and transformers, while PCBs and semiconductors are essential to inverter control and power conversion systems.
Copper prices have risen sharply in 2026. London Metal Exchange cash copper prices exceeded $14,700 per metric ton in mid-October, according to market data compiled by the International Copper Association Australia. Higher prices and tighter supplies of electronic components have added to procurement pressures for equipment manufacturers.
Huawei Digital Power is the latest in a series of Chinese inverter and energy storage equipment suppliers to announce price increases since August.
In September,
Sungrow notified customers of price increases of 5% to 15% for PV inverters, storage converters and energy storage systems, effective Sept. 20
. The company announced increases of 5% to 10% for its string, modular and matrix inverter ranges, and 10% to 15% for medium-voltage grid-connected models.
Growatt subsequently announced increases of 5% to 10% for string inverters, storage inverters and battery systems, effective Oct. 8
. KSTAR also notified customers of increases of approximately 10% to 20% for selected energy products.
In August, Inovance Technology announced increases of 5% to 15% for energy storage power conversion equipment and related products. Kehua Digital Energy followed on Oct. 29 with increases of 5% to 15% across its product portfolio, effective Nov. 1.
The announced increases for inverters and power conversion systems contrast with continued pricing pressure in China’s solar module market. Industry pricing data showed further declines in some module quotations in October, reflecting differences in supply-demand conditions and manufacturing cost structures between solar modules and power electronics.

title: Japanese developer switches on solar-plus-storage plant with 327% oversizing ratio - pv magazine Global
content:
Japanese solar project developer Sun Village has announced the grid connection of a solar-plus-storage facility with a DC/AC oversizing ratio of 327% at an undisclosed location in Japan.
Described by the company as a “low-voltage, super-oversized” solar power plant with battery storage, the facility features 163.2 kW of installed PV capacity, a 253.3 kWh battery storage system and a 49.9 kW power conversion system (PCS).
In Japan, low-voltage solar projects typically have an AC output of less than 50 kW, while super-oversizing refers to installing PV capacity substantially above the rated output of the PCS. This configuration allows developers to increase electricity generation without expanding grid connection capacity.
Super-oversizing differs from conventional oversizing in its significantly higher ratio of installed PV capacity to inverter output, often exceeding 300%. By comparison, the average oversizing ratio for solar installations with capacities between 10 kW and 50 kW commissioned in Japan in 2024 was approximately 180.5%, according to the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry (METI).
“The plant is expected to sell approximately 222,000 kWh of electricity annually,” Sun Village said in a statement. “The DC-coupled configuration allows surplus electricity that would otherwise be curtailed during peak daytime production to be stored in the batteries and sold in the evening and at night, when solar generation declines.”
According to the company’s simulations, the system is expected to maintain a stable electricity output of 49.9 kW for approximately 14 hours. Under Japan’s
feed-in premium (FIP) scheme
, Sun Village will act as an aggregator, handling generation forecasts, power generation planning and battery operations, while selling electricity on the wholesale electricity market.
Such configurations could gain traction in Japan as developers seek to maximize generation from existing grid connections amid constraints on available grid capacity and rising interconnection costs. Combining heavily oversized PV arrays with battery storage could allow operators to capture electricity that would otherwise be lost through inverter clipping, while extending electricity exports beyond daylight hours.
Japan’s gradual shift from fixed feed-in tariffs to market-linked remuneration under the FIP scheme could also support wider adoption of solar-plus-storage projects. By storing electricity during periods of high solar output and selling it when wholesale prices are higher, developers could improve project revenues and reduce exposure to low midday electricity prices. However, the economic viability of super-oversized systems will depend on battery costs, electricity price spreads and the amount of otherwise curtailed generation that can be recovered.

title: Planar heat pipes reduce peak temperatures by up to 32 C in PV cooling tests - pv magazine Global
content:
An international group of researchers has developed and experimentally evaluated five prototypes of planar heat pipes for active cooling of PV modules. These heat pipes are intended to spread heat on the rear surface and feed a compact, actively cooled water sink.
“Unlike conventional solutions that primarily target bulk heat removal, the proposed concept utilizes planar heat pipes as thermal spreaders for temperature homogenization and hot-spot mitigation,” the group said. “Heat is collected over a large module area and transferred to a localized cooling region, reducing temperature gradients and local peak temperatures.”
The researchers constructed five planar heat-pipe prototypes measuring 1,650 mm × 1,000 mm, each comprising stainless-steel plates enclosing approximately 2 mm-high cavities filled with distilled water. Internal mesh, wire inserts, and fence-like supports facilitated liquid return and reinforced the structure, while epoxy adhesive sealed the evacuated chambers.
The five configurations differed in internal structure, plate thickness, and water content. “Model 1500” used crimped mesh for capillary liquid distribution and wire inserts to maintain plate spacing. “Sandwich light” combined two mesh layers with fence-like supports that formed vapor channels, while “Sandwich” used the same arrangement with thicker 1 mm plates instead of 0.5 mm plates. “Hybrid 1” alternated crimped-mesh and fence structures to balance liquid return and vapor transport. “Hybrid 2” retained this design but halved the water filling from 0.9 to 0.45 liters. All other designs used 0.9 liters of water.
An automated rig used 32 heating pads to simulate uneven PV heating at 50- 100 C. Prototypes were tested under natural convection at 30° and 45°, and localized water cooling at 45°, against references without heat pipes. Sensors and infrared imaging assessed heat transfer and temperature uniformity. Measured temperature reductions informed a simplified PV model using Riyadh weather data to estimate annual generation gains.
“The experimental findings revealed only minor differences in thermal performance between the five planar heat pipe models over the investigated operating conditions,” the team said. “In testing, peak surface temperature reductions ranging from approximately 8 C to 32 C were observed, depending on the prototype configuration and heating-pad temperature.”
According to the findings, when applying the test results to real-world conditions in Riyadh,  Saudi Arabia, active water cooling led to 2.2% to 3.6% more energy generation, primarily due to the active cooling system. However, the planar heat pipes’ temperature homogenization was estimated to provide a theoretical upper-bound benefit of up to 4.5%.
“The assessment indicated potential improvements in annual electricity production under the investigated assumptions,” the group concluded. “The results demonstrate that planar heat pipes are effective thermal spreaders for photovoltaic applications, particularly for reducing temperature gradients and mitigating hot-spot formation.”
The article “
Experimental evaluation of planar heat pipes with active cooling integration for photovoltaic thermal hot-spot mitigation
” has appeared in
Renewable Energy.
Researchers from Finland’s
Lappeenranta-Lahti University of Technology
, Germany’s
Friedrich-Alexander University of Erlangen–Nuremberg
, and Saudi Arabia’s company Samirock have contributed to the study.

title: Rayzon Solar to start production at 5.1 GW TOPCon cell facility in December, plans ingot-wafer manufacturing by 2028 - pv magazine Global
content:
Gujarat-based solar module manufacturer Rayzon Solar Ltd is set to commence production at its 5.1 GW TOPCon solar cell manufacturing facility in December 2026, with initial deliveries expected in the first quarter of 2027. The facility marks the company’s expansion beyond module manufacturing as it seeks to strengthen backward integration and reduce its reliance on imported solar cells.
Founded in 2017 by Chirag Nakrani and Hardik Kothiya, Rayzon Solar has currently an installed solar module manufacturing capacity of 11.3 GW.
The company said it remains focused on executing its manufacturing roadmap and building capabilities across the solar value chain despite a shift from IPO proceeds to debt financing amid market volatility.
Looking ahead, Rayzon Solar plans to further expand its upstream manufacturing operations with a proposed 5.1 GW ingot casting and wafer slicing facility, targeted for development by 2028. The company is in discussions with multiple state governments to evaluate incentives and finalise a suitable location for the proposed project.
“The commissioning of our 5.1 GW TOPCon solar cell manufacturing facility in December 2026 will mark an important milestone in Rayzon Solar’s journey towards deeper backward integration,” said the company’s co-founder Chirag Nakrani. “As we advance our cell manufacturing plans, our next phase of expansion will focus on a proposed 5.1 GW ingot casting and wafer slicing facility, targeted for 2028. We are engaging with multiple states to assess incentives and finalise the location for this proposed investment.”
Alongside its solar cell expansion, Rayzon Solar has completed an aluminium extrusion and anodising facility with an annual capacity of 19,800 metric tonnes for manufacturing solar module frames.
The company is also investing in research and development, with three patent filings over the past year. Its R&D programme includes work on tandem solar cell technology and nano-coatings for next-generation solar modules, with product launches targeted by 2028.
Hardik Kothiya, Co-Founder, Rayzon Solar, said, “Our strategy is centred on building a technologically advanced and increasingly integrated solar manufacturing ecosystem in India. By expanding from modules into TOPCon cell manufacturing, and subsequently exploring upstream integration through ingot and wafer manufacturing, we aim to strengthen domestic capabilities, reduce import dependence and enhance our competitiveness in global markets. Combined with investments in research and development, these initiatives reflect our long-term commitment to India’s renewable energy ambitions and the future of solar manufacturing.”

title: Vaillant unveils 20 kW propane heat pump for large buildings - pv magazine Global
content:
German heating technology manufacturer
Vaillant
has launched the aroTherm perform, a new monobloc air-to-water heat pump designed for large residential buildings, renovation projects and small commercial properties.
The new series is available in 15 kW and 20 kW capacity classes. According to the manufacturer, the larger unit can provide space heating and domestic hot water for newly constructed buildings of up to 1,200 m², renovated buildings of up to 750 m² and non-renovated properties of up to 500 m².
The heat pump uses propane (R290) as its refrigerant and can reportedly achieve a supply temperature of 75 C at an outdoor temperature of -10 C without auxiliary heating. At an ambient temperature of -15 C, it can still deliver supply temperatures of up to 70 C, the company said.
According to Vaillant’s technical documentation, the VWL 205/8.1 A S2 Q variant delivers a heating capacity of 11.2 kW and a coefficient of performance (COP) of 5.66 at A7/W35, corresponding to an outdoor air temperature of 7 C and a water supply temperature of 35 C. At A-7/W35, the heating output increases to 19.6 kW, with a COP of 2.6.
The series has an A+++ energy efficiency classification at a water supply temperature of 55 C. The seasonal coefficient of performance (SCOP) is reported at up to 5.44 for the 15 kW model and 5.35 for the 20 kW model at 35 C under average climate conditions.
The outdoor unit measures approximately 1,230 mm × 1,890 mm × 788 mm and weighs around 310 kg. It operates on a 400 V three-phase electrical supply.
The 20 kW version has a sound power level of 50 dB(A) under energy-related product (ErP) rating conditions, while its maximum sound power level is approximately 63 dB(A). Vaillant said its Sound Safe System technology and night operating mode can reduce noise emissions, with the latter providing reductions of up to 10 dB(A).
The manufacturer has also integrated its Flexible Space Function, designed to reduce installation restrictions associated with the safety zones required for propane-based heat pumps. The technology provides greater flexibility when positioning outdoor units near windows and doors, subject to applicable installation requirements.
The aroTherm perform system also incorporates Vaillant’s iQconnect control platform, which includes a 7-inch touchscreen, commissioning assistant, connectivity gateway and system controller. It supports over-the-air software updates, remote monitoring and control through the myVaillant app.
The control platform also enables integration with energy management systems and rooftop photovoltaic installations, allowing building owners to increase the self-consumption of locally generated electricity. Up to six heat pumps can reportedly be connected in a cascade configuration to serve buildings with higher heating requirements.
