title: SpaceX taps Qualcomm as Starlink prepares a huge nationwide 5G push
content: SpaceX plans to build a nationwide terrestrial 5G network in the U.S. for its Starlink Mobile service, deploying tens of thousands of base stations from 2027 through a new collaboration with Qualcomm.The Elon-Musk led space transportation company has picked Qualcomm’s Dragonwing cellular infrastructure platforms to support the network.. The technology will combine high-capacity radio and baseband processing with power-efficient computing to support large-scale cellular deployments.Under the multi-year agreement, Qualcomm will supply its Dragonwing QRU100 and QDU100 platforms, along with commercial-grade Layer 1 software for SpaceX’s planned nationwide terrestrial wireless network. The collaboration will support SpaceX’s development of an end-to-end base station architecture for its terrestrial network.The move expands SpaceX’s connectivity strategy beyond its satellite constellation. Starlink Mobile plans to combine terrestrial cellular infrastructure with satellite connectivity to provide a more integrated network for users across the US.Massive MIMO boosts capacityA key component of the planned network is Massive Multiple-Input Multiple-Output (MIMO) technology, which uses multiple transmitters and receivers to improve wireless communication.Starlink Mobile will deploy radio units with 64 transmit and 64 receive paths, known as 64T64R. The configuration is designed to improve network coverage, increase capacity and make more efficient use of available radio spectrum.Massive MIMO uses multiple antenna elements to direct radio signals towards users, rather than broadcasting them uniformly in every direction. This technique, known as beamforming, can help networks serve more users and handle greater data traffic within a given area.SpaceX has selected Qualcomm #Dragonwing Cellular Infrastructure solutions to support @Starlink Mobile’s nationwide terrestrial 5G network in the U.S. https://t.co/Up7LxbQz5o— Qualcomm (@Qualcomm) November 4, 2026Qualcomm’s QRU100 platform will provide integrated processing for the Massive MIMO radio units. Its QDU100 platform will handle Layer 1 processing, which manages the physical transmission and reception of data over cellular networks.The two platforms are designed to improve performance per watt across radio and distributed-unit processing. This could help reduce the energy requirements and operating costs associated with deploying and running thousands of cellular base stations.Network targets 2027 rolloutSpaceX plans to begin the nationwide deployment in 2027, with tens of thousands of sites expected to be installed over the multi-year agreement. The companies have not disclosed the financial terms of their collaboration.The planned infrastructure will complement Starlink’s satellite network, which provides connectivity in areas where conventional terrestrial networks have limited reach. Ground-based cellular stations could help deliver additional coverage and capacity, particularly in populated areas where satellite connectivity alone may not meet demand.The announcement also marks a commercial step towards Qualcomm and SpaceX’s longer-term vision for AI-native sixth-generation (6G) wireless infrastructure.Although the initial deployment will focus on 5G, Qualcomm said the platforms offer an adaptable foundation for future connectivity technologies and more intelligent network operations.For SpaceX, the partnership provides access to specialized radio and baseband technology as it develops its terrestrial network. For Qualcomm, the deal expands its role beyond mobile-device processors into large-scale telecommunications infrastructure.The companies have not provided a detailed deployment schedule or specified how many sites will become operational in the first phase.

title: Sunken WWII US cargo ship with 1,400 tons of explosives made safer
content: A sunken U.S. warship, SS Richard Montgomery, long regarded as a ticking time bomb because it still houses approximately 1,400 tonnes of unexploded ammunition onboard, has been made slightly safer eight decades after it sank.Engineers removed the ship’s three masts from the fragile wreck as experts feared they could collapse one day and potentially trigger an explosion.“The vessel was starting to lean and deteriorate, so they could see some of the structures around the mast starting to collapse,” said Nolan, an architect with marine salvage firm Resolve Marine Group that carried out the mast removal operation last month.Mast’s fall could trigger explosionThe mast had remained visible above the water near Sheerness, a coastal town about 50 miles (80 km) east of London on the Thames Estuary, since the ship sank in 1944.The fear is the masts could have fallen onto the cargo itself, causing it to detonate,” he added.Before the operation, his team completed extensive surveys to understand the wreck site using radar, magnetometers and sonar systems.Special tools were then used to carry out the delicate operation, and extra caution was exercised to avoid any vibrations while approaching the wreck that may set off the unexploded bombs still inside the wreck.Divers carefully cut through the masts with a diamond wire, taking turns as they worked on the fragile deck. Although the masts remained well preserved, officials said the surrounding steel structure had become “paper thin.”The exact munitions left onboard the ship, nicknamed Monty, are yet unknown. A defense agency report projected that more than 2000 cluster bombs, white phosphorus smoke artillery, and around 300 blockbuster bombs weighing nearly 2000 pounds (900 kg) were still on the ship.The wreck continues to pose a potential hazard to nearby communities, although experts have divided views over how severe the consequences of an explosion would be.A 2004 report suggested that the blast Some could cause a small tsunami, hurling debris nearly 1.8 miles (3 kilometers) into the air, “shatter almost every window in Sheerness” and devastate the town. However, David Alexander, an emergency planning expert at University College London, wrote in a 2019 paper that considerable uncertainty remains over the true level of risk posed by the wreck.Masts preserved at MuseumBecause of their historical significance, the detached masts have been transferred to the Dockyard Chatham, a maritime museum in Kent.UK maritime minister Keir Mather welcomed the operation and said that the masts had put “significant load on the structure and their removal has reduced that risk and supports the long-term safe management of the site.”Built in 1943 at Jacksonville, Florida, the World War II cargo ship was carrying about 7,000 tonnes of ammunition to Britain. It was due to anchor near Sheerness after passing through the Thames Estuary, but dragged its anchor and ran aground on a sandbank. Although the crew unloaded about half of the cargo, a crack in the hull ultimately caused the ship to sink, leaving thousands of tonnes of explosives on the seabed.Besides removing the mast, the British government has long kept the area around the U.S. cargo ship as a shipping exclusion zone. Since last year, the government has also issued a no-fly zone for the area, and these restrictions will remain in force, the government said in a statement.​

title: US ally tests 49-foot rocket to develop next-gen hypersonic weapons
content: France has successfully launched its SyLEx sounding rocket for the second time, marking the first operational flight of a system designed to restore the country’s sovereign suborbital testing capability. The November 4 launch was conducted from the Directorate General of Armaments’ (DGA) missile test center in Biscarrosse. The launch carried an experimental payload for the French military, supporting research linked to the development of its M51.4 strategic missile.SyLEx stands for Système de Lancement d’Expériences, or Experimental Launch System. Built by ArianeGroup under the direction of the DGA, it is designed to carry experimental equipment to altitudes of 200 to 400 kilometers (124 to 248 miles). The flight followed an initial demonstration on November 28, 2025, making this the system’s second successful launch.French Minister of the Armed Forces and Veterans Catherine Vautrin said the latest mission enabled experiments considered essential to the development of the M51.4 missile. A platform for high-altitude experimentsUnlike orbital launch vehicles, sounding rockets follow suborbital trajectories, carrying instruments and experimental payloads to high altitudes before returning to Earth. They provide researchers with access to atmospheric conditions and short periods of microgravity, making them useful for testing materials, sensors, and other technologies.According to ArianeGroup, SyLEx can carry payloads weighing up to 600 kilograms, with multiple experiments accommodated on a single flight depending on the mission configuration. The system is designed for both military and civilian applications, including atmospheric re-entry research and microgravity experiments.SyLEx comprises two rocket configurations. A single-stage and a two-stage version, supported by a dedicated launch pad. The November 4 mission used the single-stage configuration. ArianeGroup said it is now working with the DGA on the next development milestone: the two-stage version.Reportedly, the single-stage setup supports up to 300 kg (661 pounds) of research equipment.Supporting France’s strategic weapons programsThe latest launch is particularly significant for France’s nuclear deterrent. The M51 family of submarine-launched ballistic missiles forms the sea-based component of the country’s nuclear forces. The M51.4 is a planned evolution of the missile system, although French officials have not disclosed the specific experiments conducted aboard SyLEx or how they will contribute to its development.Vautrin also highlighted the rocket’s potential to support hypersonic demonstrators. High-altitude experimental flights can help evaluate technologies under demanding flight conditions, including those relevant to atmospheric re-entry and high-speed flight. However, the exact hypersonic research activities planned for SyLEx have not been detailed.Une nouvelle avancée pour notre dissuasion !Cette nuit, la @DGA a réalisé avec succès, depuis le site Landes à Biscarosse du centre d’essais et d’expertise DGA Essais de missiles, un tir expérimental de la fusée-sonde française SyLEx (système de lancement d’expériences),… pic.twitter.com/Pdg0R6Mskp— Catherine Vautrin (@CaVautrin) November 4, 2026ArianeGroup described the successful launch as a demonstration of its ability to provide a sovereign suborbital testing platform for major development programs. The company said it developed the system in less than three years for the DGA, the program’s contracting authority.Beyond defense, SyLEx could support civilian research and other European applications. Its payload capacity and ability to accommodate multiple experiments offer a platform for scientific investigations that require access to high altitudes.For France, the launch marks the return of a domestic capability for suborbital flights and high-altitude testing after several decades without one. With the single-stage version now through its first operational flight, the next step is developing the two-stage configuration, which could expand the range of missions the system can undertake.

title: US nuclear fusion reactor drive taps advanced plasma tech in new deal
content: Fusion energy has long promised virtually limitless, low-carbon power by mimicking the physical reactions that fuel the Sun. But turning laboratory experiments into working power stations remains a huge problem. Connecting that power to the electrical grid is one of science’s greatest engineering challenges.Now, an international pact aims to bridge that divide. Engineering firm Amentum has agreed to a strategic partnership with Japanese developer Kyoto Fusioneering. Under a new agreement, the two companies plan to combine their technical resources. Together, they will focus their work across Japan, the United States, and the United Kingdom. Their shared ambition is straightforward, which is to move fusion from experimental physics rigs into commercially viable power plants.Building a commercial reactor is fundamentally a systems challenge. Reactors require specialized internal hardware that can endure conditions hotter than the solar core. Combining industrial engineering with digital innovationKyoto Fusioneering supplies several of these critical technologies. These include plasma heating devices, advanced fuel-cycle equipment, and “breeding blankets” designed to generate tritium fuel within the reactor walls. Amentum, by contrast, brings the nuclear safety protocols, systems engineering, and large-scale delivery management needed to construct actual industrial facilities.“Building a fusion power plant will depend on collaborations like this one,” said Kiyoshi Seko, president and chief operating officer of Kyoto Fusioneering. He noted that Amentum provides the scale of nuclear engineering experience that developers urgently need as projects advance toward physical construction.A major focus of the venture will be digital simulation. The teams intend to deploy artificial intelligence and digital engineering tools to model plant operations. In theory, testing virtual designs will cut down development cycles, predict equipment degradation, and avoid costly trial-and-error during physical builds.The agreement comes amid rising momentum in Japan. Tokyo’s national fusion strategy has channeled substantial public backing into private demonstration ventures, giving firms like Kyoto Fusioneering a springboard to pursue joint ventures across western markets.“This collaboration comes at a pivotal moment,” said Mark Whitney, president of Amentum’s energy and environment division, arguing that combining their specialisms will directly tackle the delivery hurdles stalling commercial deployment.Extreme testing and reactor hardware trialsThe initiative builds on Kyoto Fusioneering’s growing international testing footprint. In October, the company joined forces with the DIII-D National Fusion Facility in California, a testbed backed by the US Department of Energy.Inside a fusion tokamak, operators face a brutal thermal dilemma. The core plasma must stay searingly hot for atomic nuclei to fuse, but the surrounding chamber walls must stay cool enough to avoid structural failure.To help resolve this, Kyoto Fusioneering is supplying heat-resistant tiles for an advanced “divertor”—the exhaust component that expels waste heat and impurities from the plasma chamber. Alongside researchers from Columbia University, engineers will run extended operational tests on DIII-D’s reverse-D-shaped plasma.Data gathered from those California trials will feed directly into US Department of Energy roadmaps. The measurements will help physicists assess plasma stability, validate computer models, and choose the resilient materials required for the world’s next generation of pilot plants.

title: Unitree G1 humanoid suffers 'heatstroke' on mountain climb in China
content: A Unitree G1 humanoid robot overheated and had to be carried down Mount Taishan on a stretcher during a robot competition in China. The incident occurred during the inaugural CMG World Robot Mount Taishan Competition in Shandong Province of China.Unitree later suggested that the robot may have entered the competition without proper tuning, sparking online debate about humanoid robot endurance and their ability to operate in demanding real-world environments.Recently, the robotics firm demonstrated its G1 humanoid autonomously sparring with a human using its UnifoLM-X2-1.0 AI model, showcasing advances in real-time robotic control.Humanoid endurance testedThe Chinese humanoid robot faced an endurance challenge after overheating during a competitive climb up Mount Taishan on November 2, highlighting the technical difficulties of operating bipedal machines for extended periods on demanding terrain.The G1 development version, also used in China’s Spring Festival Gala, overheated during the race, and its operator had to withdraw it. Event staff subsequently placed the humanoid on a stretcher and carried it down the mountain.The competition offered a demanding test of the robot’s mobility, balance, and thermal management systems. The course covered approximately 3.9 kilometers (2.4 miles), running from Hongmen to Zhongtianmen, with more than 3,100 steps and an elevation gain of around 600 meters (1,970 feet). Unlike demonstrations on flat indoor surfaces, the route required the humanoid to navigate uneven terrain and repeated stair climbs while maintaining its balance, Global Times reported. According to experts, such conditions place considerable demands on a humanoid robot’s mechanical and electronic systems. Walking involves continuous coordination between its joints, actuators, sensors, and onboard control systems. Climbing thousands of steps adds further demands, requiring repeated adjustments to leg movements, body posture, and balance as the robot negotiates elevation changes.Thermal management is another important consideration during sustained operation. Motors, actuators, computing hardware and power electronics generate heat while performing demanding tasks. If the heat produced exceeds the system’s ability to dissipate it, internal temperatures can rise and affect operating reliability. The incident therefore raised questions about how well humanoid robots can manage heat during prolonged physical activity rather than short demonstrations.G1 faces scrutinyUnitree suggested that the G1 development version may have entered the competition without tuning. The company did not provide further technical details about the overheating incident or identify the specific component responsible for the temperature increase.The robot’s withdrawal also prompted discussion about the distinction between demonstrating mobility and sustaining it under demanding conditions. A humanoid may successfully walk, run, or perform complex movements for relatively short periods, but maintaining those capabilities over extended operations requires reliable coordination between its mechanical hardware, control software, and thermal management systems.According to analysts, the Mount Taishan competition exposed these challenges in the field. The combination of thousands of steps, sustained movement, and significant elevation changes provided a different test from the controlled conditions typically used for laboratory demonstrations. It also highlighted the importance of evaluating robots beyond their ability to complete individual movements.The incident does not necessarily indicate a fundamental limitation of the G1 platform, particularly given Unitree’s suggestion that the development model may not have been properly tuned for the event. However, it illustrates why endurance, thermal stability, and adaptability are becoming important measures of humanoid robot performance.

title: Unmanned underwater vehicle hunts and neutralizes naval mines
content: An autonomous underwater vehicle has completed an end-to-end mine countermeasure demonstration, bringing naval forces closer to safer and faster mine-clearing operations. The exercise connected underwater search, sonar-based identification, and mine neutralization within one coordinated mission.HII and Thales conducted the demonstration using an integrated network of autonomous underwater systems and specialized mine-countermeasure equipment. The setup centered on HII’s REMUS 620 unmanned underwater vehicle (UUV) and Thales’ Expeditionary PathMaster architecture.The system followed a complete Find, Fix, Finish workflow. It allowed operators to detect potential mine threats and coordinate their identification and subsequent neutralization. The approach also reduces the need to send crewed platforms close to suspected minefields.Autonomous systems hunt minesNaval mines remain a persistent threat to maritime operations. They can restrict shipping routes, disrupt commercial traffic, and force warships to avoid entire areas. Traditional mine-clearing missions often involve several platforms and repeated deployments before operators can confirm a threat.The integrated system aims to shorten that process. Its REMUS 620 UUV carries Thales’ SAMDIS 600 multi-aspect sonar to scan the underwater environment for potential mines. HII’s command-and-control software manages the vehicle and connects its operations with Thales’ Expeditionary Portable Operation Center (ePOC).The ePOC serves as the mission’s central control hub. It hosts Thales’ mission management system and sonar analysis software alongside HII’s Odyssey mission management solution. Operators can monitor mission assets through a unified operational picture.Once the sonar detects suspicious objects, Thales’ software analyzes the collected imagery. Its Automatic Target Recognition technology helps operators classify and pinpoint mine-like objects. Human personnel retain oversight of the identification process and subsequent operational decisions.Finding and neutralizing threatsThe demonstration’s final phase brought in Thales Advanced Acoustic Concepts’ ANGLER underwater effector. An accompanying remotely operated vehicle (ROV) rapidly reacquired the previously detected objects. It then conducted visual inspections to establish whether they represented mine threats.The ANGLER system provides the means to engage and neutralize identified mines. This completes the mission chain without requiring sailors to approach suspected explosives directly.The exercise also tested automated launch and recovery capabilities. HII’s Sea Launcher system deployed and recovered the REMUS 620, which carried the SAMDIS 600 sonar. This adds another layer of automation to expeditionary mine warfare operations.Thales’ open Expeditionary PathMaster architecture also supports equipment from multiple manufacturers. Its NATO-compliant framework allows allied navies to combine different autonomous vehicles, sensors and neutralization systems. This could make it easier to adapt mine-clearing capabilities across different naval fleets.Faster mine countermeasure missionsThe demonstration expands on a 2025 integration exercise involving the SAMDIS 600 sonar and REMUS 620. That earlier work focused on sensor integration and underwater performance. The newer exercise incorporated mission management, automated target recognition, and mine neutralization.“Together, we are giving naval forces a path to conduct these demanding missions faster, at greater scale and with sailors farther from the mine threat,” said Duane Fotheringham, president of HII’s Unmanned Systems group.Sébastien Guérémy, Thales‘ vice president of Underwater Systems, said the exercise demonstrated how different autonomous platforms and specialized equipment could operate within one framework.The approach could help US and allied navies reduce personnel exposure during dangerous mine-clearing missions. It also offers a more flexible way to deploy underwater systems across expeditionary operations.

title: Japan’s proposed solar panel recycling rules would leave perovskite out for now
content:
Japan’s proposed solar panel recycling rules would leave perovskite out for now
Japan’s Ministry of the Environment and Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry (METI) have proposed leaving perovskite solar cells out of the scope of the country’s new solar cell waste recycling law, at least for now. The proposal was presented at the first meeting of a study group that is drafting the law’s subordinate regulations, held on October 30.
According to the ministries’ materials, organic solar cells, a category that includes perovskite, are not yet widespread and have no established recycling technology, so they are not proposed as a covered cell type. Flexible panels made with glass fiber are also proposed for exclusion, as no recycling technology or processing route exists for them yet. The ministries say the scope would be reviewed as technology progresses and markets develop.
The proposal would cover silicon, CIGS and CdTe modules, including double-glass and building-integrated panels, with a minimum weight of 3.7 kg per panel. Commercial owners disposing of 50 metric tons or more of panels would have to file a disposal plan in advance. The ministries estimate that this threshold would cover about 38% of the panel waste expected between 2027 and 2050. Final values will be set in the implementing regulations.

title: Researchers identify the spin mechanism that limits spin-polarized lasing in quasi-2D perovskites
content:
Researchers identify the spin mechanism that limits spin-polarized lasing in quasi-2D perovskites
Researchers at the University of Chinese Academy of Sciences’ Hangzhou Institute for Advanced Study, the Shanghai Institute of Optics and Fine Mechanics of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, and Huazhong University of Science and Technology have identified the mechanism that limits spin-polarized lasing in quasi-2D perovskites, and used it to demonstrate such lasing at low temperatures. Spin-polarized lasers could be used in secure communication, optical interconnects and other photonic devices, but they need spin states that last long enough to be sustained during lasing.
Quasi-2D perovskites are promising gain media because their structural asymmetry gives strong spin-orbit coupling. The same coupling, however, makes spins relax quickly. The team found that the dominant relaxation channel is the Bir-Aronov-Pikus mechanism, driven by electron-hole exchange interactions within excitons. To get around it, the researchers compared two organic cations in FAPbBr₃-based quasi-2D films: phenylethylammonium (PEA) and 1-naphthylmethylamine (NMA). NMA, with its lower triplet energy, captures triplet excitons, and its film showed only a fast spin decay, with a temperature-independent lifetime of about 7.2 ps. In the PEA film, triplet excitons remain in the perovskite layers, where reverse intersystem crossing activates a second spin-relaxation pathway (the D’yakonov-Perel’ mechanism). The result is a spin lifetime of 35.4 ps at 77 K, about five times the BAP-limited lifetime, which falls to 17.0 ps at room temperature.
The longer spin lifetime also helped the optical gain. Under circularly polarized excitation, the PEA film’s gain threshold dropped by half compared with linearly polarized excitation, and its peak gain coefficient rose 2.1-fold, from 1,410.5 to 2,983.7 cm⁻¹. The film showed spin-polarized lasing below 200 K, with a threshold 30.2% lower than under linear polarization. Above that temperature the spin lifetime becomes comparable to the exciton lifetime in the lasing regime, and the advantage disappears.
The team describes the lasing as random lasing from the polycrystalline film. It was optically pumped, and the key results were obtained at 77 K. They say the work contributes to the development of perovskite spintronic devices.

title: China’s energy storage fleet grows to 167 GW as utilization improves - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
The NEA reported 63% annual growth in installed capacity, alongside longer storage durations and improving utilization rates.
Vincent Shaw
05 Nov 2026
Markets & Policy
Batteries
Energy Storage
Highlights
A shift in China’s energy policy has dramatically changed the revenue model for battery storage, opening up revenue opportunities from capacity payments, arbitrage, and ancillary services.
China’s operational new-type energy storage capacity reached 167 GW/435 GWh at the end of September 2026, up 63% year on year, according to figures released by the National Energy Administration (NEA) on October 30.
The data were presented at the agency’s quarterly press conference on national energy developments. China’s new-type energy storage category covers electrochemical, compressed-air and other emerging storage systems, but excludes conventional pumped hydro.
Compared with 135.93 GW/351.12 GWh at the end of 2025, the latest figures indicate a net capacity increase of approximately 31 GW/84 GWh during the first nine months of 2026.
The NEA reported that average storage duration had increased to 2.61 hours, up approximately 0.27 hours year on year. Equivalent utilization hours reached around 915 hours during the nine-month period, an increase of approximately 10 hours compared with the same period of 2025.
The improvements suggest that China’s storage expansion is being accompanied by gradual changes in system configuration and utilization, rather than growth in installed capacity alone.
According to the NEA, the rapid development of new-type storage has been supported by government policies, technological innovation, industrial supply chains and growing demand for flexibility in the power system.
China’s combined wind and solar generating capacity exceeded 2.01 TW at the end of September, accounting for approximately 48.7% of total installed power capacity. As variable renewable generation expands, storage is increasingly needed to absorb surplus electricity, shift generation to higher-demand periods and provide fast-response grid services.
The structure of China’s storage market is also changing. Official figures for 2025 showed that independent energy storage facilities accounted for 51.2% of cumulative new-type storage installations. Projects rated at 100 MW or above represented 72% of installed capacity, while systems with durations of at least four hours accounted for 27.6%.
Lithium-ion batteries remained the dominant technology, representing approximately 96% of installed new-type storage capacity, although compressed-air, flow batteries and other technologies are gradually expanding their presence.
Market reforms are expected to reinforce these trends. China has been developing arrangements allowing independent storage operators to earn revenues from electricity trading, ancillary services and capacity remuneration, gradually reducing reliance on mandatory storage requirements associated with renewable projects.
Under the country’s 15th Five-Year Plan for power system development, new-type energy storage capacity is targeted to reach 300 GW by 2030, with greater emphasis on longer-duration systems, grid-forming capabilities and improved operational efficiency.
The growing contribution of storage is already visible in renewable-rich regional grids. In western Inner Mongolia, the grid operator reported 20.23 GW/70.47 GWh of operational storage capacity in October. During emergency dispatch operations, storage supplied up to 12.25 GW, equivalent to 33% of the grid’s electricity demand at the time.
Such examples illustrate how storage can provide substantial short-term balancing capacity in electricity systems with high renewable penetration. For other countries expanding wind and solar generation, China’s deployment offers experience in large-scale storage manufacturing, grid integration and centralized dispatch.

title: Congo launches energy supply study into economic zones, industries - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
The study plans to establish a pricing benchmark for the Congolese industrial market after the country’s industrial development minister referred to current solar electricity price offers as low as XAF 130 ($0.22)/kWh as ‘opportunistic’.
Patrick Jowett
05 Nov 2026
Markets & Policy
Research & Development
Commercial & industrial
Highlights
The Republic of the Congo is working on a study examining electricity supply needs for its special economic zones (SEZs) and industrial facilities.
The initiative, which aims to assess suitable supply solutions as the country’s electricity demand increases, was launched earlier this week by Michel Djombo, the country’s Minister of Industrial Development, SEZs and Private Sector Promotion.
It will be conducted under supervision of the Ministry of Energy and Hydraulics, implemented by the National Agency for Rural Electrification and supported technically by the United Nations Development Programme.
The study will compare four potential approaches to meeting industrial electricity demand: solar paired with battery storage, biomass and cogeneration using agricultural, forestry and agro-industrial residues, connections to the national grid where available, and hybrid energy systems.
It is also expected to establish a pricing benchmark for energy solutions in the Congolese industrial market.
Speaking at a launch event, Djombo questioned solar electricity offers priced at between XAF 130 ($0.22) and XAF 150/kWh, describing some as opportunistic, and said international comparisons would help establish fair and sustainable pricing.
The minister also highlighted the cost of relying on diesel generators during periods of electricity supply disruption, saying the price of generated electricity can reach almost XAF 200/kWh.
Electricity supply constraints are impacting industrial operators in the country, the minister continued, with some companies reportedly having to suspend production lines. Despite high diesel prices, Djomobo also revealed some industrial operators remain reluctant to commit to alternative energy solutions and are waiting for market conditions to become clearer.
The initiative plans to also examine different commercial arrangements for supplying industrial customers, including turnkey installations financed directly by businesses, financing services for equipment purchases and introducing independent power producers. It is also expected to identify bankable projects capable of attracting public and private investment.
The Africa Solar Industry Association (AFSIA) has identified 35.6 MW of operational solar in the Republic of the Congo to date, according to figures available in its project database, 27 MW of which is listed as unidentified C&I projects.

title: Hoymiles plans to establish inverter factory in Oman - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Chinese inverter manufacturer Hoymiles has signed a strategic agreement with three partners to develop solar, energy storage and manufacturing projects in Oman. The proposed $100 million partnership includes a renewable energy investment fund and a solar inverter manufacturing facility targeting Middle Eastern and North African markets.
Vincent Shaw
05 Nov 2026
Markets & Policy
Asia-Pacific
Inverters
Hoymiles’ HMS-2000 micro-inverter
Chinese solar inverter manufacturer
Hoymiles
has signed a four-party strategic cooperation agreement with PCG Global, the Oman Investment Authority (OIA), and Greenwill Asset Management to explore renewable energy investment, project development, and local manufacturing in Oman.
The agreement was signed in Beijing on Nov. 2, during Omani Sultan Haitham bin Tarik’s state visit to China. The signing ceremony was attended by the sultan and Mu Hong, vice chairman of the National Committee of the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference.
The partners plan to establish the Oman New Energy Ecosystem Cooperation Fund, targeting distributed solar and energy storage projects, integrated power supply solutions for artificial intelligence (AI) data centers, and investments in renewable energy-related industries.
Hoymiles said the fund will primarily invest in renewable power generation assets in Oman, supporting local project development and operations.
In a separate announcement, OIA said it had signed a preliminary term sheet with Hoymiles and PCG Global for a proposed partnership valued at OMR 38.45 million ($100 million). The agreement covers solar project development and a solar inverter manufacturing facility serving markets across the Middle East and North Africa.
OIA, Oman’s sovereign wealth fund, is expected to act as an anchor investor in the proposed fund and coordinate with local authorities and project partners. It did not clarify whether the $100 million represents the proposed fund’s capitalization or a broader investment commitment.
Singapore-based PCG Global will focus on project development, construction, and operations, drawing on the experience of Chinese distributed energy developer PCG Power. Its planned activities include commercial and industrial solar projects, off-grid power systems, and integrated energy solutions for AI data centers.
Hong Kong-based Greenwill Asset Management will oversee fund management and investment activities.
PCG Global was established by the team behind PCG Power. In July 2026, it secured pre-Series A funding led by GenZero, an investment platform owned by Singapore’s Temasek, to support its international renewable energy expansion.
The agreement comes as Oman seeks to diversify its economy and expand renewable power generation. The country aims to generate approximately 30% of its electricity from renewable sources by 2030.
A China-Oman joint statement issued on Nov. 2 also called for closer cooperation in solar and wind power, electricity transmission and conversion, energy storage, and AI.

title: Korean researchers build all-solid battery prototype with 235.13 Wh/L energy density - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
Researchers at South Korea’s Dongguk University have developed an anode-free all-solid-state thin-film battery featuring an ultrathin tin/carbon interlayer to improve lithium deposition and cycling stability. The 2.77-micrometer-thick prototype achieved a volumetric energy density of 235.13 Wh/L after 100 cycles, potentially paving the way for more reliable solid-state batteries.
Emiliano Bellini
05 Nov 2026
Research & Development
Batteries
Energy Storage
Solid-state batteries (SSBs) remain far from mainstream adoption in battery energy storage systems (BESS), as their potential benefits have yet to outweigh high costs, manufacturing challenges and limited commercial experience. Although they promise improved safety, higher energy density and potentially longer lifetimes, grid-scale storage has different priorities from electric vehicles. For BESS applications, affordability, cycle life, reliability, safety and bankability are more important than energy density, making established lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries difficult to displace.
SSBs also also face challenges related to uneven lithium plating and stripping during operation, which can cause interfacial instability, void formation and lithium (Li) filament growth. These effects can accelerate degradation, increase the risk of internal short circuits and compromise the long-term reliability required for stationary energy storage applications.
To address this challenge, researchers at South Korea’s Dongguk University have developed an anode-free all-solid-state battery (ASSB) in which Li from the cathode is deposited directly onto a bare current collector during the initial charging cycle, forming an anode in situ. “This architecture enhances volumetric energy density and simplifies fabrication, particularly for thin-film batteries. However, it is vulnerable to Li loss caused by uneven deposition, electrically isolated ‘dead’ lithium, or loss of contact with the solid electrolyte during stripping, compromising battery stability and capacity,” they explained.
The proposed innovation relies on what the research group describes as an anode-less thin-film battery platform using an ultrathin tin/carbon (Sn/C) interlayer, which is intended to eliminate the need for a conventional lithium-metal anode during manufacturing. Instead, a very thin coating of tin and carbon is applied to the anode-side current collector to control how lithium deposits during charging.
“Our interlayer acts as a seed for Li nucleation, promoting uniform Li plating and reducing Li loss and improving the reversibility of repeated charging and discharging,” said lead author Hyun-Suk Kim.
The battery prototype features a modified copper current collector coated with ultrathin layers of tin and carbon, an architecture the researchers identified as the most effective after evaluating several metal-based, carbon-based and hybrid coatings. Their experiments showed that the Sn/C combination offered superior control over Li deposition while improving stability at the electrode interface.
The improvement stems from the different functions of the two materials. Tin provides favorable sites for lithium to accumulate by lowering the energy required to initiate deposition, while carbon helps distribute the deposited lithium more evenly. This combination limits irregular growth and supports a more stable interface during repeated charging and discharging.
To further improve performance, the team added a small amount of metallic Li to the coated current collector before cycling. This “prelithiation” step creates a lithium reserve intended to compensate for irreversible losses during early operation, addressing a key limitation of anode-free battery designs.
The researchers assembled the modified current collector (Cu@Sn/C) with a lithium vanadium oxide (LVO) cathode and a lithium phosphorus oxynitride (LiPON) solid electrolyte. The resulting cell, measuring only 2.77 micrometers thick, delivered a volumetric energy density of 235.13 Wh/L at the 100th cycle, under a reported cycling rate of 0.01 C.
Microscopic analysis also provided insight into the battery’s stability. During the first lithium deposition, a three-dimensional structure containing tin and lithium–tin alloy developed within the interlayer. This structure helped accommodate the physical changes associated with subsequent cycling, reducing disruption at the interface and supporting more consistent battery operation.
“Our approach shows how interface engineering and lithium-inventory management can improve anode-less thin-film batteries,” said Kim. “This approach could support the development of ultrathin batteries for wearable electronics, IoT sensors, and medical devices, as well as scalable anode-less ASSBs for industrial-scale power.”
The novel SSB concept was presented in “
Pushing Energy Density Limits: Anode-Less Solid-State Battery Integrated With Amorphous Lithium Vanadium Oxide Thin-Film Cathode
,” published in
Advanced Energy Materials

title: Lebanon issues solar tender - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
A tender is open in Lebanon for the operation and maintenance of solar energy facilities on the Beirut River. The deadline to submit bids is January 7.
Patrick Jowett
05 Nov 2026
Markets & Policy
Asia-Pacific
Commercial & industrial
Utility-scale
State-owned electricity corporation Électricité du Liban (EDL) has opened a tender for the operation and maintenance of solar energy facilities on the Beirut River in Lebanon.
Available tender details
state a contract length of one year. The invite adds the public tender will be procured based on price, with EDL set to finance the works through its own funds.
Interested bidders can purchase tender documents from Lebanon’s Public Procurement Authority for a fee of LBP 5 million ($55.84).
The deadline for submitting clarification requests is Dec. 28, 2026, ahead of a deadline for submitting bids, which must be delivered by post, on Jan. 7, 2027. Each bid must be accompanied by a bank guarantee amounting to LBP 250 million.
EDL previously tendered a similar operation and maintenance contract in September 2025, but cancelled the procurement in June this year, citing the need for substantial amendments to the tender documents. The cancellation was published by the country’s public procurement authority in July.
In September, Lebanon
issued new rules
for the deployment of solar PV systems up to 1.5 MW in size, with plants smaller than 1.5 MW no longer requiring approval from the Ministry of Energy and Water. Instead, these installations must follow a defined municipal administrative and safety procedure.
Lebanon’s cumulative solar capacity reached 1,505 MW at the end of 2025, according to figures published by the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA), up from 1,081 MW a year earlier.

title: Malawi launches net metering scheme - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Malawi officially launched its net-metering framework, allowing eligible consumers to export surplus solar electricity to the grid in exchange for credits. Pilot implementation is underway, targeting 34 prosumers with approximately 3.9 MW of capacity, while nationwide rollout remains unconfirmed.
Emiliano Bellini
05 Nov 2026
Markets & Policy
Highlights
Malawi’s Ministry of Energy and the Malawi Energy Regulatory Authority (MERA) have launched a net metering scheme intended at supporting residential PV deployment across the country.
“The new regulatory frameworks would enable households and businesses to generate their own electricity and supply surplus power to the national grid, reducing reliance on conventional energy sources and promoting a cleaner, more affordable and sustainable energy future for Malawi,” said Minister of Energy, Jean Mathanga.
Implementation activities had already commenced in May 2026 under the Electricity Supply Corporation of Malawi (ESCOM). An initial pilot programme is expected to involve 34 eligible prosumers, with a combined generation capacity of approximately 3.9 MW. The United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) has also demonstrated the practical application of net metering through a solar PV installation connected to the national grid.
Although the regulatory framework has been introduced and pilot implementation is underway, the extent of nationwide commercial deployment remains unclear. In particular, the availability of the scheme to all eligible customers, applicable compensation arrangements and detailed administrative procedures require further verification.
Malawi’s electricity sector has historically faced challenges related to grid instability, dependence on hydropower, renewable energy curtailment and reliance on costly diesel backup generation. To address these challenges and facilitate greater integration of renewable energy, the country has recently invested in grid-scale energy storage infrastructure.
In July 2026, Malawi inaugurated its first utility-scale battery energy storage system (BESS), located in Kanengo, Lilongwe. The facility has a capacity of 20 MW/40 MWh and was developed by ESCOM with support from the Global Energy Alliance for People and Planet (GEAPP), including $20 million in grant financing.
According to the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA), the country had 105 MW of installed PV capacity at the end of 2025.

title: Pairing residential heat pumps with potassium carbonate-based thermochemical storage - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
U.S. researchers have found that combining residential heat pumps with thermochemical energy storage could reduce electricity demand during cold spells. Improved storage efficiency and heat pump performance could increase the contribution of thermal storage in highly decarbonized power grids.
Lior Kahana
05 Nov 2026
Research & Development
Heat pumps
Residential
Illustration of the system
A research team at
Pennsylvania State University
in the USA evaluated residential heat pumps paired with thermochemical energy storage (TCES) for long-duration energy storage. The researchers aimed to determine whether storing heat ahead of cold spells could reduce heating-related electricity demand when heat pumps become less efficient and the grid faces greater pressure.
“In this paper, we model a TCES system using potassium carbonate (K₂CO₃) as the thermochemical material (TCM),” the group explained. “This system can be thermally charged by an electric heat pump well in advance and discharged to meet the building’s heating load during the heating season. The optimal operation is assessed during the most stressful time of the heating season, based on projections for 2050.”
The researchers used simulation and linear optimization to evaluate an air-source heat pump coupled with potassium carbonate-based TCES and a battery in a 220.82 m² single-family home under New York City conditions. Hourly grid projections for a 95% decarbonized electricity system in 2050 were translated into a varying building electricity-demand limit.
The TCES model represented heat storage through salt dehydration and heat release through hydration, with approximately 80 C water required for charging and 35 C water supplied to radiant heating during discharge. The team further optimized hourly operation to minimize electricity consumption while meeting heating demand and respecting the electricity limit.
Reference charging/discharging efficiencies were 45%/80% for TCES and 95%/95% for the battery. Across 96 simulations, they varied heat-pump performance, TCES specific heating power, and charging efficiency to assess their effects on required storage capacities.
According to the results, the reference system required 68 kWh of thermal storage and 168 kWh of battery capacity, with batteries providing most of the storage response. Higher warm-weather heat-pump coefficient of performance (COP), improved TCES charging efficiency, and greater specific heating power favored thermal storage, while better cold-weather COP reduced both storage requirements. In the scenario most favorable to thermal storage, the optimized TCES capacity requirement was 894 kWh.
“These findings suggest two potential pathways for future researchers and manufacturers to enable efficient, long-duration energy storage responses from heat pumps and TCES systems,” the academics noted. “The first approach involves increasing TCES’s charge efficiency from 45% to 65%, while the second involves enhancing the heat pump’s COP by at least 25%, even if it degrades in cold climates.”
The researchers said further development of the proposed configuration could focus on enhancing the thermal storage system’s specific heating power. Such advances could enable TCES to provide a greater share of heating demand during periods of grid stress, reducing reliance on battery storage. However, the viability of the combined system would depend on improvements in component performance and the ability to integrate thermal storage with residential heating systems.

title: Revolta installs first 10 kWh sodium-ion home battery in Germany - pv magazine Global
content:
Applications & Installations
The German startup has commissioned its first customer system in an unusual place, with further pilot installations planned across Germany in the coming weeks.
Tristan Rayner
05 Nov 2026
Applications & Installations
Batteries
Energy Storage
Residential
Frankfurt-based Revolta has installed and commissioned its first sodium-ion home battery at a customer property near Aschaffenburg, Germany.
The high-voltage system, oeprating at a nominal voltage of 450 V, comprises five battery modules with a combined capacity of 10 kWh. While not setting any records for installation size, the sodium-ion storage system rollout continues and provides both Revolta and the industry a look at customer site usage, with operating data to follow.
The property already has around 20 kW of solar PV and a small hydroelectric plant housed in a former mill. The hydro plant has supplied the family with electricity since 2017.
According to Revolta, the owner had been waiting specifically for a suitable sodium-ion home battery, with greater energy independence given as the motivation. Revolta team members Julian Mattheis and Florina Thaler carried out the installation and commissioning.
Each 2 kWh battery module weighs 18.7 kg and has IP64 protection according to the data sheet, with the installation using an SMA inverter. Each module uses only three battery cells, and batteries are charged and discharged at 0.4 C (or 2.5 hour power duration). In this 10 kWh configuration, a maxium 4 kW power output could be expected.
Energy density is published at 141 Wh/l, 107 Wh/kg.
Further installations at selected customer sites across Germany are planned over the coming weeks. Revolta is supplying pilot customers with an additional measuring device at no charge to collect data on how the systems perform in daily operation. The findings will feed into development of its battery management system and firmware.
The company describes the installation as the start of its commercial launch, although the rollout remains at the pilot stage. Its announcement did not disclose pricing, rated power, cycle life or efficiency figures.
Revolta notes it is sold out for 2026, but offers a resevation for 2027. It publishes a list price of €599 ($672.5) per 2 kWh module, and lists a price for give modules for the 10 kWh installation at €2,995.

title: What Class A reveals about solar PV module fire performance - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
When it comes to solar PV module safety, it’s important to understand how Class A designations differ. Any Class A claim must identify the standard used.
05 Nov 2026
Technology & Products
solar modules
While two solar modules can carry the same Class A designation, they can differ in their fire performance. The shared label can conceal differences that matter for the safety of the building below.
Class A is a defined classification reached through prescribed test criteria, and any Class A claim must identify the standard used. It should not automatically be interpreted as “fireproof”, nor does the classification itself tell a potential user how far beyond the pass threshold a particular solar module performed.
The first distinction is what the test measures: resistance to an external fire or the product’s contribution to fire development.
Under UL 790, Class A describes performance under severe external fire exposure. It does not classify the module’s materials as non-combustible.
European standards assess a product’s contribution to fire development under EN 13501-1 and a roof’s response to external fire under EN 13501-5. UL 790 Class A does not establish compliance with either; each requires separate evidence.
Even under UL 790, flames can spread farther across one module than another and both still pass Class A. Buyers need measured test results to compare them. A “pass” alone does not show how close either came to the limit.
Fire-resistant glass is only part of the design
A claim about fire-resistant glass says little about how the complete solar PV module behaves. The encapsulation beneath it can contribute to fire development, so flame-retardant materials also have a role in limiting fire propagation. Electrical faults create ignition risks that the glass does not prevent.
Cell-level current management can limit hot spots under shading, and reinforced electrical connections can reduce fault and arcing risks. A complete assessment of module fire safety must therefore examine both its response to external fire and the design features that reduce the risk of a fire starting within it.
LONGi’s Hi-MO X10 Guardian Fire-Resistant solar module incorporates these features alongside fire-resistant glass. The module passed TÜV Rheinland’s UL 790 Class A spread-of-flame and burning-brand tests. The burning source did not penetrate the module or roof covering, and the module did not sustain flaming. The test specimens were randomly selected from a normal production batch.
The Hi-MO X10 Guardian Fire-Resistant module also achieved Class B under EN 13501-1 for reaction to fire and passed testing for B ROOF (t4) under EN 13501-5 – the highest external roof-fire performance classification within the t4 method.

title: Agricultural solarisation presents 116 GW opportunity for India’s domestic solar manufacturing industry - pv magazine Global
content:
India’s agricultural sector can absorb an additional 116 GW of solar modules, creating a significant opportunity for domestic manufacturers—according to a new report by the Indian Solar Manufacturers Association (ISMA).
Titled “Powering the Farms, Building the Factory (PM-KUSUM: Solarising Agriculture and Strengthening Domestic Manufacturing,” the report was launched at the Bharat RE Summit on 2 November 2026. It highlights the potential of agricultural solarisation to support India’s clean energy transition while creating sustained demand for domestically manufactured solar modules and cells.
With nearly 2.3 crore irrigation pumps across the country, solarisation presents a substantial opportunity to expand the domestic solar manufacturing market.
According to the report, India’s agricultural sector could generate demand for an additional 116 GW of solar modules, comprising 100 GW from grid-connected pumps and 16 GW from diesel pumps, excluding those in groundwater-stressed areas.
The report highlights the growing momentum of PM-KUSUM, which added a record 7.6 GW of solar capacity in FY 2025–26, with over 28 lakh irrigation pumps solarised by July 2026. It also underscores the role of the Domestic Content Requirement (DCR) under Components B and C in driving demand for Indian manufacturers. By October 2026, 13.8 GW had been installed under these components, meeting nearly two-thirds of the 20.8 GW of demand for domestically made solar cells and modules originally projected.
Agriculture is India’s third-largest power consumer. It accounted for
of the country’s electricity consumption in FY 2024. To keep irrigation affordable, tariff subsidies billed by DISCOMs doubled from INR 1.21 lakh crore in FY20 to INR 2.41 lakh crore in FY25. Solarising agricultural pumps and feeders can help improve power availability for farmers while supporting more sustainable energy use.
Commenting on the findings, Amit Manohar, Secretary General, ISMA, said, “PM-KUSUM has emerged as an important link between India’s agricultural development and domestic solar manufacturing ambitions. The estimated 116 GW of additional module demand from the agricultural sector presents a significant opportunity for Indian manufacturers. Sustaining this momentum will require continued policy support, adherence to domestic content requirements and a predictable project pipeline to encourage investments, strengthen the domestic supply chain and expand manufacturing capabilities.”
The report recommends retaining DCR provisions, establishing clear state-wise targets and multi-year tender pipelines, and strengthening implementation models that facilitate land access, clearances and grid connectivity. It also calls for greater focus on upstream manufacturing capabilities, including wafers and ingots, to deepen India’s domestic solar manufacturing ecosystem.

title: JA unveils 510 W back-contact PV module with 25.5% efficiency - pv magazine Global
content:
China-headquartered solar manufacturer
made the Australian debut of its HyperGen Pro solar module and JA ESS 125 kW / 261 kWh liquid-cooled commercial and industrial (C&I) battery energy storage system at All Energy Australia 2026.
Designed
for the Australian market, the HyperGen Pro features a 1,762 mm module format. The white variant delivers up to 510 W of power output at a maximum efficiency of 25.5%, while the all-black version offers up to 505 W at 25.3% efficiency.
The HyperGen Pro is based on JA ‘s Hycium n-type back-contact cell technology, which positions all electrodes on the rear of the cells, eliminating front-side grid lines. Combined with zero-busbar (0BB) interconnection technology and a full-screen design, the architecture increases the light-receiving area while providing a uniform appearance, particularly in the all-black version.
JA said the HyperGen Pro weighs 12% to 14% less than comparable dual-glass modules of the same format, reducing rooftop structural loads, improving heat dissipation and allowing single-person handling. The lighter design makes the module suitable for commercial and industrial buildings with limited roof load capacity.
The module has an HW4 hail-resistance rating and can reportedly withstand hailstones up to 40 mm in diameter, addressing reliability concerns in hail-prone regions such as Victoria, New South Wales and southeast Queensland.
A chemically etched, micro-textured glass surface converts specular reflection into diffuse reflection, reducing glare and addressing reflected-light concerns in urban environments.
The HyperGen Pro has a power temperature coefficient of −0.26%/C. JA Solar specifies first-year degradation of 1%, followed by annual linear degradation of 0.35%.
The module also incorporates a bypass design enabled by its back-contact cell architecture to mitigate power losses under partial shading and reduce hot-spot temperatures. The feature is designed to improve performance under common rooftop shading conditions caused by trees, chimneys and bird droppings.
JA Solar East Asia and South Pacific Region Vice President Daniel Li said Australia is one of the world’s most demanding rooftop solar markets.
“[It has]
intense solar irradiance
, challenging rooftop installation conditions, frequent hailstorms and a rapid shift towards integrated solar-plus-storage solutions,” Li said. “HyperGen Pro was developed with these conditions in mind, combining a lighter design, enhanced hail resistance and reliable performance in high temperatures.”
JA exhibit at All Energy Australia 2026 |
Image: JA
JA ESS: 125 kW / 261 kWh Liquid-Cooled C&I Energy Storage
The JA ESS liquid-cooled C&I energy storage system combines multiple safety measures, energy efficiency and intelligent operation and maintenance (O&M) capabilities.
Safety is supported by millisecond-level insulation monitoring, a three-tier fire and explosion protection architecture, and real-time battery pack monitoring. Working together, these measures enable early detection of potential thermal runaway risks and provide multiple layers of protection throughout system operation.
The system uses long-life lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries and achieves round-trip efficiency of up to 88%. Its liquid-cooling design also reduces auxiliary power consumption by 10%, helping improve overall system efficiency and long-term project economics.
For ongoing operations, built-in AI-powered predictive maintenance is designed to minimise unplanned downtime and simplify fault management. According to JA, these capabilities can reduce downtime by up to 90% and enable more than 90% of system faults to be resolved remotely. A modular design further simplifies on-site inspection and component replacement, helping reduce maintenance requirements and operating costs over the system’s lifetime.
DeepBlue 5.0
JA also showcased the DeepBlue 5.0 n-type TOPCon series at All Energy, extending its module offering across residential rooftops, commercial and industrial installations, and utility-scale projects.
For residential applications, the 485 W JAM48D51 LR all-black module combines Tri-Cut cell architecture with Bycium+ 5.0 cell technology and 20-busbar (20BB) current collection, delivering a 0.25% improvement in low-light output.
For larger commercial, industrial and ground-mounted installations, JA presented the 550 W JAM54D50 GR and 670 W JAM66D50 GB modules. The 670 W model offers a bifaciality of 85% ± 5%, a power temperature coefficient of −0.26%/C, and a degradation rate of 1% in the first year, followed by 0.35% annually thereafter.
At All Energy Australia 2026, JA received SunWiz’s “#1 Win Rate — Panel Proposal to Sale” award and was also recognised as a Top Solar Company.

title: Johnson Controls launches industrial ammonia heat pump - pv magazine Global
content:
US-based heating and cooling specialist
Johnson Controls
has launched the Frick HeatPAC Reciprocating Ammonia Heat Pump, an industrial heating system designed to recover waste heat from ammonia refrigeration installations.
The heat pump is intended for food and beverage processing facilities, where recovered heat can be used to produce hot water for pasteurization, sanitation, and space heating. According to the manufacturer, the system can be up to seven times more energy efficient than a natural gas boiler in typical applications, based on internal modeling.
The new product offers heating capacities ranging from 200 kW to 2MW and can deliver hot water at temperatures between 54.4 C and 87.8 C. It uses ammonia (R717) as a refrigerant, with a minimum refrigerant charge of approximately 39.5 kg.
The system is based on a Mark 5 Sabroe reciprocating compressor platform and features a fully welded plate-and-shell condenser with an integrated desuperheater, designed to achieve higher water temperatures while reducing the equipment footprint.
It also incorporates two-stage oil separation technology to maintain heat exchanger performance, a crankcase ventilation system to protect against liquid slugging, and a variable-frequency drive with a 4:1 turndown ratio to improve part-load operation.
The factory-assembled and pre-tested units feature a Frick Quantum HD controller with Unity architecture. The control system includes a 15-inch touchscreen and can be integrated with existing plant control systems and refrigeration equipment, enabling coordinated operation and remote access.
The manufacturer has not disclosed a rated coefficient of performance (COP), electrical input, unit dimensions, weight, or operating pressure limits for the new model in its launch announcement.
Johnson Controls said the standardized design of the new FRICK HeatPAC can reduce upfront investment costs and shorten delivery times by several weeks compared with conventional engineered-to-order industrial heat pumps.
“As energy costs continue to rise, waste heat is becoming an increasingly valuable and often untapped resource for food and beverage producers,” said Micah Lehman, product manager at Johnson Controls. “HeatPAC applies Johnson Controls deep thermal management expertise to help customers put energy they have already generated back to work.”
The manufacturer also provides its Frick Coolware selection software to estimate heat recovery requirements, system efficiency, operating costs, and potential savings compared with conventional heating equipment.
In a modeled application involving a cheese production facility requiring 2 MW of hot water at 60 C, the company estimated that the heat pump could reduce annual energy costs by up to 40% compared with natural gas boilers. The estimate depends on the energy prices and operating assumptions used in the simulation, the company said.
Johnson Controls also offers other ammonia-based heat pumps under its Sabroe brand.
Its HeatPAC HPX range, for example, comprises 13 standard models with heating capacities from 300 kW to 2.7 MW and hot water temperatures of up to 90 C. The HPX systems use high-pressure reciprocating compressors designed for differential pressures of up to 40 bar and design pressures of up to 60 bar

title: Researchers recover rooftop PV tilt, azimuth from power data - pv magazine Global
content:
An international research team has developed a method to determine the tilt and azimuth of rooftop PV arrays using operational power data. Accurate orientation data is essential for estimating electricity generation and detecting faults, but installation records are often missing or incorrect, while site inspections are impractical for large PV portfolios.
“This study provides a method to recover panel tilt and azimuth from operational power data while accounting for partial shading and the geometric limit at low tilt,” corresponding author Hanrong Huang told
pv magazine
. “We tested it on 17 commercial rooftop systems in Australia with independently verified orientations. It offers a practical way to fill in missing or wrong tilt and azimuth records without a site visit.”
The researchers developed and tested the method using operational data collected in 2025 from commercial rooftop PV systems in Australia. The dataset included DC power measurements recorded at five-minute intervals for each maximum power point tracker (MPPT). They used pvlib clear-sky modeling and ERA5 weather data to estimate solar irradiance on panels at different tilt and azimuth angles.
After selecting periods with high direct irradiance and sufficient morning and afternoon measurements, the researchers used an optimization algorithm to identify the orientation that best matched the measured power output. The algorithm also adjusted effective system capacity to account for power losses.
The team also compared two fitting metrics, R² and Huber loss, and assessed the effects of shading, low tilt angles, data resolution, module temperature, and inverter clipping on accuracy. R² measures how well modeled power output matches observed data, while Huber loss reduces the influence of outliers, such as power deviations caused by shading, when fitting the model.
“On unshaded systems the method recovered tilt to within about 2° and azimuth to within about 4° median error using only DC power data and site coordinates,” said Huang. “Because it works on DC data, it can also find the orientation of each array separately at the MPPT level.”
Clear-sky modeling consistently outperformed ERA5, which resulted in median tilt errors of 10° to 12° and azimuth errors of 48° to 62° for unshaded systems. Shading increased clear-sky azimuth errors from 4° to 35° when using Huber loss and from 15° to 27° when using R². At tilt angles below 5°, azimuth was difficult to determine because panel orientation has little effect on incident irradiance, limiting the impact of such errors on estimated electricity generation.
“Our next step is to reduce the effect of partial shading on recovery accuracy, which is the main limitation of the method,” Huang said. “We also want to make it robust to other real operating conditions such as inverter clipping and tripping so that it can be applied reliably at large scale.”
The researchers presented their findings in “
Recovering rooftop photovoltaic array tilt and azimuth from operational power data
,” published in
Solar Energy
. The research team included scientists from the
Chinese Academy of Sciences
, Australia’s
University of New South Wales
Diagno Energy
Global Sustainable Energy Solutions

title: Spain approves methodologies to strengthen electricity system cybersecurity - pv magazine Global
content:
Spain’s National Commission on Markets and Competition (CNMC) has approved two European methodologies for assessing cybersecurity risks and classifying cyberattacks in the electricity system, under the European network code on cybersecurity for cross-border electricity flows.
The methodologies establish common criteria for identifying, analyzing and assessing cybersecurity risks, as well as determining the severity and impact of incidents. They were developed under Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/1366 of March 11, 2024, which establishes cybersecurity rules for cross-border electricity flows.
The risk assessment methodology will serve as the basis for cybersecurity assessments at national, regional and EU levels. The assessments will identify existing threats and evaluate their potential impact on the operational security of the electricity system and cross-border electricity exchanges.
The methodology will also establish indicators and thresholds to identify entities that could have a high or critical impact on the electricity system in the event of a cybersecurity incident. These could include system and market operators, transmission system operators, distribution companies, electricity producers, suppliers and aggregators.
Competent authorities will designate entities classified as having a high or critical impact, which will be subject to specific cybersecurity obligations based on their classification.
Classification of cyberattacks
The second methodology establishes a common framework for classifying cyberattacks according to their severity and impact, and determining which incidents must be reported. It aims to facilitate information sharing and coordination among operators and national authorities.
The harmonized classification is particularly relevant for incidents with potential cross-border impacts, allowing common criteria to be applied to their detection, reporting and management.
Entities classified as having a high or critical impact will be required to comply with cybersecurity requirements within the deadlines established by the network code.
These requirements include conducting risk assessments, implementing cybersecurity controls, establishing cybersecurity management systems, sharing information, and preparing for and managing cybersecurity crises.
The two methodologies were developed by the European Network of Transmission System Operators for Electricity (Entso-E) in collaboration with the EU Distribution System Operators Entity (EU DSO Entity). The proposals subsequently underwent consultation and coordination among the competent authorities of EU member states.

title: Tokyo tests solar-powered hydrogen production at high-rise office complex - pv magazine Global
content:
Nippon Steel Kowa Real Estate, Sumitomo Life Insurance and Obayashi Corp. are implementing a green hydrogen production and power generation project at Shinagawa Intercity, a high-rise office and commercial complex in Tokyo’s Minato ward.
The project is the first to receive funding under the Tokyo Metropolitan Government’s support program for the practical implementation of green hydrogen production.
The system uses electricity generated by rooftop solar panels to produce hydrogen through electrolysis. The hydrogen is stored using a hydrogen-absorbing alloy and subsequently converted into electricity by fuel cells when needed. The electricity will be used to power lighting in selected common areas of the complex.
An energy management system (EMS) will coordinate the operation of the PV array, battery storage, hydrogen production equipment, hydrogen storage units and fuel cells. The integrated system is designed to address the mismatch between solar electricity generation and building demand.
The companies have not disclosed the installed PV capacity, electrolyzer capacity, hydrogen storage volume or fuel cell power output.
Separately, the companies have introduced an off-site physical corporate power purchase agreement (PPA) to supply Shinagawa Intercity with solar electricity from external generation facilities.
The agreement is expected to supply approximately 3 GWh of renewable electricity annually through the existing grid, with an estimated reduction in carbon dioxide emissions of around 1,200 metric tons per year.
The Shinagawa Intercity complex includes offices, retail facilities and a multipurpose hall. It occupies a site of approximately 34,388 square meters and has a total floor area of around 337,126 square meters.
Nippon Steel Kowa Real Estate is a Japanese property developer and real estate management company specializing in office buildings, residential properties and mixed-use developments. Sumitomo Life Insurance is one of Japan’s major life insurance providers, with additional investments in real estate and other assets. Obayashi Corp. is a Japanese construction and engineering group active in building construction, civil engineering, infrastructure development and renewable energy projects.

title: U.S. solar PPA prices rose in Q3 as Section 232 tariffs began to take effect - pv magazine Global
content:
Power purchase agreement (PPA) prices for solar projects in North America experienced a 4.9% quarter over quarter increase in the third quarter of 2026, marking a return to an upward trend after a decrease in the second quarter. Meanwhile, wind PPA prices remained essentially flat during the quarter after jumping nearly 14% in the past year, according to the latest
Q3 2026 report
The quarterly analysis, which included 206 price offers from 166 energy projects in six ISO territories across the United States, revealed that Section 232 Tariffs on imported polysilicon solar materials set to take effect in December are already having an effect on PPA prices offered by solar developers, while similar tariffs on steel, aluminum and copper are reportedly pushing up costs for wind developers. However, a modest decline in wind prices in the large ERCOT market offset increases in other markets during Q3.
Looking ahead, the LevelTen report asserts there are good reasons for buyers to jump into the PPA market in the near term. The authors point to a deep misalignment between federal policy and voluntary frameworks, suggesting buyers should “show up soon” to benefit from IRA-era economics by helping to ensure developers can secure project financing in time to benefit from the current Investment Tax Credit.
Additionally, while the authors point to recent pauses in clean energy procurement due to uncertainty as buyers await revisions to the voluntary Greenhouse Gas Protocol (GHGP), they suggest that changes to another voluntary framework — the Science Based Targets Initiative (SBTi) — should spur buyers into action.
While the LevelTen report’s executive summary points to “a brief but golden window for buyers” looking to take advantage of current SBTi rules before updates for contracts signed after Jan. 31, 2027 become final , the authors promise more thorough advice regarding “how buyers can leverage a number of procurement fast lanes to thread the SBTi Needle” included in the full report.
New methodology
For the Q3 2026 report, LevelTen Energy has adopted a new methodology, displaying a “Market Index” number that represents the relative growth (or lack thereof) in PPA prices over the previous eight quarters.
Prior to the most recent report
, the chart displayed PPA price benchmarks for the preceding eight years.
The new figure represents an aggregate of pricing trends for individual markets, weighted based on the size of the offer pool and the number of offers within the market. In total, the market indices for wind and solar have risen 27.5% and 12.7%, respectively since Q3 2024.
The benchmark P25 (25th percentile) prices for Q3 2026 were listed as $64.23/MWh for solar and $68.27/MWh for wind.
