title: A Black Hole Could Split in Two, According to a Surprising New Theory
content:
A startling new theory suggests that black holes spinning at extreme speeds might split in two, challenging what scientists thought possible. Credit: SciTechDaily.com
Black holes might split in two under extreme conditions, theoretical calculations suggest, offering physicists a way to explore the limits of our understanding of gravity.
Two black holes can collide and merge into one. But could a single black hole divide into two smaller ones that go their separate ways? Reversing a merger might sound straightforward, but the rules governing black holes make it difficult.
The entropy barrier to splitting
One obstacle is entropy, a measure of how many different microscopic arrangements can give a physical system the same overall properties. Think of rolling two dice. Several combinations produce a total of seven, but only two ones produce a total of two. Entropy captures a similar distinction between an overall result and the different underlying arrangements that can produce it. More possible arrangements mean higher entropy.
For an ordinary black hole that is not rotating, two smaller black holes would have less combined entropy than the original. That makes splitting thermodynamically unfavorable. The usual requirement of thermodynamics is that the total entropy of an isolated system should stay the same or increase, rather than decrease.
Whether black holes can split is the subject of “When Black Holes Admit Pair-of-pants Topologies,” a theoretical study published in
Physical Review D
. The unusual title describes what a split would look like through time. A black hole’s outer boundary, called its horizon, would trace a trouser-like shape, with one section dividing into two “legs.”
Illustration of black hole splitting in two creating the shape of pants. Credit: Francesco Sannino
“In our study, we investigate which physical laws normally prevent a black hole from splitting into two. We also investigate if certain circumstances may allow a split to happen”, says Francesco Sannino, a co-author and professor of physics at the University of Naples Federico II in Italy and the Quantum Field Theory Center at the University of Southern Denmark.
Sannino’s co-authors are Giacomo Cacciapaglia, a Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique (CNRS) researcher at the Laboratoire de Physique Théorique et Hautes Énergies, a joint laboratory of CNRS and Sorbonne Université in Paris, and Manuel Del Piano and Vania Vellucci, both from the Quantum Field Theory Center at the University of Southern Denmark.
Rapid rotation offers a possible loophole
Their calculations suggest that rapid rotation could offer a loophole in the thermodynamic barrier. A spinning black hole might be able to divide under conditions that would make splitting unfavorable for a nonrotating one.
“But the two resulting black holes must also be able to separate rather than immediately fall back together. When we include this requirement, the window largely closes again, except possibly for black holes rotating close to their maximum possible rate,” says Francesco Sannino.
Uncertain odds beyond Einstein’s theory
The researchers also explore theories with additional dimensions of space. Within these theories, physicists already know of black-hole-like objects that can become unstable and begin to break apart. Under some of these conditions, splitting can be thermodynamically favorable, particularly when one resulting black hole is much smaller than the other. Even then, showing that entropy permits a split does not establish that the process will actually happen.
The possibilities also extend to primordial black holes, hypothetical objects that could have formed in the early universe.
“We cannot yet give a single probability for a black hole to split. It depends on how gravity behaves beyond Einstein’s theory, and we are working to quantify this. We expect small primordial black holes to be more prone to splitting than much larger astrophysical black holes. We may detect a split indirectly: gamma-ray telescopes such as Fermi-LAT can search for signals from tiny black-hole fragments that might form during mergers,” says Francesco Sannino.
Reference: “When black holes admit pair-of-pants topologies” by Giacomo Cacciapaglia, Manuel Del Piano, Francesco Sannino and Vania Vellucci, 22 October 2026,
Physical Review D

title: A Devastating Disease Is Threatening the World’s Chocolate Supply – but Scientists May Have Found the Answer
content:
Chocolate may be a beloved treat enjoyed worldwide, but its future is increasingly uncertain. Disease, rising temperatures, and shifting weather patterns are threatening cacao harvests, putting pressure on the global chocolate supply and the millions of farmers who depend on it. Credit: Shutterstock
A change to just two DNA letters reduced disease in cacao by about 42% under laboratory conditions, suggesting a possible way to protect future chocolate harvests.
Black pod disease is estimated to reduce cacao yields by roughly 30% worldwide, threatening the livelihoods of farmers who grow the crop used to make chocolate. Shifting weather patterns and other environmental stresses are making production even more difficult. With millions of farmers depending on cacao, these pressures are raising concerns about the future of the global chocolate supply.
Scientists at
Penn State
have developed a new variety of cacao that shows significantly improved resistance to black pod disease in laboratory tests. The researchers used gene editing and traditional breeding to strengthen the plant’s natural defenses, offering a potential way to reduce losses without introducing foreign DNA into the final plant. The promising results are now moving toward field testing and possible commercial production.
Just-harvested cacao pods display a range of vivid colors. Credit: Mark Guiltinan / Penn State
The work builds on decades of research led by Mark Guiltinan, the J. Franklin Styer Professor of Horticultural Botany and professor of plant molecular biology in the Department of Plant Sciences at Penn State’s College of Agricultural Sciences, and Siela Maximova, a research professor of plant biotechnology in the same department.
“For consumers, chocolate is something they expect to find on store shelves every day, but behind that product is a crop and industry facing significant challenges,” Guiltinan said. “Our goal is to develop tools that help growers continue producing cacao sustainably and profitably.”
Young cacao trees growing in the experiment in one of Penn State’s plant science greenhouses. Credit: Francisco Menéndez-Burns / Penn State
Cacao’s rainforest origins leave it vulnerable
Cacao is particularly vulnerable to environmental changes because of where it evolved. Native to the Amazon rainforest, the species originally grew beneath the canopy of tropical forests, where surrounding trees helped create relatively stable conditions. Today, cacao is cultivated across tropical regions of Africa, Asia, and Latin America, often in environments quite different from its original habitat.
“Cacao evolved in a very stable rainforest environment,” Guiltinan said. “It’s a delicate plant in many ways. Changes in rainfall, temperature, and humidity can all affect production, and some of those changes can also increase disease pressure.”
Mycelium of phytophthora palmivora, which can give rise to cacao black pod disease, grows from an agar plug, infecting a cacao leaf 48 hours after inoculation. Credit: Mark Guiltinan/Penn State
These environmental pressures are especially concerning because cacao trees cannot be improved quickly through traditional breeding. A tree takes roughly three years to mature and begin producing seeds, and developing and evaluating a new variety can take decades. Meanwhile, changing weather conditions, including increased humidity and variability, can create more favorable conditions for pathogens and insect pests.
“The climate is changing faster than these trees can naturally adapt,” Maximova said. “One of our goals is to develop tools that help breeders respond more quickly to those challenges.”
The fungal disease black pod rot, shown here in cacao seed pods, is a serious problem in all areas of the world where the crop is grown. Caused by the fungus Phytophthora, black pod rot causes pod losses of up to 30% and kills as many as 10% of the trees annually. Credit: PlantVillage, Penn State
A tiny DNA edit strengthens cacao’s defenses
In a study published in the
Plant Biotechnology Journal
, the team combined genome sequencing, CRISPR gene editing, and traditional crossbreeding to develop cacao plants with greater resistance to black pod disease. The disease is caused by a mold-like pathogen that attacks cacao plants and can severely reduce harvests.
The researchers targeted a gene called TcNPR3, which normally acts as a brake on the plant’s immune system. By changing this gene, they partially activated the cacao tree’s natural defense response, giving it greater protection against subsequent pathogen infections.
The genetic change was remarkably small. Rather than introducing a completely new defense system, the scientists adjusted one already present in the plant. After making the edit, they used traditional breeding to remove all transgenic material, including the foreign DNA associated with the gene-editing machinery. The resulting plants retained the beneficial change without carrying foreign DNA.
This distinction is important for how the plants are regulated. According to the researchers, the resulting cacao is no longer considered a genetically modified organism, or GMO, consistent with U.S. and European Union regulatory frameworks that treat certain gene-edited traits similarly to those produced through conventional breeding.
Native to the Amazon rainforest, cacao evolved as an understory tree growing beneath a tropical forest canopy. Credit: Mark Guiltinan/Penn State
“In one case, we only changed two bases in the entire genome of the plant,” Guiltinan said. “Out of roughly 450 million bases, that single change resulted in about a 42% reduction in disease under laboratory conditions.”
That result provides encouraging evidence that a small genetic adjustment can improve cacao’s disease defenses. However, laboratory conditions cannot fully reproduce the environmental challenges trees encounter on farms, and the researchers have not yet established whether the same protection will hold under commercial growing conditions.
Cacao’s disease defenses face field trials
Field evaluations are now underway through collaborations with the U.S. Department of Agriculture in Hawaii and Puerto Rico. These trials will help determine how the edited plants perform in actual growing environments before decisions are made about broader cultivation.
“These plants are specifically designed to improve disease resistance,” Maximova said. “The next step is proving performance in field trials. Scale-up and marketing will be the next challenges should the field testing prove encouraging. That’s where commercial partners can play an important role in helping move the technology forward.”
Penn State has recently entered into a licensing agreement with AgroNetica, a biotechnology company focused on cacao, to advance that process. The company has licensed the commercial rights to plants carrying the disease-tolerance mutation and plans to continue testing, expand production, and eventually market improved cacao varieties directly to growers in cacao-producing countries.
Turning a successful laboratory experiment into a crop that farmers can reliably grow requires considerably more than demonstrating that the genetic modification works. Plants must undergo additional testing, be produced in sufficient quantities, and reach growers through commercial distribution systems. Universities generally lack the resources needed to carry out that entire process.
Embryonic cacao is shown developing tiny flowers in a tissue culture. Cacao trees typically don’t flower until they are between three and eight years of age. The team’s work to spur early flowering promises to greatly speed up breeding to develop disease-resistant trees. Credit: Mark Guiltinan/Penn State
“It takes millions of dollars and many years to bring a new crop variety to farmers,” Maximova said. “That’s why partnerships with companies willing to invest in development, testing and deployment are so important.”
The agreement also marks a milestone for Penn State’s Program in the Molecular Biology of Cocoa, which Guiltinan and Maximova co-direct. The program traces its origins to an
industry-supported endowment
established in the 1980s. Over the following decades, Penn State researchers developed foundational tools for cacao biotechnology, mapped important genetic pathways, and established one of the world’s leading cacao research programs.
Those advances created the scientific foundation for the current gene-editing work. They also demonstrate why maintaining a research program over many years can be necessary before discoveries become practical agricultural technologies.
“Thanks to this long-term investment in research and maintaining a sustained program, we now have an opportunity to begin getting technologies developed here in the lab closer to the hands of farmers,” Maximova said. “The focus was always on helping cacao farmers and the industry. We’re now at the place where we have a partner whose expertise is moving these discoveries into real-world use.”
Improving cacao beyond disease resistance
Disease resistance is only one of the traits that researchers and commercial developers hope to improve. AgroNetica also plans to introduce additional characteristics from its development pipeline, including greater tolerance to heat and drought, reduced cadmium accumulation, and more compact trees that could allow greater mechanization. Other goals include shortening the time before a tree’s first harvest and developing caffeine-free cacao varieties. These remain development objectives rather than demonstrated benefits of the newly licensed disease-tolerant plants.
Guiltinan and Maximova are continuing to investigate traits associated with climate resilience and crop productivity. They expect accelerated breeding and genome editing to play increasingly important roles in helping cacao growers respond to environmental pressures that may change throughout the lifetime of a tree.
“The diseases are changing. The climate is changing. The challenges growers face continue to evolve,” Maximova said. “This is not something you solve once, and then you’re finished. It’s an ongoing effort to develop better plants and provide growers with new options.”
For Guiltinan, the success of the research will ultimately depend on whether these advances translate into meaningful improvements for the people growing cacao.
“We’re trying to solve real problems for farmers,” he said. “If we can help growers reduce losses, improve productivity and adapt more quickly to changing conditions, then that’s the ultimate measure of success.”
Reference: “Reduced Susceptibility to Phytophthora in Non-Transgenic Cacao Progeny Through CRISPR–Cas9 Mediated TcNPR3 Mutagenesis” by Mark J. Guiltinan, Lena Landherr, Siela N. Maximova, Dante DelVecchio, Aswathy Sebastian and Istvan Albert, 9 September 2025,

title: A Hidden Cancer-Fighting Switch Could Supercharge the Human Immune System
content:
A protein best known for preventing cancer may also help immune cells fight it. Researchers discovered that briefly activating this protein enhanced the ability of engineered human T cells to attack melanoma in laboratory experiments. Credit: Shutterstock
Temporarily activating a protein best known for preventing cancer helped engineered human immune cells kill melanoma cells more effectively in the lab, suggesting a way to improve existing cell therapies.
Engineering a patient’s immune cells to recognize cancer does not guarantee that they will keep fighting it. Repeated exposure to cancer can gradually weaken T cells’ ability to multiply and attack tumors, a decline known as exhaustion. The laboratory process used to prepare these cells for treatment can also make them mature too quickly, reducing their chances of surviving and remaining effective over time.
These problems limit engineered T-cell therapies, including chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy and T-cell receptor (TCR) therapy. Both involve collecting a patient’s immune cells, genetically modifying them in a laboratory to recognize cancer, and infusing them back into the patient to attack tumors. Such treatments have transformed care for certain blood cancers and are increasingly being investigated for solid tumors.
Researchers at the UCLA Health Jonsson Comprehensive Cancer Center have identified a possible way to improve these cells during preparation. Their study, published in
Frontiers in Immunology
, found that temporarily activating a protein called p53 helped human T cells develop characteristics associated with longer-lasting immune responses and become more effective at killing melanoma cells in the laboratory.
Activating p53 improves melanoma cell killing
Often called the “guardian of the genome,” p53 is best known for preventing damaged cells from becoming cancerous. Scientists have extensively studied that protective role, but its involvement in regulating human T cells is less understood.
The team collected human T cells and treated them with navtemadlin, an investigational drug that increases p53 activity by blocking another protein, MDM2. Normally, MDM2 keeps p53 levels under control. Comparing treated and untreated cells allowed the researchers to assess how activating p53 affected their development, energy production, and ability to fight cancer.
T cells (black) attack melanoma cells (red). Compared with the control group (left), T cells treated with navtemadlin were significantly more effective at killing melanoma cells, leaving very few cancer cells remaining. Credit: Crompton Laboratory
To test cancer-killing performance, the researchers genetically engineered T cells to recognize a protein found on certain melanoma cells. They then used specialized imaging equipment to monitor the cells for nearly seven days.
The engineered T cells prepared with navtemadlin were significantly more effective at killing melanoma cells than untreated cells. Their advantage became apparent after approximately 40 hours and continued throughout the experiment. They also showed improved cancer-fighting activity without additional interleukin-2, a protein commonly used to support T-cell growth and survival.
“This is one of the first studies to link p53, one of the most extensively studied proteins in biology, to T-cell exhaustion in humans,” said Joseph Crompton, MD, PhD, assistant professor of surgery at the David Geffen School of Medicine at UCLA and senior author of the study. “While p53 has long been known for its role in preventing cancer, our findings suggest it may also play an important role in helping immune cells maintain their ability to fight it. This opens up a new avenue for developing more effective cancer immunotherapies.”
More energy, fewer signs of exhaustion
The treated cells had greater energy reserves and were more likely to produce interferon-gamma and granzyme B, two cancer-fighting proteins that help immune cells coordinate an attack and destroy cancer cells.
They were also more likely to develop into central memory T cells, which have a greater capacity to survive and multiply when they encounter their target again. Along with fewer molecular signs of exhaustion, this shift suggested that the cells might remain effective for longer. Those characteristics indicate potential for lasting immune responses, although the experiments tested human cells in the laboratory rather than treatment outcomes in patients.
Cell survival depends on the dose
Adding a drug such as navtemadlin during cell preparation could potentially fit into existing manufacturing processes. That would offer a way to improve engineered T-cell therapies without developing an entirely new treatment or introducing additional genetic modifications.
At lower concentrations, navtemadlin encouraged the development of healthy memory T cells without substantially reducing the overall number of viable cells. Higher concentrations, however, caused more cells to die, showing why any use of this approach would require careful control of p53 activation.
Reference: “p53 activation via pharmacologic MDM2 inhibition constrains exhaustion and enhances antitumor function of human CD8+ T cells” by Alexandra Boix de Jesus, Hy B. Dao, Anthony Imani, Gabriel A. Rodriguez, Michael S. Shehata, Rachana R. Chandran, Stuart A. Fine, Sin Y. Lim, Michelle To, Serena Y. Lofftus, Nicolas Pedroncelli, Fritz C. Eilber, Brigitte N. Gomperts, Tyler R. McCaw, Cristina Puig-Saus and Joseph G. Crompton, 18 September 2026,
Frontiers in Immunology
DOI: 10.3389/fimmu.2026.1910235
The study was funded in part by the American College of Surgeons, the UCLA Broad Center of Regenerative Medicine and Stem Cell Research, the UCLA Health Jonsson Comprehensive Cancer Center, the Tower Cancer Research Foundation, the Sarcoma Foundation of America, and the National Cancer Institute of the National Institutes of Health under the Early-Stage Surgeon Scientist Program.

title: A Hidden Star May Be Plowing Through Betelgeuse’s Giant Atmosphere
content:
This artist’s illustration shows the smaller, hotter companion star Siwarha creating a wake-like disruption in Betelgeuse’s outer atmosphere as it orbits directly through it. The shape of Betelgeuse itself becomes slightly oblong as a result of Siwarha’s perturbations. Credit: NSF/AUI/NSF NRAO/M. Weiss
Radio images suggest a link between Betelgeuse’s changing outline and its companion’s expected orbit, offering clues to how a smaller star may influence a giant’s later life.
Betelgeuse, the bright red supergiant marking Orion’s shoulder, may have another star stirring its atmosphere from within. Its recently identified companion, Siwarha, is thought to orbit at a distance of only about twice the giant’s radius. New radio observations suggest that this close neighbor is leaving a visible mark on the shape of Betelgeuse’s outer gas, even though the companion itself is too faint to appear in those observations.
Researchers proposed Siwarha’s existence in 2024 to explain Betelgeuse’s mysterious 2,100-day brightness cycle. Direct imaging and spectroscopic studies of the star’s light have since supported its existence. The companion’s name means “her bracelet,” a reference to Betelgeuse’s Arabic meaning, “the hand of al-Jawza.”
Betelgeuse’s shape hints at Siwarha’s influence
The new study was led by Dr. Lynn D. Matthews, Principal Research Scientist and Assistant Director at MIT Haystack Observatory, with colleagues from the Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian, the University of Manchester, and the European Southern Observatory. The team combined observations from the U.S. National Science Foundation’s Karl G. Jansky Very Large Array (NSF VLA) and the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA), collected between 2021 and 2026 at seven radio frequencies ranging from 22 to 485 GHz.
Radio waves at different frequencies reveal different depths in a star’s atmosphere. Using both observatories allowed the researchers to build a picture of Betelgeuse layer by layer, from just above its visible surface to several times the star’s radius.
“It was the combination of the incredible data from the NSF VLA and ALMA that gave us a convincing result here,” said Matthews. “The fact that we can use these facilities to actually resolve the disks of nearby stars is amazing.”
Detecting Siwarha directly was beyond the observations’ reach. The team calculated that the companion would be tens to hundreds of times too faint to see at radio wavelengths. They could, however, measure the ellipticity of Betelgeuse’s radio-emitting atmosphere, meaning how stretched or egg-shaped it appeared, at different observing times.
The atmosphere looked noticeably more elongated near the times when Siwarha was expected to be at its greatest apparent separation from Betelgeuse. It appeared rounder when the companion was expected to pass in front of or behind the giant star. That correspondence suggests that the smaller star’s gravity and movement are disturbing the surrounding gas.
“This companion is orbiting so close to the star that it actually passes through its extended atmosphere,” Matthews explained. Its passage could leave a wake, much as a boat leaves one as it moves through water.
The team will need observations covering more of Siwarha’s orbit, particularly at frequencies that have not yet been well sampled, to confirm and refine these findings.
Warming again after the Great Dimming
The same radio data also show that Betelgeuse’s extended atmosphere has largely recovered from a much more conspicuous disturbance. In late 2019 and early 2020, the star faded to its faintest level in more than a century of record-keeping. During that episode, known as the Great Dimming, Betelgeuse ejected a billion tons of stellar material that partially blocked our view.
Months before the dimming, a 2019 study led by Matthews had found that Betelgeuse’s atmosphere was unusually cool at radio wavelengths. That team proposed that convection, the circulation of gas carrying heat from deep within the star, had triggered a shock wave. The wave could have disturbed gas in the outer layers, setting the stage for the massive dust-forming outburst that followed.
The new measurements show that the atmosphere’s brightness temperature, a temperature inferred from the strength of its radio emission, has returned to more typical levels at those same wavelengths. At a distance from the center of about 2.7 times Betelgeuse’s radius, the gas now registers around 3,500 kelvin, or about 5,840°F. That is comparable to the temperature of the star’s visible surface.
A temperature dip above Betelgeuse’s surface
Closer to the surface, the highest-frequency ALMA measurements revealed a much cooler layer. These observations probed nearer to Betelgeuse’s surface than previous radio measurements and found temperatures of roughly 2,200 kelvin, or about 3,500°F. That is more than 1,000 kelvin cooler than the photosphere, the star’s visible surface.
The measurements confirm a long-suspected “temperature minimum” between the photosphere and the chromosphere, an atmospheric layer above it. This cool region coincides with the “MOLsphere,” a shell of molecular gas that astronomers had long inferred from infrared observations but had rarely examined so directly at radio wavelengths.
Future observatories, including the Next Generation Very Large Array now in development, are expected to make such detailed studies more routine. Sharper views could help researchers understand how red supergiants shed material and evolve in the final stages of their lives, and how the gravitational pull of a nearby companion might shape that process.
Reference: “New Spatially Resolved Observations of Betelgeuse from the VLA and ALMA: Evidence for Atmospheric Perturbations from a Close Companion” by L. D. Matthews, A. K. Dupree, A. M. S. Richards and W. R. F. Dent, 32 August 2026,
The Astronomical Journal
DOI: 10.3847/1538-3881/ae953d

title: A Woman Who Lived 30,000 Years Ago Is Changing What We Know About Ice Age Europe
content:
Cave of Isturitz, the cavity in which the bone of a Gravettian woman was found. Credit: Severine Dabadie
DNA preserved in ancient cave sediments reveals how some Ice Age Europeans endured extreme cold, while genetic evidence from France uncovers unexpected connections across the continent.
A woman who lived in southwestern France around 30,000 years ago carried a genetic history that stretched far beyond her corner of Ice Age Europe. Most of her ancestry was western European, but part of it was related to populations in central and eastern Europe. Her DNA challenges the idea that ancient populations on opposite sides of the continent remained largely separated from one another.
For archaeologists, evidence of these distant connections is not entirely new. The Gravettian culture, which spread across Europe roughly 34,000 to 25,000 years ago, left behind evidence suggesting extensive contact between groups. Ancient DNA, however, seemed to tell a different story, pointing to relatively stable eastern and western ancestry groups. The two lines of evidence had been difficult to reconcile.
Now, an international research team led by the
University of Vienna
has found genetic evidence that helps bring those pictures together. In a study published in
Science Advances
, researchers combined new and previously published genomes with human DNA recovered from cave sediments, uncovering evidence of both long-distance genetic exchange and populations that endured in the same regions for thousands of years.
Eastern and western populations exchanged genes
The clearest evidence of those distant connections came from a woman whose remains were discovered at Isturitz Cave in southwestern France. Her remains yielded the oldest genome-wide dataset yet obtained from a modern human in southwestern Europe. Genetic modeling places the exchange between eastern and western populations around 32,500 to 31,500 years ago, before she lived.
“Our results show that eastern and western European populations were not as genetically isolated as previously assumed,” says first author Pere Gelabert, Department of Evolutionary Anthropology at the University of Vienna. “Gene flow across such large distances adds a new dimension to our understanding of how Gravettian populations were connected.”
She was not the only person to carry evidence of these connections. A previously studied individual from Ormesson, France, showed a similar genetic signal. When considered alongside archaeological findings, the results also strengthen the possibility that Isturitz served as a meeting place for different groups, although the DNA cannot reveal exactly how those encounters occurred.
Western European ancestry survived the Ice Age
Yet contact across Europe did not necessarily mean that established populations disappeared or were replaced. In northern Spain, researchers uncovered another part of the story: western European ancestry persisted for thousands of years, including through some of the harshest conditions of the last Ice Age.
Genomic evidence from Chufín Cave points to this long-term continuity. At El Mirón Cave in Cantabria, the researchers went a step further, recovering human genetic information without relying on bones or teeth. A sediment layer dating back approximately 22,000 years contained enough human nuclear DNA to identify the genetic ancestry of people who had occupied the cave, despite the absence of human skeletal remains in that layer.
The DNA revealed that western European ancestry had persisted through the Last Glacial Maximum, when Ice Age conditions were particularly severe. Together with the evidence from Chufín, this supports the idea that the Iberian Peninsula served as a refuge where human populations endured during a period of extreme cold.
“Sedimentary DNA allows us to recover genetic information from periods where human remains are missing,” says senior author Ron Pinhasi, Department of Evolutionary Anthropology at the University of Vienna, whose team led this study. “This gives us a way to connect archaeological layers with the genetic ancestry of the people who occupied a site.”
Ancient family offers clues to inbreeding avoidance
In southern Italy, the team examined a different aspect of ancient population life through the remains of Ostuni1b, a male fetus who was most likely the son of a previously studied woman known as Ostuni1. Genetic analysis suggests that his father probably belonged to the same population as his mother, yet the parents were not closely related. The researchers interpret this as a possible sign of mating practices that helped prevent high levels of inbreeding, even among people who shared a common genetic background.
These findings offer a more complicated picture of Ice Age Europe than one divided into isolated eastern and western populations. Genetic ancestry could endure in a region for thousands of years while connections between populations extended across much greater distances. The evidence suggests that remaining part of an established regional population did not necessarily mean being cut off from people elsewhere.
Gelabert’s team is now extending this research by combining sedimentary DNA with advanced proteomic analyses, which examine proteins, to investigate the earliest expansions of modern humans across Europe. The approach may also help researchers understand how these populations interacted with carnivores at archaeological sites where organic remains are too scarce to provide a clear record of the past.
Reference: “Early Gravettian genomic data from Western Europe reveal population movements before the LGM” by Pere Gelabert, Susanna Sawyer, Vanessa Villalba-Mouco, Olivia Cheronet, Victoria Oberreiter, Diego Gárate, Christian Normand, Lawrence G. Straus, Manuel R. González Morales, Igor Gutiérrez-Zugasti, David Cuenca-Solana, Joëlle Darricau, Henry de Lumley, José-Miguel Tejero, Mareike Stahlschmidt, Thomas Higham, Maddalena Giannì, Laura G. van der Sluis, Carla Gómez-Montes, Miriam Ibáñez-Herranz, Michelle Hämmerle, Brina Zagorc, Florian Exler, Florian Brück, Stefan Franz, Fernanda Tenorio Cano, Kristin Stewardson, Lijun Qiu, Ana B. title: NASA’s Parker Solar Probe Discovers Something Unexpected Hidden in the Chaos of Space
content:
Artist’s illustration of NASA’s “Parker Solar Probe” mission. Credit: NASA/Johns Hopkins APL/Steve Gribben
NASA’s Parker Solar Probe has uncovered hidden order in space turbulence, a finding that could help scientists understand magnetic storms on Earth.
Smoke rising from an incense stick can begin as a thin, steady stream before curling and spreading unpredictably. The smoke makes turbulence in the air visible. Turbulence also occurs in space, where the moving material is plasma, an ionized gas containing electrically charged particles. Electric and magnetic fields strongly influence how those particles move, making this turbulence different from the movements of ordinary air.
Space plasma is also so dilute that its particles rarely collide, making it effectively collisionless. Physicists are still working to understand how turbulence develops under these conditions and how its energy is distributed. Measurements from NASA’s Parker Solar Probe have now revealed an organized pattern within that irregular activity.
Magnetic fields reverse rotation at smaller scales
At large scales, plasma behaves like a fluid, and turbulence develops through swirling motions called vortices and through electromagnetic waves. The fluctuations become random. At smaller scales, the dynamics of individual particles become important. These are different ways the same material behaves depending on the size of the disturbances being examined.
Using high-precision magnetic field and particle data from Parker Solar Probe, an international research team directly demonstrated, for the first time, that turbulent magnetic fields reverse their preferred direction of rotation across this transition. Picture the magnetic field’s direction as an arrow that can turn as the field fluctuates. Viewed looking radially away from the Sun, the fields preferentially rotate counterclockwise at larger scales. At smaller scales, they rotate clockwise.
Reversal of the field rotation from left-handed rotation (blue) to right-handed rotation (red), plotted on the frequency spectrum (y axis) against distance from the Sun x axis). Analysis based on the data from the Parker Solar Probe. A low frequency corresponds to a long wavelength in the spectrum. Credit: Iizawa et al., Astrophys. J. Lett., 2026
The reversal occurs at the wavelength, or spatial scale, where fluid-like behavior gives way to particle-like dynamics. Farther from the Sun, the reversal becomes more pronounced and shifts toward longer wavelengths, corresponding to larger spatial scales.
“We see a clear structure in the spectrum, even though the turbulence represents unstructured motions,” says Dr. Masatomi Iizawa of Technische Universität Braunschweig (TU Braunschweig), the article’s first author.
The study brought together researchers from the Institute of Theoretical Physics at TU Braunschweig and the University of Tokyo, in cooperation with Tohoku University, Kyushu University, Osaka University, and other research institutes. The collaboration spanned ten countries, and the results are published in
The Astrophysical Journal Letters
Turbulence shapes space weather
Dr. Yokoi of the University of Tokyo says, “The results are of great significance for both plasma physics and astrophysics.”
Plasma turbulence plays an important role in the solar wind, solar eruptions, and interplanetary space, as well as in Earth’s magnetosphere, the region dominated by our planet’s magnetic field. It also matters in accretion disks, where material orbits and moves inward toward a central object. In interplanetary space, turbulence can influence the shock waves and magnetic clouds produced by solar eruptions, making it an important factor in predicting geomagnetic storms.

title: NASA’s Voyager 1 Is About to Become the First Spacecraft One Light-Day From Earth
content:
Nearly 50 years after launch, NASA’s Voyager 1 is overcoming mysterious glitches and dwindling power as it approaches an extraordinary milestone 16 billion miles from Earth. Credit: NASA, ESA, and G. Bacon (STScI)
Voyager 1 is nearing a distance from Earth that light takes a full day to cross, while NASA engineers stretch its dwindling power to keep it exploring.
NASA’s Voyager 1, humanity’s most distant spacecraft, was about 16 billion miles (25.75 billion kilometers) from Earth when its radio signal disappeared in October.
NASA’s Deep Space Network
, which uses large antennas at three facilities around the globe to communicate with spacecraft at the Moon and beyond, could not detect the probe during two scheduled contacts on October 18 and 19, 24 hours apart.
The signal returned on October 20, ending the 48-hour interruption before engineers had sent commands to troubleshoot the problem. The team has remained in contact with Voyager 1 since then.
Engineers are still investigating what caused the communication loss. They have determined that one group of thrusters went offline and its backups switched on. Thrusters are small rocket engines used to control a spacecraft’s movement or orientation. Voyager 1 is programmed to make the switch automatically if its computers detect something wrong with the active thrusters. This response, called fault protection, puts the spacecraft into a safe, stable configuration and pauses normal operations, giving engineers time to diagnose the problem and act.
“This is the first time we’ve seen the spacecraft do something like this, but we are also at a point in the mission where we have to expect the unexpected,” said Kareem Badaruddin, Voyager mission manager at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) in Southern California. “We’re relieved to be back in contact with Voyager 1 and are eager to understand what happened.”
This image, taken on April 27, 1977, shows one of the Voyagers in the 25-Foot Space Simulator thermal vacuum chamber at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California. Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech
Interstellar science on a shrinking power supply
Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 are the only spacecraft ever to study interstellar space directly. Both now travel beyond the heliosphere, the bubble of particles and magnetic fields created by the Sun. Keeping their instruments running preserves access to measurements that no other spacecraft can provide.
Both probes draw electricity from radioisotope thermoelectric generators, which convert heat from decaying plutonium into electrical power. As that fuel supply diminishes, each spacecraft loses about 4 watts of power a year. Nearly half a century after the mission’s 1977 launch, little spare power remains, and engineers have been shutting down nonessential devices and systems to conserve energy.
The mission began with 10 dedicated
science instruments
. Some were shut down after the spacecraft completed their planetary encounters, while others stayed on to study the heliosphere’s outer region. In recent years, dwindling power has forced the team to turn off two science instruments.
Three simultaneous swaps extend Voyager’s science mission
Saving electricity also requires keeping the spacecraft warm enough to work. In early September, engineers completed a months-long effort to turn off three devices aboard Voyager 1 and replace their functions with three lower-power alternatives. The operation, nicknamed the “Big Bang,” came about six weeks after the team
performed the same swap on Voyager 2
All six devices involved help keep the spacecraft warm in the cold of space. To reduce electricity use while maintaining the proper distribution of heat, engineers had to make all three swaps simultaneously. The successful operation will allow Voyager 1’s
remaining science instruments
to work longer than previously anticipated. Without it, the team would have needed to shut down another instrument as early as summer 2027.
A two-day wait for Voyager’s reply
Voyager 1 is traveling at 38,000 mph (61,155 kph) toward another milestone. On November 18, it will be 16.09 billion miles (25.89 billion kilometers) from Earth. That distance equals one light-day, the distance light travels in a day. A radio message from Earth will take 24 hours to reach Voyager 1, and its reply will need another 24 hours to travel back.
Crossing that threshold will cause no change in the spacecraft’s surroundings or anything aboard it. The milestone marks the reach and endurance of humanity’s most distant explorer.
“If you want to say ‘hello’ to Voyager, you send your message and then you go home and you wait two days before you finally get a response,” said Suzanne Dodd, Voyager project manager at JPL.

title: New Research Reveals That Honey Beehives Act as a Living Immune System
content:
Honey bees are social insects that live in highly organized colonies consisting of a queen, workers, and drones. Best known for producing honey and beeswax, they also play an important role in pollinating flowering plants and agricultural crops. Credit: Stock
Scientists have discovered that honey beehives possess a surprisingly sophisticated system for protecting colonies against disease.
A honey bee colony relies on more than its workers to fight disease. The hive itself acts as a “living immune system,” using carefully arranged natural materials to create layers of antimicrobial protection around developing bees and stored food. New research shows that these defenses are closely linked to the surrounding landscape, with local vegetation influencing how effectively a colony can resist harmful microbes.
“Hives are not only homes for bees, but also act as their workplaces, restaurants, and hospitals, and now we can add immune systems to the list,” said lead researcher Dr. Kenya Fernandes.
How Beehives Build Layers of Protection
The strongest antimicrobial defenses were found in parts of the hive most exposed to the outside environment. Honey showed particularly powerful antimicrobial activity, while propolis, a sticky plant-derived substance bees use to seal cracks and openings, provided additional protection. Both materials contained biologically active compounds, including hydrogen peroxide in honey and plant chemicals called flavonoids in propolis.
Deeper inside the hive, where eggs and larvae develop, the defenses became more selective. Beeswax combs, stored pollen, and substances produced by the bees themselves helped suppress harmful bacteria and fungi while supporting beneficial microbial communities.
“As we travel closer to the hive center, the antimicrobial defenses became more targeted, with wax comb, stored pollen, and the bee’s own bodies helping to filter out harmful bacteria and fungi, while encouraging helpful species,” said Fernandes, a 2026 NSW Tall Young Poppy Award recipient.
“We already know honey, beeswax and propolis have antimicrobial properties independently. But what came as a surprise was how these materials were placed in the hive wasn’t random, but organized. The hive’s antimicrobial properties worked together to protect the eggs and larvae, as well as the fermented pollen the bees consume.”
Close-up of bees extracting pollen. Credit: Elizabeth Frost
Why the Surrounding Landscape Matters
For the study, published in
ISME Communications
, scientists examined 24 honey bee colonies across five apiaries at Tocal College in New South Wales, Australia. They analyzed the chemical composition and antimicrobial properties of honey, pollen, beeswax, and propolis. They also investigated microbes living in the bees’ digestive systems and tested the antimicrobial activity of their tissues and secretions.
The researchers found that many microorganisms in hive materials likely originated from floral nectar. Colonies located closer to native bushland also showed measurable differences in chemical defenses compared with those near agricultural land. These differences suggest that the plants available to foraging bees influence the protective properties of the materials they bring home.
“This shows healthy hives depend on and are influenced by healthy ecosystems. Land clearing and intensive farming could be quietly eroding the bees’ natural defenses. This builds a strong case for protecting diverse flowering habitats that support healthy hives,” said co-author Elizabeth Frost, Technical Specialist Bees at the NSW Department of Primary Industries and Regional Development (DPIRD).
Why Bacterial Diseases May Shape Hive Defenses
The hive’s protective system was generally more effective against bacteria than fungi. Researchers suggest this imbalance may reflect the greater threat posed by certain bacterial infections. One example is American foulbrood, a highly contagious disease that kills honeybee larvae and can destroy entire colonies.
“There are direct threats to bee populations such as the varroa mite, but many don’t realize the indirect threats: the shrinking of healthy ecosystems has a domino effect. Landscapes with diverse plant species can increase the bees’ chances of being resilient to disease.”
The findings also raise questions about other colony-building insects. Although the study focused on European honey bees, Fernandes hopes to investigate whether Australian native stingless bees have comparable nest-based defenses and whether similar systems occur in other social insects.
“I’d love to see if other social insects such as native stingless bees, ants, and termites, which also build incredibly complex homes, also have the same system,” Fernandes said.
Reference: “Spatially organized chemical defences shape microbial communities in honey bee colonies” by Kenya E Fernandes, Aviva Levina, Elizabeth A Frost and Dee A Carter, 19 October 2026,
ISME Communications

Funding: Australian Research Council, New South Wales Bushfire Industry Recovery Package Sector Development Grant

title: Researchers Discover Earth May Have Made Its Own Water 4.5 Billion Years Ago
content:
Artist’s illustration of early Earth, showing rocky debris raining through a scorching atmosphere onto a molten surface. Credit: University of New Mexico
Laboratory experiments suggest that rocky planets could generate their own water as they form, potentially giving distant worlds an essential ingredient for life.
Rocks, hydrogen gas, and intense heat might sound like an unlikely recipe for an ocean. Yet experiments suggest that these ingredients could have produced much of Earth’s water while the planet was still taking shape.
One leading explanation for Earth’s water involves small particles containing ice, known as icy pebbles. These formed in colder regions of the early solar system, where water could remain frozen, and may have carried that water to the growing Earth. Questions remain about how the particles traveled such long distances and whether those deliveries can fully explain Earth’s chemical composition.
Water in minutes from rock and hydrogen
Graduate student Susmita Garai led the new research with Zachary Sharp, professor and director of Earth and Planetary Sciences, and Peter Olson at the University of New Mexico. Their study, published in
Nature Geoscience
, investigated whether iron-bearing silicate rocks could react with atmospheric hydrogen under conditions resembling those of early planetary formation.
Experimental apparatus heating silicate rock samples. Credit: University of New Mexico
“In order to evaluate the possibility of ‘pebble’ rain’ being a source of water, we needed to construct and execute some very challenging high-temperature experiments. Dr. Garai’s efforts paid off mightily, as she found that water is produced in just minutes in the high-temperature environment of the Early Earth’s atmosphere,” Sharp said.
The researchers heated silicate rock samples to between 1,200 and 1,400 degrees Celsius, or about 2,192 to 2,552 degrees Fahrenheit, in experiments lasting from 15 minutes to three hours. Some samples were exposed to streams of hydrogen. Others were heated in helium for comparison, allowing the team to test hydrogen’s role in the reaction.
In the hydrogen experiments, nearly 80% of the iron oxide in the samples was converted into metallic iron, producing water vapor in the process. Hydrogen reacted with oxygen bound to iron in the rocks, leaving the iron as metal and forming water. The same reaction did not occur in helium.
Pebble rain could supply Earth’s oceans
“Previous ideas about the source of water to Earth rely on an external source, such as comets or meteorites. Here we show that virtually any Earth-sized planet should have water by this newly identified mechanism,” Sharp explained.
Results from the experiment. Left showcases the molten iron in silicate melt. Right shows the solid iron crystals in silicate melt. Credit: University of New Mexico
For this chemistry to supply a growing planet with water, rocky material, and hydrogen would need to meet under suitable conditions. That could happen during pebble accretion, a process in which small rocky particles accumulate to build a larger planetary body. Once the growing planet became sufficiently massive, it could develop a hot, high-pressure atmosphere rich in hydrogen. Silicate pebbles falling through that atmosphere could then undergo the water-producing reaction tested in the laboratory.
“We had suspected and hoped that we would produce iron metal and water in our reduction experiments, but we really had no way of knowing how fast and how much. We were quite surprised to find that extrapolation of our work suggests that hundreds of oceans worth of water were likely produced in this way. Looking out over a large body of water, it is hard to imagine that that water may have been produced 4 ½ billion years ago in a hell-like atmosphere, but it very well may have,” said Sharp.
AI generated illustration of pebble rain. Credit: University of New Mexico
Earth-sized worlds could make their own water
If comparable conditions developed around other rocky planets during their formation, the reaction could provide a widespread route to water on Earth-sized worlds beyond our solar system.
“The idea of pebble accretion is still relatively new. It’s only been around for the last decade. But it seems to solve many problems that exist with the existing paradigm for planet formation,” Sharp said. “And now we see that it also can explain why our planet is habitable. By extension, it is reasonable to expect that other Earth-sized bodies circling other stars would also have water and possibly life.”
The experiments demonstrate a potential mechanism for producing water during planetary formation. Determining how much of Earth’s water actually originated this way will require further research.
Reference: “Dry pebble rain could have delivered water to Earth through hydrogen reduction of iron oxide”, 12 October 2026,
Nature Geoscience
DOI: 10.1038/s41561-026-02138-3

title: Scientists Sound the Alarm As Colorectal Cancer Reverses a 20-Year Decline
content:
Colon cancer develops when abnormal cells grow uncontrollably in the large intestine, often beginning as small growths called polyps. Although the disease is more common in older adults, cases are increasing among younger people. Credit: Shutterstock
After decades of decline, colorectal cancer rates are showing a concerning reversal.
Colorectal cancer rates in the United States are rising across a much wider range of ages than previously recognized, reversing a long period of declining diagnoses. A new study published in
NEJM Evidence
found that the increase is no longer concentrated among adults younger than 50, with rates now climbing in people approaching their 70s.
Colorectal cancer is the second leading cause of cancer-related deaths overall in the United States and the leading cause among adults younger than 50. As more generations reach ages when the disease becomes increasingly common, researchers warn that growing numbers of diagnoses could place additional demands on cancer treatment and long-term survivorship care.
Colorectal Cancer Rates Reverse a Decades-Long Decline
Researchers led by Caitlin Murphy, PhD, MPH, Professor of Pediatrics and Public Health Sciences at the University of Chicago, analyzed National Cancer Institute data to track changes in colorectal cancer incidence over more than two decades. The age-adjusted rate dropped from 55.2 cases per 100,000 people in 2000 to 36.7 in 2022, before increasing to 38.3 in 2023.
“This is the first time that we have seen an increase in the overall rate since in more than 20 years,” Murphy said. The study also found rising incidence across age groups through 65 to 69 years, indicating that the trend extends well beyond the younger populations that have received much of the attention.
The increase among older adults is particularly concerning because colorectal cancer screening has historically produced substantial benefits in these age groups. Rates are now rising among people ages 65 to 69 and have stopped declining among those ages 70 to 74, despite approximately 80% of people in these groups being up to date with screening. Researchers suspect that unidentified risk factors may be counteracting some of the progress achieved through earlier detection and prevention.
A Generational Pattern May Help Explain the Increase
Murphy believes the expanding age range reflects a phenomenon known as the “birth cohort effect,” in which people born during particular periods experience different disease risks as they grow older. In this case, evidence suggests that individuals born in the 1960s and afterward may face an elevated risk of colorectal cancer that persists as they advance into middle and older adulthood.
“I think of a birth cohort effect as the interaction of age and time,” Murphy explained. “As people born around the same time move through time and age together, we’re going to see more colorectal cancers being diagnosed.”
The pattern could help connect the growing incidence among younger adults with the increases now appearing in older populations. American Cancer Society statistics show that colorectal cancer incidence among people ages 20 to 49 rose approximately 3% annually from 2013 to 2022.
“There are many unique challenges when you’re diagnosed with cancer at a young age, so it’s important that we shine a spotlight on that problem,” Murphy said. “But in terms of understanding the root cause, I think our study shows that we can consider that whatever might be causing colorectal cancer in younger people is now also causing it to increase in older people as well.”
Screening Changes Explain Only Part of the Rise
The steepest increase occurred among adults ages 45 to 49, whose colorectal cancer incidence rose by 12.76% annually between 2019 and 2023. Researchers believe this unusually rapid increase largely reflects expanded screening following a change in national guidelines that lowered the recommended starting age from 50 to 45.
Screening can temporarily raise reported incidence by detecting cancers that were already present but had not yet been diagnosed. “That means that screening is doing as we intend it to do — it’s catching cancer earlier,” Murphy said.
However, increased screening cannot fully account for the broader rise across age groups, especially among older adults who already have high screening participation. The researchers also examined whether disruptions caused by the COVID-19 pandemic contributed to the trend. The increase persisted even when data from 2020 and 2021 were excluded, and screening activity had largely returned to pre-pandemic levels by January 2021. These findings suggest that pandemic-related delays are unlikely to explain the overall increase observed in 2023.
Scientists Investigate Environmental Exposures
The underlying causes of the rising incidence remain uncertain. Researchers are now examining whether exposure to chemicals in the environment could contribute to colorectal cancer risk, although no specific exposure has been established as responsible for the observed trends.
“These results motivate us to understand reasons for this rise, so risk factors can be identified and possibly reduced,” said Sonia Kupfer, MD, director of the Gastrointestinal Cancer Risk and Prevention Clinic at UChicago Medicine.
Murphy is collaborating with Xin Hu, PhD, a toxicologist at Emory University, to investigate thousands of environmental chemical exposures using small blood samples. This approach will help identify substances that may warrant closer examination.
The researchers then plan to work with Kupfer to study selected chemicals using colon organoids, laboratory-grown models that reproduce some features of human colon tissue. These models will allow scientists to investigate how particular exposures affect colon cells and potentially identify biological processes involved in cancer development.
Early Detection Remains Essential
Until the causes become clearer, colorectal cancer screening remains one of the most effective ways to identify the disease early and prevent deaths. Current national guidelines recommend routine screening for adults at average risk beginning at age 45 and continuing through age 75. Screening decisions outside that range should be individualized based on factors such as family history, symptoms, and other medical conditions.
Colonoscopy remains the gold standard because it can both detect cancer and remove precancerous polyps. Other screening methods include home-based stool tests and newer blood-based tests, although their capabilities and recommended testing intervals differ.
“There are several ways to do screening that should be discussed with a clinician, so people know what the different screening tests are intended for and how often these need to be repeated,” Kupfer added.
For adults younger than 45 who do not qualify for routine screening, recognizing possible warning signs is particularly important. Blood in the stool, persistent changes in bowel habits, and unexplained weight loss should prompt medical evaluation, even in people without a known family history or genetic risk.
The research team also recommends continued monitoring of national cancer registry data as new figures become available. If the upward trend persists as large generations of Americans grow older, healthcare systems may face increasing demand for cancer treatment, follow-up care, and long-term support for survivors.
Reference: “Colorectal Cancer among U.S. Adults, 2000–2023” by Caitlin C. Murphy, Folasade P. May, Sonia S. Kupfer, Xin Hu and Samir Gupta, 27 October 2026,
NEJM Evidence
DOI: 10.1056/EVIDpha2600217
The study was supported by funding from the National Institutes of Health and the Eli and Edythe Broad Center of Regenerative Medicine and Stem Cell Research Ablon Scholars Program.

title: Study Reveals How Brain Function Changes When We Learn Something New
content:
Scientists have detected measurable changes in brain activity after beginners completed just one violin lesson. Credit: Shutterstock
A beginner’s violin lesson may seem worlds apart from dementia research, yet wearable brain scans are revealing signals that could help scientists understand both learning and neurological disease.
Playing a familiar tune on a violin is no simple task for someone who has never held the instrument. Each movement must produce the intended sound, and the brain has to learn how to coordinate those movements. Researchers at the University of Nottingham have now captured changes in brain activity as beginners learned to play, revealing measurable differences after just one violin lesson.
The study, published in the journal
Imaging Neuroscience
, involved 22 novice violin players. Using a wearable brain scanner, the scientists tracked patterns of neural activity while participants attempted to play “Twinkle Twinkle Little Star.” They found that those who improved the most also showed the greatest changes in certain brain signals associated with movement and learning.
A metal-free violin enables brain scans
Capturing those signals while someone plays an instrument presents a technical challenge. The electrical activity of neurons generates extremely weak magnetic fields, which can be measured to study brain function. However, the equipment must be sensitive enough to detect these signals without interference, while still allowing the person being studied to move naturally.
The researchers used a technology called OPM-MEG, developed in Nottingham, that incorporates brain-scanning sensors into a lightweight helmet connected to a backpack-mounted control unit. Unlike scanning systems that restrict movement, this wearable design allows researchers to monitor brain activity as people perform everyday tasks.
There was still one problem. A conventional violin contains metal components that would interfere with the scanner’s measurements.
To overcome this obstacle, the team enlisted Alan Kirby, an expert violinist and violin maker from Nottingham. Kirby sourced a standard violin and replaced every metal part with alternatives he crafted himself, producing an entirely wooden instrument operating at frequencies associated with Baroque music.
“Bringing together the ancient art of violin making, with the quantum physics underpinning this brain scanner, has been amazing. Perhaps even more impressive was to actually see the effects of my lessons on peoples brains. That was quite an experience,” Kirby said.
Alan Kirby working on a Violin. Credit: University of Nottingham
Reading the brain’s musical predictions
Kirby also served as the participants’ violin instructor. At the beginning of the experiment, all 22 beginners watched a video of him playing “Twinkle Twinkle Little Star.” They then attempted to perform the same melody during their first scanning session, while the researchers recorded their brain activity.
After completing that initial recording, the participants received a violin lesson from Kirby. They then returned for a second scanning session, following the same procedure and attempting to play the tune again. By comparing recordings from before and after the lesson, the researchers could examine how the brain responded to a brief period of musical training.
Their attention focused on brain waves, rhythmic fluctuations in electrical activity that occur across groups of neurons. In particular, they examined oscillations in the beta frequency range, which are thought to help signal whether an action produces the result the brain expects.
When learning the violin, that process could involve predicting the sound of a note before playing it and registering whether the actual sound matches the prediction. Unexpected notes provide information that the movement did not produce the intended outcome.
“Your brain works by making predictions about what will happen as a result of your actions. So, if I am playing a violin, my brain will have an expectation of what sound it will make. If I play the expected note, my brain receives information that the outcome matched its prediction; if I hit an unexpected note, it receives information that it did not. In this experiment, we were able to measure these signals in real time while the instrument was being played,” said Joe Gibson, a Ph.D. researcher in the School of Physics and Astronomy.
A participant plays the violin while wearing a specialized brain-scanning helmet that allows researchers to monitor neural activity in real time, revealing how the brain adapts as new motor skills are learned. Credit: University of Nottingham
Greater brain changes accompany better playing
The recordings revealed changes in beta-wave activity following the lesson, providing evidence that even a short period of musical instruction can alter measurable patterns of brain function. The researchers also found a relationship between those neural changes and improvements in playing ability.
Participants with the largest differences in beta-wave activity between the two scanning sessions also showed the greatest improvement in their violin performance. Although the findings do not establish that the changes in brain activity caused better playing, they suggest that beta oscillations are closely associated with how people acquire new motor skills.
Brain scanning could reach beyond music
Making these measurements possible required expertise extending well beyond neuroscience. Professor Matthew Brookes of the University of Nottingham’s School of Physics and Astronomy has spent more than a decade leading the development of OPM-MEG technology. The violin experiment brought together specialists in physics, engineering, mathematics, and music to create a system capable of studying movement as it happens.
“This is a study that we have been working on for years, and it’s taken a unique combination of skills: the physics required to measure brain activity; design engineering to create an ergonomic scanner that people can wear; the mathematics required to model the signals; and of course, Alan’s knowledge and abilities as a violin player and maker. Without this wonderful diversity of talent, we simply couldn’t have done the work.”
The researchers believe the technology could eventually help scientists investigate more than musical learning. Some of the patterns of brain activity measured during the experiment can also be affected by neurological conditions, including dementia. Studying these signals during natural movements could offer another way to examine how brain function changes in health and disease.
“The results provide a greater understanding of motor learning. It’s also fascinating that some of the effects that we measure here are among those that can be affected by disorders like dementia. Hopefully this type of study will bring about a new understanding of not just healthy brain function, but also disease,” said Brookes.
Reference: “Beta-band dynamics during a naturalistic motor task: an OPM-MEG study” by Joseph Gibson, Jessikah Fildes, Alan Kirby, Niall Holmes, Lukas Rier, Karen J. Mullinger, Matias Ison, Peter G. Morris, Elena Boto, Ryan M. Hill and Matthew J. Brookes, 27 July 2026,
DOI: 10.64898/2026.07.27.740561
Disclosure: The University launched a spin-out company, Cerca Magnetics Limited, in 2020 to commercialize OPM-MEG scanners and related technologies. The wearable system has been installed in a number of high profile research institutions across the globe and is being used to investigate a range of neurological and psychiatric conditions, including epilepsy and dementia.

title: “Schrödinger’s Penguin”: Scientists Discover a Bizarre Paradox Among Endangered Penguins
content:
A new Otago study has investigated Erect-crested penguins on the Antipodes and Bounty islands. Credit: Thomas Mattern / Tawaki Project
Endangered erect-crested penguins are holding steady on tiny islands while declining on a breeding ground 40 times larger, challenging assumptions about where the species’ best hope for survival lies.
An endangered penguin species could receive a less severe global risk rating even as one of its only two breeding populations suffers a steep decline. A survey of erect-crested penguins in Aotearoa New Zealand shows how a single assessment of an entire species can conceal very different conservation needs.
The erect-crested penguin is among just four penguin species worldwide listed as “Endangered” on the International Union for Conservation of Nature Red List. Another is New Zealand’s hoiho, or yellow-eyed penguin. Yet while the hoiho has attracted sustained public and conservation attention, the erect-crested penguin remains largely overlooked and is one of the country’s least-studied penguin species.
Steady on Bounty, shrinking on Antipodes
These birds breed only on the Bounty and Antipodes islands, two remote island groups about 800 kilometers (500 miles) southeast of the South Island. Between 2022 and 2024, researchers used drones to photograph and count every breeding colony across both groups, the first time this had been done for the entire species.
The study, published October 21, 2026, in
PLOS ONE
, was led by Dr. Thomas Mattern of the Tawaki Project, whose researchers are based in the Departments of Zoology and Marine Science at the University of Otago (Ōtākou Whakaihu Waka). The team collaborated with the Antarctic Research Trust and the Global Penguin Society.
Mattern says, “Comparing the new counts with historical records going back to the mid-1990s, the Bounty Islands population has remained essentially unchanged for at least 25 years.
“The Antipodes Islands population, by contrast, has declined by more than 40 percent since 1995.”
The counts also challenged the historical view of where most of the species breeds.
“The results overturn a long-standing assumption,” Mattern says.
“The tiny Bounty Islands, at just 50 hectares, were found to hold almost as many breeding pairs (about 27,800) as the Antipodes Islands (about 29,800), even though the latter is 40 times larger and historically considered the species’ stronghold.”
The researchers have dubbed the situation “Schrödinger’s Penguin” after the well-known thought experiment in which a cat sealed in a box is imagined to be simultaneously alive and dead until someone opens it and checks. For the penguins, Mattern says, the logic runs in reverse.
A pair of Erect-crested penguins on the Bounty Islands. Credit: Thomas Mattern / Tawaki Project
“With Schrödinger’s cat, opening the box settles the question one way or the other.
“With Erect-crested penguins, it’s the opposite. From a distance, without proper surveys, everyone assumed there was a single answer for the whole species.
“Once we actually opened the metaphorical box and looked, we found there wasn’t one state at all, but two: stable on the Bounty Islands, declining on the Antipodes Islands.”
Shrinking colonies give predators an opening
On the Antipodes Islands, a shrinking colony may become increasingly difficult for the penguins to defend. Mattern describes how that can compound the losses.
“As Antipodes colonies have shrunk over recent decades, the collective defense they once provided against native subantarctic bird, the skua, a natural predator of eggs and chicks, has weakened, allowing predation losses to increase and colonies to fragment further.”
The islands’ eastern rockhopper penguins had already experienced a population collapse. Their numbers crashed “catastrophically” during the second half of the 20th century, leaving fewer than 1,000 breeding pairs on the Antipodes Islands. The decline mirrored trends elsewhere across the species’ Southern Ocean breeding range and was likely driven by ocean warming.
Co-author Dr. Klemens Pütz of the Antarctic Research Trust suggests that this loss may have changed which penguins the predators targeted.
“As Rockhoppers disappeared, skuas may have turned to Erect-crested penguin eggs and chicks instead,” Pütz says.
Increasingly severe storms, consistent with broader climate trends in the Southern Ocean, have also triggered landslides that break colonies into smaller fragments and put them at further risk. Differences in the birds’ ocean habitats and migration routes likely add to the pressures.
Outside the breeding season, Antipodes birds travel far into the Antarctic Polar Frontal Zone, a region of the Southern Ocean, Mattern says. Bounty Islands birds stay close to their breeding sites in more sheltered waters that may also be more productive.
Bounty’s penguins remain exposed to industrial fishing
The contrasting population histories complicate how the species’ extinction risk should be assessed. According to Mattern, its current Endangered ranking rests on inflated population estimates from the 1970s. Reassessing that status against the new data broadly supports the ranking for the Antipodes population, but not for the Bounty population.
“Averaged across both populations, the global ranking would actually improve to “Vulnerable”, masking the severity of the Antipodes decline, and downplaying how exposed the Bounty Islands, likely the species’ last secure stronghold, are to industrial fishing.
“A single, ostensibly improved threat ranking is like putting the lid back on Schrödinger’s box, trading a convenient illusion for the stronger protection the Bounty Islands population actually needs,” Mattern says.
Reference: “Schrödinger’s Penguin? Divergent population trajectories and the challenge of assessing the threat status of the Erect-crested penguin” by Thomas Mattern, Klemens Pütz, Hannah Mattern, Robin Long, Dave Houston, Bianca Keys, Jeff White, Richard Seed, Myrene Otis, Ursula Ellenberg, Pablo Garcia-Borboroglu and Benno Lüthi, 21 October 2026,
PLOS ONE
DOI: 10.1371/journal.pone.0359075
The study was funded by the Vontobel Foundation (Switzerland) through the Antarctic Research Trust, the Global Penguin Society, and conducted under permits from the New Zealand Department of Conservation.

title: Blue Wave Could Engulf Data Center Industry
content: Election Day’s blue wave is set to crash into the data center industry. In 12 states, the winning or leading candidate for governor has called for a pause on data center development, including Alaska, Georgia, Kansas, Maine, Michigan, New Hampshire, New Mexico, New York, Ohio, Oregon, Texas and Wisconsin. And in even more states, winners have also pledged other restrictions on data centers including ratepayer protections, environmental limits and the elimination of tax incentives for building the facilities. And of the 24 incoming governors who did not call for a pause, 22 back at least one limit on data centers. Ratepayer protections, which would make sure households don’t shoulder the costs of increased power demand or energy infrastructure buildouts, were nearly universal: 34 of 36 winners support them. And 27 back restrictions relating to water usage or the environment. Fifteen leading candidates say they would cut or end the tax breaks that states have used to court developers. (For a detailed pre-election analysis of the data center positions of state candidates, see this story .) Governor candidates calling for data center pauses lost races in nine states, but only a few of these races were ever close. Florida was the tightest toss-up, and a key battleground on the issue. Republican Byron Donalds, who opposed a statewide pause and was backed by millions in spending from super PACs affiliated with Anthropic and OpenAI’s Greg Brockman, beat Democrat David Jolly by about a percentage point. Some of the states where winning candidates would restrict data centers are at the center of the industry’s building plans. OpenAI’s Stargate project with Oracle has massive sites in Texas, Michigan and New Mexico. SoftBank’s SB Energy plans to build an 8-gigawatt campus for OpenAI in Ohio. Microsoft, Amazon and Nvidia have lined up Texas sites . In Georgia, the Atlanta metro area has overtaken Northern Virginia as the busiest market for data center construction, according to real estate firm CBRE. In an interview on The Information’s TITV on Wednesday, Charles Hua, founder and executive director of Power Lines, a nonprofit focused on energy regulation, said that the election results in Ohio, Texas and Georgia were particularly noteworthy. “Those are three of the fastest growing markets for data center development for electricity demand growth and and all three saw pretty dramatic outcomes that folks maybe weren’t actually expecting,” Hua said. How (and whether) governors put in place their moratoriums will vary—in duration, strictness and path of action. But the narrowing map could lead to higher costs and more red tape for the data center and AI industries. It introduces even more uncertainty for investors about the payoff on the large AI investments of big tech firms. If neoclouds and other data center developers can’t turn borrowed money into revenue quickly enough, the delay could ripple, with developers paying interest on buildings that are not earning rent, lenders waiting longer to be repaid and AI companies going without the computing power they’ve committed to buy. Some deals could unravel entirely, if missed deadlines give tenants the rights to terminate. SB Energy warned in its IPO filing that permit delays could lead to this at OpenAI’s Ohio campus. Even if data centers weren’t the deciding issue in elections, the sweep matches American public opinion. In an August poll from Pew Research Center, six in 10 U.S. adults said they would be uncomfortable with a new one operating in their area, with more than half calling them bad for the environment and half considering them bad for home energy costs. Few saw a bright side: Less than a quarter agreed they would be good for local jobs or tax revenue. The moratoriums would join more than 500 data center pauses or bans at the local level, as shown by The Information’s ban tracker . At the year’s start, only about 40 towns and counties had bans in place. By August, the count had topped 500, driven by worries about power bills, water usage, noise and blight.
