title: India’s installed solar PV capacity to exceed 350 GW by 2030, says IEA - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Growth will be supported by utility-scale projects, rooftop solar and corporate procurement, although grid and storage investments remain critical.
Uma Gupta
07 Nov 2026
Markets & Policy
Highlights
A solar power plant in the Indian state of Maharashtra
India’s installed solar PV capacity is expected to exceed 350 GW by 2030, according to the IEA’s India Renewable Energy Market Report 2026.
The report, launched at the Bharat Renewable Energy Summit in New Delhi, forecasts that India’s total installed renewable power capacity will reach around 530 GW by 2030, with solar PV accounting for the largest share of growth. Wind capacity is expected to approach 90 GW, while hydropower capacity is projected to reach 75 GW as large hydro projects come online and investment in pumped storage accelerates.
The expansion is expected to put India on track to meet its target of 500 GW of installed non-fossil fuel power capacity by 2030, a key milestone toward its goal of achieving net-zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2070.
Competitive costs, sustained auction activity, growing open-access procurement and accelerating rooftop installations are expected to drive solar PV deployment.
Utility-scale projects have accounted for around 75% of solar PV capacity additions over the past five years. The IEA expects that share to gradually decline to approximately 70% by 2030, as policy support, improving economics and simplified administrative procedures boost distributed solar deployment.
Distributed solar PV capacity for self-consumption is projected to triple to more than 100 GW by 2030. The PM Surya Ghar Muft Bijli Yojana scheme is accelerating residential rooftop installations, while PM-KUSUM supports the solarization of agricultural feeders and irrigation pumps.
Corporate procurement is also emerging as a major source of demand. Open-access reforms have simplified renewable energy procurement for commercial and industrial consumers, with corporate power purchase agreements expected to support around 20% of utility-scale solar PV and wind capacity additions by 2030.
India’s installed renewable power capacity has almost quadrupled over the past decade, surpassing 300 GW in 2026, according to the report. The country is now the world’s second-fastest-growing renewable energy market and second-largest solar module manufacturer. India also reached its target of 50% non-fossil fuel installed power capacity in 2025, five years ahead of schedule.
The IEA said renewable energy deployment is already delivering substantial energy security benefits. Renewable electricity saved India more than $100 billion in coal and natural gas import costs between 2011 and 2025, with cumulative savings expected to more than double by 2030. Without the solar PV, wind and bioenergy capacity added since 2010, India’s coal imports in 2025 would have been around 110 million metric tons higher.
“India’s renewables expansion is delivering major benefits for its energy security at a time of heightened uncertainty in global energy markets,” said IEA Executive Director Fatih Birol. “As countries look to strengthen domestic energy supplies, India’s experience shows how consistent policies can help drive down renewable energy costs and attract investment, offering valuable lessons for other emerging economies. We look forward to supporting India as it builds on these achievements.”
“India’s emergence as a new giant of renewable energy reflects the progress we have made in recent years,” said India’s Minister of New and Renewable Energy Pralhad Joshi. “As India’s electricity needs continue to rise, we are laying the foundations for the next phase of growth by strengthening domestic manufacturing, mobilising investment and expanding transmission infrastructure.”
The report said competitive auctions have helped India achieve some of the world’s lowest solar PV generation costs and become a global leader in procuring hybrid renewable energy projects. Growth is also extending beyond utility-scale power plants, supported by rooftop solar, corporate electricity procurement and expanding domestic manufacturing.
However, sustaining the expansion will require faster investment in electricity grids, energy storage and system flexibility, alongside stronger utility finances and fewer project delays. Addressing these challenges could accelerate renewable power capacity deployment by more than 20% between 2026 and 2030, according to the IEA.

title: Maintaining trust in new tech - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
Rapid technological advances, particularly in AI, are challenging traditional approaches to conformity assessment and standardization. International standards bodies are adapting their frameworks to ensure products remain safe, reliable and trustworthy throughout their lifecycles.
International Electrotechnical Commission (ICE)
07 Nov 2026
Research & Development
Standards are often invisible to the people who rely on them, yet they underpin the confidence that products will work together, operate safely and perform as expected. But rapid technological change resulting from digitalization and the widespread use of AI is challenging traditional ways of assessing conformity to standards.
“Standardization and confirmity assessment (CA) bring tremendous value by providing trust in new technology,” says Wolfram Zeitz, executive secretary of two of the IEC CA systems, IECEE, which is the IEC System of Conformity Assessment Schemes for Electrotechnical Equipment and Components, and IECRE, which is the IEC System for Certification to Standards Relating to Equipment for Use in Renewable Energy Applications.
“What has changed is the speed of development. In the past, product cycles took up to three years before prototypes appeared,” he adds. “Now change happens far, far quicker and this creates a feeling of uncertainty. Consumers lose trust when they think development was rushed and conformity is not being adhered to.”
Henrike Gördes, head of governance at DKE, the organization hosting this year’s IEC general meeting, agrees: “A product that conforms to relevant standards provides assurance that it will behave in predictable ways and interact appropriately within a wider technological ecosystem. This ability to create trust has been one of the foundations of the success of standardization over many years. But maintaining that trust is becoming more challenging as technology changes at an accelerating pace.”
The potential undermining of a standards-based order is particularly acute when software, data or AI can alter a product’s behavior. The question is no longer simply whether the product was safe when it was tested. It is also how organizations can ensure that it remains safe and operates as intended following updates, changes in data or advances in AI, which are happening faster and faster.
Keeping pace with AI
The problem with attempting to standardize systems and products in an emerging environment is that the technology may not be mature enough to stabilize. “Particularly for AI, we don’t yet have industrial consensus on the technological framework,” says Zeitz. “AI tools are using different technological setups almost daily. Standardization and conformity assessment are struggling to keep up with the speed of development.”
Progress is being made, however. CASCO, the ISO committee for CA, is working with ISO/IEC SC 42 on ISO/IEC 42007, a draft standard offering a high-level framework and guidance for the development of CA schemes for AI systems.
Cybersecurity is one of the challenges related to AI, and in this area the IECEE Industrial Cyber Security Programme, which is based on the IEC 62443 series of standards, is already well established. A new pilot CA program has also recently been initiated with IEC TC 62, the technical committee that prepares standards for medical devices, to look at how AI can be assessed.
All new technologies need to be trusted
While AI is very much the focus of global attention, a host of new technologies required in our evolving world – notably to meet net-zero targets – also require standards and CA to be used safely and effectively. Different countries around the world need to trust that manufacturers providing the technology and products meet the appropriate benchmarks.
The difference is that these technologies are not evolving at the same pace as AI-based systems and are therefore easier to assess. For instance, IECEE provides a testing and certification scheme for electric vehicle (EV) battery systems, assessing their safety, performance, interoperability, energy efficiency, electromagnetic compatibility and hazardous substances. It also operates a specific EV program, which can test and certify charging systems, stations and plugs against relevant IEC standards, including IEC 62196-1 and the IEC 61851 series.
IECEE is also the go-to body for ensuring that solar panels and components are safe and perform as planned through its national certification bodies and recognized testing laboratories. The system relies on IEC standards for module performance, durability and safety. IEC 61215 covers design qualification and type approval of terrestrial photovoltaic modules, while IEC 61730 addresses electrical and mechanical safety through construction and testing requirements.
IECRE was established a little more than 10 years ago to help provide third-party certification and testing services for all power plants producing, storing or converting energy from wind, marine and solar PV energy. The CA system ensures that the essential quality and safety requirements in standards are met and, as a consequence, that reliable performance can be expected from all these systems.
For the wind sector, for example, that means checking that the industry aligns with the IEC 61400 standards, developed by IEC TC 88, the technical committee that produces standards for wind energy systems.
Conformity assessment is evolving
Traditionally, CA has often followed a relatively linear model: a product is developed, tested and assessed, and then the assessment provides assurance about that product. Digital and AI-based technologies complicate this.
“Take the introduction of autonomous control in cars, for example. You could have a software update that basically changes the way the self-driving vehicle operates,” says Gördes.
This raises an important question for conformity assessment: What does it mean to demonstrate that a product remains safe and performs as intended when the product itself can continue to change?
“Rather than assessing a product only at a particular point in its development, assessment needs to take account of what happens throughout the product’s lifecycle,” Gördes says.
DKE advocates a shift from a linear model of CA toward a more continuous, cyclical approach. “Such an approach could help connect CA more closely with the reality of digital products, where development, deployment, updating and monitoring can form an ongoing process rather than a sequence that ends when a product is first assessed.”
The aim, as outlined in this DKE white paper, is to develop an approach that better reflects products and technologies that can change throughout their operational life.
DKE is working with stakeholders from different industries and in cooperation with DIN and VDE, Germany’s national standards bodies, to develop the concept. “DKE has a strong interest in ensuring that emerging thinking can ultimately contribute to international standardization,” Gördes says.
Independent assessment is essential to ensure trust
The international dimension matters because standards and CA operate across markets. Manufacturers, regulators and users need confidence that assurance mechanisms are meaningful not only within individual national systems but also across increasingly global technology ecosystems.
“Our entire framework of requirements is based on international agreements and consensus,” explains Zeitz. “Every member country, no matter how big or small, has the same voting rights. The voice of Germany or the US has the same weight as Kenya. This is embedded in our governance and this matters because the community and the public need to know that a requirement – whether technical or procedural – is not just the opinion of one party. International agreement and consensus building is a strong factor in trust.”
“Only third-party assessment gives full independence,” Zeitz insists. “That’s why our CA systems rely on completely impartial laboratories, certification or inspection bodies. Only such a set-up can give the market full trust and confidence in the safety, efficiency and interoperability of the different products.”
The International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC) is a global, not-for-profit membership organization that brings together 174 countries and coordinates the work of 30.000 experts globally. IEC International Standards and conformity assessment underpin international trade in electrical and electronic goods. They facilitate electricity access and verify the safety, performance and interoperability of electric and electronic devices and systems, including for example, consumer devices such as mobile phones or refrigerators, office and medical equipment, information technology, electricity generation, and much more.

title: Portable solar-powered system produces 1.64 liters of drinking water in 8 hours - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
Researchers at Soochow University in China have developed a portable solar-powered system that converts saline, turbid and contaminated water into drinking water using an electrothermal evaporator and concentrated sunlight. The device produced 1.64 liters of clean water in eight hours, achieving an energy efficiency of 93.31%.
Pilar Sánchez Molina
07 Nov 2026
Research & Development
A research team from
Soochow University
in China has developed a portable solar-powered device that produces drinking water from turbid, saline, oily and highly acidic water. The prototype produced 1.64 liters of clean water in eight hours using an evaporation surface measuring just 30.72 cm2.
The system uses an electrothermal evaporation process in which an electrically powered heating element heats a surface that absorbs contaminated water, causing the water to evaporate. The resulting vapor is collected and condensed into clean water, while salts and other contaminants remain in the source water.
The device’s main innovation is an interlayer electrothermal evaporator. Instead of heating the entire volume of the wet material, the researchers positioned the heating element within an internal layer of the structure.
This configuration reduces heat losses to the surrounding water and air. According to the study, the design reduced heat losses and energy consumption by nearly two-thirds compared with a conventional electrothermal evaporator based on volumetric heating.
The system also combines two sources of solar energy.
It features foldable solar cells that generate electricity to power the electrothermal evaporator, alongside a foldable Fresnel lens that concentrates sunlight directly onto the evaporation surface. The study does not specify the rated capacity or electrical characteristics of the PV system.
When accounting for concentrated solar energy, the device achieved an apparent energy efficiency of 93.31% and a water production rate of 69.46 liters per square meter per hour.
Outdoor tests showed that the prototype could produce 1.64 liters of drinking water in eight hours using an evaporation surface of 30.72 cm2, smaller than a standard bank card.
The researchers tested the system with different types of water, including sediment-laden water, oil-contaminated water, highly saline wastewater and strongly acidic water.
The tests also included real seawater, with the researchers analyzing water samples before and after treatment. Under concentrated sunlight, the system achieved evaporation rates exceeding 90 kg/m2 per hour.
The device integrates PV modules and an optical solar concentration system, allowing it to operate without a grid connection or external fuel supply. The researchers said the configuration could be used in areas where conventional water supply infrastructure is damaged or unavailable.
They also suggested that the technology could serve as a portable water treatment solution in emergencies, including floods, earthquakes and conflicts, where access to safe drinking water may be disrupted.
The researchers presented their findings in “
Solar-operated interlayer electrothermal evaporator enabling instant high-flux freshwater production across multiple scenarios
,” published in
Nature Water
. Outdoor tests were conducted using a small-scale prototype on selected days in January and February 2025.
The results demonstrate the feasibility of the concept, but larger systems and longer-term testing under real-world conditions are still needed to assess its potential for large-scale deployment.

title: Researchers develop 10.56 kW solar-powered pleasure boat - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
Researchers in Canada have designed a solar-powered pleasure boat featuring a 10.56 kW PV array and a 19.68 kWh battery system. Simulations under solar conditions in Cyprus showed that the system could meet propulsion demand while providing a 39.8% surplus energy margin.
Lior Kahana
07 Nov 2026
Research & Development
Residential
The proposed pleasure boat
A research team from Canada’s Memorial University of Newfoundland has designed a solar-powered pleasure boat. The researchers developed and sized the system using a two-stage evaluation method combining energy yield estimates from HOMER Pro with multi-domain dynamic modeling in MATLAB/Simulink.
“The real-world applicability of this solar-electric drive system underscores significant environmental and operational benefits for the marine sector,” the researchers said. “By eliminating onboard fossil-fuel consumption, the proposed architecture avoids localized greenhouse gas emissions, reduces acoustic pollution, and prevents potential fuel-spill contamination in fragile marine ecosystems.”
The researchers designed the solar-electric propulsion system for an 11.8-meter-long, 5.8-meter-wide boat capable of accommodating five to six adults, taking into account solar conditions in Larnaca, Cyprus. Based on a full-load displacement of approximately 2,250 kg and a target speed of 5.4 knots, they selected two 2.5 kW brushless DC motors, with an estimated energy requirement of 30 kWh for six hours of daily operation.
Using HOMER Pro and local solar resource data showing average daily irradiation of 5.43 kWh/m2, the researchers assessed power generation, energy balance and life-cycle economics. The proposed system features 32 solar modules rated at 330 W each, providing a combined capacity of 10.56 kW across approximately 62.4 m2. The modules are divided into four independently controlled subarrays. Eight lead-acid batteries form a 48 V, 410 Ah battery bank with a nominal storage capacity of 19.68 kWh, providing two hours of backup power.
The team modeled the system in MATLAB/Simulink, connecting each subarray to a common 48 V DC bus through a boost converter equipped with incremental-conductance maximum power point tracking (MPPT). A central energy management system limits battery charging current to approximately 50 A and curtails surplus generation. Hall-effect sensors and closed-loop proportional-integral-derivative (PID) control regulate motor speed at 2,000 rpm. The simulations covered solar-only, combined PV-battery and battery-only operating modes, assessing power tracking, voltage stability and motor response.
“Dynamic simulation results under localized clear-sky irradiance peaks confirm that the decentralized PV system achieves a maximum output of nearly 10.98 kW,” the researchers said. “Evaluated against the logical profiles of Larnaca, Cyprus, the array fully satisfies the baseline propulsion demand while delivering a robust 39.8% excess energy margin.”
The results also showed that the four incremental-conductance MPPT controllers effectively minimized power-tracking oscillations, while the energy management system maintained DC-bus voltage fluctuations within ±3% of the nominal 48 V rating.
“While this simulation-based work establishes a rigorous computational foundation for system control and dynamic sizing, several avenues remain for future development,” the researchers concluded. “Furthermore, experimental validation through physical full-scale sea trials could be conducted to verify real-world hydrodynamic drag effects, alongside detailed techno-economic sensitivity analyses evaluating levelized cost of energy (LCOE), net present cost (NPC), capital paybacks, and cycle degradation under fluctuating market interest rates and fuel prices.”
The researchers presented their findings in “
Integrated modeling and performance assessment of a stand-alone PV-battery system for a solar-powered pleasure boat
,” published in
Next Research

title: Study finds 0.5-meter spacing between solar module rows improves cooling in floating PV systems - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
A study by Italian researchers has found that 0.5-meter spacing between module rows optimizes cooling in floating PV systems by improving airflow. The findings highlight the importance of row spacing in thermal management, although further research is needed to assess its impact on electricity generation.
Sergio Matalucci
07 Nov 2026
Research & Development
Floating PV
Utility-scale
A computational fluid dynamics study of a proposed floating PV installation at the Occhito Dam reservoir in southern Italy has found that spacing module rows approximately 0.5 meters apart delivers the best cooling performance in a three-row configuration. The researchers found that the intermediate spacing outperformed both narrower and wider arrangements, highlighting the importance of airflow management in floating PV system design.
At a wind speed of 3.5 m/s, the optimal configuration achieved an average module temperature of 27.16 C, compared with 31.07 C for the most compact arrangement. Under weaker wind conditions of 1.5 m/s, the same configuration recorded an average module temperature of 37.02 C.
The study notes that the efficiency of crystalline silicon PV modules typically decreases by approximately 0.3% to 0.5% for every 1 C increase in cell temperature. The findings underscore the importance of airflow management in floating PV design and challenge the assumption that proximity to water alone ensures better cooling.
The researchers said row spacing should be considered not only in terms of installed capacity, shading, and floating platform requirements, but also as a key thermal design parameter.
The research, conducted by scientists from the University of Naples Parthenope and the University of Campania Luigi Vanvitelli, also identified a less intuitive aspect of floating PV cooling. Although the widest spacing allowed airflow to recover more fully between rows, it did not consistently produce the lowest module temperatures. The researchers attributed this to reduced airflow acceleration between rows.
The findings suggest that effective cooling requires a balance between aerodynamic wake recovery and airflow acceleration, with the optimal configuration depending on site-specific conditions.
Airflow acceleration and differences between module rows
Cooling performance depends on several interacting factors, including wind speed, array geometry, airflow pathways, and the formation of aerodynamic wakes behind individual module rows.
These wakes can restrict air movement around the modules, reducing convective heat transfer and increasing operating temperatures. While greater row spacing can allow airflow to recover before reaching the next module, wider gaps do not necessarily improve cooling. The researchers found that excessive spacing can weaken airflow acceleration between rows.
At a wind speed of 1.5 m/s, spacing equivalent to 0.5 times the module length delivered the best performance, with an average module temperature of 37.02 C. The widest configuration, with spacing equal to one module length, performed worst, reaching 37.74 C.
The differences became more pronounced at 3.5 m/s. The configuration with spacing equivalent to 0.5 times the module length recorded an average temperature of 27.16 C, compared with 29.26 C for spacing of 0.75 times the module length, 29.75 C for the widest arrangement, and 31.07 C for the most compact configuration.
The study also found that cooling performance varied between module rows. The middle row was particularly sensitive to changes in spacing.
At 3.5 m/s, the middle row reached a temperature of 23.30 C with spacing equivalent to 0.5 times the module length, compared with 29.66 C in the most compact configuration and 30.17 C in the widest arrangement. According to the researchers, this behavior reflects the middle row’s exposure to the competing effects of upstream wake formation and airflow recovery.
The simulations also showed that the relationship between row spacing and module temperature is nonlinear. An analysis of airflow velocities under different operating conditions helped explain these differences.
At the lower wind speed, airflow velocity between the first two rows remained below 0.5 m/s in the most compact configuration. Increasing the spacing to 0.5 times the module length raised local airflow velocity to approximately 0.9 m/s to 1.1 m/s.
At the higher wind speed, the difference was even more pronounced. The intermediate spacing produced airflow velocities between rows of approximately 2.5 m/s to 3.0 m/s, compared with 1.0 m/s to 1.5 m/s for the most compact arrangement.
Four configurations
The researchers developed a two-dimensional conjugate heat transfer model to simulate interactions between PV modules, the surrounding air, and the underlying water.
The proposed installation was modeled using three consecutive rows of modules, each tilted at 15 degrees and positioned 25 cm above the water surface. The modules were approximately 0.99 meters long.
Four row-spacing configurations were examined, corresponding to 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, and 1.0 times the module length. The simulations considered two incoming wind speeds, 1.5 m/s and 3.5 m/s, representing relatively weak and stronger convective cooling conditions.
Meteorological inputs were derived from hourly ERA5 reanalysis data for 2024 covering the Occhito reservoir, which lies on the border between the Italian regions of Apulia and Molise.
The model used an annual average air temperature of 15.37 C, a water temperature of 14.67 C, and a net shortwave radiation flux of 146.65 W/m2.
Further research needed
The findings are particularly relevant to inland reservoirs in Mediterranean climates, where high summer temperatures and variable wind conditions can affect PV module operating temperatures.
However, the researchers cautioned against treating the identified spacing as a universal design recommendation.
The analysis was limited to a two-dimensional model comprising three module rows and two wind speeds. It did not account for three-dimensional turbulence, changes in wind direction, shading effects, detailed floating support structures, or the full range of meteorological conditions experienced over a year.
The study, “
Influence of row spacings on the thermal performance of floating photovoltaic arrays at the Occhito Dam reservoir, Italy: A numerical study
,” published in
Solar Energy
, focused on thermal behavior rather than directly calculating electricity generation or annual energy yield.
The authors recommended extending the research through three-dimensional computational fluid dynamics simulations, additional wind speeds and directions, and integrated electrothermal modeling to determine how the observed temperature differences translate into actual electricity generation gains.

title: U.S. solar developers navigate policy stack as Section 232 deadline nears - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
With national inventory surging 126% in the second quarter of 2026 ahead of shifting trade cutoffs, utility-scale developers are altering procurement strategies and contracts to manage multi-layered regulatory uncertainty.
Ryan Kennedy
07 Nov 2026
Markets & Policy
Utility-scale
The Permian Energy Center in Texas
U.S. solar equipment inventories expanded by 126% during the second quarter of 2026 as project developers accelerated procurement to clear a series of federal trade cutoffs.
Developers across the country are working to reconcile overlapping federal policies with distinct regulatory objectives. The industry spent the summer navigating the July 4 construction-start deadline, the July 24 tariff transition, Foreign Entity of Concern restrictions, and Federal Communications Commission rules regarding inverter components. Attention has now turned toward Dec. 4, when new Section 232 measures take effect for polysilicon, wafers, cells, and modules.
For utility-scale solar and energy storage developers, operating in this environment requires restructuring multi-party contracts and building operational flexibility into project financing rather than speculating on spot market prices.
Sabah Bayatli, chief executive officer of San Antonio-based developer OCI Energy, said the market spent late summer and early autumn focused on how Section 232 will dictate post-December pricing dynamics.
Under the Section 232 proclamation, minimum import price thresholds sit at $0.22 per watt for solar cells and $0.38 per watt for finished solar modules.
“Without further guidance from the government, it is hard for the market to price solar modules today, because there are two scenarios for modules post-December 4,” Bayatli told
pv magazine USA
. “It comes down to whether a manufacturer who imports cells from outside the country is able to sell finished panels for less than 38 cents.”
In addition to price floor interpretations, developers are awaiting administrative guidance from federal trade agencies. U.S. Customs and Border Protection and the Department of Commerce are expected to issue procedural instructions detailing the self-certification forms importers must execute to clear shipments at entry ports after the deadline.
Equipment delivery schedules for funded projects undergoing active construction remain largely insulated from immediate balance sheet shocks, as hardware for those sites was under contract prior to the proclamation. The primary exposure sits in long-term procurement structures for pipeline projects scheduled for construction in 2027 and beyond.
To absorb regulatory volatility, OCI Energy relies on collaborative contract structures that spread policy risk among project sponsors, equipment vendors, EPC contractors, lenders, and off-takers.
“These multiple stakeholders need to come together through you as a sponsor to make sure there is flexibility on managing future tariffs that you do not have visibility on today,” Bayatli said. “In the contract, you see change in law or change in tariff clauses that allow the developer to share risk across multiple stakeholders so no single entity carries the full exposure.”
When trade policy generates expenses that cannot be absorbed within fixed construction budgets, the cost is ultimately transferred to electricity buyers.
“Eventually, any additional tariffs that you did not bake inside your financial model will flow into the power pricing,” Bayatli said. “What that translates to is having a higher PPA pricing to make the project economically work.”
Despite the friction created by shifting trade mandates, market fundamentals and long-term project pipelines remain firm as developers continuously adapt to regulatory shifts.
“As a developer, you are always on your toes these days,” Bayatli said. “You have to catch up with the market and adjust to regulatory changes, but developers will always find a way to navigate through it.”

title: A Hidden Substance in Drinking Water May Be Linked to Heart Problems in Children
content:
A large study involving millions of children has uncovered a possible connection between naturally occurring lithium in drinking water and a rare heart rhythm disorder. The condition, known as Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome, involves an abnormal electrical pathway in the heart that can trigger episodes of dangerously rapid heartbeats. Credit: Shutterstock
The water we drink may hold clues to a rare heart condition in children, but whether naturally occurring lithium plays a role in its development remains unknown.
A dangerously fast heartbeat can begin with an extra strand of heart muscle that forms before birth. The strand creates an abnormal electrical connection, allowing the heart’s rhythm to go awry. Doctors can eliminate these connections, but a larger question has remained largely unanswered. Why do they develop in the first place?
A study led by
UC San Francisco
researchers points to a possible environmental clue in drinking water. Children living in areas with higher levels of naturally occurring lithium were more likely to be diagnosed with Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome, or WPW, a rare condition involving a particular type of abnormal connection. The findings, published online in
The Journal of Clinical Investigation
, show an association, but do not establish that lithium causes the condition.
These connections, known as accessory pathways, usually occur in people with no family history of the condition. That suggests environmental exposures during fetal development could play a role. Lithium attracted the researchers’ attention because medicinal doses taken during pregnancy have been associated with an increased risk of congenital heart defects, including Ebstein’s anomaly. This rare defect is frequently accompanied by accessory pathways, prompting the team to investigate whether lithium in drinking water might also be associated with changes in the developing heart.
Higher lithium, greater odds of WPW
The researchers analyzed health and water-quality data for more than 2.3 million children in California. Just 686 had a documented WPW diagnosis. Children living in counties with lithium levels in the highest 25% had 71% greater odds of a diagnosis than those in counties with lower levels.
The team then tested its main finding among nearly 2 million children in New York. There, children living in areas with lithium levels above 10 parts per billion also had greater odds of a WPW diagnosis.
Higher lithium levels in California were also associated with palpitations, fainting, and supraventricular tachycardia, or SVT, a rapid heart rhythm that can cause palpitations and other symptoms. Accessory pathways are among the most common causes of SVT. WPW is also associated with a small increased risk of sudden death. Doctors can treat accessory pathways with catheter ablation, a minimally invasive procedure that eliminates the small area of heart tissue responsible for the abnormal electrical connection.
“We’ve known about these pathways for decades, and we know how to treat them, but we haven’t known why people develop them,” said Gregory Marcus, MD, MAS, an endowed professor in atrial fibrillation research in the UCSF Division of Cardiology and senior author of the study. “This is an exciting step because it points to a potential environmental factor that may be modifiable. But we need more research to determine whether lithium is actually contributing to their development.”
Individual lithium exposure remains unknown
The study estimated exposure from the county of residence. Researchers did not know how much lithium individual children or their mothers consumed, and other environmental or genetic factors could help explain the association. Studies in other populations and research that measures exposure during pregnancy more precisely are needed to determine whether lithium plays a causal role.
Marcus said the findings should not alarm people about the safety of their drinking water, including those who are pregnant. Despite the association, WPW was rare in the children studied.
Lithium occurs naturally in groundwater, and its concentration varies widely by location. Groundwater used for drinking water across the United States and elsewhere contains lithium, raising questions about the findings’ potential public health significance beyond California and New York. The researchers said the results underscore the value of collecting environmental data to understand how ordinary exposures may affect health.
“We’re exposed to things in our environment every day, including substances that occur naturally,” Marcus said. “The more precisely we can measure those exposures and connect them with health outcomes, the better we can understand what may be influencing health.”
Lithium in drinking water is not currently regulated in the United States, although the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency requires monitoring through its program for unregulated contaminants. The U.S. Geological Survey also measures lithium in groundwater.
“The next step is to determine whether lithium itself is contributing to the development of these pathways and, if so, how much exposure matters and when during development it matters most,” Marcus said. “That will require studies that can measure exposure much more precisely.”
Reference: “Elevated lithium levels in drinking water are associated with higher prevalence of Wolff-Parkinson-White diagnoses” by Justin T. Teraoka, Anushree Agarwal, Janet J. Tang, Thomas A. Dewland and Gregory M. Marcus, 13 October 2026,
The Journal of Clinical Investigation

title: Chemical Breakthrough Could Unlock the “Holy Grail” of Solid-State Battery Technology
content:
Technology
Solid-state batteries are a promising alternative to conventional lithium-ion batteries because they replace flammable liquid electrolytes with solid materials. Credit: Stock
A simple chemical treatment could overcome a persistent weakness in next-generation solid-state batteries.
Scientists in China have developed a thin protective coating that could help overcome a major obstacle to longer-lasting, high-capacity batteries. In laboratory tests, solid-state batteries using the treated lithium metal retained 82.3% of their initial capacity after 300 charging cycles, compared with just 43.0% for batteries using untreated lithium.
The researchers at Xidian University developed a simple liquid coating that reacts with lithium metal to form a protective barrier. Their findings, published in
Science China Chemistry
, suggest a possible route toward safer, more durable batteries for electric vehicles and energy storage.
Solving a Persistent Battery Problem
Lithium metal has been called the “holy grail” of energy storage because it can theoretically store nearly ten times as much charge per gram as the graphite used in conventional lithium-ion batteries. Its exceptional capacity could enable lighter batteries that store more energy and potentially support longer driving ranges.
To address this problem, researchers led by Professors Siwu Li, Weiwei Wu, and Chuang Yu combined a silicon-based polymer with indium chloride. When applied to lithium, the mixture forms lithium fluoride and lithium-indium alloy nanoparticles within a flexible protective film just 12 micrometers thick (about 0.00047 inches).
“This hybrid layer acts like a smart fortress,” explains corresponding author Siwu Li. “The polymer backbone provides flexibility to absorb the mechanical stress of lithium expanding and contracting. The lithium fluoride phase blocks electrons to prevent dendrite nucleation. And the lithium-indium alloy nanoparticles act as traffic conductors, guiding lithium ions to deposit evenly rather than piling up in dangerous spikes.”
This illustration depicts the in-situ formation of the PFSIn-Li interlayer on a lithium metal anode. A liquid precursor containing a fluorinated siloxane polymer and indium salt reacts on the lithium surface to generate a multifunctional hybrid film. The organic polymer network interpenetrates with inorganic lithium fluoride, lithium-indium alloy, and lithium silicon oxide nanodomains, simultaneously suppressing dendrite growth and stabilizing the interface with the sulfide solid electrolyte. Credit: Science China Press
Stronger Performance in Laboratory Tests
The coated lithium electrodes withstood a critical current density of 3.5 milliamperes per square centimeter, more than four times the 0.8 achieved by untreated lithium. In complete batteries containing a nickel-cobalt-manganese oxide cathode and a sulfide solid electrolyte, the protected electrodes delivered an initial capacity of 129.8 milliampere-hours per gram and retained 82.3% after 300 cycles at 0.5C.
Spectroscopy and electron microscopy confirmed the coating’s composition and revealed a dense, uniform layer without visible cracks or gaps.
A Simpler Path to Better Batteries
The coating could help address the chemical instability between lithium metal and sulfide solid electrolytes, a major challenge in solid-state battery development.
Because the protective layer forms from an applied liquid, it may be compatible with existing industrial coating equipment without requiring expensive vacuum processing. The researchers also plan to explore alternatives to indium, including tin and zinc.
Although commercial performance remains unproven, the findings offer a promising approach to making high-energy lithium metal batteries more stable and longer-lasting.
Reference: “In situ reductive construction of a silicon-based polymer/indium alloy hybrid layer for stable lithium metal anodes in sulfide solid-state batteries” by Kun Song, Qun Zhao, Xianbo Zhao, Siwu Li, Jun Liu, Haitao Chen, Weiwei Wu and Chuang Yu, 6 August 2026,
Science China Chemistry
DOI: 10.1007/s11426-026-3450-y

title: Could Type 2 Diabetes Be Reversed? 14-Year Study Reveals Remarkable Results
content:
Weight-loss surgery may offer more than significant weight reduction for people with type 2 diabetes. Research suggests it can improve blood sugar control and even lead to remission. Credit: Shutterstock
In a long-term trial, weight-loss surgery led to more type 2 diabetes remissions than intensive medical and lifestyle management, while patients’ disease histories offered clues to who might benefit most.
For some people with type 2 diabetes, keeping blood sugar under control without medication is possible. This state, known as remission, raises a question that could shape years of treatment decisions: Which approaches give people the best chance of reaching it, and what makes it more likely to last?
A long-term study found that 58% of participants assigned to weight-loss surgery achieved remission during follow-up, compared with 3% of those assigned to intensive medical and lifestyle management. Participants were followed for a median of 11 years, with some followed for up to 14 years. Those percentages describe how many people reached remission, rather than how many remained in remission throughout that time.
Researchers analyzed data from 262 people with type 2 diabetes, including 166 assigned to metabolic-bariatric surgery, commonly called weight-loss surgery, and 96 assigned to medical and lifestyle management. They defined remission as an A1C below 6.5% without blood sugar-lowering medication. A1C is a blood test that reflects average blood sugar levels over approximately three months.
The findings were published in
Diabetes Care
, a journal of the American Diabetes Association®. They come from the Alliance of Randomized Trials of Medicine vs. Metabolic Surgery in Type 2 Diabetes (ARMMS-T2D), the largest, longest-running trial of metabolic surgery for diabetes. The study’s lead author is Donald Simonson, M.D., MPH, Sc.D., of Brigham and Women’s Hospital and Harvard Medical School in Boston.
Diabetes history offers clues to lasting remission
Participants who had lived with diabetes for fewer years, did not use insulin, and took fewer types of blood sugar-lowering medications before treatment were more likely to achieve remission. Greater weight loss during the first year after treatment was also associated with a higher likelihood of remission.
John P. Kirwan, Ph.D., is the principal investigator of a recently published clinical trial showing that people with type 2 diabetes were much more likely to achieve remission after weight-loss surgery than after intensive medical and lifestyle management. Kirwan is executive director of the University of Oklahoma Health Harold Hamm Diabetes Center. Credit: University of Oklahoma
Among people who initially reached remission, diabetes was more likely to return in those who had lived with the disease longer and those who took more types of blood sugar-lowering medications before treatment. Together, these associations suggest that a patient’s diabetes history and response to treatment may help physicians assess both the likelihood of remission and its potential duration.
A case for considering surgery earlier
The study’s principal investigator, John P. Kirwan, Ph.D., was named executive director of the University of Oklahoma Health Harold Hamm Diabetes Center this summer. He also serves as Vice Provost for Diabetes Programs at the University of Oklahoma and holds the Chickasaw Nation Endowed Chair in Diabetes Research.
“For years, one of the most consequential questions in diabetes care has been whether the benefits of metabolic surgery endure,” Kirwan said. “Now we have a durable answer. Over 14 years, 58% of surgical patients achieved remission, compared with just 3% on medication and lifestyle alone. By identifying who is most likely to achieve lasting remission, including shorter diabetes duration, no insulin use, and greater early weight loss, we can offer surgery to the right people earlier, rather than as a last resort.”
Kirwan has led the study since its inception, through his years at the Cleveland Clinic and the Pennington Biomedical Research Center at Louisiana State University. He now brings his expertise in translational and clinical research to the OU Harold Hamm Health Campus.
“Recruiting Dr. Kirwan to lead the Harold Hamm Diabetes Center brings to Oklahoma one of the world’s foremost authorities on long-term treatment for type 2 diabetes,” said Gary Raskob, Ph.D., Senior Vice President and Provost of the OU Harold Hamm Health Campus. “Research of this caliber is exactly what this center, and Harold Hamm’s investment in it, was created to advance.”
Reference: “Predictors of Type 2 Diabetes Remission and Relapse After Metabolic-Bariatric Surgery or Medical-Lifestyle Therapy in the ARMMS-T2D Study” by Donald C. Simonson, David E. Cummings, Philip R. Schauer, Ali Aminian, Bo Hu, David E. Arterburn, John M. Jakicic, Sangeeta R. Kashyap, Ashley H. Vernon, William F. Gourash, Anita P. Courcoulas, Mary Elizabeth Patti and John P. Kirwan, 20 October 2026,

title: Kids Who Learn To Swim Early May Have an Unexpected Advantage in School
content:
Early swimming lessons may offer unexpected advantages in childhood development. Credit: Shutterstock
Children who learn to swim early may have a head start in classroom skills, with research finding developmental advantages even after accounting for socioeconomic background.
When family budgets tighten, swimming lessons can be among the first expenses to go. Most swim schools operate as commercial businesses, and cost is the biggest barrier to participation. Yet the consequences of missing out may extend beyond water safety and fitness to the skills children need when they start school.
A four-year study involving nearly 7,000 survey respondents and individual testing of 177 children suggests that children who learn to swim early have developmental advantages over their peers. Participants younger than 5 could be 5 to 18 months ahead of typical milestones in literacy, numeracy, and following instructions compared with the general population of children their age. Those advantages remained when socioeconomic background was taken into account.
Robyn Jorgensen, Emeritus Professor at the University of Canberra in Australia, examines and expands on the research in her new book,
Why Young Children Should Learn to Swim
Swimming may offer a classroom head start
Jorgensen does not interpret the findings as evidence that children who learn to swim are innately smarter. Instead, she argues that lessons develop skills and habits children can carry into the classroom. A child counting kicks from one to ten with an instructor, for example, is practicing number sequencing and one-to-one correspondence, matching each number to a single action.
The project grew out of a conversation between Jorgensen and Laurie Lawrence, an Olympic swim coach inducted into both the Australian and U.S. Swimming Halls of Fame. Lawrence thought children who learned to swim early generally seemed more “school-ready.”
“There was no formal evidence to support this observation, but it was one that Laurie felt he and many others in the swim industry observed,” Jorgensen explains.
To investigate that “industry hunch,” Jorgensen and her colleagues used the Peabody Developmental Motor Scales and Woodcock-Johnson III assessments. These internationally recognized testing tools were normed against national census data, providing reference standards for comparing the children’s performance with that of the wider population.
The results surprised even Jorgensen, who said, “My early observations of the young learners piqued my interest while retaining some sense of skepticism about what could be achieved. I am not from a swimming background, so had no vested interest in the ‘proving’ or otherwise of Laurie’s hunch. My only interest in swimming was as a grandparent and around water safety for my children and grandchildren, and as a recreational activity.”
Beyond the literacy and numeracy findings, the research suggests that early swimming participants are more sociable and have measurable advantages in cognitive development, language skills, and emotional regulation. These findings point to potential benefits for academic success.
“It is reasonable to claim that swimming prepares children for the schooling years, particularly the early years and the transition into schooling,” Jorgensen explains.
Costly lessons and faraway pools
Access to those potential benefits is sharply unequal. Jorgensen’s analysis identifies the United States and China as having the greatest inequities in access, with regular swimming lessons affordable only to very affluent families. Singapore, Australia, Brazil, and South Africa also face substantial economic and geographic barriers.
One respondent from Zimbabwe described how lessons compete with basic necessities. “So swimming is still seen in Africa in general as elite. But basically, if you are a working-level person well below average, swimming lessons will not be a priority; what will be a priority is feeding your family.”
Even reaching a pool can be difficult. In Australia, families on remote farming properties can face journeys of hundreds of kilometers to the nearest one. The study describes “a double whammy” for children from low-income and rural communities, who are both the least likely to have access to lessons and the most at risk of drowning.
The case for subsidizing swimming lessons
With cost-of-living pressures affecting families worldwide, Jorgensen is calling for broader government support. She argues that governments have both a moral and a financial incentive to intervene, given the billions they already spend trying to close gaps in school achievement.
“What this study has shown is that even when socioeconomic backgrounds are accounted for, children who participate in quality lessons achieve better than the general population. It would make sense for the government to consider investing in providing or subsidizing early years swimming for families who would otherwise be excluded from participation in early years swimming lessons,” Jorgensen explains.
“Investing in quality swimming lessons would make a politically wise move. The cost of lessons can be quite high, but if policies were created to offer subsidies for parents or to create swim programs for disadvantaged families, there is considerable potential for adding capital to these cohorts of learners,” she explains.

title: Scientists Find That Older Brains React Very Differently to a Night of Poor Sleep
content:
A new study reveals that younger and older brains respond in surprisingly different ways to a single night of sleep deprivation. Credit: Shutterstock
A single bad night’s sleep may be easier on a healthy older brain than a younger one, though regularly missing sleep still carries risks.
Sleep quality often declines with age, yet older adults can seem less affected by a single bad night than younger people. Understanding that apparent mismatch means looking at how the brain responds when sleep runs short.
A study from
Simon Fraser University
offers a possible explanation. After just three hours of sleep, certain connections in younger and older brains changed in opposite directions. The findings suggest that healthy older brains may adapt to acute sleep loss in ways that help preserve function, although the study measured brain activity rather than cognitive performance.
The research, published in
Imaging Neuroscience
, compared brain networks in younger adults ages 20 to 30 with those in older adults ages 65 to 75. Lead researcher Josh Neudorf, an affiliate member of SFU’s Institute for Neuroscience and Neurotechnology, says earlier research on the effects of poor sleep provided a reason to investigate the difference.
“Older adults tend to better handle the effects of poor sleep, whereas younger adults, as we know, have the common symptoms of decreased mood and cognitive ability following poor sleep,” says Neudorf.
“This study tries to get at the heart of this difference – how does the older brain react to lost sleep.”
How brain networks handle a short night
Brain connectivity describes how activity in different regions is linked. Stronger connections do not automatically mean the brain is working more efficiently. The arrangement matters, too. In a more modular network, regions are organized into groups, with relatively stronger connections within each group than between groups.
“What we found was quite striking in that older and younger brains actually responded in opposite ways to acute sleep loss.
“Certain connections in the brains of younger adults showed increased connectivity as a response to less sleep, while those same connections in the brains of older adults showed decreased connectivity.
“That decrease in connectivity promotes more efficient modular connectivity for the brain as a whole. In other words, the brain is acting in a more efficient way to maintain cognitive function. In contrast, the increased connectivity in younger brains suggests the brain is having to work harder to maintain function.”
Whether those network changes actually helped the older participants think or perform tasks better was not tested. The proposed benefit is an interpretation of the brain activity, consistent with previous research suggesting that older adults are often less impaired by a single night of poor sleep.
The reason for the opposite responses also remains open. One of several possible explanations is compensation, in which an aging brain reorganizes its networks and uses different strategies to maintain function.
“The quality of sleep starts to change and deteriorates somewhat in older adults,” says Neudorf.
“The theory of compensation is the idea that older brains adapt or compensate for those changes.”
Chronic sleep loss still harms health
Being able to adjust to an occasional short night would not make regularly missing sleep harmless. Researchers emphasize that good-quality sleep matters throughout life. Although the response to one or two nights of lost sleep may differ with age, chronic sleep loss is detrimental to brain health and cognitive ability. Its cumulative effects over a lifetime also have the potential to increase the risk of cardiovascular disease, hypertension, diabetes, weight problems, and colorectal cancer.
Dementia presents another concern. Study co-author Brianne Kent is an assistant professor of psychology, associate director of SFU’s Institute for Neuroscience and Neurotechnology, and Canada Research Chair in Translational Neuroscience and Dementia. Her research focuses on Alzheimer’s disease, the most common cause of dementia.
“A lot of sleep disruption could increase your risk of dementia,” says Kent.
“What we know is that there’s a protein called amyloid beta, which accumulates in the brain and causes these plaques in the brains of individuals who have dementia. Amyloid beta is this toxic protein, a waste product of your brain. These plaques accumulate for, on average, about 20 years before dementia starts.”
Sleep plays a role in how quickly that protein is removed, linking repeated sleep loss to a process that can unfold over decades.
She concludes, “During sleep, that protein is cleared out at a faster rate. So if you’re continuously missing sleep, then that protein and those plaques will accumulate at a faster rate. Not everyone who has poor sleep will get Alzheimer’s disease, but if you are somebody who has the predisposition for the disease, then missing sleep over time will drive the process.”
Reference: “Young and old adult brains experience opposite effects of acute sleep restriction on the functional connectivity network” by Josh Neudorf, Leanne Rokos, Kelly Shen, Brianne Kent and Anthony R. McIntosh, 18 June 2026,

title: Scientists Find a Clever Way to Read Quantum Information Without Destroying It
content:
Schematic of a readout of an Andreev qubit without using auxiliary qubits. Credit: Marcus Egues and José Carlos Egues, with assistance from ChatGPT
Simulations suggest that one type of qubit could reveal its state through its own electric current, helping researchers monitor quantum computers with less disturbance and fewer components.
Like a bit in an ordinary computer, a qubit stores information using states labeled 0 and 1. A qubit can also be prepared in a superposition, a quantum combination of the two. These states belong to a physical system that researchers build and control. In the design explored here, that system is a tiny wire connected to superconducting materials.
The aim of quantum computing is to use quantum behavior to perform certain calculations more efficiently than conventional computers. That requires control: researchers must prepare qubits and change their states deliberately. Unwanted interactions with the surroundings can disrupt them, and measuring a qubit can alter it, too.
A theoretical study proposes reading one type of qubit through an electric current it produces itself. This could let researchers follow its behavior with minimal disturbance and without the extra qubits used in many existing methods.
Quantum information in a tiny wire
Andreev qubits hold information in states formed between superconducting materials, which carry electric current without resistance. They are named after Soviet physicist Alexander Andreev (1939–2023), who described the underlying process at the boundary between normal and superconducting materials in 1964.
“In the system under consideration, this region is a quantum dot—that is, a nanoscale structure in which electrons are spatially confined – formed in an indium arsenide [
] nanowire connected to superconducting materials on both sides. It’s in this environment that the states characterizing the Andreev qubit are formed,” explains José Carlos Egues, a full professor at the São Carlos Institute of Physics at the University of São Paulo (IFSC-USP) in Brazil.
Schematic of a readout of an Andreev qubit without using auxiliary qubits. In the proposed device, the qubit’s quantum information appears as an oscillating supercurrent circulating in a large superconducting loop. The magnetic signal generated by this current is detected by a small coil coupled to a SQUID, allowing the qubit’s state to be inferred with minimal perturbation. Credit: Marcus Egues and José Carlos Egues, with assistance from ChatGPT
“In the conventional formulation of quantum mechanics, a projective measurement causes the system to assume one of the states associated with the measured quantity. Thus, if a qubit has been prepared in a certain superposition of 0 and 1, its direct measurement tends to destroy that superposition and, consequently, the information it contained,” says Egues.
Many existing methods use a helper quantum system called an ancilla. Researchers prepare it, connect it to the qubit, transfer information to it, and measure it to preserve the original qubit as much as possible. These steps add time and equipment. “Our strategy is different. Instead of transferring the information to an auxiliary qubit, we seek to obtain it from a signal produced by the qubit under study itself,” says Egues.
Reading the signal a qubit produces
The qubit would sit in a closed superconducting circuit carrying a supercurrent, an electric current that flows without resistance. The calculations predict that interference between the states in the qubit’s superposition makes part of this current oscillate. “It’s precisely that property that we use to read the qubit. It’s that supercurrent that lies at the heart of our proposal,” Egues points out.
An applied voltage usually causes this kind of oscillation, known as the AC Josephson effect. “Our system generates a supercurrent that varies over time like an alternating current but without voltage. It’s the very evolution of the qubit’s state that produces that oscillation,” says Egues.
A nearby superconducting quantum interference device, or SQUID, would act as the detector. These instruments are extremely sensitive to weak magnetic fields. Egues explains, “We can think of the qubit as one compass and the SQUID as another compass. The current in the circuit produces a magnetic field, and the SQUID ‘senses’ that field. Since the coupling between the two is very weak, the effect of the measuring instrument on the qubit tends to be very small.”
Identifying the qubit’s state requires knowing both the balance of 0 and 1 and their relative phase, or how the two components line up.
“Our study showed that this information is encoded in the supercurrent itself. The supercurrent has a constant component and a fluctuating component. The value of the constant component and the amplitude of the oscillation reveal the proportion of each state (0 and 1) in the superposition, and the moment when that oscillation begins reveals the phase relationship between them. Thus, by measuring how the current varies over time, it’s possible to reconstruct the initial state of the qubit,” Egues explains.
Researchers could also track the qubit through repeated readings without resetting it to its initial state after each measurement.
The design still needs experimental testing
Simulations included measurement noise and feedback from the small detection coil. They indicated that the detector’s influence could become negligible, with readout accuracies of 99.52%, 99.81%, and 99.85%, depending on the number of measurements. These values fall within standard thresholds adopted in quantum error correction schemes.
“Our method doesn’t eliminate the fundamental problem of quantum measurement. But it can approach the limit of a non-destructive readout and, at the same time, avoid the use of auxiliary qubits – the ancillas – employed in other non-destructive quantum measurement protocols,” Egues notes.
The work, published in
Physical Review B Letters
, was led by Egues and Yugui Yao of the School of Physics at the Beijing Institute of Technology in China. SQUID detection of extremely small currents and magnetic fields is already established, and Egues says the proposal would not require future advances in materials or device fabrication.
“All the numbers we used are realistic. In principle, this can be achieved. In fact, we used parameters from existing systems in our calculations. What doesn’t yet exist is that geometry, that setup that we proposed,” he argues.
Reference: “Andreev qubit readout from dynamic interference supercurrent” by Xian-Peng Zhang, Chuanchang Zeng, Zhen-Biao Yang, Jose Carlos Egues and Yugui Yao, 5 August 2026,
Physical Review B

title: The Secret to Saving Shellfish From Acidifying Oceans Could Be Hiding in Crushed Shells
content:
In the study, UC Davis researchers added crushed shells, pictured here, to sand to better understand how the practice can protect shell-making animals from the negative effects of ocean acidification. Credit: Hannah Kempf/UC Davis
Crushed shells helped young clams grow larger shells in laboratory tests, showing how a long-standing Indigenous coastal practice can offer local protection against ocean acidification.
For a young clam, the surrounding water can threaten the shell it is trying to grow. When seawater absorbs excess carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, it becomes more acidic, making shell growth more difficult and energetically costly for animals such as clams, oysters, and mussels. Acidic seawater can even dissolve shells. Larvae and juveniles are thought to be especially vulnerable to this process, known as ocean acidification.
Indigenous communities have long added crushed shells to coastal sands to help keep these ecosystems healthy. Research from the
University of California, Davis
now helps explain how this material, called shell hash, can protect young clams from some of acidification’s effects. Published in
Biogeosciences
, the study connects the chemistry of water between sand grains with changes in clam growth and gene activity.
Raising groups of Pacific littleneck clams in four different conditions, the researchers monitored their growth and the water’s chemistry over a 90-day period. Credit: Hannah Kempf/UC Davis
Crushed shells help young clams grow
At the UC Davis Bodega Marine Laboratory, researchers raised baby Pacific littleneck clams in four conditions. Two groups burrowed in sediment beneath either non-acidified or acidified seawater. The other two experienced the same seawater conditions, but their sediment contained shell hash. During the 90-day experiment, the team tracked shell growth and sampled the seawater three times a week, monitoring acidity, salinity, temperature, and dissolved oxygen.
“We found that, on average, clams grew larger shells when shell hash was present in their treatment,” said study first author Hannah Kempf, an environmental scientist at the California State Water Board who graduated from UC Davis with a Ph.D. in earth and planetary sciences in 2024. “Interestingly, we also found that, on a genetic level, the ‘acidification’ signal was dramatically minimized when shell hash was present.”
The crushed shells altered the chemistry of the water filling the tiny spaces between sand particles, reducing its overall acidity and creating better conditions for shell growth. That finding places the protection at a very local scale, in the water surrounding the burrowing clams.
A weaker acidification signal in clam genes
“Adding crushed shells removed the negative genetic changes that occur when young clams are raised in acidified water,” said study corresponding author David Gold, an associate professor of earth and planetary sciences at UC Davis.
A UC Davis researcher holds a Pacific littleneck clam. Credit: Hannah Kempf/UC Davis
To examine gene activity, the researchers collected samples of the clams’ mantle tissue, which produces their shells, after 90 days and used them for follow-up gene sequencing. The analysis revealed gene expression profiles, or patterns of activity across genes. In clams raised in acidified seawater with shell hash, those profiles were largely indistinguishable from those of clams raised in non-acidified water.
“This was the first time the question was studied from a genetic perspective,” Gold said.
Indigenous expertise could shape coastal research
Traditional ecological knowledge provides significant evidence that shell hash benefits shell-making animals, said study co-author Tsim Schneider, an associate professor of anthropology at UC Santa Cruz. In the Pacific Northwest, some Indigenous communities build large-scale structures that expand intertidal spaces, the areas of shore between high and low tide. These structures promote habitat for invertebrates and other marine organisms.
“For me, one of the interesting aspects of this research is the potential to engage more fully with tribes on designing projects that promote their long-standing expertise and Indigenous science,” said Schneider, who is also affiliated with the National Science Foundation’s Center for Braiding Indigenous Knowledges and Science. “If there’s a history of adding shell hash to clam beds in California, for example, western science might be able to better support communities interested in reawakening dormant cultural knowledge and coastal stewardship practices.”
Reference: “Shell hash promotes growth in Pacific littleneck clams (
Leukoma staminea
) by altering pore water chemistry” by Hannah L. Kempf, Alyssa J. Griffin, Gabriel Ng, Tessa M. Hill, Tsim D. Schneider, Sandra J. Carlson and David A. Gold, 29 October 2026,
Biogeosciences
DOI: 10.5194/bg-23-7627-2026
The research was supported by a California Sea Grant and the Russell J. and Dorothy S. Bilinski Fellowship.

title: The Blue Wave May Not Stop Musk’s Texas Data Center Ambitions
content: Elon Musk moved early to build AI data centers in Tennessee and Mississippi and reaped the rewards. Later, he began working on ambitious plans to open SpaceX data centers in Texas, following on the heels of OpenAI and others that are farther along in the state. Democrat Gina Hinojosa’s surprise election as governor this week could delay parts of Musk’s projects, though, even if it doesn’t derail them completely. New details are emerging on bold data center plans from Musk’s SpaceX that could face a hard look from Hinojosa. Public records, job listings and rapidly rising steel structures with gas turbines parked beside them suggest SpaceX has begun building a multigigawatt “Starbase supercomputer”—the term used in one SpaceX job post —in its expanding City of Starbase. That’s the sprawling SpaceX property on the Texas-Mexico border in the Rio Grande Valley from which it launches its gigantic Starship rocket. Musk has also made previously unreported down payments to secure as much as a gigawatt of floating power at the nearby Port of Brownsville from Turkish modular power provider and shipbuilder Karpowership, according to a person familiar with the financing discussions. SpaceX is also preparing to use 700 to 800 megawatts of grid-connected power at its existing satellite manufacturing site in Bastrop, Texas, near Austin, according to utility board approvals for a substation and land deeds analyzed exclusively for The Information by Corey Trinetti, author of the Measured AI infrastructure newsletter. That could power another large AI data center or industrial operation, though its purpose remains undisclosed. Trinetti also cites a job listing for a Bastrop-based data center technician as another sign of SpaceX’s intentions for the location. A county commission hearing in rural Grimes County revealed plans for data centers inside SpaceX’s Terafab chip foundry, about 80 miles from Houston. APR Energy, a turbine reseller SpaceX acquired earlier this year, had previously sought to build a data center in Pampa, in the Texas Panhandle, and placed mobile turbines there—another possible site for Musk. Musk told SpaceX shareholders on Oct. 20 that he could build and energize 10 gigawatts of terrestrial data centers by 2027. These quiet preparations, along with his estimated $224 million in donations to Texas Republicans who lost in the midterms, appeared to be part of his blueprint for building at an unheard-of scale and speed in a state he had assumed would be friendly territory. The odds of a quick SpaceX data center build-out are now much lower with Hinojosa taking office Jan. 19, 2027. During Hinojosa’s campaign, she vowed to block new data center approvals while lawmakers considered new safeguards. Hinojosa grew up in the Rio Grande Valley and campaigned explicitly against Musk and other billionaires “buying up Texans’ land, energy and resources.” Data centers that generate their own power must also get pollution permits if they combust fossil fuels. Even before Tuesday’s election, Gov. Greg Abbott paused both grid connections and air permitting for data centers in the state, holding up the approval of SpaceX’s application during state audits that won’t conclude until December and could go longer. SpaceX filed an air permit application for on-site power at Starbase in September, but the application has been held up by the pause. “Air permitting is the chokepoint,” says Christian Okoye, whose analysis for infrastructure risk analytics firm Occam Edge suggests a 444-acre Starbase parcel could support 1.5 to 2.6 gigawatts of on-site gas power. Permitting delays pose two risks for SpaceX. First, they could cut future revenue: The company rented out immediately available cloud capacity to customers at a premium in Tennessee and Mississippi, but customers won’t pay such excess rates for capacity that’s ready much later. Second, SpaceX may have to pay for chips it recently agreed to lease from Apollo Global Management , with some coming in the first half of 2027, even if it lacks a powered data center ready to house them. Selling AI compute to customers like Anthropic has grown by leaps and bounds to become SpaceX’s biggest business. During the third quarter, sales from what it calls its SI business unit—for super intelligence—nearly tripled from the prior quarter to $7.56 billion. Any serious disruption to that business could make it harder for Musk to pull off a merger of SpaceX and Tesla, a deal that board committees from both companies are considering. SpaceX buildings on the shore in Boca Chica, Texas, near the company's Starbase facility. Photo by Getty Images Had Abbott won reelection, the Texas data center projects might have become the latest examples of Musk pushing past barriers that stop others. He has already moved to tackle one bottleneck by setting up a Texas turbine-blade castings foundry, which we revealed in August. SpaceX and Karpowership, the floating power provider, did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Musk has warned of “guppy-level death” for cloud upstarts unable to compete at SpaceX’s level. But in posts this week , he acknowledged the election could make terrestrial data centers harder to build—and increase his interest in space-based computing. Even so, Musk may pull off more than expected. My reporting suggests politicians are overestimating what a Democratic administration can or would block in pro-business Texas. Starbase controls its own zoning and can obtain low-cost municipal bond financing. SpaceX and Starbase rushed from August through October to annex land, negotiate water infrastructure and route underwater gas pipelines at the port. Those moves may have come just in time, unless opponents can reverse them. Two nearby towns, including Brownsville, have just enacted temporary data center moratoriums, but Starbase succeeded at getting Brownsville to “disannex” land at a rowdy Aug. 29 meeting so Starbase could then annex it, just days before Brownsville began hearings to consider its moratorium. The SpaceX and Tesla industrial complex that stretches across Texas amounts to hundreds of billions of dollars in investments in rocket launches, chip fabrication, solar module and battery manufacturing and data centers. Greater Brownsville is experiencing a historic boom, driven not only by SpaceX but also by new defense projects and data center companies including Fluidstack. Just before the election, a coalition of local governments in Hinojosa’s home region, the Lower Rio Grande Valley, drafted a term sheet outlining what communities should demand from tech companies seeking to build data centers. Rather than reject the digital economy, the coalition wants companies to subsidize high-speed internet access, including for telehealth. There is also a possibility that Musk and Hinojosa could find a compromise. The governor-elect struck a moderate tone this week, telling CNN on Nov. 5, “It is not that I hate data centers. I hate the way they are taking advantage of Texas.” She noted a Republican on her transition team and added: “We can have a strong working relationship with Elon Musk and his companies, but it has to be on our terms. It cannot be just running over the people of Texas.” In the meantime, Abbott could conceivably lift parts of his permitting pause, giving some regulatory reviews a brief window to advance before Hinojosa takes office, says John K. Arnold, a Houston-based energy regulatory partner at Troutman Pepper Locke. But a case backlog and the holidays make securing an air permit before the new governor is sworn in an extreme long shot for Musk, and such a move would play poorly with voters. Abbott “could lift the pause, but the permitting process itself still requires significant input,” Arnold says. Still, it’s not clear Hinojosa could block air permits, either. The commissioners at the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality were all recently appointed by Abbott and have several years left in their terms unless they resign, Arnold says. The agency paused air permits more in political deference to Abbott than because the governor had the legal authority to order it, he says. Hinojosa would face the same limit and, he expects, also not want to chase investments out of state. In Texas, “you can’t alienate people by being anti-business. It needs to be about business being done the right way,” he says. SpaceX is nonetheless hedging its bets by unveiling a data center project in another state, where it continues to shock small communities with its audacious, rapidly unfolding plans. The day after the midterms, Riley Trettel, SpaceX’s head of energy and data center development, appeared at a town hall in rural Cochise County, Arizona, to explain that SpaceX wants to put as much as six gigawatts of data centers, battery storage and backup gas generation on a 747-acre site. It would draw power from a rural cooperative but also need new power generation and transmission upgrades, says the analytics firm Occam Edge. Builders and financial partners I interviewed agreed Democratic victories will moderate but not stop the national AI build-out. “Data centers are happening,” says Mike Mathews, global digital infrastructure head at insurance broker Marsh. “Society and technology are pregnant with the next wave of data center demand, so the question is not whether data centers will be built, but where, when and under what conditions.” New From Our Reporters Exclusive TSMC Weighs Making Advanced Memory Chips to Capture More AI Spending By Qianer Liu Upcoming Events Monday, November 9 — Intimate Dinner with The Information and EY Consulting in San Francisco Trust is quickly becoming the defining question of the AI era. Over dinner, Jessica Lessin, Founder & Editor-in-Chief of The Information, and Whitt Butler, EY Americas Vice Chair – Consulting, will talk candidly about how leaders can build that trust and keep it.
